en: Preface to the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Zhizhin* (The Sound-Knower of the Lotus Sutra), composed by the monk Ru-yu of Jiangxia, a student and non-student at Shitou Monastery in Jinling.

When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, it is like a compassionate father instructing his beloved son; there is not even a hair’s breadth of concealment or guile, for they know all that ought to be known.

These words leave nothing unsaid, just as an enlightened master instructs his young disciples. When one analogy does not suffice, another is drawn from elsewhere, with the sole aim of enabling those who are like children to understand.
Thus, instruction is given until the point is fully grasped. If this is so, what need is there for building house upon house within a house, or adding a handle to a bowl?
What further use is there for commentaries and exegeses? For it is thus that the Buddha-dharma has come down to us.

In the Western Regions, their language cannot avoid the concurrent use of both Chinese (Huā) and Sanskrit (Fàn) terms; and their meanings cannot avoid the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.

For this reason, the great Bodhisattvas, by the power of their compassion and vows, come to be born in this land, sometimes manifesting themselves as kings or ministers, sometimes as elders or lay devotees, and sometimes as śramaṇas or Śākyas.

My son, apply your mind to the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures). Whether you are a translator of the texts, a commentator on the commentaries, one who offers worship and offerings, or one who specializes in preaching and expounding, there is none among you who is not a person entrusted with the Buddha’s mandate.
Furthermore, how could there be any distinction of superiority or inferiority based on likes and dislikes or right and wrong?
However, at the time of receiving the Buddha’s entrustment, there were those who were sincere and those who were insincere.
They arrive at the same goal. Although they have been born in this land, there are certainly varying degrees of depth in their protection and propagation of the teachings.

Those who are deep in their commitment are like a son carrying out his father’s affairs; knowing that his father’s family estate is his own, he does not cease his efforts even when undergoing hardship.

Those who are shallow are like a hired laborer performing a task; they do no more than complete it for the time being. Receiving the Buddha’s entrustment is a matter of the human sentiment of the moment.
Consequently, those who write commentaries and sub-commentaries move about like the sun and moon [illuminating all], yet those who read them merely scatter chaff and thus darken their eyes.
Those who preach strike the drum while seeking a lost child, yet those who listen call a rat a jade gem.
Thus, while this sutra is fundamentally clear, the commentators obscure it; while people are fundamentally wise, the preachers delude them. One seeks...
To treat it as a mere object of affection while failing to regard it as the instruction for a deluded disciple is impossible.

I have observed that although the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is simple and easy, its meaning is truly extraordinary; although its matters are clear and direct, its principle is indeed profound and mysterious.

Though it is said to be neither carved nor adorned, this teaching of the One Great Vehicle contains the most exquisitely refined and sublime expressions, such that nothing can surpass the profundity of this One Great Vehicle.

Consider, for instance, the essays written by candidates for the three examination halls: there is not one that does not exhaust their mental and physical strength, flaunting their aspirations, adorning them with elegant rhetoric, and pushing their stylistic refinement to its ultimate limit.
They seek the extraordinary within the extraordinary and seek brilliance within the brilliant, fearing only that the examiners might fail to recognize their subtlety and accuracy.
Yet, as for this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is as if it were produced [from a different realm].
The text for proclaiming names at a public examination does not require ornate embellishment or artistic refinement; it merely states, "First place: [Name], Second place: [Name].

Furthermore, in the great teachings of the world, when officials examine the merits of those under their jurisdiction to recommend or dismiss them, they must employ refined appraisal and literary polish.
Only this Vajra King’s Precious Enlightenment is like... [receiving imperial appointment].

The texts of imperial edicts do not rely on elaborate circumlocutions or the exchange of "duyu" (harmonious responses), but simply state "it is so" or "there is. The use of punctuation marks is merely functional.
Nevertheless, when one attains the singular truth, those who first excel in literary refinement begin to rank themselves as superior or inferior;
otherwise, the former skill in ornate beauty would have it that all such things are reduced to empty flowers and bubble-like reflections—of what use are they?

Ah! It is for this reason that this sutra alone, by bestowing predictions upon the śrāvakas and naming them as specific Buddhas, constitutes one of the great causal conditions for the appearance of Buddhas in the world.
To cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is its ultimate and final discourse.
Indeed, regarding the Great Teaching of One Time, it is said that all sentient beings— [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*
Do all possess the Buddha-nature? Is it not said that one first realizes that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the beginning?
Yet, one has not yet truly known what kind of Buddha they have become; who this Buddha is; in which kalpa he appeared; in which land he resides; and what his retinue is.

What Buddha-dharma is being taught here? Furthermore, whom is he prophesying? This is a general statement regarding those who read books, meaning that all may pass the examinations and become officials.

How can this compare to this sutra, which truly bestows upon Śāriputra and the twelve thousand śrāvakas the manifest prophecy of attaining the ten titles of a Buddha and the adornments of their future lands and kalpas? Although Maitreya was once recorded in the Āgamas, [this is far superior].

Nagarjuna was a Bodhisattva; he was not among the śrāvakas recorded in this sutra. This is truly a sutra within the Buddha-dharma that proclaims names by issuing a public notice in accordance with the holy intent. How could it be compared to the teachings of the One Great Time?

The teachings of the One Great Time are indeed the blossoming of flowers, whereas this sutra is the fruition of the fruit. This is because the various śrāvakas initially did not believe in their own minds.

He became a Buddha. It was because he had harbored the patience of a Buddha for forty years that, when the karmic conditions for his manifestation as a Buddha were finally activated, he could no longer restrain his forbearance;
he immediately emitted light, shook the earth, and preached through three cycles of nine parables.

Within these teachings, he manifested the profound and the mysterious through the use of simple and accessible language; thus, while they appear superficial to those who look at them, they are in fact deep.
There is indeed a profound flavor in its purport. Is the Tiantai school not profound? Yet one has not yet recognized what is profound within this [text]. Is the Wenling school not essential?
Yet one does not yet know what is essential therein. Those from various quarters who lecture on the plain prose version surely say they are expounding the great meaning of the sutra;
yet they have not reached the fact that the great meaning lies in the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa)—that we ourselves shall attain Buddhahood in a future kalpa and realm.
It is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that adorns [all things]. What is this "Buddha’s knowledge and vision"? It is the true mark (dharmatā) inherently present within my own mind.
What is this "true mark inherently present within my own mind"? In the sutras, it is sometimes called the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows;
sometimes it is called the *utpala* flower that blooms at unseasonable times; sometimes it is called the white ox-cart outside the gate of the burning house; and sometimes it is called the elder.
The great treasure-trove within the chamber; alternatively, it is named the ambrosia that universally rains down upon the three types of grass and two types of trees;
or it is named the transformation-city of skillful means spanning the past, present, and future; or it is named the bright pearl tied within one's robe;
or it is named the water close by when seeing the mud on its bank; or it is named the Many-Jeweled Stūpa; or it is named the Three Pure Lands; or it is named the Sage Asita.
Some call her the Dragon Girl of Sāgara; some call her the Peaceful Joy of the Four Practices, who, upon meeting one of great merit, bestows the jewel from her topknot.
Some call her the Disciple as Numerous as the Sands of the Ganges; some call her the One Who Increases Life Span Upon Meeting Her Father Return.
Some call her the One of Distinguished Virtue; some call her the Ever-Disregarded; some call her the Tathāgata Manifesting Supernatural Powers; and some call her the Entrustment of Bodhi.
Sā. He is also named "One Who Causes All Sentient Beings to Rejoice upon Seeing Him" because he willingly takes medicine;
or named "Universal Gate Sovereign Avalokiteśvara" who practices the art of healing well; or named "Wondrous Sound Dāra"; or named "Adornment of Samantabhadra’s Conduct. In short, [he is these].

The Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon—all the *sūtras*—do not surpass the sharp shaft of this scripture. Like a fool born in the final age, I have heard nothing beyond superficial learning;
yet, like one who seeks a ring from a neighboring tree, I possess many latent habits and deep vows, and thus I have willingly undertaken this task myself.
The matter was not delegated to another, for my nature is one of shame, and though I am a son of love, my character is that of a child; I do not measure my own talent against it.
It is difficult to avoid being self-important while disparaging others. Nevertheless, I recognize that the Buddha is truly my compassionate father; his mind is as straight as a bowstring.

Therefore, I seek the Buddha’s words directly through the Buddha’s mind, refusing to establish separate categories outside of the sutras, fearing I might incur the fault of "cutting the crane short and extending the duck.

Furthermore, I recognize that the Buddha is truly my enlightened teacher; his words are like the most precious treasure. Thus, I seek the Buddha’s mind directly through the Buddha’s words. Although the words are weighty, the intent—
There must be a reason for this. Therefore, when encountering all manner of elaborate formalities and redundant words, one must strive to investigate their fundamental source.

Although the categories are not established externally, they are nonetheless delineated through chapters and sections. Seeing that the scriptures are orderly, it is clear there is an inherent sequence;

the methods are not applied arbitrarily. Only then does one rely upon the natural principle (*tianli*) of the ox and wield the blade with ease upon the sinews and joints, avoiding the tough, knotted parts.
I have never [forgotten it]. As for the provenance of this scripture, there is Master Xuan’s preface;

as for the rises and falls of its prose and the sequence of its shallow and profound meanings, these are fully contained within the commentary on the twenty-eight chapters. Let one cultivate them daily and month by month.
He completed his studies with composure. The assembly requested that he carve the woodblocks for the printing so that it might be widely circulated.
The scripture states: "That which all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know, only a Buddha and a Buddha can know. For this reason, the title was given as *Zhīyīn* (The Knower of Sounds).
May all those throughout the various regions who possess eyes and feet surely await this work to achieve their fulfillment; I hope you will not dismiss it merely by hearing of it.
When you discern with your own eyes and follow that which is good, you will not have betrayed the vow you made before the Buddha on Vulture Peak in days of yore.

Thus, this sutra and its commentary are today once again offered to the world as the sacred mandate of our Buddha, a proclamation that re-reveals the path to attaining Buddhahood through the chanting of names. Were it otherwise, the Buddhas and Patriarchs would have had no reason to act as they did.
There are instances where characters were not established; if this was indeed that person, what cause for suspicion is there in the calculation of skipping levels? The commentary was completed.
In total, he traveled through three prefectures and one county:
first, he annotated two chapters at Shitou Ān (Stonehead Hermitage) in Bifeng Temple, located in the Nanjing Prefecture of Yingtianfu; next, he [proceeded] to Zhenjiangfu.
He annotated one chapter at Jiaoshan Temple; subsequently, he annotated four chapters at Songluo Hermitage in Huizhou Prefecture;
and finally, he annotated fifteen chapters at Chunxi Hermitage and the Zhizhai Hermitage in Hanxiang, Gaochun County.
Finally, at Shitou Hermitage, he annotated six chapters. This took a total of over three years,

Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: "Knowing the Sound" (Zhīyīn).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dào Xuān of Zhōng Nánshān during the Táng Dynasty;
annotated by Rú Yú, the Abbot of Hùguó Jīngāng Monastery during the Míng Dynasty.

The five characters "Miao" (Wondrous) and so forth constitute the title of the sutra. The three characters "Hong" (Vastly) and so forth are established based on the sutra’s title; they constitute the title of the prologue.

Now, first the title of the sutra will be explained, and subsequently the title of the prologue. Regarding the former, the titling of most sutras requires an appropriate request from those present, after which the Buddha expounds them.
However, the title of this very sutra was [established] by the Buddhas of the past, such as Candrasūryapradīpa, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, and Raśmiprabha.

O King and others, within the teachings of all Buddhas, this very name has already been established. Furthermore, while the Buddha was in meditative absorption, Mañjuśrī had already spoken the answer to Maitreya;
and when the Buddha emerged from concentration and granted permission to speak, he likewise did not exceed the ancient theme of past Buddhas, saying:
"Such a wondrous Dharma is taught by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, only at certain times. This wondrous...
The two characters for "Dharma" (法) can clearly be seen as having been spoken by the Buddha himself. Furthermore, it is said: "It is like the *udumbara* flower, which appears but once in an age.
In Sanskrit, this is *udumbarapuṣpa*. According to various sutras, śāstras, and poetic compositions, this refers to a rare, auspicious, great precious blue lotus (*nīlotpala*).
Thus, the two characters for "Lotus Flower" (蓮華) are likewise the Buddha’s own metaphor for the wondrous Dharma. (This is the analogy for the Dharma.)
Thus, one knows that the title’s two characters, "Lotus" (Liánhuá), do not refer to the ordinary red and white lotuses found in the mundane world,
but rather to the auspicious, great-treasure blue lotus known as the *udumbara* mentioned in the sutra.
Because the great jewel of the blue lotus is rare in the world, a sutra states: "For example, the udumbara flower is rare in the world;
however, as for the red and white lotuses, how could they be rare? Their appearance is an auspicious omen of the emergence of a Golden Wheel-Turning Sage King.
According to the scriptural text, the Buddha used this flower as a metaphor for the Sublime Dharma.

All [other teachings] emphasize the single moment; for whenever the Buddhas appear in the world, they preach the dharmas of the Small, Great, and Triple Vehicles according to the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings, teaching as appropriate to the occasion without being restricted by time. Only this sutra fully expresses the Buddha’s original intent.
One must wait for the time to arrive before speaking. Why is this? Because this sutra does not speak of the three vehicles, but speaks only of the one vehicle.

Yet the one vehicle is precisely the aforementioned three vehicles; the three vehicles were originally intended as the present one vehicle. This is because it is most difficult to believe and most difficult to understand.
It would have been better not to speak of it at all, for if it were spoken, none of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas of the past would have been permitted [to hear it].

As for those who have attained Buddhahood, they have all now received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of their own future buddhahood. This is just like the *udumbara* flower—a rare and auspicious great treasure, a blue lotus—which, if it does not emerge, is that;
but once it emerges, there will certainly appear in the world a Golden Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
The lifespan of the people and the adornments of the land will all increase. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, you should know that all..."
The Dharma attained by the Buddha is expounded for the sake of sentient beings through immeasurable powers of skillful means.
Sometimes he speaks in sūtras, gāthās, and itivṛttakas; yet he has never said to you, "You shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
The reason he has not spoken thus is that the time for such a teaching had not yet arrived. Now is precisely that time; I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna. I...

These nine divisions of the Dharma take entry into the Mahāyāna as their fundamental purpose. By this one may know that within the scriptures, both the metaphors and the titles emphasize the word "one-time" (*ekakāla*).
The title conforms to the name of the sutra; since the sutra is the Buddha’s own word, it must not be altered by one’s own composition.

Because the root and flower are simultaneously the fruit, and because it remains eternally pure while dwelling in defilement, the lotus possesses six meanings, and the wondrous possesses ten wonders. And...

This is a forced interpretation. To claim that the statements regarding the identity of the causes and effects of defilement and purity are all doctrines from the Vaipulya teachings of forty years prior, rather than the ultimate discourse of this final sutra, is untenable; for regardless of whether one is defiled or pure, the white ox is bestowed equally upon all.
Regardless of whether it has been long or short, all are entrusted with the family inheritance; this may be deliberated upon. (The Sūtra says: "This great elder possesses immeasurable wealth.

These young children are all my sons, and my love for them is without partiality. I have such great seven-jeweled chariots, numbering immeasurably; I ought to give them to each with an equal mind, and it is not fitting to differentiate between them.

This shows that regardless of the duration, there is the evidence of the family inheritance through which one is prophesied to attain Buddhahood). This is where the title of the sūtra originates. If one wishes to explain its meaning:
Regarding the principle, it is likewise more appropriate to rely on the self-explanation provided in the sutra itself. The sutra states: "The Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is suitable.

This explains the character *fa* (Dharma) in the title (for forty years prior, the ninefold scriptures of the Small and Great Vehicles were spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; hence, it is said to be "according to what is suitable").

"Its underlying intent is difficult to understand" explains the character *miao* (wondrous) in the title (as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "You all should believe the profound sutras spoken by the Tathāgata with sincerity and truth, for their meaning is exceedingly subtle and wondrous"; this is it). These are the explanations within the sutra.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, he investigates and explains this, asking: "Why is this so? The Dharma taught according to what is appropriate has an intention that is difficult to understand;
this is sublime. By means of countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions, I have expounded all dharmas.
These dharmas cannot be understood through the conceptualization or discrimination of those of the Two Vehicles; they can only [be understood by the Bodhisattvas]."

There are Buddhas who are able to know this. Why is this so? Because although the worlds from which the Buddhas emerge differ, they are the same in their purpose for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-karaṇa-hetu-pratyaya*): to reveal, show, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It continues, saying: "It is solely by means of the One Buddha Vehicle that I preach the Dharma for sentient beings; there is no other vehicle."
Whether it be two or three [aspects], it is therefore called "wondrous" (miao). Within this sutra, the subject is presented, its significance is raised, and its meaning is explained;
that which constitutes the Dharma and that which constitutes the wondrous are clearly and unerringly set forth in explicit text. If one follows the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (Qixin lun):
Regarding the direct and clear exposition of the Dharma and its subtlety, the *Treatise* states: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings.

This mind, in its aspect of true suchness (*tathatā*), reveals the essence of Mahāyāna; in its aspect of the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing, it can reveal the self-nature, characteristics, and functions of Mahāyāna.
Since this mind encompasses all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms.

Therefore, it is called "Dharma. In its substance, characteristics, and function, these three greatnesses constitute that which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden upon and that which all Bodhisattvas shall ride upon;
they are the wondrous functioning of both awakening and non-awakening. Therefore, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma.
Once sentient beings clearly realize the wondrous nature of this mind-Dharma, their six sense organs—such as the eyes born of their parents—are, in this very moment, the [Buddha-nature] itself.

This is the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas. Because sentient beings do not dare to accept it (as the sutra says: "When the impoverished son saw his father possessed of great power, he immediately felt terror and regretted having come here," continuing until:
"Having had this thought, he fled quickly away"—this refers to not daring to accept it), and because they are unwilling to accept it (the sutra says: "At that moment, the elder... [and so forth]).

He further gave him a name and called him "son. At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer; even until now, he had not yet abandoned his inferior mindset and was unwilling to accept [the responsibility].
Therefore, forty years prior, the Buddha, in accordance with what was appropriate for sentient beings, taught within the Āgamas that this mental dharma exists (for a period of twelve years).
Sentient beings, having heard the Dharma, realized the nirvāṇa of the small fruits of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding the Prajñā teachings, it was said that this mind-dharma is empty (a period of twenty-two years). When sentient beings heard this Dharma, they became Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.
Regarding the Vaipulya teachings, it was said that this mind-dharma is neither empty nor existent, yet is both existent and empty (a period of eight years).
When bodhisattvas heard this Dharma, they realized the ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the One Vehicle.
Such distinctions between the Small, Great, and Three Vehicles—how could these be the intent with which the Buddhas and all the Buddhas appear in the world?
When the Buddhas and all the Buddhas appear in the world, their original purpose is simply for sentient beings to directly take responsibility [for their own minds].
If one sees for oneself that this mind is Buddha, then a single, most great matter—along with all its causes and conditions—is completely finished. (As the Sūtra says: Śāriputra...)

"You should know that I originally made a vow: 'I desire to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself. As I vowed in the past, it is now fulfilled. To transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way—this is it."

Because sentient beings find it difficult to believe and difficult to understand, the Buddha—the King of all dharmas, untainted and unconditioned—endured for more than forty years the status of an inferior being among those ordinary people who grasp at signs, teaching them according to their needs.
Only after forty years had passed, when the time for the Buddha’s nirvana arrived, could he no longer restrain his impatience; he simply took the full platter and set it out before them.

Because he has thoroughly acted for the sake of others, there is this text consisting of twenty-eight chapters concerning the emission of light, the manifestation of auspicious signs, emerging from meditative concentration, and the proclamation of virtues.

This clarifies that when Buddhas and all other Buddhas appear in the world, they do so solely to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s innate knowledge and vision—what is called the "one great causal condition.
This is nothing other than the desire to lead those of small, medium, and large capacities [to the same goal].
This is the manifest record of those who ride [the vehicle] attaining the adornments of the land and kalpa of the One Vehicle, and the manifestation of the ten titles of a Buddha.
Therefore, the teachings previously expounded for over forty years according to what was appropriate are all unified into the wondrous Dharma of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the One Vehicle.
Thus, the title "Wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma) refers to this. However, one must [also consider] the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...

Regarding the Buddhas and the Buddhas: if one hears even a single verse or a single phrase from those who have passed away in the past, and rejoices in it for even a single thought-moment, the time for receiving the prediction of enlightenment has arrived;

the time for the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa has come, and only then can this be spoken. It is like the *udumbara* flower—a rare and auspicious great treasure, a blue lotus—that does not appear in ordinary times;
it must wait until the time arrives when a Golden-Wheel Turning Sage King appears in the world. Only once in a while does it manifest.

It appears in the *Ārya-śrī-bhadracarī-praṇidhāna-rāja*. Therefore, the title’s metaphor of the lotus flower refers to this. As for the explanation of the first fascicle of the sutra, it may follow the various existing commentaries.

Regarding *utpala* (or *udumbara*), the old translation was "Auspicious Response" (*shuìyìng*). Those with knowledge of phonology [the *Yīnzhī*] explain it as a "spiritual and auspicious great treasure, a blue lotus flower. (Examination and verification appended).
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "How does the Tathāgata preach this Dharma? It is like the auspicious *utpala* flower, which is seen only from time to time;
the Dharma praised by the Buddha is rare and occurs only after a long interval."
The *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: At that time, within the Jeta Grove, a precious lotus flower emerged from the earth, seven *tāla* trees in height.
This flower possessed eighty thousand layers, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
within each layer was a Buddha, surrounded before and behind by immeasurable multitudes, preaching the wondrous Dharma.
[The Buddha] said, "Śāriputra, because he wished to make offerings to these Buddhas, he used his supernormal powers to circumambulate this Flower King for eighty-seven days;
yet even with a hundred thousand million parts, he could not complete even one [turn]. (In this context, "zhī" should be understood as meaning "great" and "treasure.")

Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha, "What is the name of these flowers? Among the Buddhas, they preach the treasury of the sublime Dharma to immeasurable great assemblies. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Good son, these flowers are named *udumbara*.
The Buddhas therein are all named Śākyamuni. You all should make offerings [to them]. (The previous heading states: "Jewel...")

"Lotus. Later, the commentary explains it as *utpala* (or *utpala-bhara*). This is the same as the title of this sutra, which is marked "Lotus," while within the text, the *utpala-bhara* flower is used as the standard term.

This indicates why only the Buddha explained *utpala* as the great precious blue lotus (*mahāratna-nīlotpala*). Question: The scriptural text uses the same character for both, yet the additions and subtractions differ.
I fear that this sutra merely says *utpala* and has never had the character "la" (羅). This is why Dharmarakṣa translated it as "Numinous Auspiciousness" (*ling-shui*), as its name...

As for why the *Yìjí* translates [the term] as "Auspicious Response" (*ruìyìng*), since the *Fāngděng tuóluóní jīng* adds an extra character "luó," the *Yìjí* consequently uses it to gloss "precious lotus. The answer is: Not so. The text cited in the *Yìjí* also directly states "udumbara";
it is only in the gloss that the character "luó" is specifically added, which is then explained as "Auspicious Response. Thus we know...
"Udumbara" is the same as *udumbarapuṣpa*. "Auspicious response" (*ruìyìng*) refers to the great precious blue lotus; there is no doubt of this.
In the original sutra, it is stated that when the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara comes to this land, he will first manifest eighty-four thousand precious lotuses.
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions did this omen first appear? This was also because seeing the precious lotus flower constituted a miraculous response (prātihārya).
He asked: "If the precious lotus flower constitutes a miraculous response, then that is so; however, you speak of the blue lotus flower—is this not in contradiction with the miraculous response?
According to the *Mingyi ji* (Collection of Names and Meanings), the *udumbara* is translated as [the flower of] rare appearance.

The *śrīphala* is translated as *utpala*, which refers to the blue lotus; thus, these two flowers each have their own distinct name and color, and one cannot therefore equate the *śrīphala* with the blue lotus.
In response, it is said: according to the *Vaipulya Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, these two flowers were originally one flower;
the *udumbara* is precisely the *utpala*. This is because that sūtra employs this as a metaphor for the Buddha on three occasions.
It is difficult to encounter. Though the phrasing differs, the meaning is one and the same. Thus, when Subhadra first sought an audience with the Buddha, he said:
"The Buddha is difficult to encounter; he appears but once in a long while, like the *utpala* flower. At first, there was no mention of the name "Pātra" (Maitreya).
Subsequently, the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus regarding the Buddha’s own appearance, saying: "After one hundred and forty million years have passed, Maitreya Buddha shall appear once more."

His ancestors were descendants of the Hù (Hù) clan, chieftains of the Western Róng. His army numbered one hundred thousand; he styled himself King of Qin and fathered Jiàn.

On his back was a character written in grass script; he changed his surname to Fu. He usurped the throne for four years, with his capital at Chang’an. Fu Jian’s courtesy name was Yonggu; he was also the son of Fu Hong. Possessing both martial prowess and strategic wisdom, he brought the entire Central Plains under his control.

He reigned for twenty-seven years and led a million troops to invade the Jin dynasty, but was defeated by Xie Shi, Xie Xuan, and others. Later Qin’s Yao Chang, courtesy name Jingmao, was a Qiang from Chiting. His ancestors were descendants of the Youyu clan.

His father, Yao Yizhong, had twenty-four sons, of whom Chang was the youngest. Initially serving Fu Jian, he suffered defeat during a southern expedition and subsequently strangled Jian to death. Yao Xizhi usurped the throne for eight years. His son, Yao Xing, courtesy name Zilüe, reigned for twenty-two years. This is a general outline of the "Five Barbarians" (Wuhu) disrupting China. Emperor Yuan crossed the [Yangtze River].

Regarding the River: according to the *Zhuanjian*, in the first year of Jianxing (the Guiyou year), the tenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Min of Jin, the Han ruler Liu Cong held a banquet for his ministers in the Guangji Hall. He ordered Emperor Hui to serve wine in the attire of a common servant. Yu Min, Wang Jun, and others could not restrain their indignation and wept aloud.

Liu Cong detested this and executed more than ten Jin officials. The Emperor was also killed. When the news of this calamity reached [the south], the high ministers enthroned Ye, the son of Prince Yan of Wu, to ascend the throne; he was known as Emperor Min. At that time, fewer than a hundred households remained within the city of Chang’an; weeds and briars had formed forests.

The officials lacked ceremonial robes and seals of office, and they designated their titles by wearing mulberry-tree garments. Later, he too was captured by Liu Cong and forced to serve wine and wash out goblets. Subsequently, the Emperor was made to wear military attire and hold a ceremonial parasol. Furthermore—

The Secretariat Official Xin Bin embraced the Emperor and wept bitterly. Fu Chong led him out and executed him. It was for this reason that Emperor Yuan crossed the Yangtze River to Jiangdong. The *Fozu Tongzai* states: "Emperor Yuan of the Eastern Jin was the great-grandson of Emperor Xuan and the son of Prince Gong Wang Jian.

His personal name was Rui, and his courtesy name was Jingwen. At the time of his birth, there was a divine light within the room that illuminated it entirely; a white tuft of hair grew from the left side of his 'sun-peak' (the area between the eyebrows). He held successive offices until he became the Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Yangzhou and Left Chancellor."

After the defeat of Emperor Huai and Emperor Min, the hundred officials were scattered; some fled to the south of the Yangtze River, while others were taken captive or killed. Chang’an lost its seat of power, and the Emperor was confined in Pingyang at Jiangdu. At that time, five suns suddenly appeared together in the sky. The assembled ministers urged Liu Yu (Rui) [to take action].

It was appropriate to title him Prince of Jin and entrust him with the myriad affairs of state to preside over the billions of subjects. When Emperor Min was murdered, he ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jianwu. He subsequently established his capital at Jianye;

to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Min, it was renamed Jiankang. Previously, there had been a children’s rhyme: "Five horses float across the river; one horse transforms into a dragon. During the chaos of the Yongjia period, among the members of the imperial clan, only the five princes of Langya, Xiyang, Runan, Nandon, and Pengcheng managed to escape to safety. Of these, Shi Rui was the first to establish the foundation as the Son of Heaven.
Emperor An’s personal name was Dezong. He was the Crown Prince of Emperor Xiaowu. On the day of Bingshen, he succeeded Emperor Xiaowu and ascended the throne.
In the following year, Dingyou, he changed the era name to Long’an, which lasted for five years. He then changed it to Yongxing, lasting for three years. He further changed it to Yixi.
This lasted for a total of fourteen years. Later Qin was the surname Yao; details regarding this are found in the preceding notes. Hongshi was the reign title of Yao Xing.
Kucha is the name of a kingdom located to the southwest of Yanqi. The śramaṇa was named Yúnqín. Kumārajīva means "Child Longevity.
When Fú Jiān, the King of Former Qin, heard of the Master’s reputation, he dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry Lǚ Guāng to lead seven... [thousand troops].
In the year Renwu, the seventh year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, [Fu] Jian invaded Kucha to capture Kumārajīva. Having obtained Kumārajīva, they returned together to Liangzhou.
Upon arriving at Liangzhou, they heard that Jian had already passed away and that Yao Guang had seized control of Liangzhou, immediately assuming the title of King of the Three Rivers.
He changed the state’s name to Daoliang and altered the era name to Dà'ān; this was the eleventh year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin. When Guang died, his son Yao Shao [succeeded him].
He was established [as king], but was killed by Lü Zuan, the Duke of Taiyuan. Upon Zuan’s accession, he was in turn deposed by Lü Chao, who established Lü Long.
In the third year of Yao Xing’s Hongshi era, he dispatched an army to attack Long; Long surrendered, and consequently, Kumārajīva was escorted to Chang’an.
The King of Qin treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher. This was in the *xinchou* year, the fifth year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty.
In the eighth year of Hongshi, Kumārajīva first translated this sutra at Cūtang Monastery in seven fascicles; these are the titles used today.
However, it was during the *bingwu* year of the Yixi era of the Jin that he produced the preface, which refers to the Long’an era because he was speaking from the time he entered Chang’an. (Sui...)
The one surnamed Ren-shou was Emperor Wen of the Sui Dynasty, Gaozu. His clan name was Yang and his given name was Jian.

He was a native of Honglong in Huayin and the fourteenth-generation descendant of Yang Zhen, the Grand Marshal of the Han dynasty. Initially, Yuwen Tai served the Wei dynasty and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhou;

his son Yuwen Jue subsequently received the abdication of the Wei, establishing the state with the name Zhou. Jian’s father, Yang Zhong, served the Zhou dynasty with merit and rose to the rank of Grand Tutor (Taifu).

The Duke of Sui, Zhong, died; Jian succeeded him to the rank. In the thirteenth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty, the year of Xinchou, Jian received the abdication from the Zhou and established his capital at Chang’an.
He made “Great Sui” (Dàsuí) his dynastic name. From Emperor Wendi to Emperor Gongdi, there were three sovereigns in total, for a combined duration of thirty-seven years.
Because he took the dynastic name as his surname, he was called the Sui clan. Renshou was the era name of Emperor Wendi. North.

Regarding "Tianzhu" (India): there are five regions of Tianzhu, collectively named India, which here is translated as "Moonland. To distinguish it from the other four, it is called "Beiyu" (Northern Region).

The *Xiyuji* states: "The designation 'Tianzhu' is subject to various divergent interpretations. Formerly it was called Shendu, or Xiandou; now, following the correct pronunciation, it should be called India.

'India' is the Tang-language term for 'moon. The moon has many names, and this is one such appellation. As for Jñānagupta, according to the preface to the *Addendum to the Lotus Sūtra*, he must have been the second [to arrive].
[This is] a person. However, in the preface to that sutra, there is no Śīlajñāna; instead, there is Xuemaduō (Kumārajīva).
In the *Fanyi zaji* (Collection of Records on the Translation of the Tripitaka), above the name Jīmūta, there are the two characters "Dharmā" [i.e., Dharmagupta]. The preface states:

In the first year of the Renshou era of the Great Sui dynasty, the year of Xinyou, the śramaṇa Shangxing of Puyao Monastery invited the two Dharma Masters Kumārajīva (here translated as Dezhi) and Jīmūta (here translated as Fami) to the Daxingshan Monastery to [re-]translate...
This sutra was translated in eight fascicles and titled *The Expanded Version of the Sublime Dharma*. Here, the titles of two [versions] are taken together and combined into a single phrase:
"Jñānagupta. Regarding the phrase "the three sutras being redundant," etc., this is a transitional expression used to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one;
it means that although the sutra comprehensively covers the fundamental purpose of the various Buddhas' descent into the world, its transmission from the West to the East occurred at specific times.

In total, it has undergone three translations. To avoid the redundancy of repetition (where "repetition" refers to a second translation and "cumulation" to a third—thus having versions of ten, eight, and seven fascicles, resulting in a layering of layers and a cumulating of cumulums)—the phrasing and essential meanings of each have been presented side by side;
they appear to be without distinction in quality. However, as for what people of the time have venerated:
As for those who favored and esteemed [this work], it was primarily the Qin dynasty that transmitted it most extensively.
This is why the Preface mentions only the Qin translations and does not mention the Jin or Sui translations; this was done to accord with the times.

Regarding the mutual presentation of the textual meanings—for instance, the passage "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena," specifically the phrase "the nature of all phenomena is thus"—Dharmarakṣa’s translation states: "The Tathāgata fully understands the source of all phenomena; from where they come, all phenomena are spontaneous (*svabhāva*); he distinguishes the appearance of phenomena, their various marks, and their roots."

Fundamentally, one knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are spontaneous (*svabhāva*). When compared with the translation by Kumārajīva, while the phrasing may not reach [the original's elegance], the essential meaning is indeed presented. Why is this?

It is because all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, including the faculties, objects, and elements—are the source from which the Buddha and the various Buddhas, throughout forty years of teaching, established the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and nine divisions of scripture. These are the phenomena whose characteristics, natures, origins, and ultimate ends are equal; they have as their source the mind-nature of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), the untainted (*anāsrava*) true reality (*tathatā*).

From what do these phenomena come? The Buddha knows they come from true reality. That "all phenomena are spontaneous" means that since they come from true reality, they are so of themselves; they are not attained through cultivation, nor are they lost through non-cultivation. [End of Section]

Regarding "the differentiation of the characteristics of dharmas": this means that although all dharmas share the same single true reality (*dharmatā*), there are nevertheless distinctions in their characteristics, natures, essences, functions, causes, conditions, fruits, retributions, origins, and ends, as well as in their respective dharmas and appearances.

Regarding "knowing that the root of all characteristics is the spontaneity of dharmas": this means that although the dharmas of characteristics, natures, powers, and functions are numerous and vast, they all have the single-vehicle (*ekayāna*) untainted true reality of the mind-nature as their root. This is why this Buddha and all Buddhas know that [all things] are spontaneously so, ultimately equal.
As in the two translations of the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* (The Simile of the Medicinal Herbs), the text is still incomplete by more than half a chapter; in Kumārajīva’s translation, however—

In the *Wú* (無) translation, following the "Parable of the Herbs," there are many passages such as those comparing [the Buddha] to the sun and moon, a potter fashioning vessels, and a person born blind meeting a skilled physician, as well as the analogies and teachings concerning the King of Medicines from the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*).

Furthermore, in Dharmarakṣa’s translation, prior to the "Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples" chapter, there are many passages such as the Guide entering the sea to gather treasures. Prior to the "Dharma Master" chapter, there is the "Bhaiṣajyarāja Tathāgata" chapter. By cross-referencing these three translations, it appears that the [present] version follows the Jin (晉) edition;

it contains the account of Bhaiṣajyarāja Tathāgata and connects with the section where, following Bhaiṣajyarāja’s address to the eighty thousand great beings, the narrative begins its progression. It is not like the Qin (秦) edition, which inexplicably omits these parts. Upon reading the preface to the *Extended Version of the Lotus Sūtra*, I finally...

It is known that because the translators originated from different countries, they brought with them various versions of the Sanskrit text; thus, there are discrepancies regarding what is present or absent in each. The preface states: "Dharmarakṣa [translated] from palm leaves; Kumārajīva [translated] from the script of Kucha. All such instances represent the mutual presentation of the textual meanings.

For example, in the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment), Kumārajīva’s translation places it as the twenty-second chapter, whereas Dharmarakṣa’s translation places it at the end of the volume.

Kumārajīva regards nineteen chapters as the *mūla* (the authentic core), while the eight chapters beginning with "The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers" constitute the *pariṇāmanā* (the dissemination). Dharmarakṣa, however, considers the chapters beginning with "Supernatural Powers" to all belong to the *mūla*, assigning the *Parīndanā-parivarta* alone to the dissemination section.

For the purpose of circulation, all [versions] are acceptable). As for the remaining chapters such as the *Zhipin* (Separate Chapters), since the Qin edition was already venerated by its time, both its phrasing and intent are excellent; why then would one need to provide a commentary on twenty-eight chapters?

Regarding those that were not covered in the commentary, these are all the individual verses of the *Zhipin* (such as the *Jian Baota Pin*, which exists as a separate chapter in the canon titled *Safang Fenduo*).

The *Lìjīng* (Expedient Means Chapter) and the *Pǔménpǐn* (Universal Gate Chapter) are individually titled the *Pǔménjīng*. Therefore, the preface focuses solely on the chapters within the three cycles of the Dharma—namely, the "Introductory Chapter," "Expedient Means," "The Burning House," "The City of Illusion," "The Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples," and "The Stringing of Pearls and Digging the Well"—while judging all other parts to belong to the separate branches (*zhībié*).
That it is not without its own tradition, as seen in works such as the *Xùlì* (Chronicle of the Preface), means that since they are indeed separate branches.
Why should it be included in the orthodox canon? It is because each has its own distinct category. Since there are these categories, one should follow the stream to reach the source;
by adhering to the sequence of the chapters and sections, the words and principles will become clear and easy to understand.

Therefore, following the analogy of "digging a well," this preface reveals that after awakening there is much that remains unrecorded; it records only the fundamental descent of the Buddhas into the world.

This is as explained in the following section (regarding those who are not without their own particular tendencies: the *Devadatta-parivarta* corresponds to the teaching on the Bodhisattva Dharma for the sake of the Master of the Law;

it concerns the stream of those for whom the Buddha acted as a royal disciple, who did not shrink from hardship in their quest for the Dharma. The *Sadāparibhūta-parivarta* corresponds to the teaching on the Bodhisattva Dharma for the sake of the Master of the Law; it concerns the stream of those who, as bhikṣus acting as teachers, preserve the sutras and are able to endure insults.

The *Dharmakośa-stūpa-parivarta* clarifies the stream of those who are protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness and possess the *nirmāṇakāya*. The *Ayuḥpramāṇa-parivarta* clarifies the stream of those who are protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness and possess the *dharmatākāya*. The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta* [concerns] maintaining the sutra through ascetic practice.)
As for the "streams" (of the Dharma), Avalokiteśvara acts as a stream through the sovereignty of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*).

Now, the descent of spirits upon sacred peaks cannot occur without the transformative influence of a Great Sage; and that the reach of such transformation extends to others cannot happen without past conditions to guide their minds.

Thus, when the Perfected Garden (*xian yuan*) reached completion, there was a distinction between the capacities of small and great vehicles; and when the Golden River witnessed the final charge, [the teachings were entrusted].
The Way distinguishes between the partial and the full teachings; is this not because the instruction adapts to the capacities and times of those who ride upon it?

To examine the essence of these sublime assemblies, one knows that the five thousand disciples withdrew from their seats to advance those of arrogant disposition, while the five hundred received predictions of enlightenment as traces of the joint veneration of the esoteric transformation.

Thus, the radiance was emitted and auspicious signs manifested to open up the source of the teaching requested; emerging from meditative concentration, virtue was extolled to fully unfold the Buddha’s wisdom.
The broad strategy of the "Decayed House" provides a textual track for entering the Great [Vehicle], while the "Transformation City" draws upon past conditions so they do not fall into ruin.

The "Tying of the Jewel" clarifies that the rational nature is eternally present; the "Digging of the Well" demonstrates the manifold methods of awakening. The phrasing and meaning are perfectly complete, and the metaphors presented are truly profound.
Were it not for the vast salvation of Great Compassion, which pulls those submerged in the flowing currents of stagnation, and the ultimate heart of pity that rescues the ignorant—how could this be?

Since the Han dynasty until the Tang, for over six hundred years, throughout the study of more than four thousand scrolls of various scriptures, none has surpassed this sutra in terms of those who have received, upheld, and propagated it.
Is it not because the capacities of beings and the teachings have met, being the lingering traces of the wisdom of the Victorious One (Śākyamuni), such that upon hearing it, one feels deep reverence?
Or perhaps it is due to the remaining achievements of King Udayana, such that I have now composed this preface at the head of the scripture to synthesize its essence, hoping thereby that—

"May we early purify the six sense organs to partake in the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One, and swiftly accomplish the four virtues to follow the profound path to the Land of Bliss.
This explains that the fundamental purpose for which all Buddhas descend as spirits is to extensively praise [the Dharma]. Now, "with regard to" (*fuyi*) is a particle used to introduce a statement.

What was previously called "the descent of the spirits of all Buddhas" is here termed "the numinous mountain" (*lingyue*). While the former refers generally to the ten directions and the three periods of time, this...

This text describes only Śākyamuni Buddha; therefore, it distinguishes him by means of the "Numinous Peak" (the Vulture Peak). The reason for this is that Śākyamuni is the primary teacher of this sūtra.
While the fundamental intent of all Buddhas emerges [from the source], it is Śākyamuni who proclaims and manifests it;

when Śākyamuni’s fundamental intent is fully realized, then the fundamental intent of the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of infinite and boundless transformation Buddhas is likewise fully realized. The Numinous...
"Yue" (the mountain) refers to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. In the Sanskrit language it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa; here it is translated as "Spiritual Vulture. "Yue" is a term of honor.

Regarding the phrase "the descent of the spirit," it was refined by quoting from the *Shijing* (Book of Odes), specifically the eighth chapter of the eighth section of the *Songdaoya* (Greater Odes of the Mountain):

"Lofty indeed is the mountain, reaching up to the heavens. From this mountain descends the spirit, giving birth to Fu and Shen. Fu and Shen are the pillars of Zhou, spreading [its influence] to the four quarters and proclaiming it to the four directions. This was not [said of] an ordinary person.

"Those who could not be transformed through other means" refers to the fact that while the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas pervades the trichiliocosm, it was not without cause and condition that Śākyamuni, the Great Sage, alone descended his traces to Gṛdhrakūṭa.
His coming here to reveal the provisional (*upāya*) and transform beings toward the ultimate (*bhūtārtha*) was precisely for this purpose.
"Just as the reach of transformation extends" correctly clarifies that there is indeed a cause; it means that he has appropriately arrived at and reached [them]. This refers to those who possess...

What is the cause? It is because one thousand two hundred arhats, while currently on this mountain, have received the Buddha’s transformation and teaching, and have attained the prediction that the time for their attainment of Buddhahood has arrived; this is the reason. Since these arhats have received their predictions and the time has arrived—
This explains the reason for the Buddha’s descent of his spirit. Why is it that within the sutras there are those whom his transformation reaches and those whom it does not reach?

Those whom his transformation reaches are those who formerly possessed the conditions for the Mahāyāna, such as the twelve hundred arhats and the two thousand learners and non-learners who have received predictions of enlightenment.
Those whom his transformation does not reach are those who formerly lacked the conditions for the Mahāyāna, such as the five thousand who regressed.
Regarding the "seat": although the Buddha possesses the means to transform others through equanimity, he would likewise have no way to guide their minds.

Therefore it is said: "Without the conditions of the past, there is no way to guide the mind" (meaning that without a Great Sage there is no means to open and transform them; though he may again apply his transformative teachings, without the conditions of the past, there is no way to guide the mind).

This discourse on the capacities to whom the teachings are addressed serves as a record for future occasions when the capacities and the teachings will mutually correspond and bring about subduing [of afflictions]. Regarding the phrase "The Garden of the Immortals was completed," etc., this clarifies that there is a specific origin for the Great Sage’s beginning and end regarding the sites where he transformed beings.
It means that the Buddha first appeared in the Garden of the Immortals; therefore, it was in the Garden of the Immortals that he announced his completion [of his work].
Furthermore, one must distinguish between the great and small capacities [of those to be taught]; in the end, there is a specific origin in the Golden River.
Because he gave his final instructions by the Kim River, the Path—though its doctrines distinguish between the Half and the Full—is not it true that the latter serves as the language of realization?
This refers to the stages of the Small, Great, Half, and Full as expounded in that sutra;

is this not indeed the basis for the beginning and end of the Buddha’s teaching according to the capacities and times of those to be converted? Yet, it cannot compare to the sacred mountain where the Sage descended in spirit.
Examining their high assemblies, he preached this wondrous Dharma of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that those of the two vehicles would attain Buddhahood.

(The "Garden of Immortals" refers to the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*). Because many immortals of antiquity attained the Way there, it is called the Garden of Immortals. Furthermore, as it was the park where King Śuddhodana raised deer, it is also named the Deer Park. It belongs to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. After attaining perfect enlightenment, [the Buddha] reflected for twenty-one days;

knowing that sentient beings were not yet capable of receiving the Mahāyāna, he then proceeded to the Deer Park and addressed the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, saying: "I have already attained perfect enlightenment," and thus he performed the three turnings of the Four Noble Truths ten times...)

Regarding the second, the Wheel of Dharma, it is said: "This is suffering; I have known it. This is its origin; I have abandoned it. This is the path; I have cultivated it. This is its cessation; I have realized it," and so forth. The Sūtra states: "Having reflected upon these matters, he proceeded to Vārāṇasī. The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words;

yet, by the power of skillful means, he preached it for the sake of the five bhikṣus. This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma. Thereupon, there arose the sound of Nirvāṇa, as well as the distinct names of Arhat, Dharma, and Saṃgha," and so on.

As for the distinction between the capacities of the small and the great, this refers to how the Buddha himself, from the Deer Park, taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, thereby establishing the Āgama teachings for twelve years. Although this was accomplished through equal and impartial transformation, it did not hinder the [threefold distinction].

According to the circumstances, there is naturally a distinction between the "small" [teaching] of the four truths of arising and ceasing, and the "great" [teaching] of the four truths of non-arising. Regarding the *Kinnara* River: according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are eight great rivers, and the *Kinnara* is the fourth.

The sūtra states: "Just as with the eight great rivers: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Yamunā; third, the Sarayū; fourth, the Aciravatī; fifth, the Mahī; sixth, the Sindhu; seventh, the Vakṣu; and eighth, the Sītā. The *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings), citing the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), says:

"Aciravatī means 'Possessing Gold' in this language; it is the place where Jambūnada gold is produced. Master Zong of the Liang dynasty said: "The Buddha came to the bank of this river to enter parinirvāṇa, symbolizing the flow of the river."

The rushing torrent is like the swiftness of birth and death; the unmoving golden sand is a metaphor for the eternal abiding of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Some say that because the Buddha cast off his body here while on the path of practice (*bhūmi*), he likewise enters *parinirvāṇa* at this very spot.

Regarding the title "Guming" (Bequeathed Testament): when King Cheng was about to pass away, he summoned the Duke of Zhou and the various feudal lords to assist King Kang. This is the "Guming" chapter. Zheng Xuan’s commentary states: "To look back is called 'gu'. Thus, at the end of his life, King Cheng looked back toward his ministers and issued his testament.

In the *Taijia* [Annals], it says: "He looked back upon the bright mandate of Heaven (*tianming*). This is borrowed here as an embellishment. When the Buddha was approaching his final extinction, he preached the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; thus, it serves as his "Guming Sūtra. The sūtra says: At one time, the Buddha was in the city of Kuṇāla, at the birthplace of the Malla clan, in Ārāḍa...

By the banks of the Bahudā River, between a pair of *śāla* trees, accompanied by eighty billion hundred thousand great bhikṣus, on the fifteenth day of the second month, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha, through his supernatural power, produced a great sound that reached the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*), universally proclaiming to all sentient beings:

"Today, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is about to enter parinirvāṇa. All sentient beings, if you have any doubts, you may now ask them all; let this be your final question. These were the words of the Buddha’s final testament.

Thereupon, together with Kāśyapa and other bodhisattvas, he preached the forty-two fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "the path distinguishes the categories of the Half and the Full": "path" (*dao*) refers to the Way; "distinguishes" (*shu*) means to differentiate; and "categories" (*ke*) carries the meaning of grades or stages. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

It is like an elder who has an only son. Having sent him to a teacher to study, fearing he might not achieve mastery quickly, he diligently instructs him in the "half-syllables" day and night, but does not teach him the *Vyākaraṇa* treatise, because the child is too young and his strength is not yet sufficient.
...and so forth, it says: "Good son, that great elder refers to the Tathāgata; 'only one son' refers to all sentient beings. The Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as if they were his only son.

'Teaching the only son' refers to the śrāvaka disciples. 'Half-syllables' refers to the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-dharma-pravacana*). 'Vyākaraṇa-śāstra' refers to the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras. Because the śrāvakas lack the power of wisdom, the Buddha preached the half-syllable ninefold canon for them, but did not preach the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra for them.

By this standard, the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra is a metaphor for the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras as the 'full-syllables. Furthermore, in the eighth sūtra, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa asks about the meaning of these characters, and the Buddha [explains] with ten..."

The four sounds replied to him, saying: "The half-syllables (*ardhakṣara*) are the foundation for all worldly scriptures, records, treatises, and literary compositions; the full-syllables (*pūrṇakṣara*) are the foundation for all supramundane wholesome dharmas. Just as a person who commits evil is called a 'half-person'."

One who performs good deeds fills the world with their fame. The Tathāgata and those in perfect liberation do not enter into the "half-letters" (*ardhākṣara*), for they are free from all words and letters. If there is one who can know that the Buddha has appeared in the world and is able to extinguish the half-letters, such a person is called one who understands the meaning of the letters.

Judging by this, how could the "half" and "full" [teachings] of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, or the "small" and "great" *Āgamas*, be compared with this sutra to evaluate their relative superiority? To clarify the extent to which the transformative influence reaches and does not reach is the meaning of "unconditioned" and "conditioned.

"For example, there was a man who went to the house of a close friend and lay down, intoxicated with wine. The Buddha is also like this. When he was a bodhisattva, he taught and transformed us, causing us to resolve upon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*); yet we soon forgot it. By this, one can further know that both [the Buddha and we] revere the traces of his secret transformation. The above is a general preface to the teachings of the One Great Vehicle, explaining from beginning to end the descent of the Buddha’s spirit.
Below this, the narrative enters the present sutra, specifically clarifying the descent of the Buddha’s spirit. [Question: Since the five [aspects] were already enumerated above...

therefore, it is provided as an explanatory clarification. As for the emission of light and so forth, it means that because of these departures, the sutra provides the conditions for further progress.

Advancement serves as the basis for the exaltation and manifestation of the Esoteric and Exoteric teachings. Therefore, in the introductory chapter, the Buddha emits light from between his eyebrows as an auspicious omen.

The dialogue between Maitreya and Mañjuśrī at this single assembly is nothing other than the opening of the minds of Śāriputra and the twelve hundred arhats, causing them to aspire to request the appearance of all Buddhas in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*).

This refers to the source of the teaching (meaning that the single chapter, the "Introductory Chapter," is the fountainhead from which this teaching flows). Regarding "Emerging from Samādhi to Proclaim Virtues" and so forth:

this means that in the "Chapter on Expedient Means," because Śāriputra and the others did not comprehend the meaning of the Introductory Chapter, the Buddha immediately emerged from his samādhi and extolled the virtues of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—none of which fail to expound upon the Buddha and all Buddhas.

This refers to the grand strategy of wisdom (*prajñā*). (The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi. This describes his emergence from meditative concentration. Furthermore, it says: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;

its gateway to wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, such that it cannot be known by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. This extols his virtues. *Hong* (grand) means great. This corresponds to the passage in the Sūtra:

"The Buddha has personally attended upon countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas," up to "the Tathāgata knows this to be vast, profound, and far-reaching," and so forth. *Lüe* (strategy/essential) means the essential. This corresponds to the passage in the Sūtra: "Śāriputra, to state the essentials: the immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas, the Buddha has fully realized them all.")

“Stop, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further,” and so forth—this is the passage. The intention of the Preface is that the textual portion of the “Chapter on Expedient Means” (Upāya-paṭala), which proclaims his virtues after emerging from samādhi, is still but a general outline. It is only after the three requests that the Buddha provides a detailed and analytical exposition, which constitutes the complete first cycle of the Dharma-discourse (dharmadeśanā).
Regarding the phrase “the dilapidated house allows for universal entry” and so forth: this refers to the first cycle of the Dharma-discourse, wherein Śāriputra receives his prediction (vyākaraṇa).
The other śrāvakas had not yet attained faith or understanding; therefore, Śāriputra requested on their behalf, and the Buddha again spoke through parables.
He compared the triple world to a burning house, the Buddha to the elder, and the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to the children within that burning house.

First, he used the three vehicles as an inducement (representing the three vehicles taught by the Buddha during the forty years prior); subsequently, he bestowed equally upon them the great treasure carts drawn by white oxen.

(Analogous to the Buddha now preaching the wondrous Dharma. Although it consists of a mere few thousand words, there is nothing that does not serve as a text for clarifying the path to the Mahāyāna for those of the two vehicles;
they follow the same standard. This text and its standard are recorded [in the preface]:

"Today under Heaven, the carriage ruts are the same, the written characters are the same, and conduct is the same. This is the refinement [of the *Puhua pin*]. Therein, the three realms are likened to a burning house, yet the introduction refers to it as a "decayed house," for the sutra states: "This decayed old house belongs to one man."

Regarding the phrase "The City of Transformation leads back to the past," etc.: Kāśyapa and the other four great disciples, having received the Parable Chapter, recounted the Parable of the Poor Son to repay the Buddha.
The Buddha then further preached the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs for them.

Although he did so for the sake of the four great disciples to complete their understanding of their own limitations, his actual intent was for the twelve hundred people to attain simultaneous awakening through the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

He bestowed upon them knowledge and vision, as well as the prediction of their future Buddhahood. Consequently, his five hundred disciples, through the rain of the single flavor, moistened the flowers of humanity;
they gradually advanced in their practice and all attained the fruits of the Path. Furthermore, regarding the teaching that "the path you all practice is the Bodhisattva path;
by practicing and studying it progressively, you shall all become Buddhas," they remained settled in the minor fruits and became deluded regarding the Great [Vehicle].

"Vehicle. This means that since the dharmas of the beginning and the end constitute a single vehicle (*ekayāna*) and all people are already bodhisattvas, what need is there for diligent cultivation or further seeking of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)?

Therefore, after the Buddha bestowed predictions upon his four great disciples, he further preached the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter as a teaching based on causes and conditions, clarifying this through one question:
"In the past, when the Buddha was among the *jñānabuddha* [Dharmakāya] Buddhas, he served sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras..."

For a long time, he had planted the causes for the Mahāyāna within twelve hundred people; now that he has attained Buddhahood, he still first delivers those twelve hundred people by means of the Hīnayāna.
This is because the small vehicle serves as the expedient condition for leading them into the Great Vehicle.

The Great Vehicle is like a precious destination, while the small vehicle is like a conjured city. He causes his five hundred disciples to know that there was formerly a precious destination of the Mahāyāna.
This is the causal condition. One does not fall into the provisional nirvana of the small fruit—the illusory city—nor does one settle for gradualism rather than making immediate progress.

Regarding the "Tying the Jewel" and the clarification of the principle: the five hundred disciples, having received the Buddha’s teaching on causes and conditions, attained the prediction of their future fruition after one cycle of the Dharma.
Moved by the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue, they spoke the parable of tying the jewel, using the Buddha as a metaphor for a kinsman.
Friends, I have compared myself to a drunken man. The rational nature of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the One Vehicle is likened to that pearl.

Now, as the Buddha has preached the Dharma in three successive turnings and five hundred people have attained awakening, it is like realizing after the wine has worn off that one possesses the pearl from before which can now be used.

Although the distance between the Wisdom Buddha and the present Buddha spans eons as numerous as motes of dust—indeed, though it is so remote—the pearl of the rational nature of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision remains.

It has never been lost for even a single moment; therefore, it is said to be "constantly present. (The Sūtra says: "The Buddha was likewise. When he was a Bodhisattva, he taught and transformed us, causing us to give rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).

Yet we soon forgot it, neither knowing nor perceiving it. Once we had attained the path of Arhatship, we considered ourselves to have reached *nirvāṇa*. We struggled for our livelihood and were content with little. Our vow for omniscience remains, yet we did not realize it.

Regarding the metaphor of "digging a well to reveal [the pearl]" and so forth, this refers back to the preceding text. It means that although the pearl of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) within the Buddha's knowledge and vision exists, though...
If one does not obtain the method for cultivation—namely, the opening, showing, awakening, and entering provided by this sutra—one will likewise be unable to realize its present enjoyment.
Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the Buddha again and again exhorted them to diligently read, recite, receive, and uphold this sutra, providing the analogy of digging a well.
He stated that whether lay or ordained, those who study the Bodhisattva path and seek...
Regarding Bodhi, there are those who practice according to other sutras; it is like seeking water on high ground:
one sees only dry earth, and though one exerts effort in digging, the water is still far off.

If one practices according to this sutra, it is like continuing one's labor until one begins to see moist soil and gradually reaches mud, knowing that the water must be near. By means of this sutra...

To explain, manifest, reveal, awaken, and lead others to enter [the Way], there are many kinds of skillful means for attaining Buddhahood through the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (a term used in various ways, much like the *Zhuangzi* employs various methods to embellish benevolence and righteousness).
Regarding the phrase "the words and meanings are perfectly clear," this refers to the sections from the Introductory Chapter to the Chapter on the Dharma Master.

Although the words and meanings of these three cycles of teaching are indeed perfectly clear and evident, they are presented through numerous metaphors; thus, while contemplating their actual substance, one perceives that it remains distant.
"Great. This term, in its literal meaning, appears to be a conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), a common discourse that is easy to see and easy to understand;
yet, when presented as a metaphorical exposition, it clarifies the causes and conditions of the one great matter (*ekamahā-kṛtya*) which is difficult to believe and difficult to comprehend.

From "Thus, above, I have extensively praised this sutra" onwards, he extols the sutra to clarify the excellence of the Dharma taught therein. From "Were it not for his great compassion" onwards, he extols the Buddha to clarify... [the excellence of the teacher].

The speaker is endowed with a sublime mind of compassion; that is to say, were it not for the Great Pity and vast salvation of Śākyamuni, who else could have spoken this wondrous Dharma, whose words and meanings are so perfectly refined?

Who else could have extracted those of the two vehicles who were stalled and unable to progress, or submerged and unable to ascend, drifting in the depths of the stream? Were it not for the ultimate compassionate heart of the Muni, who [could have done so]?
This analogy can be compared to the *udumbara* lotus described by Chen Weiyuan: it is utterly dark and lacks clarity;

it is one of delusion rather than awakening, a being who has lost their true nature (the term "sinking in the stream" refers to those of the Two Vehicles, as they are submerged in the flow toward minor fruits;

How profoundly moving! To explain this sutra: from the Han to the Tang dynasties, a period of over six hundred years elapsed—how long that time was!
In total, across all the scriptural collections, there were over four thousand fascicles of sutras, vinayas, and śāstras—how vast that body of Dharma was!
Yet among people, no other sutra was as widely upheld as this one; it alone was maintained for such a long duration and with such great vigor.
This is verified as the great compassion and ultimate heart of pity of the Buddha’s empowerment.

For over six hundred years, it has illuminated the previous three hundred-odd years, clarifying that the Tang was distinct from the Jin. That the practice of upholding [the teachings] flourished most intensely must correspond to what was revered and esteemed in earlier times;
thus, it cannot be considered spurious. Having already extensively praised the Buddha above, one will likewise extensively praise him below.

I praise these monastics and laypeople for possessing the wondrous quality of having their faculties and the teaching harmoniously accord; they have heard [the Dharma] and deeply revered it. To clarify what has preceded this:

"opening up transformation" constitutes the teaching (*jiao*), while "having the conditions to guide the mind" constitutes the faculty (*ji*). This refers to the mutual striking and meeting, the convergence of cause and response.

It means that in the past, when the Buddha was in the world and personally preached this sutra, there were still many who felt resentment and jealousy, such that five thousand people withdrew from their seats. Now, the Buddha...

I have therefore humbly and respectfully placed myself at the forefront, weaving together the threads of the entire tapestry, with its myriad billions of warp and woof.

Having been thus selected, the author of this preface considers that he knows the capacities [of others] and that his teachings accord with them; furthermore, those who heard [the teachings] and held him in deep reverence have all passed away.

Placing this preface before the scripture is like using a loom’s shuttle to pull the threads together, so that people may see the preface and thereby understand the scripture;

through the scripture, they may attain awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. May they thus be able to purify their six sense faculties early on, rather than waiting until it is too late to look up to and revere the Compassionate Honored One Maitreya, receiving the prediction of Buddhahood beneath the Dragon Flower Tree at that magnificent and sublime assembly, and swiftly accomplishing the four virtues.

Without delay, one proceeds directly toward the blissful land of the *sadaśāntaprabhāsvara* (Eternally Quiescent Light), realizing the profound principle of the *ekayāna-satyalakṣaṇa* (the True Aspect of the One Vehicle).

[To achieve this,] one should early on purify the six sense faculties, as explained in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" and the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Despising. Looking up to the compassionate Honored One, the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" states:

Maitreya Bodhisattva possesses the thirty-two marks [of a great man]."

Surrounded by a great assembly of Bodhisattvas, and amidst hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial maidens as his retinue, he was born therein. Regarding the phrase "a magnificent assembly" (*jiāhuì*): according to the *Yìwén*, "hēng" (亨) signifies a "magnificent gathering.

As for the "moistening text," the four virtues (*sìdé*)—according to the old commentaries—were explained as permanence, bliss, self, and purity. and fourth, generating the mind to save all sentient beings. This is considered more appropriate. Since the introduction has already extensively praised the Triple Gem, it proceeds to the "Chapter on Exhortation to Resolve" of Samantabhadra.
