"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, if there should be a woman who hears this sutra and practices according to its teachings, at the end of her life here, she will immediately go to the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Anala-loka*), to the dwelling place of Amitābha Buddha surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas, and be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne.

This is what is meant. As for "incapable of being burned by fire or swept away by water," O Xuanyou, such is the merit of yours; with the exception of the Tathāgata, none among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even the wisdom of the bodhisattvas can compare to it.

"In meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there is none who can equal you. By this standard, if a single woman upholds a sūtra, her merit shall surpass that of the multitudes of the Three Vehicles; how could this not be a profound principle?"

"To propagate and extol [this teaching] boundlessly, so as to perpetuate it for all posterity"—thus concludes the title of the preface. The author of the preface states that he has composed this introductory discourse;

though his person is humble and his words insignificant, they are like a handful of soil aiding Mount Tai or a ladle of water benefiting the vast ocean, such that one can never exhaustively fathom the merit of the Sūtra.

It is but one ten-thousandth part. I only wish that by means of this preface, this sutra may be perpetually transmitted to future generations, manifesting my humble sincerity in protecting the Dharma for even a single moment.
The phrase "yúnrě" (云爾) refers to what is stated in the preface, meaning it is exactly so, precisely so.

Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
*The Key to Understanding the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
The four characters "Miao deng" (The Wondrous [Lotus]) by the current abbot of Huguojin'gang Monastery, Ruyu, constitute the "signified" (*vācya*).
The scripture itself is the "signifier" (*vācaka*). Regarding the title consisting of the dharma and the metaphor, the explanation of their meaning has been seen previously.
The Introduction, Chapter One of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This chapter title is established based on the title of the sutra. As for the practice of attaching each chapter title to the name of the sutra title:

the sutra title serves as the general designation, while the chapter titles serve as the specific designations. Although the chapters each have their own thematic groupings, they are collectively subsumed under the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Therefore, this sūtra consists of twenty-eight chapters, which, according to the standard practice, are divided into three parts. The first chapter, the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta), constitutes the introductory section (nidāna-bhāga).

From the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya) to the "Chapter on Never Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta), comprising nineteen chapters, constitutes the main body of the teaching (saddharma-bhāga).

From the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers" (Tathāgatarddhy-abhisamskāra) to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" (Samantabhadrotsāhana), comprising eight chapters, constitutes the dissemination section (pariṇāmana-bhāga). Within the single chapter of the introductory section, there are both general and specific aspects.

Thus have I heard. [The assembly] proceeded until each had paid homage at the Buddha’s feet and withdrawn to sit on one side; this constitutes the general introduction (*pūrvayoga*), a format common to all sūtras.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly. [The Buddha] arrived so that he might sever and exhaust [the afflictions] for their sake, leaving nothing remaining;
this constitutes the specific introduction (*nidāna*). Although it is called the introductory section, it specifically sets forth the causes and conditions for the inception of this sūtra.
The core teaching and its dissemination—its great significance is truly exhausted here.

As for the titles of the various chapters, only the "Chapter on the Original Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" and the "Chapter on Devadatta" were spoken by the Buddha himself; the others were perhaps added by the translators.

This allows those who read, recite, and uphold the sutra to understand the great significance of each individual chapter upon seeing its title. As for the "Introductory Chapter," it sets forth [the narrative].

This is the source and foundation for initiating the teaching. It clarifies who spoke this sutra, in what location it was spoken, for whom it was spoken, on account of what matter it was spoken, and what fruit or retribution results from its being spoken. Therefore, it is called the "Preface Chapter" (*nidāna-varga*).
(The *Madhyama Āgama* states that *varga* is translated here as "chapter" [*pin*]. Tiantai says: "When categories of meaning are gathered together, it is called a chapter.")
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling... [omitted] ...having exhausted all fetters of existence, he attained mastery of mind.

This is called the "Preface of Certification and Faith. That is to say, all sutras contain such a sequence of phrases and words that enable people to realize and enter the Dharmakāya, because they engender faith in the Three Jewels.
Regarding the term "thus" (*evam*), according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it serves for the purpose of faith.
This is the accomplishment. The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma can be entered through faith; with faith one says, "It is so," and without faith one says, "It is not so.
Therefore, among the five stages, the stage of faith occupies the first. Among the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith is likewise the foremost.
Prior to the arising of faith, there is no dharma superior to it. Based upon this foundation of faith, the stages of understanding, practice, and realization are first established.

Liu Qiu said: "When the Sage preaches the Dharma, he does so only to manifest Suchness (tathatā). Since only Suchness is what is true, it is called 'Thus' (evam). 'I have heard' (evaṃ mayā śrutam) refers to the accomplishment of hearing.
'I' is the conventional designation for the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), namely Ānanda; 'hearing' refers to the consciousness produced by the faculty of the ear."
Setting aside the specific to follow the general, it says, "I heard. This combines with the preceding "Thus" (*evam*) to serve as a term for pointing to the Dharma;
thus, it means: "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha. Now, there are four kinds of "self": first, the self of the universal conceptualization of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

There are four types of "self": first, the self of the non-Buddhist *puruṣa*; second, the provisional self of followers of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; third, the true self of the *dharmakāya*; and fourth, [the aforementioned].
Here, it is distinguished from the others; thus it is called a "provisional name. It follows worldly convention for the sake of guiding sentient beings, and is designated as "self" accordingly.
Those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools differ in their explanations regarding hearing. Some say it is the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*); some say it is the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*);

and some say it is the conjunction of the faculty and consciousness. Here, we follow the latter view. A question is raised: since it is said that the ear-faculty gives rise to consciousness, one should properly say "the ear hears."
"What do you mean by 'I hear'? He replied, "The ear is but a specific part of the six sense organs, whereas the 'self' (ātman) is the master of the entire body.
By setting aside the specific ear and following the general 'self,' one says 'I hear. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In this land, the true essence of the teaching..."

"Purity lies in hearing. If one wishes to attain samādhi, it is truly through entering via hearing. Thus, the single character "hearing" (wen) constitutes the teaching-body (dharmakāya) of this Sahā world;
for this reason, it is placed at the beginning of all sutras. Regarding the phrase "at one time": this refers to the perfection of time.

Because the teacher and disciple have met and the exposition and listening have reached their conclusion, it is called "one time," without being restricted by the seasons of spring, summer, autumn, or winter.
At times such as the hours of Zi, Wu, Mao, and You, because the Buddha’s forty-nine years of teaching the Dharma constitute, in total, a single great period of time, the term "Buddha" (in full:

*buddha*)—which here means "the Awakened One"—refers to one who has awakened himself and awakened others, whose practice of awakening is perfected, and who is thus the Lord of the Dharma for preaching this sutra.
This is the "Lord Accomplishment" (*nātha-siddhi*) among the six types of accomplishments; this is the explanation.

"Kāśyapa" refers to Kāśyapa-Munīndra Buddha. "Dwells" (*viharati*) is one of the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*). From the perspective of the agent who dwells, "dwelling" belongs to the Buddha;

from the perspective of the location where one dwells, "dwelling" belongs to places such as Rājagṛha. Furthermore, these few phrases were spoken when Ānanda inquired of the Buddha, shortly before his parinirvāṇa, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras.
The Buddha commanded that the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) be placed there.

"This is what I have heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in such-and-such a place. This serves to let future generations know that the Buddha-dharma has its source and origin, and is not something that can be fabricated by worldly people.
First, it cuts off doubt; second, it quells dispute; third, it distinguishes the heterodox.
Because these three benefits exist, the Buddha commanded that this be placed at the beginning of the sutras. Regarding "cutting off doubt": when Ānanda ascended the seat, his [physical] marks...
"It is excellent, like the Buddha. The assembly gave rise to three doubts: first, the doubt that the Buddha had arisen again; second, the doubt that a Buddha from another direction had come;
and third, the doubt that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood. When these words were spoken, the three doubts were immediately extinguished. Regarding "extinguishing disputes":

this means that one does not say, "I heard this from the Buddha," for if one claims it was one's own composition, then disputes will arise. Regarding "discerning the heterodox": [this refers to distinguishing the true teaching from false doctrines].
This means that at the beginning of the heterodox scriptures of the non-Buddhists, the two characters "A-yu" are always placed; "A" signifies non-existence, and "Yu" signifies existence.
The non-Buddhists claim that although the myriad phenomena are numerous, they do not transcend the auspiciousness of existence and non-existence. The Buddha-dharma is different from theirs.

Therefore, it is said that this excludes heterodox views (this phrase was added to supplement the absence of the old commentary). Regarding "Rājagṛha" and so forth: this refers to the perfection of the location.
In the past, King Bimbisāra and his thousand sons together established their capital there as a residence, hence it is named Rājagṛha (King’s Abode).
It is the kingdom of Magadha; its king is Ajātaśatru. Gṛdhrakūṭa means "Vulture Peak"; the explanation is found in the previous preface. This is where the Buddha [dwelt].
The place of residence where this sutra was preached is first a city and later a mountain; it is the honored land of the Lord of the Earth.
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus" refers to the perfection of the multitude. These are the individuals who shall receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood through this sutra.
Regarding the bhikṣus and arhats, their translations and exegeses according to other sutras need not be elaborated upon here; they shall be explained solely according to this present sutra.
"Great bhikṣus" (one phrase): this enumerates their number (in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, only "twelve hundred people" is enumerated).
"All" (downward) explains the reason for their being called "great. That is to say, they are already called bhikṣus; why then are they called "great"? It is because they are all arhats.

This is stated in contrast to the two thousand learners and non-learners (śaikṣa and aśaikṣa) mentioned below, in order to manifest that [the former] have not yet realized the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
A Great Arhat is merely called a "small bhikṣu" [in comparison]. One whose outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted has lost the fruits of the three realms;
one who is free from further afflictions (*kleśa*) has extinguished the causes of the four abodes. Those who equally leave the household life to become *saṃgha* are all disciples of the Buddha;
fundamentally, there is no distinction between great and small. It is only that those who have exhausted their outflows and are free from affliction are "great," while others are "small."

Regarding the phrase "attaining one's own benefit" and so forth: on the surface, it appears to praise virtue, but in reality, it covertly censures faults. This is because [such practitioners] are unwilling to share in the Bodhisattva’s self-benefit and benefit for others;
instead, they merely seek to extinguish within themselves the fetters and delusions of the three realms—namely, the views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana and kleśa-saṃyojana).

By causing the causes of the three realms to perish, they ensure that in the future they do not leak back into the pit of afflictions; thus, the fruits of the segmented existence (paricchinna-bhava) are lost. Three... [text fragment].
He clarifies the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Acting according to his heart's desire, he seeks only benefit and causes no harm; he is simply autonomous.

This "autonomy" refers to the autonomy of the mind, not the autonomy of a Bodhisattva. Since this sutra is about to bestow predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon those of the two vehicles who study the Bodhisattva path and resolve their minds on Great Awakening, there is a tone of restraint embedded within the praise of his virtues. Below, his name is revealed.
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya (and so on), up to these great arhats renowned by all.
In the Sanskrit language, *Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya* means "First-understood. *Mahā* means "Great. *Kāśyapa* means "Drinker of Light" (*Pītabhāsa*).
*Uruvilvā* refers to the "Wood-apple Grove" (*Bilva-vana*); he was named after the grove in which he resided. *Gayā* means "City."
The name is derived from where one dwells; for example, "Nadi" means river, so one who dwells by a river is named accordingly.
Śāriputra means "Son of Śārī. Mahāmaudgalyāyana means "Bean-Planter. Kātyāyana means "Ornamented. Aniruddha means "Free from Poverty.
Kapphiṇa means "Lunar Mansion (Kṛttikā). Gavāmpati means "Ruminator. Revata...
Nakṣatra is translated as "Star. Piṅgalavatsa is translated as "Vestiges of Past Habits.
Bakula is translated as "Fine Appearance. Mahākauṣṭhila is translated as "Great Thighs. Nanda is translated as "Joy. Sundarananda is translated as "Radiant Joy.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is translated as "Son of Maitrāyaṇī, the Full One. Subhūti is translated as "Born of Emptiness. Ānanda...
It is said: "O Ānanda," and "Rāhula is like a covering. These refer to the leaders of the twelve thousand [bodhisattvas]; hence the phrase "such as these.
Their names, virtues, and origins are manifold; they are fully described in other sūtras, so they are not cited here at length.
(This concludes the section on those who received the prediction [of enlightenment] through the three cycles of teaching.)
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
These are what are called *bhikṣus*, but they are not *mahā-bhikṣus*. Those who investigate the truth and sever delusions are called "those in training";

those for whom the truth is fully realized and delusions are exhausted are called "those beyond training. These two thousand persons were disciples of Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others who were themselves still in training.

The sons [of the Buddha]— namely, those who have attained the first and second fruits of the path (for the subsequent "Chapter on Bestowing the Prediction of Learners and Non-learners," see the appendix)—
and Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī, together with her retinue, also arrived.
The above refers to the male monastics; this refers to the female monastics. Mahāprajāpatī means "Great Love-Path" (Mahāprajāpatī);

she is also called the "Leader of the Nuns" and was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Yaśodharā means "Flower-Colored"; she was the Buddha’s consort during his lay life, and thus her name is coupled with that of the Buddha’s son, Rāhula, to designate them.
This introduction concerns the two assemblies who left the household life (serving as the basis for the record of their receiving predictions in the subsequent Chapter on Holding).
"Eighty thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas... [omitted] ...are able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.

Here, the number of the Bodhisattvas is first indicated, and their virtues are subsequently extolled. The reason why Bodhisattvas differ from those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) is that they seek enlightenment above while transforming beings below;
they cultivate both merit and wisdom and are fully endowed with the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). Regarding this—

Non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is great joy (*mahāmuditā*). Attaining *dhāraṇī* and eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and planting the roots of all virtues is great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
They are constantly praised by all Buddhas. To cultivate the body with loving-kindness and skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom is great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).
When worldly people attain a single name or rank, they feel joy at never losing it; how much more so for one who never regresses from *bodhi*!
Is it not because they do not rejoice? This is why the first stage (*bhūmi*) is named "Joyful" (*pramuditā*).
Furthermore, it can be known that Mañjuśrī and others, who are Bodhisattvas of the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*), have no regression from Bodhi and possess great joy.

When one pities the suffering of the poor and lowly in the world and seeks to rescue them with wealth and honor, there is nothing that exceeds what is occasional and limited in number. Since the Bodhisattva has already rejoiced for himself...
The family attained the dhāraṇī of total retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*). Furthermore, they joyfully acquired the eloquence of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

Throughout immeasurable eons, by means of their brilliant eloquence and skillful means, they turned the non-retrogressive bodhi they themselves held over to countless sentient beings, causing them to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. How could there be anything that surpasses the greatness of their compassionate vows?

How could one fail to attain non-retrogression for one's own benefit? How could one fail to turn toward non-retrogression for the benefit of others? Can those of the Two Vehicles act in such a manner?
When worldly people offer with a mind of renunciation to a single worthy or a single sage, their offerings are limited in number;

the merit of such renunciation does not exceed the pursuit of the minor fruits of the human and celestial realms. Yet, when a Bodhisattva renounces body and life to make offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands [of Buddhas], [the merit is boundless].
The Buddhas do not seek the karmic rewards of humans or devas; they only wish to plant the roots of all virtues under the presence of the Buddhas.
Thus, the greatness of their renunciation can be known. When worldly people receive praise from a king, a noble, or an elder, they still harbor attachment to it;
yet, through such kindness and non-violence, they may attain the wisdom of great beings. It is by means of this joy that Bodhisattvas [proceed].
The great power of the vow of compassionate equanimity is constantly praised by all Buddhas.

How could one not cultivate the body through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and thereby skillfully enter the Buddhas’ profound and immeasurable wisdom of reality? Regarding "attaining mastery over great wisdom" and so forth:
this refers to attaining *bodhi* through its causes and turning the wheel of Dharma, thereby benefiting oneself and others; thus, one penetrates great wisdom and reaches the other shore.
The other shore is itself bodhi. By making offerings to the Buddhas, one plants the root; by means of compassion, one cultivates the self;
and by means of wisdom, one delivers others. When there is such reality in benefiting oneself and others, there arises such a name.
Thus, his reputation is heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and he is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. Can those of the Two Vehicles do as he does?
Indeed. Joy and sorrow: wisdom encompasses these within merit; this clarifies the gift of Dharma. Renunciation and loving-kindness: merit encompasses these within wisdom;

this clarifies the gift of material wealth. Therefore, by taking the four immeasurable minds as the core of training, one gathers both the two adornments of merit and wisdom, as well as the six pāramitās. This is precisely what constitutes a bodhisattva as a "Great Bodhisattva."
Their names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva (through to) eighty thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, together with them. [The preceding section] praised their virtues; this [section] lists their names.

(This serves as the underlying basis for those who are suited to the teachings in each subsequent chapter. Tiantai said: "Śrāvakas have forms that have emerged from the net of worldly entanglements, and their traces are close to the Tathāgata;

they hear the Dharma as intimates, and thus are listed first. Deva and Mānuṣa beings have forms that differ and attire that is distinct; their traces do not consist of serving attendance; they hear the Dharma as outsiders, and thus are listed later. Bodhisattvas have forms that are not constrained by conventional decorum, and their traces have no fixed location; since they are neither the same as the laity nor different from [the Śrāvakas]," [they are placed in between].)

Regarding the Sangha, it is placed in the middle position between the first and last [of the Triple Gem], hence its placement in the center. "Mahā" signifies "Great," as explained extensively in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, together with his retinue of twelve thousand devaputras, arrived.

This introduction concerns the heavenly kings and the celestial hosts of the three realms. At that time, the various devas of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the various devas of the form realm (rūpadhātu)—the latter being referred to as "Sahā" [or "below"]—were present;
those of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) were few, because, lacking physical form, they were unable to hear the Dharma.
Śakra Devānām Indra: fully expressed as Śakrendra, this means "The Able One" (Nengzuo), because he is able to act as the lord of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Furthermore, there is a subordinate official of this "Able One" named Candra, who is the deity of the Moon Palace.
Samantagandha is the deity of the lunar palace; Ratnaprabha is the deity of the solar palace. These three sons of gods are the inner ministers of Śakra.
As for the Four Great Heavenly Kings, they are Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south, and Virūpākṣa in the west.
In the north is Vaiśravaṇa, who governs the four continents and serves as an external minister to Śakra. The fifth [heaven] is Paranirmitavaśavartin;
the sixth is Maheśvara’s Paranirmitavaśavartin. These, along with the Four Kings and Trāyastriṃśa, constitute the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
By mentioning the lowest and the highest, the two intermediate heavens of Yāma and Tuṣita are included. Sahā means "Endurance."
The Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) is divided into four levels. The First Dhyāna is the realm of the Lord of the Sahā World; Śikhin means "Crest" and refers to the Lord of the First Dhyāna Heaven.
*Prabhāsvara* means "Radiant Light" and refers to the Lord of the Second Dhyāna Heaven, who manifests through the light of his halo for the sake of teaching and transforming beings. The word "etc.
(*ādi*) encompasses the entirety of the Third and Fourth Dhyānas.
There were eight dragon kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues:
Nanda, translated as "Joy"; Upananda, translated as "Excellent Joy"—these two brothers are dragon kings;
Sāgara, translated as "Salt Sea"; Vāsuki, translated as "Many Heads"; and Takṣaka, translated as "Manifesting Poison," also known as...
Bahuvaktra means "Many-Tongued. Anavatapta means "Without Heat or Affliction," which is the name of a lake. Mahāmanasa means "Great-Body.

Utpala means "Blue Lotus," which is also the name of a lake. These eight dragon kings each obtained their names either due to their virtuous nature or their place of residence, as explained extensively in other commentaries.
There were four Kinnara kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
"Kinnara" means "doubtful deity"; they resemble humans but have horns on their heads, and those who see them doubt [their nature].
They are the musical deities of Śakra. They dwell on the Ten Treasure Mountains; whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, they manifest their forms and sing in the sky.
The various devas, having heard this, all came to listen to the Dharma; therefore, it is named "The Sublime Dharma" and so forth.
There were four gandharva kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
*Gandharva* means "one who travels by seeking fragrance. They are the deities who perform music for Śakra. Whenever Śakra is about to perform music, he first burns incense;
this deity dwells amidst mountains of ten kinds of jewels, and upon merely smelling the fragrance, he immediately arrives at Śakra’s abode to play music.
As for "music," it refers to acrobatic feats such as swinging from poles and tumbling; "musical sounds" refer to the rhythmic coordination of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments.
Regarding sound: those who excel in the "beautiful" [mode] toss it upward; those who excel in the "harmonious" [mode] join the rhythmic intervals.
There are four asura kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.

Asuras are called "Non-Gods" (*asura*). They are also called "The Ugly. Because they performed meritorious deeds while harboring anger during their causal stage, the fruit they experience is similar to that of the gods, yet it is not the same as the enjoyments of the gods;
thus they are called "Non-Gods. This is because the males are ugly while the females are beautiful.
Furthermore, it is said that Asura Vemacitra means "not upright"; Bala means "round"; Kharaskandha means "broad-shouldered";
Vemacitra means "pure-minded"; and Rāhu means "obscuration. When he battles with Śakra, he obscures the sun and moon.
If the people of Jambudvīpa perform many good deeds, Śakra is victorious; if they perform many evil deeds, the Asuras are victorious.
The reason the Four Heavenly Kings constantly observe the good and evil in the human realm is that they wish for the heavens to prevail.
There are four Garuḍa kings, each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
The *garuḍa* is called the Golden-Winged Bird (*suvarṇapakṣa*). Its wings are golden in color; when both are spread wide, they span three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
By fanning them open, it parts the waters of the ocean to seize dragons as food. It subdues all other species, and is thus called "of Great Majestic Virtue" (*mahā-tejas*).

Its form exceeds that of all other species, and is thus called "of Great Body" (*mahākāya*). Having eaten its fill of dragons, it is thus called "Greatly Satiated" (*mahā-pūrṇa*). Upon its neck there is...
Because it is a *maṇi* jewel, it is called "as one wishes" (*yathā-manas*). From the heavens down to this world, they are named the Eight Divisions (*aṣṭa-nikāya*).

Among them, two divisions—yakṣas and mahoragas—are somewhat lacking. Yakṣas are called "swift ghosts"; they are a class that feeds on humans and are subsumed under the jurisdiction of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Mahoragas are called "great serpent deities"; they are subsumed among the eight Dragon Kings (*nāgarāja*).
Within these divisions, they are not mentioned separately. Those with many precepts and few vehicles serve as the retinues of the devas.
Those with urgent pursuit of the vehicle but laxity in precepts serve as the retinues of the other seven classes. Those with both urgency in vehicle and precepts are Bodhisattvas.

Those with both laxity in vehicle and precepts fall into the three miserable realms. All who are kings among these eight classes are the emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Bodhisattvas through the power of their great vows. Thus it is said:

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). These serve for the purpose of conversion (as a celebration when Śāriputra later receives his prediction, as well as in the "Dharma Master" chapter regarding the bestowal of the extensive prediction).
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, was present together with several hundreds of thousands of followers.
"Vaidehī" means she who contemplates; she was the wife of King Bimbisāra. "Ajātaśatru" means he who has no enemy, and is also called "Unborn Enemy";
he was the king of Rājagṛha. Initially, while Vaidehī was pregnant with King Ajātaśatru, [the physiognomist] observed his marks...
The master’s divination stated: "Once this child is born, he will certainly harm his parents. The King believed these words;

as soon as Ajātaśatru was born, the King ordered him to be struck down and killed, but only one finger was damaged, hence he was named Aṅgulimāla (the Fingerless). Palace attendants raised him in secret and called him Sudarśana (Good Vision).

Later, he indeed harmed his parents just as the physiognomist had predicted, and thus he was also known as Ajātaśatru (Unborn Enemy). He subsequently received the Buddha's teaching and transformation.

Realizing his error, he repented; one [part] fell into hell, while another was immediately reborn in the heavens. (The *Wenju* quotes the *Puchao jing*, stating that King Bimbisāra repented before Mañjuśrī.)

Having attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), at the end of his life he entered the Piñchila hell; entering and exiting it immediately, he was reborn in a buddha-field above. When Maitreya appears, he will be named Acala Bodhisattva and later shall become a buddha, titled Śuddhaloka Tathāgata.

According to the nineteenth and twentieth fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, this was due to receiving the Buddha’s transformative teaching, whereby he realized his error, repented, and gave rise to the bodhicitta, thereby being born in heaven.
Each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.

This refers to the fourfold assembly, the eight classes of beings, and others—regardless of whether they were monastics or laypeople—all of whom bowed their heads to the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side to await his preaching of the Dharma.
"On one side" means that when the Buddha preaches the Dharma among the assembly, there is no distinction between front and back.

Those on both sides all see the face of the Buddha; therefore, it is said here that there is "one face. What follows below speaks of "surrounding," meaning they surround him from the front, back, left, right, and one face.
The explanation of the general introduction is complete. Below is the explanation of the specific introduction. The specific introduction consists of three sections.
This is the expedient means for revealing, showing, causing to awaken to, and entering into the one great causal condition.
It begins from "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly" and ends with "with joy, they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with single-mindedness.

This is because the Buddha was about to bestow the prediction of Buddhahood upon those of the two vehicles; fearing that they might rest content with the minor fruits and remain deluded regarding the Great Way.

Therefore, he first preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, which is called "the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas," intending for those of the Two Vehicles to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Furthermore, his entry into the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings was for the sake of the followers of the Two Vehicles;
it was the Buddha entering samādhi to manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. First he preached the sūtra, and subsequently he entered meditative concentration. From—
Now, the time has come to reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is what is meant by "first moving through meditative concentration.
From the point when the Buddha first emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, up until the construction of the seven-jeweled stūpa with the Buddha’s relics,

this was the Buddha’s manifestation of the Dharma in its full perfection by emitting light from the white tuft between his eyebrows— specifically because he saw that those of the two vehicles did not understand how to move within meditative concentration.

The elements, phenomena, and the arising of characteristics constitute the beginning and end of the Buddha. It is shown that every person inherently possesses the "True Person of No Rank," who dwells at the gateway of the six sense organs, emitting light and shaking the earth day and night;
this is intended for those of the Two Vehicles who wish to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Third, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva arose" until the end of the chapter where Mañjuśrī says,

"The Buddha shall eliminate and sever [these obstacles] so that they are exhausted without remainder," it is shown that the Buddha, seeing that the faculties of those of the two vehicles were dull and they did not awaken,
secretly dispatched two people to seek out the impoverished son. He fully recounted the aforementioned matters, desiring that those of the two vehicles enter into the knowledge of the Buddha.
Those who have seen it [the light] know this: while in samādhi, he emitted light, and the two Great Beings engaged in further dialogue.
This represents the "subsequent extraction by wisdom" from the time of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) until the present moment.

Since those of the Two Vehicles cannot enter therein, our World-Honored One laboriously arose with composure from his samādhi and delivered these words of skillful means; thus begins the section on the True Doctrine (*samyak-artha-bhāga*).
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly... [until] ...with joy they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with single-minded attention.
From "At that time" onwards, the text follows the preceding passage to describe how the Buddha had previously preached sutras without distinguishing between those of the two vehicles;

however, on this day, he preaches a Mahāyāna sutra for the sake of the bodhisattvas, thereby distinguishing them from those of the two vehicles. It is titled "The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings. Thus:
This reveals that the meanings previously heard by those of the Two Vehicles are all limited. The passage beginning with "teaching the bodhisattvas" asks:
"What is the Great Vehicle? because it is the teaching of the Dharma for bodhisattvas. It asks: "Why is it called the 'Teaching of Infinite Meanings'?
because it is that which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Thus, within this "Expedient Means" chapter, there exists the gate of wisdom that is difficult [to fathom].

This is the skillful wisdom for entering [the path] by resolving difficulties (according to the *Awakening of Faith*, there are three great meanings: essence, characteristics, and function; as for the "vehicle," it has two meanings:
that which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden, and that which all Bodhisattvas shall ride). The Buddha spoke thus because he wished to stir the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*).
When those of the Two Vehicles remained unmoved, their intention was: "Since this teaches the Bodhisattvas, what does it have to do with me? Therefore, after the Buddha had preached this sutra...

"Or there may be those who practice giving" and below provides a detailed explanation of the seven treasures such as gold and silver, as well as male and female slaves; it includes the giving of both sentient and insentient things.
From the small, such as carriages, to the large, such as palanquins and litters, one gives both light and heavy items. This is done with a mind of joy as the cause.
Taking the objects bestowed as conditions, one simply dedicates them toward the Buddha-way. "May I obtain... and so forth are the words of dedication;

this means that while worldly material gifts such as the seven treasures may be limited, one prays to attain the supramundane Mahāyāna, which is praised by all Buddhas as the foremost within the three realms.
Regarding the term "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*), it refers to the ten dedications in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
This is because it was previously also called the "Ten Vows. Regarding the phrase "or there may be bodhisattvas" and so forth:

this means that one may see bodhisattvas who do not merely give vehicles and the like, but further give the four horses that draw such vehicles, as well as the decorative railings and so forth for palanquins and carriages.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "again seeing bodhisattvas" and so forth: this means that they do not merely give external things such as chariots and horses.
Furthermore, one gives internal wealth such as the body, flesh, hands, and feet, which are extremely difficult to relinquish.
Just as our Śākyamuni Buddha gave his head for the sake of King Candraprabha, and the Seer Sunetra gave his eyes, they all joyfully delighted in giving;
had it not been for their true faith and understanding, this would have been impossible. From the passage on Mañjuśrī below, [the text] praises various characteristics in a single line.
That is to say, by means of the Buddha’s light, one sees bodhisattvas in those many lands;
some appear in the guise of kings and preach the Buddha-way while practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), relinquishing both internal and external wealth;

others take on the appearance of monks, shaving their hair and beards and donning the dharma robes, thereby practicing patience (*kṣānti*) and maintaining the precepts (*śīla*). (This refers to the case of King Wonderful Adornment. A question is asked: "Why shave the hair and beard?"
It is appropriate to don the Dharma robes and practice the observance of the precepts. Why is it called "the perfection of patience" (kṣānti-pāramitā)? The answer is:

because the subsequent text states that the Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and forbearance. Or, as seen below in the passage beginning with "or seeing the Bodhisattva," it means that the Bodhisattva, while remaining a householder, manifests the appearance of one who has left the home life.
(Question: Above, it was stated that shaving the hair and so forth constitutes being a bhikṣu; why then do you speak of this again? (Answer: As for what was said above...
"Possessing the status of a bhikṣu" is the point that clarifies the meaning of the name. "Frequenting secluded places while reciting the sūtras" is the mark of being widely learned (*bahuśruta*).
"Being courageous" is the mark of diligence (*vīrya*). Furthermore, "seeing the departure from desire" is the mark of seeking meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

"Deeply cultivating the lower [stages]" means that by attaining supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one manifests the appearances of a thousand transformations and myriad changes.

Furthermore, "seeing the Bodhisattvas in tranquil meditation (*dhyāna*)" and so forth refers to the appearance of performing Buddha-works (*buddhakārya*) through sound while in a state of tranquil meditation, as a response to the Buddha’s grace and virtue.
"Again seeing the Bodhisattvas" and so forth indicates that because their wisdom is profound, they are able to inquire.
The sublime Dharma of all Buddhas is firm in resolve; thus, having heard it throughout billions of eons, one receives and upholds it.
All of these are the characteristics of wisdom. The above verses describe the characteristics of self-benefit.

Furthermore, the line "seeing the Buddha-sons with meditative concentration and wisdom equal" describes the characteristics of benefiting others. This means that because Bodhisattvas have deeply cultivated meditative concentration, they...
Concentration is fully perfected through deep wisdom and firm resolve; being able to inquire and uphold [the teachings], wisdom is fully perfected.

When concentration is perfected, the essential principle of one's own nature is penetrated; when wisdom is perfected, one receives the lineage of the teacher’s transmission. Thus, within, one does not lose oneself.
Only when one does not lead others astray externally can one draw near analogies and preach the Dharma for the multitude using immeasurable parables to benefit them.
"Rejoicing" refers to preaching the Dharma for the multitude; this is spoken in terms of those with middling and inferior faculties who rejoice in the teaching of the Dharma.

"Transforming all bodhisattvas" refers to those of the supreme One Vehicle. Since bodhisattvas are already able to observe the capacities of beings and preach the Dharma accordingly, [they are so described].

This refers to striking the Dharma drum prior to destroying the demonic armies. Furthermore, regarding the passage "seeing the Bodhisattva in profound stillness" and so forth, it means that whether the Bodhisattva moves or remains still, whether speaking or remaining silent, everything is non-other than Buddha-work. When speaking with wisdom, it is sharp and effective; thus, one strikes the Dharma drum.
Thus he destroys the armies of Māra. As for "steadfast silence," it means that even when gods and nāgas pay him homage, he does not take pleasure in it.

Furthermore, regarding the passage on seeing the Bodhisattva dwelling in the forest and so forth: this means that because the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), he is able to dwell in the forest while emitting light, rescuing beings in the hells from suffering, and suddenly causing them to enter the Buddha-way. This is the verse on the faith in causes and conditions.
[The commentary] explains: "To represent [the perfections] through their general characteristics, one uses only the single perfection of *dāna* (giving) as a symbol;

yet, to describe their specific manifestations, one employs all six perfections. Otherwise, there would be no way to perceive their various distinct forms. Maitreya may indeed be called one who asks well, for his inquiry is orderly and systematic.
Master Kumārajīva may indeed be called one who translates well, for he wields his chisel with such mastery that it moves like the wind without confusion. Otherwise, the scripture...
The literary talent [of the commentator] first mentions "giving" (*dāna*), and again says "giving"; first mentions "vehicles," and again says "precious chariots.

One sees only the redundancy, the confusion, and the inversion of the words. Now, by following the prose commentary (*gadya*) and carefully examining the verse (*śloka*), one finally realizes how marvelous it is:
the sacred scripture contains not a single superfluous word, nor a single phrase that is not virtuous. Why have the masters of antiquity not [noticed this]?
Have you carefully examined [the teachings] and then, following your own whims, falsely engaged in speculative interpretation?
Furthermore, I see that the sons of the Buddha have never slept [in this manner], seeking the unsurpassed path through this sublime wisdom.

This verse, from the prose section, addresses the single phrase "practicing the bodhisattva path" by dividing it into the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Each perfection concludes with the phrase "the path of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, seeing the sons of the Buddha" refers to the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

The reason the six perfections take vigor as their foremost is that it serves as a warning to those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who lack vigor and merely contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, while neglecting the bodhisattva path.
The Dharma consists of sporting in supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-lands, and bringing sentient beings to maturity, without giving rise to even a single thought of attachment or delight.
This sutra is the essential transmission for those of the Two Vehicles, a manifest record of the ten titles of a Buddha and the adornment of his lands and kalpas;
therefore, through diligence, one’s mind is stirred. Thus, he later bestowed a prediction upon Ānanda, saying: "I..."

Ānanda and I simultaneously resolved our minds for enlightenment at the time of the Buddha Śūnyarāja. Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning, whereas I always applied myself with diligent vigor;
therefore, I have already attained Buddhahood, while Ānanda has protected and upheld my Dharma without ever sleeping, thereby removing dullness and distraction.
He practiced walking meditation in the groves to collect right mindfulness and diligently sought the path of the Buddha. Not...
They seek the lesser fruits. Furthermore, seeing those who possess the full precepts, they apply themselves to the *śīlapāramitā*. Their deportment is without defect;
their marks of morality (*śīlākāra*) are complete. Pure as a precious jewel, the nature of their morality is pure like a gem, capable of clarifying the muddy dregs of broken precepts.
Furthermore, seeing sons of the Buddha who abide in the power of patience, they apply themselves to the *kṣāntipāramitā*.
Those with overweening pride may insult them verbally, reviling them with harsh abuse, as the later text describes:
"These ignorant bhikṣus," and so forth. Or they may insult them physically, beating them;

"beating" (*chui*) refers to striking indiscriminately with objects, while "topping" (*ding*) refers to piercing directly with a staff, as described in the later text. Or they may use sticks, wood, tiles, or stones...
They strike and cast them down; even to the point of being repeatedly seen expelled and banished from the stūpas and monasteries—this is what they do.

That one can endure all of this is the mark of a hero or a noble man. To glare with murderous intent and seek immediate revenge, or to be subjected to flogging and humiliation in the marketplace, is what a gentleman finds shameful.
Now, that the Bodhisattva can endure all of this is for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way. How could the Buddha harbor anger or resentment? And yet, he desires [to teach].
Does this not repay the grievance of those who treat one with violence? Such is the power of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, seeing that the Bodhisattva has abandoned frivolous laughter reveals his diligent cultivation of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). When frivolous laughter is abandoned, one’s own mind becomes concentrated;
when foolish companions are abandoned, external circumstances do not disturb it. Those close to wisdom seek the means to attain concentration and enter [into it].
The mountain forests provide the opportunity to eliminate distracted thoughts; thus, one can maintain focused mindfulness for hundreds of thousands of millions of years without wavering.
This is not like the two vehicles' delight in the extinction samādhi of solitary tranquility, but rather the desire to attain the Buddha-way.

If one sees a bodhisattva providing fine delicacies and food and drink, this is the diligent practice of the *dāna-pāramitā*. Among all forms of giving, *dāna* is most urgent; among these, food and drink are primary.
When illness arises from food and drink, then medicinal decoctions become urgent. For cold and heat, clothing is required;
thus, one gives away famous garments and superior robes worth ten million taels of gold. Even if such famous garments are worth ten million, they are still wearable.
If it has a price, it seems easy to give away; however, if it is a priceless robe, even its value is difficult to determine, making its relinquishment difficult.

When a Bodhisattva wishes to fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they do not begrudge anything when bestowing upon the Buddha and the Sangha, as seen in the later passage where Ajita-akṣaya (Unfailing Intent) gives the pearl necklace and various precious ornaments from his own neck to offer to Avalokiteśvara. This is an example of that.
For the hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of precious sandalwood palaces, they do not require ordinary materials; they provide them with palaces made of precious sandalwood.
For the couches required for sitting and reclining, they do not require coarse or inferior ones; they provide them with various exquisite bedding and furnishings.
Thus the four requisites are fully provided. If there are no gardens or ponds for the sake of sporting in the ground of samādhi, then they are likewise not required.

It is the sandalwood that fulfills all wishes. Therefore, the Bodhisattva further gives away gardens with flourishing flowers and fruits, bathing pools with flowing springs and pure water—giving such various and subtle things with joy, seeking not the rewards of fortune among humans or devas, but only the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
Or there may be Bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma of quiescent extinction.
One exerts oneself in the *prajñāpāramitā*. As for the benefit to others through *prajñā*, one teaches and instructs countless sentient beings in various ways without weariness.
As for the benefit to oneself through *prajñā*, one contemplates that the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without dual characteristics, being like empty space;

thus one realizes the two emptinesses of self and phenomena, as well as the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional. Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, seeing the sons of the Buddha" onwards is [the section on] *prajñā*.

Not adhering to the two extremes, one achieves the non-emptiness of the emptiness of both self and phenomena. When one attains the wisdom of the Middle Way, this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In observing that the nature of all phenomena belongs to oneself, while the instruction and guidance of sentient beings belong to others, one reaches the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
Therein, the non-dual nature of all phenomena—self and other—is like space, vast and expansive.
It is signless (*animitta*). Since its nature is signless, how could the mind be attached? The wisdom that does not cling to the two extremes is called "sublime wisdom" (*prajñā*).

By means of this sublime wisdom, one seeks the unsurpassed path; thus, one will certainly attain Buddhahood. The verses concerning sentient beings, the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and the fourfold assembly are abbreviated.
The verses concerning the various causes and conditions, the characteristics of faith and understanding, and the practice of the Bodhisattvas are explained in detail.
Thus it is vast. The Buddha has already attained the Way; his merits cannot be fully described in words. Sentient beings have not yet attained Buddhahood;
the manifestations of their karmic suffering are likewise difficult to describe. Only the Bodhisattvas are those who seek the fruit of Buddhahood above and deliver sentient beings below.
It is upon them that the Buddhas rely to transmit the Dharma, and it is upon them that sentient beings rely to escape from suffering. Their burden—
The responsibility for bearing this is also grave. It is intended that those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) should study as Bodhisattvas;

therefore, they are alerted by this. Whether it be the conduct during the causal stage of our single Buddha Śākyamuni, who was so diligent in seeing the Buddhas and seeking the Dharma, or the conduct of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, who realized Buddhahood through seeking the Dharma—[it is for this purpose].

Such is their identity. This may be the practice of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bhaiṣajyarāja, and others, who, in accordance with the Buddha’s entrustment, uphold this sutra with such firm resolve. In the world there is no coming or going; in the realms there is no distance or nearness.
At one time, in a single assembly, within the luminous mind of the eternal quiescence of Vairocana for all sentient beings, there clearly and simultaneously manifests the Great Teaching of One Time.
How could there be anything more marvelous than this? For this reason, this sutra is the king among all sutras.
That which is seen within the light of the Buddha’s white tuft of hair is the Mahayana Bodhisattva of those many lands.

Such was the scene. [Question: Why does the Buddha’s light illuminate only eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction and not the other nine directions? [Answer: The east belongs to the trigram *Zhen*, which is the source of all movement.

The Buddha’s intention is for those of the Two Vehicles to abandon quiescence and move toward activity, to traverse from emptiness into the provisional, to enter [the realm of phenomena] as if stretching down a hand, to cultivate the six perfections to transform sentient beings, and to realize Great Nirvana.

Therefore, the light illuminates only the east, signifying that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are still within movement; amidst active function, he accomplishes the great causal conditions of the Bodhisattva path. Otherwise, everyone would merely emulate those of the Two Vehicles, seeking emptiness and realizing quiescence, leaving sentient beings without [a refuge].

[He asked: "Whom do you intend to save? Furthermore, the sunlight in the world mostly travels from the east to the west; since the Buddha’s light pertains to the supramundane Dharma, it moves contrary to worldly patterns and thus mostly shines from the west toward the east. Later, he beheld the jeweled stupa.

The multitude from the surging sands reaches down to the lower direction to transform the pure lands and assemble the Buddhas; this then extends universally throughout the ten directions. As the sutra says: "In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—wherever the light of the white tuft mark shines, it is likewise so. This is indeed the case.

When the Dharma assembly was nearing its conclusion, and the Buddha was about to entrust this sutra to Shangxing and others for its dissemination, he first manifested his supernatural powers. The colored light and the sound-light again illuminated the ten directions outside the three transformed pure lands.

Thereafter, within the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, time is not divided into three and space is not divided into ten; all together constitute the single, eternal *dharmadhātu* of tranquil light. As the sutra says: "At that time, the ten directions were unobstructed and pervasive, as if they were a single Buddha."

Regarding the "earth" [element]: it should be understood in this way that when the sūtras speak of one direction or the ten directions, each has its own sequential order and its own established textual phrasing; there is no need to force an interpretive correlation between them.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas (up to) who are like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.

This verse, based on the prose section, concerns seeing those many lands and Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa through the Buddha’s light, as well as seeing the construction of stūpas made of the seven precious jewels from the Buddha’s relics after those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa. This is the sixth matter.
This is the seventh matter. From the passage "Mañjuśrī" downward, the text does not follow the prose narrative;
instead, it versifies the events concerning the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, yet it only versifies those who make offerings to the *śarīra* after the Buddha’s extinction.

This was done by the translators so that the scriptural text would not be as rigid as a fixed peg, allowing for an inclusive interpretation. Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, seeing the sons of the Buddha" downward, it speaks of the abundance of stūpas, their number exceeding that of the Ganges.
"Sa" refers to the fact that because the lands and worlds are numerous, their adornments and decorations are infinite and boundless. Question:
Regarding the sixth matter above, it has already been stated that one makes offerings to the *śarīra* after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Why, then, is the seventh matter further described with the phrase "constructing various stūpas and temples," and so forth? Answer: The sixth matter merely mentions making offerings.
Regarding the veneration of the *śarīra*: when the Buddha’s physical remains were displayed for public worship immediately after his *parinirvāṇa*, no stūpas had yet been constructed.

This seventh point, concerning the construction of various stūpas and temples, refers to the period following the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*, when it was desired that the Buddha’s physical remains be concealed rather than left exposed, so that people might worship them only within stūpas.
It is a temple. Therefore, although there is a subsequent phrase regarding the offering of śarīra, it is not redundant; for those were one occasion and these are another.
Regarding the "precious stupa," the height of the stupa is stated as one yojana (forty *li*), and at five thousand yojanas, the height of that stupa would be two hundred thousand *li*.
"Vertical" refers to length (*zòng*); "horizontal" refers to breadth (*guǎng*).
"Perfectly square" means that its horizontal and vertical dimensions are equal at two thousand *yojanas* each, which amounts to a width and breadth of eighty thousand *li*.
This explains the height of the stūpa. Previously it was mentioned that there is "one stūpa";
here, by explaining its excellence, it further describes the many stūpas. Each stūpa is equipped with banners and bells; therefore, it says "each has a thousand. Within the banners and streamers...
Hanging [banners], they destroy the arrogance of material things and give rise to reverence. Bead nets interlace with curtains of dew;
when the sun shines, light is produced—how magnificent! They reflect and vyingly outshine one another. Precious bells hang all around the tiers;
moved by the wind, their sounds proclaim themselves—how harmoniously their resonance accords and converges! One beholds the wondrous splendor of the adorned stupa, which cannot [be fully described].
Sight and hearing have reached their limit. The various devas, nāgas, and spirits descend, saying that there is such a stūpa as this.
Spontaneously moved, the eight classes of devas and nāgas constantly offer worship with flowers, incense, music, and dance.
Thus, Maitreya again calls upon Mañjuśrī to conclude, declaring its sublime excellence: "The sons of the Buddha in those eighteen thousand worlds are just like this."
The purpose of adorning and embellishing stūpas and temples is fundamentally to make offerings to the śarīra, not to beautify the realm.
Nevertheless, it is not that the realm does not naturally become exceptionally sublime and extraordinary through the adornment of the stūpa—wondrous beyond thought and excellent beyond words.
This is what is meant by the saying: "When the mounds are leveled, the abysses are filled. It is like heaven.
Regarding the "King of Trees" and so forth: in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, to the northeast, there is a tree known as the *pārijāta*. This tree grows upon the summit of Mount Sumeru;

among all the trees in the human world, none surpass it in height and grandeur. Furthermore, because it is the object of the Emperor Śakra’s particular affection, it is called the "King of Heavenly Trees.
When its flowers bloom, the various devas gather around it to enjoy themselves in play. It is surrounded by a dense thicket.
They circumambulated it. Among them were devas, nāgas, humans, and spirits who made offerings to this stūpa and gave rise to profound reverence.

By means of a single ray of light from the Buddha, they beheld those many lands and the scenes of the offering of relics and the construction of stūpas and temples after the parinirvāṇa of various Buddhas—such as these were there (relics are called "body-bones"; stūpas and temples are called "square mounds").
"The Buddha emits a single ray of light, and we, along with the great assembly... we behold this and have attained what we have never before experienced.

From "The Buddha emits a single ray of light" onwards, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent section is introduced; that is to say, the Buddha merely emits a single ray of light, yet it is able to bring about this for us.

Seeing those eighteen thousand world-systems with their boundless, immeasurable, and variously exquisite features—the aforementioned seven matters—all were brought about by the power of the Buddhas' spiritual penetrations (*ṛddhi*) and wisdom. Having never seen such things even during the forty years prior, they are called "rare" (*āścarya*).
The emission of a single pure light below clearly illustrates this rarity. (Alternatively, it is explained that the Buddha emitted a single ray of light...)

It is capable of illuminating. "I and the assembly" refers to those people who, by relying on the light, are able to see. As for those eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction—regardless of how many *yojanas* they are from Mount Ling, or how high, thick, distant, or near they may be—it is said that "this realm is seen.

Later it says, "that realm is seen"; because of the illumination of the Buddha’s light, whether far or near, it is as if before one's eyes, such that the distinction between "this" and "that" is forgotten. It is like sentient beings who, being separated from external objects by a layer of paper or film, cannot see them.

The eyes that cannot see the five viscera through the skin distinguish self from other; yet the Buddha’s five eyes exhaustively perceive even the pure lands within a single mote of dust, and know the number of drops of rain as far as the world-systems beyond the sands of the Ganges.

Thus, even the eighteen thousand worlds are directly within the house of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—how could one distinguish between a mote of dust and a great matter? Therefore it is said, "seeing this land"; "land" refers to the realm perceived by the assembly.

Regarding the rare power and wisdom of the Buddhas: it means that the worlds are vast, high, and deep, numbering eighteen thousand, and are reckoned according to the causes and effects of sages and ordinary beings, as well as the duration of the kalpas and the ages of the environment and its inhabitants.

The causal conditions from beginning to end, and the various manifestations of faith and understanding, are manifold, immeasurable, and boundless. Yet, without shifting from this, one perceives that; there is no distinction between near and far. Without shifting from a single moment, one perceives many kalpas;

there is no distinction between past, present, and future. Buddha is Buddha; birth is birth; good is good and evil is evil; the holy is holy and the ordinary is ordinary; the hidden is hidden and the manifest is manifest; fruit is fruit and cause is cause; this is this and that is that.

Briefly stated, there is not the slightest moment when these are not seen simultaneously, nor is there the slightest confusion among them. Were it not for the two kinds of power—the divine and the cognitive—of the Buddhas, how could it be thus? Therefore, it is called "rare. Regarding the phrase "emitting a single pure light," it refers to the capacity to illuminate, which possesses distinct aspects.

This is the limit. As for "illuminating immeasurable lands," it means that the objects illuminated are immeasurable. Therefore, we say, "We have attained what we never had before; truly, it is unprecedented.

According to what is expounded in the sutra, outside the bodies, minds, and worlds currently before us, there truly exist boundless, peerless Buddha-dharmas, bodies, minds, lands, and retinues. It is simply because our Buddha-knowledge and vision have not yet opened that we remain deluded and distressed, failing to awaken and enter [this realization].
"O Son of the Buddha Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly" (up to) "I gaze upon you, O Benevolent One; please tell me what [you have said].
From the initial verses down to the preceding section, all serve to express the doubts of Maitreya alone.
This corresponds to the prose passage from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya had this thought" up to the text ending with "I shall now ask. This...
And regarding the preceding section: the verse has Maitreya expressing his doubts on behalf of the great assembly.
This corresponds to the prose passage beginning with "At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs arose" and ending with "all saw the adornments of that Buddha-land.
Therefore, at the beginning of the preceding verses, it says: "I dwell here," next: "I see that land," and thirdly: "I see the various kings."

All [the speakers] refer to themselves as "I. Having completed the seven matters observed in the preceding section, and wishing to seek an answer to dispel their doubts, they include the great assembly, saying, "I and the assembly. Initially, they referred to themselves by including others;
now, however, they specifically represent the assembly to make their request. Therefore, the text refers to them as "sons of the Buddha."
The "extraordinary vows" resolve the doubts of the multitude. Regarding the phrase "the fourfold assembly looks up with joy," this follows from the preceding text;
it refers to the six auspicious omens and the seven matters. If these were things that had occurred previously, people would not have doubted.

Because they doubted, [the Buddha] thought, "I, Maitreya, can also resolve these for the multitude. This is because such things had never occurred before, yet now they are suddenly seen. Thus, the fourfold assembly...
Therefore, those who look up to you with admiration and those who gaze upon me each give rise to doubt, wondering:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One now emit this light from between his eyebrows, illuminating distant realms, the beginning and end of Buddhas, and the phenomena of the dharma-realm?
Since I am unable to resolve these doubts for the assembly, and the assembly does not dare to request it of you, I—[therefore speak].

"Although this is requested on behalf of the assembly, it is in truth requested for oneself as well. If you, O Benevolent One, resolve my doubts, then the doubts of the assembly will naturally be resolved.
Therefore it is said: 'The Son of the Buddha answers in a timely manner, resolving doubts and bringing joy.

To answer 'in a timely manner' means that, like the seasonal growth of living things which responds to the proper time without delay, one seeks a prompt response. As for the phrase 'What benefit does it provide? and so forth, this is the actual explanation."
Their doubt was this: "When the Buddha usually preaches the sutras, he does not enter meditative absorption; when he enters absorption, flowers do not rain down;

when flowers rain down, the earth does not tremble; when the earth trembles, he does not emit light; and when he emits light, such a multitude of wondrous phenomena has never before been seen within that light.
Now the Buddha acts in this way—shaking heaven and moving the earth, emitting light and manifesting auspicious omens—is this truly so?"
What benefit for sentient beings is there such that you first expound this radiance?

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), does this mean that by now manifesting this radiance, you intend to clarify the sublime Dharma obtained when the Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the tree? Or is it for the sake of... [granting]...?
"Have the various great bodhisattvas been granted the prediction of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becoming buddhas? [The Buddha replied:
"From the passage 'He showed them the various buddha-fields' onwards, it means that if the Buddha were to explain the Dharma obtained at the site of enlightenment, he has already explained it;
if he were to grant the predictions of buddhahood to the various great bodhisattvas, he has also previously granted those predictions. [In this assembly,] they have not seen [anything new]."
Within the light from between the Buddha’s eyebrows, he revealed eighteen thousand buddha-fields adorned with various jewels and utterly pure;

yet, I had never before seen so many Buddhas within those fields. Now, as he reveals these lands and manifests these Buddhas, I know for certain that this is not due to minor causes or conditions, but must be for the purpose of preaching the wondrous Dharma.

This is a great causal occasion for the bestowal of a prophecy. I simply do not know for what reason the Buddha is preaching the wondrous Dharma again, nor who it is that he is bestowing this prophecy upon.

Since you, Mañjuśrī, have witnessed many Buddhas in the past and possess great wisdom, you must certainly understand the auspicious signs of the manifestation of lands and Buddhas. I pray that you will not fail me, nor the fourfold assembly and the nāgas.
