From the beginning, he never—though acting with subtle and profound secrecy—used minor dharmas to draw them into the Buddha-wisdom; in truth, he never did so.
"I shall clearly proclaim that you, Śāriputra and the other twelve hundred people, shall receive the prediction of attaining the Buddha-way.

Below this, he provides the reason why he had not previously spoken of it explicitly. Regarding the word "time" (*shí*) in the phrase "it was at the time when [the long discourse] was being delivered," this means that the reason he did not explicitly state that you would attain Buddhahood was not because the Buddha was unwilling.
I did not speak of it earlier because the time when the Buddha preached this sutra, as well as the time when you yourselves would receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, had not yet arrived.

Now it has truly come down; that is to say, since the time for you to receive the prediction of becoming Buddhas has now arrived and the time for the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is also at hand, the Buddha does not make his words double or triple, but resolutely and directly teaches the One Vehicle.
The Mahāyāna is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Regarding these nine divisions of the canon taught by me:

since the Mahāyāna now preached is the reality, we know that the ninefold teachings spoken by the Buddha forty years ago were indeed expounded through the provisional wisdom that accords with the capacities of sentient beings;
yet, tracing back to the Buddha’s own mind, his sole intention was to lead those of lesser capacity into the Mahāyāna.
This is the fundamental intent. Therefore, it is said that "entering the Mahāyāna is the foundation," and so forth;
this refers to all these śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who do not understand the underlying meaning and purpose of the Buddha’s teachings given according to his expedient means.

From the passage beginning "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure" onwards, the author explains that even forty years prior, the Buddha had already taught the meaning of the Mahāyāna, asserting that since the Buddha [first] used the *hīnayāna*...
As for the fruit: how is it that for forty years prior [to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*], the Buddha also taught the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) to various bodhisattvas?

It was because there was a class of sons of the Buddha belonging to the Great Vehicle whose minds were pure and gentle, whose faculties were sharp and keen, who had made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, who practiced the profound and wondrous path, and who cultivated both merit and wisdom. Therefore, for the sake of these [beings], I... the Buddha.

"Son, when I preach this Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtra and bestow upon such individuals the prediction that they shall attain Buddhahood in a future life, it is because internally they deeply mindfully recollect the Buddha and externally they cultivate and maintain the pure precepts.
Upon hearing the sound of their own attainment of Buddhahood, these people give rise to great joy that pervades their entire bodies; they do not give way to fear or retreat. Therefore, the Buddha—

Regarding the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): because he knows that the mind and conduct of those bodhisattvas are no different from the Buddha’s, he preaches the Mahāyāna for them.
Thus, although the Buddha also occasionally preached the Great [Vehicle] during the forty years prior [to his enlightenment], this was due to the resonance of their specific capacities (*indriya*);
it was not because the Buddha had any partiality or preached with inequality. (One should understand that when the Bodhisattva speaks of "purity of mind," it refers to the two vehicles...)

If one says that the minds of humans are not yet pure, then the minds of those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are still rigid and strong; they are merely able to sever delusions but cannot deliver sentient beings. If one says that Bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties, then those of the Two Vehicles have dull faculties.

Because Bodhisattvas practice the profound and wondrous Way in the presence of all Buddhas, their faculties are supple and sharp. Because those of the Two Vehicles do not practice the profound and wondrous Way in the presence of all Buddhas, their faculties are dull and rigid.

Bodhisattvas contemplate the Buddha with a deep mind, unlike those of the Two Vehicles who take pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma. Bodhisattvas cultivate and maintain the pure precepts, unlike ordinary people who are merely greedy for and attached to birth and death. Because they are attached to birth and death, they are afflicted by suffering; because they take pleasure in the Lesser Dharma, [the Buddha] speaks to them.

The Hīnayāna seeks liberation from suffering; this [state] is filled with joy. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is taught so that one may attain Buddhahood. This distinction between Great and Small prior to the forty years [after the turning of the wheel] was because the Lesser Vehicle’s concentration (*samādhi*) could not be spoken of as Great, and its partial concentration (*ardha-samādhi*) could not be spoken of as Full.
Regarding the passage "Whether Śrāvaka or Bodhisattva," etc.: although there was previously a Mahāyāna, it was a "Great" only in contrast to the "Small";
it permitted those of sharp faculties to be Bodhisattvas and those of dull faculties to be of the Two Vehicles. Now, however, it is not so; it makes no distinction between Śrāvakas...

It is heard that whether a bodhisattva’s faculties are small or great, sharp or dull, if they have heard even a single verse—however minute—of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna teachings spoken by the Buddha, they shall all now receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, leaving no room for doubt.
This is because it accords with the fundamental intention of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition. (No doubt)
These two phrases are words intended to encourage those present to give rise to faith.
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma" (up to) "...because [the Buddhas] preach the wisdom of the Buddhas."
This verse is the third section of the long prose. From "In the ten directions" onwards, it is a verse that follows upon the preceding section.
It means that whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, if they hear even a single verse, they shall all attain Buddhahood; this is because within the buddha-fields of the ten directions...

This is because there is only one, and not two or three. "Except for the Buddha" and below means that, setting aside the Buddha, the two or three vehicles are taught as the skillful means (*upāya*) for the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle; thus, it is said that there are *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
However, these are merely the provisional names (*prajñapti-nāman*) of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, used to guide those of a certain class who prefer the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding "the fruit for sentient beings": it refers to the Buddha’s wisdom, which is described as attaining greatness from small beginnings.
Since both *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*), it can be known that the Bodhisattva is the true designation.
"The Buddhas appear in the world; this alone is the one true reality" (up to) "there is only the One Vehicle, no second.
This verse corresponds to the fourth section of the prose (*chāng-háng*). In the prose, there is only the single sentence: "The Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise thus.
That which is expanded in the verse is because the fourth section of the long text is originally a concluding confirmation (*kṣepa-siddhi*).

Section Three. Since there is no textual passage stating that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), without any other vehicles—whether two or three—the verse portion likewise directly passes over the Buddhas in general with a brief summary, while singularly emphasizing the fundamental intent of our Śākyamuni, the One Buddha.
Throughout this section of seventy-nine lines, the first three [lines] are as follows:
The first thirteen lines explain the meaning of the preceding verse: that within the lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle Dharma, neither two nor three.
Next, the thirty-two lines explain the meaning of the preceding verse:
that, setting aside the Buddha’s skillful means, he uses only provisional names to guide sentient beings, thereby preaching the Buddha’s wisdom. Finally, the last ten [lines]...

The four lines conclude the preceding section on the meaning that whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas hear the Dharma taught by me—even down to a single verse—they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood;
they also introduce the following section, the verse concerning the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

"From 'The Buddhas' onwards," [the text] returns to explain the preceding passage. This means that because within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle, the fundamental Dharma, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they do not go beyond expounding this fundamental Dharma; thus it is said, "This alone is the one reality.
Since within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there has never been a second or third vehicle from the beginning, the reason the Buddhas speak of other second and third vehicles is...
This is not true; [the teaching] will ultimately not be set aside. This is because, throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, the One Vehicle alone is the truth.
Therefore, from the very beginning of their preaching until the end, the Buddhas will never, by means of the other two or three non-true Small Vehicle teachings, deliver sentient beings.
(The preceding verses on the Buddhas are concluded. From where the Buddha himself resides downward, he again recites my explanation.
When Kāśyapa today speaks directly of the One Vehicle, he follows the fundamental Dharma of all Buddhas to deliver beings with equanimity.

As stated below: since the Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna Dharma, he likewise uses that very Mahāyāna Dharma which he has attained and in which he dwells—whether it be concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), power (*bala*), or adornment (*vyūha*)—to deliver sentient beings. From himself...
"Realization" (zhèng) below refers to the Buddha’s saving of sentient beings by means of that which he himself has realized.

Although the Buddha’s own realization of unsurpassed *bodhi* is called the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*), it is nonetheless a Dharma of equality wherein both sentient beings and Buddhas, as well as others and oneself, all possess an equal share.
Within this Dharma of Great Vehicle equality, if one were to use the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to transform even a single person, this would be [a violation].
The Buddha himself would fall into stinginess and greed if he were to give great things to himself while giving only small things to others; this would instead constitute an inequality.
Even an ordinary gentleman would not do such a thing, let alone the Buddha, who would ever consent to act like a stingy ghost?
Therefore, it is said that this matter is impossible. If a person’s faith is inferior, they might claim that the Buddha did not [do so].
Regarding this stingy and greedy person: once a person has taken refuge in the Buddha and placed their faith in him, one should treat them with sincerity;

thus, they do not deceive themselves through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, nor do they deceive others. Deception refers to the karma of speech consisting of mad, grandiose, and unreal words.
As for the greedy and jealous person, they desire only their own excellence and harbor a heart that cannot endure the prosperity of others.
Regarding mental action (*manas-karman*): when the Buddha declares by his own mouth that a person will become a Buddha, he does not deceive people; thus, his verbal action (*vāc-karman*) is pure.

When he abides himself in the Mahāyāna and desires that others also abide in the Mahāyāna, his mind is free from greed and envy; thus, his mental action is pure. [Conversely,] when the mind and speech involve deception and envy, [the actions are impure].
These are the root and secondary afflictions of both the Great and Small Vehicles, which constitute the ultimate evils among all phenomena.
Since the Buddha has already purified and severed them, he alone throughout the worlds of the ten directions is free from fear.

Consequently, he has attained a body adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, possessing a purple-gold hue; its radiance is so brilliant that it illuminates the entire world. Thus—

His physical karma is especially pure. From the heavens down to the human realm, there are immeasurable and boundless multitudes who, upon seeing the Buddha’s three karmas purified, do not fail to revere and honor him.

Therefore, with a sincere and truthful intention, he speaks this Seal of the True Mark that all sentient beings shall become Buddhas. As for this "Seal," neither celestial Māras nor external paths can alter it.
This refers to the passage beginning with "Śāriputra, you should know. Furthermore, it traces the cause back from the fruit.

This means that the Buddha’s three karmas wait for such sincere people; for when the Buddha first resolved upon bodhicitta while on the causal ground as a bodhisattva, he originally established a vow, desiring that all sentient beings be no different from himself, which has reached its fruition in the present.
Above: "I shall transform you, Śāriputra, and all sentient beings, bestowing upon them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
If the fruit is obtained according to the cause, then the Buddha’s vow will finally be fulfilled. "If I were to encounter sentient beings... and so forth:

This means that although the fruit and the cause are as one, if from the very beginning the Buddha did not observe their faculties and provide teachings accordingly, but instead taught all exclusively the path to Buddhahood of the One Vehicle, then—
Sentient beings are also difficult to transform. Why? Because those lacking wisdom, upon hearing the Buddha say that all sentient beings are Buddhas, immediately misinterpret the Buddha’s intent.
They claim that the false does not hinder the true, and they recklessly conjecture about the Buddha’s words, asserting that the true is itself the false.
Thus, they become confused regarding the sequence of view, cultivation, realization, and attainment, which constitutes a refusal to accept the teaching. This I know.

Regarding these inferior beings: I know that although these beings who do not accept the teaching possess the vision and knowledge of a single Buddha’s manifest enlightenment—which serves as the root of all virtues—because they saw little of the Buddha and cultivated only slight goodness during their past causes, they have never attained awakening;
thus, their consciousness cannot break through the five desires, and they remain stubbornly attached to them.
Attachment. From attachment arises delusive craving; from delusive craving arise afflictions. This refers to the turbidity of affliction within these five desires.
Regarding the phrase "with the various desires as causes and conditions," this means that delusive craving serves as the cause and the five desires serve as the condition.

Due to these causes and conditions, one falls into the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, and transmigrates through the six destinies of humans and devas, fully experiencing all their bitter sufferings. This is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) within these five desires.
Regarding the phrase "the subtle form of the womb" below: it means that because of this bondage to the fruit of the defilement of sentient beings, one subsequently...

Having cast aside and disregarded the vast and boundless nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one instead undergoes the union of paternal seed and maternal blood—foul and rank—to become a minute physical form within the womb.
Having not yet finished enduring the bitter fate of one lifetime, one further increases another lifetime;
thus, with virtue thinned and merit diminished, one is oppressed by the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Regarding body and mind, among these five desires, this is the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
Entering the dense forest of false views below refers to the sentient beings of the six realms who are tormented and oppressed by their miserable lives;

they fail to reflect upon the causes of their karma and instead recklessly enter the dense forest of false views—namely, speculating on existence or non-existence, annihilationism or eternalism, or regarding fortune, misfortune, longevity, and early death as being left entirely to fate rather than to human effort.

This was due to the influence of their own [erroneous] powers. From that point on, the various factions barked and clamored; some asserted both existence and non-existence, while others denied the continuity of being and further clung to the notion of impermanence.
Consequently, they each established their own schools, fully embracing sixty-two kinds of false views.

These teachers rejected the Buddha-dharma and the principles of cause and effect. As for these teachers, they did not realize that such false views are all merely the conceptual discriminations of a deluded mind. Deeply...

They become attached and cherish it themselves; as for their disciples, they do not recognize its error, transmitting falsehood upon falsehood, and they receive it with even greater firmness, unable to relinquish it.
This is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) within these five desires.

As for those who are arrogant and self-conceited due to this turbidity of views—the Sage’s eye of wisdom gazes upon them and already regards them as pitiable, yet they remain arrogant and self-conceited. And so...
They boast of lofty words, claiming, "My Way has a transmission; my practice has a tradition. Yet they are right-faced and wrong-backed, outwardly liberal while inwardly grasping.
They flatter others and act with crooked compliance toward themselves. Taking the unreal for the real, they claim their own path to be the True Way.
To turn away from this and instead follow such [desires] is to enter a heterodox path.
Consequently, for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they shall not again hear even the name of a Buddha, let alone encounter one in person.
Since they cannot see the Buddha, how could they ever hear the True Dharma? Such people have their minds turbid with these five desires and their bodies agitated and distressed by them.

Truly difficult to deliver! This refers to the *kalpa-kāṣāya* (degeneration of the age) within these five desires. Therefore, from the passage beginning with "Śāriputra," the text provides an explanation:

because these people are so difficult to deliver, the Buddha did not initially speak directly of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), but instead established expedient means (*upāya*) to teach the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), the path for exhausting suffering, and thereby showed them [the way to] *nirvāṇa*.

This means that one addresses them according to their inclinations. Regarding the passage "Although I preach *nirvāṇa*," it means that although the Buddha accords with their capacities by showing them the small fruit of *nirvāṇa* and permitting those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) to attain extinction, this is merely a provisional, skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and is not true extinction.
Regarding the passage "All dharmas from the very beginning," it means that one must attain true extinction in order to enter the Great *Nirvāṇa* of the Buddha.

You should know that the various dharmas—the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses possessed by sentient beings, as well as their characteristics, nature, beginning, and end—have, from the very beginning, never moved even a single hair’s breadth.
Their nature is inherently true and eternal; their essence is inherently quiescent and extinguished.
If you can awaken to this, then you, Śāriputra and the others, will no longer be śrāvakas, but shall be called sons of the Buddha. What you have attained...
Nirvana is not called a "fruit-virtue" (phala-guṇa), but is itself the causal practice (hetu-caryā).

The Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination constitute the completion of the path of practicing the Six Perfections. Possessing these great causes for practicing the Way, one will certainly attain the great fruit of becoming a Buddha in a future life.
From the words "I have expedient means" onwards, the conclusion is finalized; that is to say, since the Buddha possesses these...
The true Dharma of the Great Nirvana—why would it initially employ minor fruits?
Because the Buddha possesses the power of skillful means and provisional wisdom, he reveals the One Vehicle by opening it up as the Three Vehicles.
Nevertheless, the Three Vehicles revealed by the Buddha are not other than those spoken by all the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions and three periods of time.
This is the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). From the passage "Now, this great assembly... onwards, [the Buddha] exhorts them to believe in its reality.

That is to say, once they know that my three vehicles are precisely the one vehicle of those Buddhas, then your doubts regarding the former three and the present one may be removed, and the words of the Buddha—that he and all Buddhas are one and not two—may be trusted. This...
The structure of the text proceeds as follows: it begins by introducing the theme through all Buddhas, next provides an explanation through Śākyamuni, and concludes with all Buddhas.
From "In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa" up to "have all already attained the path of Buddhahood."

This verse is the fifth section of the long prose passage. It clarifies that the Buddhas of the past did not merely employ countless causes, conditions, and parables to teach the Dharma of the three vehicles as the primary skillful means for the One Vehicle;
rather, because the inclinations of sentient beings' deep minds differ, they even employed the causes and effects of humans and devas as alternative skillful means for the One Vehicle.
"Alternative skillful means" refers to tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*), which originally was not permitted to achieve Buddhahood; yet now it is still utilized to complete the fruit of Buddhahood.
How much more so for the untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—how could they not be accepted and granted the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood?

Therefore, the alternative skillful means are explained in detail so that those who are ready may gain deep faith and enter [the path]. From "In the past, countless... onwards, the verse summarizes the main point.

"Expedient means. Furthermore, from "All the Great Sages" onwards, [the text] introduces alternative expedient means. From "If there are sentient beings" onwards, it enumerates and explains the six perfections as these alternative expedient means.
A question is asked: "The six perfections are the primary expedient means for a bodhisattva to attain buddhahood."
Question: Why do you say they are different? Answer: Does the Sūtra not say that they assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?

Within the ultimate truth, even the single word "Buddha" is itself a provisional means (*upāya*). How much more so is the phrasing in these verses, which all state that he has already completed the Buddha-way?

Since the Buddha-way has already been fully accomplished, to then speak further of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) is like a person who, having already reached home, continues to describe the path.
The aforementioned matters are none other than this. If a person is virtuous, gentle, and humble, this is the mind of skillful means for distinguishing between humans and devas.

Making offerings to the śarīra and erecting stūpas and temples are the virtuous and gentle deeds that distinguish humans from devas. These may be done with the seven precious jewels, or even with sand and soil.

Whether using fragrant wood, bricks, or tiles, although the sincerity of their playfulness may differ, there is nothing that does not arise from a virtuous and gentle mind to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth;
therefore, all such acts result in the attainment of Buddhahood. When people act for the sake of the Buddha, stupas and temples are completed and images of the Buddha are produced;
thus, some carve and sculpt fragrant gems, some cast or mold with gold and clay, and some lacquer, weave, or paint with colors.

Whether one acts for oneself or causes others to act, and whether using a wooden stylus or one's fingernails—though there may be distinctions between noble and base objects—the sincere spirit of playfulness is no different.
There is nothing that is not a mind of goodness and gentleness, for it assists in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus, they have all already completed the path to Buddhahood themselves, yet they continue to transform only bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable sentient beings. If a person, regarding...

Below the stupas and temples, the physical forms [of the Buddhas] are fully present, and the implements for making offerings are arrayed. Thus, there may be various banners and canopies, various musical performances;
whether it be the faintest of a single sound or the smallest of a single flower, some arise from reverent joy and some from the settling of turbulence, yet none are not of a virtuous and gentle mind.
Because they assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they all together bring about the perfection of Buddhahood.
It is so. There may be those who prostrate themselves and offer worship at one’s feet; this is because the ritual etiquette and its formal measures bring it to completion.

Or there may be those who perform the five-limb prostration with full devotion, which differs from the mere joining of palms. Or there may be those who, with a light heart, lower their heads with a single hand; this differs from the simple utterance of "Namo.
Yet there is nothing here that is not a virtuous and gentle mind, for it serves to manifest the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Thus, it spontaneously becomes the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
They ascend to the Buddha-way and further deliver countless sentient beings, together realizing Great Nirvana, like fire being extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Thus we know that past sentient beings who relied upon minor good deeds and subtle causes have all already attained Buddhahood;
how much more so for the present disciples of our Śākyamuni Buddha—how could they be limited to merely the two or three vehicles?
"The future World-Honored Ones shall be immeasurable in number" (up to) "...the Guide speaks through skillful means.
This verse constitutes the sixth section of the long prose. The first ten lines can be understood by referring to the long prose.

Regarding the passage "The fundamental vows of all Buddhas," it refers to the Buddhas of future ages who, while originally in the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), practiced the Way and made vows, desiring—

All sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood just as I have; even when reaching the stage of fruition, although countless Dharma-gates are taught, they are all for the sake of the One Vehicle alone—this vow should be understood in this way.
From the verse "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among Two-Legged Beings" onwards, it clarifies that the Dharma should be understood in this way:
namely, the reason why the Buddhas are called the Honored Ones who are "Two-Legged Complete in Merit and Wisdom" is because they have realized and known all things.
The dharmas of the world—the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—are from the beginning truly eternal and without intrinsic nature.

This is not like those of the Two Vehicles, for whom these dharmas lack intrinsic nature because they have severed the afflictions of views and thought; thus, while their wisdom is sufficient, the seeds of Buddhahood are planted only for future lives.

Although one knows that all dharmas are truly eternal and without intrinsic nature—which constitutes the seed of the Buddha Vehicle—this does not prevent taking that very absence of intrinsic nature as a condition.
One initiates the six perfections and myriad practices to deliver sentient beings; this is unlike those of the Two Vehicles who merely sit within emptiness. Thus, one’s merit is fulfilled.
Now, the fact that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is the cause for attaining Buddhahood—who lacks this cause?
The Buddha-seed arises from conditions; this is the condition for attaining Buddhahood—who lacks this condition? All phenomena lack intrinsic nature.

This is the nature (*prakṛti*). That the seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions (*pratyaya*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Nature does not obstruct characteristics; the cause is itself the condition. Although they are called "two feet," they are fundamentally one mind.
Therefore, it is said: "For this reason, I preach the One Vehicle. Regarding the phrase "this Dharma": this Dharma is precisely the aforementioned Dharma of the One Vehicle.
"Abiding" means never having been separated from it for even a moment, whether long or short. "Dharma-position" refers to the dharmas of the sense organs, objects, and elements.
Each has its respective states of seeing, hearing, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding":

this means that by virtue of the Dharma of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the One Vehicle, it never for even a moment or briefly departs from the positions of the faculties, objects, and dharmas within the world.

Therefore, the characteristics of the worldly faculties, objects, and so forth are themselves the eternally abiding True Suchness (*tathatā*). As for the passage below concerning the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it refers to future ages.
The Buddhas, within the bodhimanda of the *araṇya* dharma, attained equal and perfect enlightenment;

having realized and known for themselves that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding and that the One Vehicle Dharma has been attained, they also employ the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to lead from the great to the small, teaching by means of the Three Vehicles.
These few phrases [serve as] the praise of virtues while emerging from meditative concentration; it is only the Buddha who...
The Buddha alone is able to exhaustively investigate the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

He specifically provides a detailed verse on this matter because Śāriputra and the other twelve hundred arhats are Buddhas who have received their predictions for future enlightenment; it is for this reason that he speaks of them in particular.
"Offered by devas and humans, the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions" (up to) "expounding according to appropriate skillful means.
The section beginning with "devas and humans" is the seventh section of the long prose.

It means that there are many Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who appear in the world and bring peace and security to sentient beings; these Buddhas likewise teach only the characteristics of the world as being impermanent.
Abiding. This is the Dharma of the One Vehicle. "Knowing the foremost" and below correctly clarifies peace and security.

This means that although the Buddhas of the present know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—which is inherently true, eternal, and characterized by the quiescence of nature and marks such that no verbal expression is possible—they do not, for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, refrain from employing the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to provisionally manifest causes.
Based on the path of various verbal expressions through parables, the Three Vehicles are taught. Although the Three Vehicles are taught, in reality, they are intended only for the One Vehicle.
Regarding the passage "knowing the dispositions of sentient beings" and below: this refers to the present Buddhas.

The reason they know the One as being one, yet further speak of three, is because the capacities of beings possess differences in their conduct, thoughts, karmic habits, diligence, indolence, sharpness, and dullness.
Because illnesses differ, within the first [truth]—the quiescent state where no skillful means exist—I employ the skillful means of verbal expression to teach it.
Now I do likewise; in order to bring peace and security to sentient beings, I preach the dharma of non-discrimination.

This verse constitutes the eighth section of the prose commentary, totaling one hundred and twenty-two lines. The final eight lines beginning with "Now I" summarize the provisional and ultimate wisdoms of the prose commentary.

Specifically, this refers to how the World-Honored One, following the example of all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions who assist sentient beings with a mind of peace and security, likewise employs various provisional means of the Three Vehicles.
The Dharma-gate of Wisdom proclaims the Buddha-way of the true wisdom of the One Vehicle.

Because the Buddha possesses the power of true wisdom, he is able to know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings; thus, through the provisional wisdom of skillful means, he preaches the Dharma to cause sentient beings to attain joy.

(One should know that the first line shows how the provisional leads to the real, while the second line clarifies how the provisional is for the sake of the real. By means of the provisional leading to the real, there is peace and security; by being for the sake of the real...)

[This is] expedient means (upāya). [The phrase] "Śāriputra, you should know" and so forth consists of one hundred and fourteen lines, which separately versify the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real (*prajñapti-tattva-jñāna*) as set forth in the prose. There are four layers to the meaning of this separate versification.

First, from "Śāriputra, you should know" up to "and gives rise to a heart of great compassion," it clarifies that the Buddha perceives sentient beings who take suffering for pleasure and are tormented by what they seek as pleasure.

Because they were not at peace, he gave rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Next, from his initial sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) until his swift entry into *nirvāṇa*, he clarified that the Buddha, for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings, leads the great toward the small—that is, he reveals the provisional (*upāya*) within the real—to perfect great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
Third, from his own recollection of past Buddhas until "I always speak thus," [he demonstrates this].

[The section] from "Śāriputra, you should know that I see the sons of the Buddha... up to "...preaching the Dharma of non-discrimination" clarifies that the Buddha does not fear the capacities of those below, nor does he oppose the Buddhas above; thus, he fulfills his original vow and achieves [his purpose]. This explains that the Buddha’s constitutional principle is that the yang is small and the yin is large, opening the provisional to manifest the real, and by opening the great, he relinquishes the four [self-attachments].

Śāriputra, you should know... [as above]... up to the preaching of the Dharma of non-discrimination. This clarifies that the Buddha, below, does not fear the capacities of sentient beings, and above, does not oppose the Buddhas; thus he succeeds in fulfilling his original vow and accomplishes [the goal].
Great joy! These four layers of prose text conclude by returning to the meanings of the second, third, and fourth sections of the preceding verses;

they thus serve as the foundation for the following "Simile Chapter. This is why the prose is brief while the verses are extensive. (The above constitutes the division of chapters; the following is the word-by-word explanation of the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "I, with the Buddha-eye," etc.: the Buddha possesses five eyes. The fleshly eye is the same as that of humans; the heavenly eye is the same as that of devas.
The wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is the same as that of the two vehicles; the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) is the same as that of bodhisattvas. What they perceive all has limits.

Only the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) is the same as what all Buddhas perceive; it has no limits. When it is now said that one observes with the Buddha-eye, it means that one has attained true vision and, moreover, that it is universal.
Sentient beings in the six realms lack merit and wisdom; this is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). They enter into birth and death.

The perilous path represents the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), for suffering continues without interruption. Being shrouded by attachment to desires represents the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Not seeking the Buddha or the Dharma that severs suffering represents the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Deeply entering into false views represents the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Because they lack wisdom, they are impoverished and enter the perilous path; because they lack merit, their destitution and suffering are unceasing. That the path is perilous and suffering continues is the fruit of suffering.
Attachment to desire blinds oneself; it is the cause of suffering. When cause and effect are not understood, it is like the yak that loves its tail and thereby destroys its own body;
hence, they are called "blind and ignorant. Because of this blindness, they obscure the causes for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, failing to seek the method for severing suffering.
They obscure the conditions for the opening, showing, awakening, and entering—the Great Matter of Cause and Condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*). Within, there is none...

Regarding what is seen: externally there is nothing sought; thus, relying on deluded conceptualization and discrimination, one gives rise to false views such as nihilism, eternalism, existence, or non-existence.
Taking the act of lying upon thorns or smearing oneself with ashes as the cause, one seeks birth in realms such as the Non-conceptual Heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*) as the fruit.
This is to abandon suffering by means of suffering. How could such a bitter fruit ever be abandoned? [The character] *mao* (犛) is pronounced *mù*; its eyes are blocked by hair. One does not see.

Regarding the meaning of "True" (Zhen): The Buddha possesses great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and is able to bestow the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha possesses great compassion and is able to uproot the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, he is called the Buddha of Great Power (*Mahāsthāmaprāpta*). As for the method for severing suffering: it is like knowing suffering, one then severs its origin (*samudaya*).

This is that Dharma, yet the non-Buddhists do not know it. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of these sentient beings," it means that he gives rise to great compassion for these beings who suffer due to the five turbidities and greed, desiring to rescue and deliver them.

This section serves as the introduction to the "Parable Chapter" (*Upamā-parivarta*); from the words "If in a kingdom, city, or village" until "having no intention to seek liberation," it establishes the foundation. I—

"Regarding 'first sitting at the site of enlightenment' (bodhimaṇḍa)': this refers to when the Buddha himself described the time of the *Avataṃsaka*, when he first attained perfect enlightenment within the Aranya-dharma Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha—the place where the principal and the retinue are infinitely interpenetrating.
Regarding 'also observing the trees while practicing': this describes how, without departing from any bodhi tree, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and other celestial realms."
"During the twenty-one days of contemplation" refers to observing the capacities of beings and adapting the teaching accordingly. "That which I have attained...

and below refers to contemplating the greatness of the Dharma realized by the Buddha himself. "The capacities of sentient beings... and below refers to contemplating the smallness of the capacities of sentient beings. "In this manner... and below [refers to the subsequent application].
This means that to apply the subtle and wondrous Great Dharma to those of dull faculties and small capacities is like trying to fit a square block into a round hole.
To instruct sentient beings who are ignorant and blind with the foremost wisdom is like beating a drum while searching for a lost child.
Since the Dharma does not meet their capacity, the teaching falls into a double bind; therefore it is said: "How can such types as these [be saved]?"
They can be saved. This refers to the Buddha’s account of the first seven days, when no one requested instruction and he remained in solitary contemplation.

At that time, while the various Brahma Kings descended and the Buddha was reflecting on how the Dharma is profound and difficult for those with inferior capacities to realize, he encountered the gods of the three realms who came to request his teaching.
Had he complied with their request and taught only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings would have been overwhelmed by suffering.

[The Buddha] passed away. [Śāriputra] fundamentally did not believe that his own mind is the Buddha. Because of this single lack of faith, it was not only of no benefit; rather, it actually caused him harm.

Thus, he remained hesitant and could not resolve his doubts, contemplating entry into *nirvāṇa*. This is the Buddha’s account of the second week, during which he reflected upon the requests made by the devas.
This section constitutes the "Parable Chapter. From the words "Śāriputra, you are like an elder... onwards [is the subsequent text].
This is the arising of reflection. Up to the point where he merely runs about here and there playing and looking at his father, it serves as the introductory basis.

From "He then reflected" (*samanvāharati*) downwards, this describes the reflection during the third week. During the first week, he followed the Dharma; however, because it was subtle and difficult to enter, the teachings of the Buddhas did not manifest before him.
During the second week, he followed the capacities of sentient beings; however, because they were difficult to believe, the teachings of the Buddhas [did not manifest].
They did not yet appear before him. Upon reaching the third seven-day period, he forgot the person [who had guided him];

looking upward toward the Buddhas and downward toward sentient beings, the Dharma of the Buddhas finally appeared before him. Therefore it is said: "When he engaged in this contemplation, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared.

(This refers to the sixteen princes of the *Parable of the Phantom City* chapter, who have now attained Buddhahood in the ten directions. Below the term "Brahma-sound" (*fan yin*), the text describes the fulfillment of the ten directions.
The words of consolation from all the Buddhas: "Having attained this unsurpassed Dharma, you are foremost among all the Buddhas in following [the truth].

To manifest the provisional by resorting to the real, it is well said: 'We too shall all descend. Thus, we describe how the Buddhas of the ten directions cite themselves as an analogy to clarify the manifestation of the provisional by resorting to the real;
and the manifestation of the provisional is precisely for the purpose of transforming toward the real, Śāriputra."

"Furthermore, you should know that below [this point], the Buddha again personally recounts his own dedication to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the practice of the meaning of the consolation and exhortation provided by those Buddhas.
The statement from the preceding text—that 'only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust [this matter]'—is made even clearer here.
From the passage 'Contemplating this matter' onwards, it clarifies how the Buddha follows the teachings of the Buddhas to reveal the provisional means (*upāya*)."
Vārāṇasī is the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), the place where the Śrāvaka teachings of the Āgamas were expounded for twelve years.
That "the mark of the cessation of all phenomena cannot be proclaimed in words" refers to the Buddha’s own realization of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"By the power of skillful means, he taught it to the five bhikṣus" refers to the opening of the One Vehicle’s reality by manifesting the three [vehicles].

This is spoken by means of provisional wisdom. Regarding the phrase "this is called turning the wheel of Dharma" and below: it refers to when the Buddha first attained the Way and sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

For twenty-one days he engaged in contemplation; the names of the Three Jewels had already flourished for a long time, yet because the Dharma did not yet accord with the capacities of beings, the world was unaware of the matter of turning the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings. It was only upon reaching the Deer Park...
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the provisional is opened through the realization of the ultimate; thus, for the first time, the names of the Three Jewels appear in the world.
"Nirvāṇa" refers to the Dharma, the small fruit, the Arhat as the Sangha, and the stage of the Worthy One (*bhadra*).

From the passage beginning with "Since long ago," it means that from the time the Buddha attained enlightenment until this very long duration, he has praised the Dharma of attaining Great Nirvāṇa, wherein the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted.
"O noble monks, the Buddha has always spoken thus; it is only that those of the Two Vehicles do not see or hear it.

This section constitutes the "Parable Chapter. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the elder immediately had this thought" up to "striving to escape from the burning house," the foundation is laid.
The above clarifies how the provisional is established upon the real. "Śāriputra, you should know that I see the sons of the Buddha..."

The following clarifies how the provisional leads to the ultimate. Continuing from the preceding statement, it means that although the Buddha has, since time immemorial, praised and revealed the Dharma of Great Nirvana and the holy Sangha for whom the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted, those of the Two Vehicles do not yet know this.
For whom, then, was this taught? It was taught for a certain class of sons of the Buddha who possess the Mahāyāna aspiration and seek the path to Buddhahood;
because they are numerous and their minds are reverent, and because in the past they have already heard from various Buddhas the teachings on skillful means (*upāya*), the Buddha thought:
"There is no need to speak further of skillful means; I shall simply teach them that Buddha."

Wisdom. It is precisely appropriate for this time. This refers to those who, though their faculties are dull, yet act in accordance with their original aspiration by preaching the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* of the Buddha.
Śāriputra, you should know that for those of dull faculties, small wisdom, and inferior capacity... [and so forth].
This means that at that time, he taught the Mahāyāna exclusively to the sons of the Buddha and did not teach it universally because there was a class of people with dull faculties,
small wisdom, attachment to signs, and arrogance who were unable to believe in this Mahāyāna Dharma. From the passage "Now I rejoice and am fearless" onwards,
it means that the Buddha initially feared that such followers— mere branches and leaves— would destroy the Great Dharma.

Because [speaking of it] would have entailed them and caused them to fall into evil realms, he remained patient and did not speak of it. Now, forty years later, their faculties have matured and the Dharma has become pure;
the branches and leaves have withered away while the true fruit remains. Therefore, the Buddha rejoices and is without fear;
amidst the assembly of bodhisattvas, he directly sets aside the former provisional and expedient teachings and speaks only of the unsurpassed One Vehicle.

This is the Way. When Bodhisattvas hear such things as these—referring to those of superior capacity among the Bodhisattvas at the assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Vaipulya* sūtras—they have already transcended the Great Vehicle;
thus, it goes without saying that their doubts and delusions are eliminated. However, as for you, Śāriputra and the other twelve hundred Arhats, who were formerly known as...
Those of the Hīnayāna also all enter the ultimate truth through expedient means; they shall likewise receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood as Bodhisattvas.

As for the phrase "equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time," this means that those who formerly followed the Hīnayāna now all attain Buddhahood through the Mahāyāna because the Buddha, like all the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the three periods of time, brings expedient means back to the ultimate truth.

This is the ritual for preaching the Dharma. "I now do likewise," and so forth, means that since all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have no distinction between small and great, they equally bestow predictions of Buddhahood upon their disciples;
how could I, Śākyamuni, be any different? This section constitutes the Parable Chapter. From here, it says: "At that time, the elder saw his sons... and so on.
Having safely emerged from the burning house, they have attained what was never before experienced and was not originally expected;

this serves as the foundation for the passage [extending] from "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote and difficult to encounter" to "knowing for themselves that they shall become Buddhas."
This verse concludes the ninth section of the long prose passage, thereby completing the first and second sections of that long prose.

Regarding the phrase "the appearance of the Buddhas," this refers to the five turbidities of the evil world (*pañca-kaṣāya*). In such times, even ordinary sages and saints remain hidden and concealed; how much more so, then, for a Buddha?
Thus, throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, it is rare indeed to encounter a Buddha appearing in the world. It may be said: [it is difficult].

It is understood. Even were all Buddhas to appear in the world, because the faculties of sentient beings are dull, the teachings of the gradual vehicle of the three vehicles—concerning the blessings and retributions of humans and devas—are still difficult to speak of abruptly; how much more so the wondrous Dharma of the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle?
Thus, it can be known that speaking the wondrous Dharma is difficult. The phrase "immeasurable and innumerable" and below refers to the difficulty over immeasurable numbers of kalpas.
Regarding the phrase "having obtained the Dharma to hear": among the five thousand people present in the assembly, even though the Dharma reached their ears, they departed from afar.

Thus, it can be known that it is difficult to obtain the hearing of this wondrous Dharma. The passage "one who is able to listen to this Dharma" and below means that once one has obtained the hearing, if one is nevertheless unable to listen with faith, then one is the same as those who did not hear it at all; therefore it says, "such a person is likewise..."

Difficult. As stated below, "like the udumbara flower," this means that because such an encounter is difficult to meet even by way of number, one who hears [the teaching] and is able to listen with faith gives rise to the thought of its being hard to encounter;
such a person is also like the udumbara flower, which all people see and love.
This can be understood. The reason for this is that such a person and such a flower have been rarely seen, both in the heavens and among humans, since time immemorial;
it is because they appear only when the proper time has come, and not easily. (This extended parable uses the metaphor of the wondrous Dharma being taught according to the timing.)
In the verse, the person who hears the Dharma is likened to the sun emerging at its proper time; this serves as a response to the first two sections of the long prose.

Regarding the passage "hearing the Dharma with joy and praise," it means that not only is it difficult to hear and then believe what is taught, but it is even more so to hear it and respond with joy, or to utter a single word of praise.
This is even more difficult than encountering an udumbara flower. These are words of extreme intensity; the essential meaning is that one must be able to believe them.
Only when the character "to listen" (聽) is interpreted as "to believe" (信) does it become coherent. Otherwise, "hearing" (聞) and "listening" (聽) are synonymous.
In that case, the word "text" (or "writing") would be redundant. To reach the ears is called "hearing" (*wen*); to register in the mind and receive it is called "listening" (*ting*).
If there is one who hears yet does not believe, they simply should not listen; thus, "listening" and "hearing" likely have distinct meanings.
You should not harbor doubts below this point, thinking that merely hearing a single word of praise is still superior to encountering an *udumbara* flower.
"Difficult! You disciples, Śāriputra and others, who listen with faith, are rarer than the udumbara flower; you need not harbor doubts. You should believe that one’s own mind creates the Buddha.
When I say 'I am the equal of all Buddhas,' it means that while Buddhas are difficult to encounter, I have already become the Dharma King;
thus, a Buddha is not difficult to meet. The wondrous Dharma is difficult to expound, yet I have already proclaimed it universally to the great assembly."

Thus, this wondrous Dharma is not difficult to expound. Although the assembly of the three vehicles finds it difficult to hear, if one now teaches and transforms all bodhisattvas solely through the path of the One Vehicle, there will be no disciples who are śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
then the Dharma may be said to have those who hear it without difficulty. You, Śāriputra and those below you, refer to the aforementioned [beings] as follows:
It is neither difficult nor easy. That which is difficult lies in hearing it without doubt and being willing to listen with faith.
Since you are all willing to listen with faith, you should know that this wondrous Dharma is the essential secret of all Buddhas and must not be recklessly bestowed upon others.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Because of the five turbidities," it means that having already explained it, he further entrusts it to you for secrecy; it is not... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
I cherish the Dharma. I fear that in future ages, wicked people may fail to believe in this teaching and instead fall into the evil realms.
Therefore, those who possess a sense of shame and purity, and who aspire to seek the Great Way, must not only refrain from concealing it, but should also widely praise this path for such individuals.
In this way, one may avoid the fault of failing to speak or failing to reach the right person. Śāriputra.

"Vasumitra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus," and so forth, concluding with an exhortation. This means that all Buddhas first teach the Three Vehicles and subsequently the One Vehicle;
first the Small and subsequently the Great, not because there is anything else, but because the fundamental Dharma is thus throughout the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
All Buddhas employ billions of skillful means to preach according to what is appropriate for each being's capacity. Those who do not study and practice [this]...
Such people are certainly unable to understand the matters of small and great skillful means adapted to circumstances.
Since you all already know that the Buddhas are the teachers who discipline the world and transcendence, you know what it means for them to be Buddhas;
furthermore, since you know the matters of the small and great skillful means adapted to circumstances, you know what it means for their Dharma to be [the Dharma].
This is the Dharma. Since you now know all of the Buddha’s teachings, you should no longer harbor doubts regarding smallness or greatness, priority or sequence.
You ought to give rise to great joy, knowing for yourself that in a future life you will certainly attain Buddhahood.

As for this "great joy," it means that having been an ordinary person submerged and sinking within the sea of birth and death, or having become a follower of the Two Vehicles—this may indeed be called joy.
How joyful! Furthermore, since one can attain the Buddhahood of the One Vehicle through the Two Vehicles, how could this joy not be great?

This Buddha, the World-Honored One, may be said to possess a compassion that is most earnest and poignant; his words are bitter and his heart is revealed, such that his kindness is difficult to repay.
This section constitutes the Parable Chapter. From "Śāriputra, what do you think? through "Would that elder ever speak falsely?
it serves as the introductory foundation for the subsequent discourse, concluding with "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said."
Like the yak that loves its tail (*Song Shi*, Western Xia Prince Li Yixing presented one yak).
*The Sound-Knower of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle One;
*The Sound-Knower of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Composed by Ruyú, Abbot of Jinkong Temple, Ming-hùguó.
The Parable Chapter, the Third, of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma.
Regarding the "Parable Chapter" (*Upamā-parivarta*): according to the scriptural text, it is named in reference to its causes and conditions (*nidāna*). The Sūtra states:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions, various parables, and innumerable skillful means (*upāya*)."
To guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments, the preceding chapter’s passage stating that "the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
appear in the world for the sake of the one great causal matter" and so forth, employs various causes and conditions to lead Śāriputra—
among the assembly of twelve hundred— to depart from his attachment to the Two Vehicles; having done so, this chapter establishes a parable.
These two statements further employ various analogies to lead the four great disciples, including Kāśyapa, away from their attachments to the Two Vehicles among the assembly of twelve hundred people.
Therefore, in the following passage, Śāriputra speaks on behalf of the twelve hundred, requesting:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be liberated."

[The assembly] was filled with doubt. Then the World-Honored One replied: "Did I not previously state that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma through various causes, conditions, parables, and skillful means?

Now, I shall once again clarify this meaning by means of a further parable, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables. Thus, although Śāriputra’s request was made by way of [causes],...
As for the conditions, the World-Honored One’s response was given by means of parables; therefore, this chapter is titled "Parables.

In fact, the textual structure of this entire sutra, though repeated again and again, does not go beyond various causes and conditions and various parables, extensively expounding the verbal teachings to guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments, as expressed in several phrases such as those in the preceding chapter. This is the fundamental discourse.
The causes and conditions for the appearance of the Buddhas in the world include the use of the *udumbara* flower as a metaphor for the Sublime Dharma;
thus, within these causal conditions, there are parables. From this chapter up to the "Chapter on the Prophecies for the Four Great Disciples," all are parables.
At the very end, it says, "The karmic conditions of my past lives and yours"—this, moreover, contains [a parable] within the parables.
The "Parable of the Phantom City" and the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples" fundamentally discuss the causal conditions from the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,
elaborating upon them through the metaphors of the phantom city and the tied jewel.
From the "Dharma Master Chapter" to the "Life Span Chapter," it fundamentally discusses the causal conditions of the present Śākyamuni Buddha and future Buddhas, and...

Furthermore, it is expounded through the analogies of the well-digger and the physician; all of these are analogies discussed within the context of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), using analogies to illustrate those very causes and conditions.

Therefore, the title of this chapter does not necessarily require an explanation such as "the prophecy for Śāriputra," which is merely a supplementary detail (*śeṣa*) to the discourse on the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).
This title is joined to the end of the preceding chapter as a designation for the supplementary section consisting of the analogical discourse (*aupamyadeśanā*).
Subsequently, regarding the debate over whether the text was expanded or not, it was simply divided into seven fascicles because the volume was so extensive.
The translator followed the sequence of the sūtra text, selecting one or two phrases to serve as the titles for each fascicle, and further interwove the preceding and following passages;
this was done so that those who read, recite, and uphold the text would know that although the fascicles are divided into seven, the meaning of the text remains undivided. What else could it be?
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy (until the passage) "lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
From this point downward, Śāriputra summarizes the Buddha’s one great causal condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu*), explaining it in detail.

Having awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he recounts the gains and losses of the past and present, presenting his understanding to the Buddha. Seeing the place where he has taken up the responsibility, [the Buddha] deems him worthy of receiving [the teaching].

This is a record. Therefore, the compiler of the sutra describes the signs of the six sense organs (ṣaḍ-indriya) being filled with joy: [the mental faculty] leaps up; [the physical body] immediately rises; [the visual faculty] gazes upward;

and regarding the two characters "joyful," they correspond to the mind generating great joy (as seen in the subsequent phrase, "my heart is greatly joyful"). Then, [the verbal faculty] speaks, describing what has now been attained.

The reason for this is to recount former failings. It means that now, upon hearing the Dharma-sound of the Two Vehicles receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, they hear that they have attained the same as others;
therefore, they rejoice. Although they also heard this Dharma in the past and saw Bodhisattvas receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, they themselves were not included;
thus, they heard that they had attained something different from others, which caused them grief. This is what is meant by "grieving."

They have lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision, and thus cannot become equal to the Bodhisattvas in practicing the Mahāyāna. (Regarding the phrase "lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision":

the two characters "Tathāgata" are a general designation for the Buddhas of the superior grade and for Śākyamuni Buddha. The two characters "immeasurable" refer to the profound and immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas.

The two terms "knowledge and vision" refer to the vast, deep, and far-reaching knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata, as well as that which all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones desire to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter.)
“World-Honored One, I constantly dwell alone in mountain forests and beneath trees... (until) whenever I encounter [the Dharma], I believe and accept it, contemplate it, and realize it for myself.
World-Honored One, I have always descended [to explain] below, clarifying the meaning of what I previously felt sorrow over not having attained, while dwelling in mountain forests and beneath trees.”
This is the place where those of the Two Vehicles practice; whether walking or sitting, they contemplate within their minds, yet they do not find satisfaction in being of the Two Vehicles.
Since the single dharma of nirvana is attained in common by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practitioners, it is said: "We have entered equally into the dharma-nature.

As for the phrase "How could it be... and so forth, it means that since what is realized and entered by those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is the same, that which they deliver and save should likewise be the same.

Yet how is it that the Buddha rescues bodhisattvas with the Mahāyāna so they may obtain an inexhaustible treasury of jewels, while delivering us śrāvakas with small fruits and providing only a limited wage? The Buddha’s heart seems to be unjust (this fault of injustice seems to lie with the Buddha).
We, being inferior, take this blame upon ourselves, saying that we have now heard the Buddha preach the equality of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the Dharma: if I were to transform even a single person by means of the Lesser Vehicle, I would fall into stinginess and greed;
such a thing is impossible. It would mean that I have lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision, and it would be our own fault for abandoning the vast to take the meager.
It is not that the Buddha possesses this inequality of "great" and "small. Therefore, it is said: "Not of the world."
Venerable sir! As for why we have sought clarification: we previously seemed to place the blame on the Buddha, yet today we say it is our own fault.
Why is this? Because when the Buddha first taught the Hīnayāna, it was precisely as a means to lead us from the small toward the great.
Yet, we did not wait for him to explain the underlying cause; instead, we ourselves adhered to the Hīnayāna. Had we waited for the Buddha to speak...
"These ninefold teachings of mine are the fundamental cause for entering the Mahāyāna;
thus, we naturally ought to attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Yet the Buddha will surely deliver us by means of the Mahāyāna" (*Anuttara* means "unsurpassed";
*samyak* means "perfectly equal"; *saṃbodhi* means "perfect enlightenment. The above is an explanation, not the words of the World-Honored One). Now, from "However, I... onwards:
Furthermore, [the text] again clarifies the reason why [we] did not wait [for the teaching], thereby explaining the completion of the phrase "it is our own fault.
This means that the reason we did not wait for the [teaching] to be so was because we were originally people attached to false views;

having only just come to take refuge in the Buddha, we did not understand that the Buddha’s light uses the *Hīnayāna* as a skillful means, and thus we merely followed according to our own faculties and conduct.
He speaks according to what is appropriate; therefore, upon hearing it once, they immediately believe and accept it.

To take this as a realization through the conceptualizing mind of the sixth consciousness is to mistake the provisional for the real. Who would have known that the Buddha further possesses the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna?
(This section should be read in conjunction with the second verse-paragraph of the "Expedient Means" chapter.)
“World-Honored One, from the past until this very day, throughout both day and night, I have been born through transformation by means of the Dharma and have attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma.
World-Honored One, from this point forward, I shall clarify today the meaning of attaining joy. This follows the preceding text.

I thought to myself: "Although I did not initially understand the skillful means and attained only a minor fruit, since ancient times I have seen various bodhisattvas receive predictions of their future buddhahood;
throughout the day and night, there has never been a moment when I have not suppressed and diminished [my own pride]."
I have been self-critical and exacting of myself, grieving that I have not made further progress and have not attained the prediction of Buddhahood like the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas.
Now, suddenly hearing the Buddha say that whether it be Śrāvakas or Bodhisattvas,
if they hear even a single verse of the Dharma I preach, they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood— this is what I have now heard from the Buddha.
"This is a Dharma never before encountered. Thus, his doubts regarding the Buddha were severed;

his regret for having pursued the Lesser Vehicle vanished, and his body and mind, along with the six sense faculties, all became thoroughly tranquil and at ease, attaining swift peace and security. 'Today I have finally come to know' refers to this."
That is to say, when it was first stated that the Bodhisattvas are truly the sons of the Buddha, while we Śrāvakas are like foster children,

although we had attained the minor fruits of our practice, our hearts were truly not at ease. Now, hearing that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only Bodhisattvas and have no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas,
and further hearing that these twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas, we finally understand.
Today we are truly the Buddha’s sons and bodhisattvas; we are not of the stream of the śrāvakas.

"Born from the Buddha’s mouth" means that the words for attaining Buddhahood have issued from the Buddha’s mouth. By believing the Buddha’s words and becoming his sons, we are born from the Buddha’s mouth.
"Transformatively born from the Dharma" means being transformed by the One Vehicle Dharma to eliminate afflictions.
Afflictions are transformed into bodhi; birth and death are transformed into nirvana without remainder. Regarding "attaining a portion of the Buddha-dharma":

"dharma" refers to the *dharmakāya*, and "portion" refers to partial realization. This means that although one still dwells in the stage of a causal ground (*hetubhūmi*) and has not yet reached the ultimate, since one is truly a son of the Buddha, one has indeed attained partial realization of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*. Śāriputra, having heard this—

The Buddha explains and analyzes this: there are those who enter through direct faith (who, throughout the day and throughout the night, remain steadfast—unlike Laozi, who said, "A whirlwind does not last a morning; a torrential rain does not last a day").
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"When I heard this sound of the Dharma, I attained what I had never experienced before... (omitted)... hearing it also removes my grief and affliction."

"Then, at that time," and so forth, summarizes the first section of the prose commentary, describing the present attainment. "I heard this sound of the Dharma" refers to the text of the chapter on Expedient Means (*upāya*).

"Attaining what has never before been attained. That a follower of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) attains Buddhahood was something that had never occurred in the forty years prior; because what had not existed now exists, their hearts are filled with great joy and their doubts are eliminated). "From of old... and so forth.
The verse refers to what was previously lost. This means that while dwelling within the net of past doubts which had not yet been removed, it appeared as though one had lost the Mahāyāna;

now that the net of doubt has been cleared away, one knows that from time immemorial, having received the Buddha’s teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), these were precisely the steps for attaining the Mahāyāna in the present.

Regarding "the Buddha’s voice and so forth," this means that because one has received the Lesser Vehicle since the past, one is thus able to eliminate the conceit of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Sentient beings were once filled with sorrow and distress; now they have not lost their greatness.

Furthermore, it can eliminate the sorrow and distress of thinking that one might become an Arhat or a sage but fail to attain Buddhahood. Thus, these small and great sounds of the Buddha from the past and the present are both exceedingly rare.

Whether I am dwelling in a mountain valley or beneath the trees of a forest (up to "I am deceiving myself")—this verse is explained in the second section of its prose commentary (*vṛtti*). [Note: Where the prose commentary is expanded, it develops what was not fully expressed.
"Whether I am dwelling" below marks the stage of initiating reflection (the two of the four postures: sitting or walking). "Alas" below explains the nature of that reflection.

Regarding the phrase "of its marks" (*zhi xiāng*): "Ahu" (Alas) is a sound of lamentation, arising from the intensity of distress and affliction. "Deeply reproaching oneself" means to truly reproach oneself; it does not mean daring to reproach the Buddha. The passage beginning with "How could... consists of words of self-reproach, expressing a sense of self-deception.

The commentary states: "To be sincere in one's intentions means not to deceive oneself. Regarding the passage "we, the [Arhats] below," this means that while the Bodhisattvas are certainly sons of the Buddha, we twelve hundred Arhats are likewise sons of the Buddha, because we have entered together with the Bodhisattvas into the dharma of untainted *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the passage "cannot [at the level] below," this means that since our entry into the Path is identical, our exposition of the Path should also be identical;

yet, as we are currently unable to do so, we are deceiving ourselves regarding the causal mind for expounding the Path in the future. Regarding the passage "the golden-colored [body] below," it further refers to oneself...

This deceives one regarding the essential nature of the fruit of attaining the Way in the future. [The thirty-two marks are: (1) The soles of the feet are level and even, like the bottom of a casket; (2) on the soles of the feet are wheels with a thousand spokes;

(3) the fingers and toes are long, surpassing those of gods and humans; (4) the hands and feet are soft and supple; (5) the hands and feet have webbed membranes like those of a royal goose; (6) the heels are full and rounded; (7) the insteps are high and well-formed;

(8) the calves are like those of the *eṇeya* deer king; (9) standing upright, the hands reach and touch the knees; (10) the private parts are concealed as in a horse-king; (11) the body is proportionate in height and breadth; (12) the body hairs are blue-black, soft, and fine; (13) the body hairs curl to the right; (14) the body is of a true golden color.

15. His body emits light, each side of which extends for one *zhang*. 16. His skin is so fine and smooth that dust and water do not adhere to it. 17. Seven parts of his body—the two hands, the two shoulders, and the two shoulders-blades—are flat and full.

18. The area beneath both armpits is full. 19. His body is like that of a lion king. 20. His body is upright and straight. 21. His two shoulders are rounded and handsome. 22. He possesses forty teeth. 23. His teeth are white, pure, even, and closely set; they are deep-rooted. 24. His four canine teeth are white and large.

25. His jaw is like that of a lion. 26. He has attained the supreme among subtle perceptions. 27. His tongue is thin and broad, covering his face up to the hairline when extended. 28. His Brahma-voice is deep and resonant, like that of the *kalaviṅka* bird. 29. The color of his eyes is like...
The golden essence; (30) eyelashes like those of a bull king; (31) the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows; (32) the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head). The ten powers:

(1) the power of knowing what is possible and impossible; (2) the power of karma; (3) the power of meditative concentration; (4) the power of the faculties; (5) the power of aspiration; (6) the power of temperament; (7) the power of the path leading to all destinations; (8) the power of recollecting past lives; (9) the power of the divine eye; (10) the power of the exhaustion of outflows). The various liberations (that is, the eight liberations):

(1) the liberation of one who perceives external forms while possessing internal perception of form, abiding in the first dhyāna; (2) the liberation of one who does not perceive internal form but perceives external forms, abiding in the second dhyāna; (3) the liberation of the perception of purity, fully perfected, abiding in the third dhyāna; (4) the liberation of the perception of infinite space.

They are fully endowed with liberation. They abide in the four dhyānas. Fifth, they contemplate the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Sixth, they contemplate the liberation of the sphere of nothingness. Seventh, they contemplate the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Eighth, they contemplate the liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception. Thus they transcend the triple world).

"Together and equally below" means that since the śrāvakas are the same as the bodhisattvas in awakening to and entering the outflow-free (anāsrava) power of liberation regarding the characteristics of the superior nature of dharmatā, they are all things within the same single dharmatā and ought to attain it together; yet we—

One cannot obtain them alone. Regarding the eighty minor marks of excellence: they begin with the slender and long nails of the toes and end with the *svastika* on the chest. Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*):
they begin with being free from all faults and end with knowing the three periods of time without obstruction or attachment;

these are not shared with those of the two vehicles. (Regarding such merits as these: "such" refers to their equality with the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the one hundred and forty kinds of merit. However, [the total] is one hundred and forty...)

The various merits consist of the aforementioned thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), the four kinds of purity, the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the three ways of non-protection (*arakṣa*).
