To these are added great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*), the permanent destruction of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), as explained at length in the *Huayan jing hui xuanyi* (Profound Record of the Avataṃsaka Assembly). Regarding the phrase "I alone" (*ahaṃ kevalam*): if one acts alone, one cannot act in concert with the multitude like the Buddha; thus, one's practice will fail to achieve its benefit.
My name is heard throughout the five regions of India, whereas the Buddha’s name is heard throughout the ten directions. Thus, my fame is lost [in comparison].
It is a loss. While I have personally benefited from my own virtuous conduct within the mountains and forests, the Buddha’s virtue brings vast and abundant benefit to devas and humans;

thus, I have truly suffered a loss. As for the phrase "reflecting upon myself," it means that I reflect upon whether in my practice, my reputation, or my actual realization, I have failed to achieve the same benefit as the Buddha.
That I am not equal to the Buddha—could it be that the Buddha has deceived me? It is rather I [who am at fault].
Since we ourselves have not studied how a bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of the Great Vehicle, our hearts deceive themselves and our words delude ourselves.
This is what is meant by the statement in the prose section: "This is our own fault."
"I constantly, day and night, reflect upon this matter" (up to) "to teach and transform all bodhisattvas.
This verse clarifies the third section of the prose. The first eight lines correspond to the three phrases in the prose from "Since the past" up to "I constantly reproach myself.
The next twenty lines correspond to the prose from "Now, following... [up to the end].
The Buddha’s hearing of the Dharma never heard before consists of three phrases. This also summarizes the six phrases from the preceding section, beginning with "Why is that?

and ending with "contemplating and attaining realization. The subsequent forty phrases correspond to the prose section from "severing all doubts and regrets" to "attaining the stage of the Buddha-dharma," which comprises seven phrases.
By assigning them in this manner, one ensures that the prose and the verses are clearly distinguished, avoiding any confusion or overlap between the brief and the detailed.
Regarding the literary structure, since the verses themselves possess an internal coherence of introduction and conclusion, they must not be fragmented;
therefore, each line must be explained in turn. "I constantly, beneath the sun," refers to the preceding statement:
although I am aware that self-deception leads to loss, I nevertheless constantly contemplate this day and night, fearing that my understanding may still be incomplete. It is from this that I proceed.
Falling back into the cycle of transmigration, he could not resolve it himself and wished to request the Buddha to decide upon its merits and faults;

thus he said, "I wish to ask the World-Honored One," and so forth. From the passage "I have always seen the World-Honored One" onwards, it means that the reason I could not remain at ease regarding my failure and wished to pose this question was because I had always seen the World-Honored One praising [the Mahayana] before those of the two vehicles.
A Mahāyāna bodhisattva reflects within his own mind: "Since the Buddha is such as this, might he not also require us followers of the two vehicles to become Mahāyāna practitioners?
Thus, day and night, he deliberates upon the matter of its merits and faults.
Now, suddenly hearing the Buddha’s voice declare that all twelve hundred arhats shall likewise become buddhas, he finally realizes that for forty years...
Previously, you preached the Dharma according to what was appropriate; it was truly untainted and difficult to conceive.
It was never intended for us to practice the Lesser Vehicle, but rather to lead us to the site of enlightenment where one attains Buddhahood. I originally clung to false views... [and so on].
This refers to the Buddha’s original intention: "I shall lead you all to the site of enlightenment.

Without waiting for me to explain the reasons, those who quickly contemplate and seek realization in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) do so because they were originally people attached to false views, and furthermore, I was a teacher to various Brahmins who were attached to false views. The World-Honored One knew that I was within the ocean of birth and death.
People’s minds are easily satisfied; therefore, the Four Noble Truths of the Lesser Vehicle were taught to uproot their false views and bestow upon them nirvana.
Following the Buddha’s teachings, I abandoned the heterodox for the orthodox and attained realization of the Dharma of emptiness.
At that time, my mind thought to itself that I had truly reached extinction (nirvana), and thus I did not seek the site of enlightenment on the path to Buddhahood. But now...
He then realized for himself that he had fallen into a lower state. He thought: "Now I have received the Buddha’s instruction as he has arisen from samādhi and told me:
'Although I speak of nirvāṇa, this is a lower state and not true extinction. All dharmas, from their very origin, are eternally characterized by quiescence.
Once a Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall become a Buddha in a future age. I have now begun to realize that what I previously took as realization was not true extinction."

One will certainly attain the same prediction of enlightenment as a bodhisattva and become a Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks, revered by the eight classes of beings including the devas, and like a Buddha in the great assembly, with fame filling the ten directions and extensively benefiting sentient beings;
at that time, one may truly be said to have attained extinction, forever exhausted and without remainder. As for the phrase "like a Buddha in the great assembly," it refers to my [teaching].
Regarding the realization that "the present is right and the past was wrong": this is because the Buddha, amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, declared, "I shall become a Buddha.
Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Buddha, my doubts and regrets have been entirely eliminated. The phrase "when first hearing" refers to the time before those doubts and regrets were removed;
at that time, upon hearing the Buddha say that a person of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) could become a Buddha, my mind...

At that moment, he was also greatly startled and filled with doubt, thinking: "Could it not be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha to preach this? Is he perhaps seeking to disturb and confuse my mind in meditative concentration?

The Buddha, perceiving his doubts, employed various causes, conditions, parables, and skillful means—as in the passage beginning with "The Buddha, by means of various..."—explaining that he had divided the One Vehicle into three vehicles for the sake of teaching. Only then did his mind begin to settle.

"Tranquil as the ocean. This means that the net of doubt regarding the Māras has been completely severed. When the Buddha says "In the past," etc., it means that the Buddha further feared that my doubts about severing [delusions] might arise again;

thus he extensively cites all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions to testify that from the beginning of his birth until the end of his attainment of the Way, and throughout his preaching in the interim, there was nothing but the One Vehicle. For this reason...
I have now reached a definitive certainty that the words regarding the attainment of Buddhahood are indeed the true path of the World-Honored One.
The evil Māra Pāpīyān could never have uttered such things; therefore, it is said that this was not a fabrication by Māra.

As for the phrase "I fell," etc., it means that since I have reached a definitive certainty that these are the Buddha’s teachings, why did I previously suspect them to be the words of Māra? It was because I had fallen into doubt.

This is because of the net [of doubt]. Regarding the phrase "hearing the Buddha’s gentle and supple [voice]," it means that having already fallen into the net of doubt, how can his mind now be as peaceful as the ocean?

It is because he hears the Buddha’s composed and supple voice—profound, far-reaching, and subtle—which expounds the pure Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; therefore, my heart rejoices and my doubts are dispelled.
"Repentance is forever exhausted. "Abiding securely in true wisdom" means not abiding in the provisional wisdom of former skillful means.
"I shall certainly become a Buddha" means not contemplating the attainment of the minor fruits of the two vehicles.
Abiding securely in true wisdom is the cause for the great task of opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. One shall certainly become...

"Buddha" is the fruit of the great matter of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Because he possesses these great causes and great fruits, he is revered by devas and humans; this is self-awakening (*svabodhi*).
By turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and teaching and transforming all bodhisattvas, he awakens others;

this is the perfection of awakening and practice (*bodhicaryā-paripūri*). [The passage] "My heart is filled with great joy; I shall certainly become a Buddha" corresponds to the "great joy" arising from the superior grade of mind, where one knows for oneself that one shall become a Buddha. Thus, the two passages illuminate one another.

According to the profound principles of the Avataṃsaka Assembly, it is said that upon first attaining the nature of a sage, one fully realizes the three types of emptiness and is able to benefit both oneself and others, thereby giving rise to great joy. Thus we know that when Śāriputra and others experienced joy upon receiving their predictions of enlightenment, they had all ascended to the first stage among the ten stages of a Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra... [down to] "the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind.

From "At that time" onwards, Śāriputra recounts his past sorrow and present joy to present his understanding; the Buddha likewise recounts his past teachings and his current forgetfulness to bestow a prediction of enlightenment.
By saying, "I am now among devas and humans," he certifies that [the teaching] is not false, so as to cause [others] not to...
One may again forget the great and grasp for the small. Furthermore, based on what was stated in the verse regarding being "venerated by devas and humans," you said:
"If you require veneration from devas, humans, and others, I shall speak before a great assembly of devas and humans."

"In the past," etc., refers to the narration of former events. Regarding the "twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas," according to the scriptural text, these must be the twenty-two thousand Buddhas of the *Vibhāṣin* (King of Majestic Sound) era when [the Buddha] was the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta.
"For the sake of the unsurpassed path" means that while he was a bodhisattva under those Buddhas, he never taught Śāriputra anything inferior; how much less so now that he has attained Buddhahood?
Furthermore, how could one be delivered by means of the *hīnayāna* (Small Vehicle) teachings?

As for the phrase "you also, throughout the long night," it means that not only did the Buddha never teach Śāriputra the *hīnayāna* during his immeasurable kalpas, but Śāriputra himself also never studied the *hīnayāna* teachings during his own immeasurable kalpas.
That he is said to have "received and studied" [the teachings] throughout the "long night" is known by the Buddha himself.
"Seeing that [his mind] was not yet opened, although he had received instruction from the Buddha, he remained entirely within the long night of ignorance.

Regarding the phrase "I used skillful means," this describes the present situation. It means that whereas in the past he taught the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) to those of great capacity, he now first delivers those of small capacity.
This is the Buddha’s skillful means of first leading Śāriputra by means of the Small Vehicle and subsequently introducing him to the Great Vehicle. Śāriputra...
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha did not previously [teach me]," it means that since the Buddha formerly instructed you to aspire to the Mahāyāna path of the Buddha,
he now employs the skillful means of the lesser fruit to guide you. This is because, having studied under him in the long night of ignorance in the past,
you have completely forgotten the Mahāyāna aspiration taught by the Buddha and have instead settled for the lesser fruit.
"You claim for yourself that you have attained extinction; how could the Buddha’s vision of saving you be so meager?

When I say, 'I now wish to treat you as an equal,' it means that although you are skilled at forgetting, I am skilled at remembering. I do not wish for you to forget now; rather, I wish for you to remember."
Therefore, for you who are followers of the Hīnayāna Śrāvakas, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is called "Mahāyāna" because it is a teaching of the Bodhisattva-dharma and a sūtra protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
Otherwise, for you Hīnayāna followers, I would have merely taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to deliver sentient beings.
"It is sufficient to reach ultimate *nirvāṇa* through aging, illness, and death. Know that these were spoken for the sake of the *śrāvakas*.
The *śrāvaka* was originally a *bodhisattva*. Since the *śrāvaka* is already a *bodhisattva*, how could you have ever lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision?
Why do you rejoice in the present while lamenting the past? (The five phrases following "for the sake of" constitute a major textual crux of this sutra.)

Regarding the great essential points and major pivots of the sutra’s meaning and principle: the first three phrases extend directly from this chapter to the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Learners and Non-learners. The latter two phrases extend directly from the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation.

As for these great essential points, one thereby knows that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition, revealing to all beings the knowledge and vision of attaining Buddhahood—something they have never before taught to the śrāvakas.
"Śāriputra, in the future age, even until the Semblance Dharma remains in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas,
this shall be precisely for the sake of all śrāvakas to preach the Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,

which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas. Thus he concludes the meaning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, wherein the World-Honored Buddhas rely solely upon—
Regarding the passage on "appearing in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition":

it is because this sutra causes those of the two vehicles to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which constitutes the "wondrous Dharma"; and because they receive the prediction of receiving a land adorned with majestic splendor for kalpas, which constitutes the "great matter.
It is like the *udumbara* flower—a rare and auspicious great treasure, a blue lotus—that appears only once in a long time.

[The passage] beginning with "Furthermore, in the past, I was once at the places of twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas for the sake of the unsurpassed path," etc., is the section where the Buddha recounts the causes of great events from the past to Śāriputra. This section is [the dialogue] between the Buddha and Śāriputra.
This serves as the condition for accomplishing great matters in the future. Its text consists of eight sections, recording those great matters.
For all sentient beings, it may be that they do not attain Buddhahood at all; yet once they do attain Buddhahood, these [sections] are certainly indispensable.

They are precisely the ritual for the preaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, as mentioned in the preceding chapter. All subsequent passages concerning the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa) are based upon this.

Although there are differences between the extensive and abbreviated versions, they do not differ from this. Śāriputra, regarding the initial bestowal of the prophecy for the stage of the causal ground at the beginning of the *Nidāna-parivarta*, it says:
"One who makes offerings to several thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas" refers to the fulfillment of merit (*puṇya*).
This is what is meant in the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta* by "having drawn near to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas. It is [the fulfillment of] wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, "upholding the True Dharma and fulfilling the path practiced by Bodhisattvas" refers to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃbhāra*).
This is what is meant in the "Expedient Means" chapter when it says, "fully practicing all the immeasurable paths and dharmas of the Buddhas.

Regarding the prediction of the two adornments of merit and wisdom, the phrase "passing through immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas" is used because sentient beings are infinite and their afflictions...

Afflictions are inexhaustible, for the Dharma-gates are immeasurable and the Buddha-way is unsurpassed. This refers to what was mentioned in the preceding passage as "the teaching of the Bodhisattvas.
From the words "you shall attain Buddhahood" onwards, it is the second section: the bestowal of the prediction of the fruit, including the ten titles of a Buddha.
This refers to what is called "his fame being heard everywhere" in the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*.

"Flower Radiance" (*Puṣyarāja*) is his name. The ten titles of a Tathāgata, such as "Tathāgata," are his epithets; these epithets signify that beneath the name there is reality. Regarding "Tathāgata":

the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that all phenomena are according to their true nature (*tathatā*). Because they come from nowhere and go nowhere, they are called "Thus-Come" (*Tathāgata*). This refers to the three virtues.

"Middle" (*madhya*) is a designation for the *dharmakāya*. "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*) refers to what the subsequent sutra states: "Universally among devas and humans, one is worthy of receiving offerings.

This is a designation for liberation (*vimukti*) among the three virtues. "Perfectly Complete Knower" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*): "Perfectly" (*samyak*) distinguishes this from the heterodoxy of non-Buddhists;
"Complete" (*saṃ*) distinguishes this from the partiality of the Lesser Vehicle. It means that all various things manifest before one—whether pines are straight or thorns are crooked—are fully known.

The crane is white and the crow is black; he fully understands their fundamental causes. Even as far as beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows the number of drops in a single drop of rain.
Therefore, he is called the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (*Samyak-saṃbuddha*), which is the designation for *prajñā* among the three virtues. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
The Buddha’s body fills the Dharma-realm; this is the Tathāgata. He manifests universally before all sentient beings; this is the Arhat.
He responds to conditions and meets with those who seek him without exception; this is the Samyak-saṃbuddha. Yet he eternally dwells upon this seat of Bodhi;

this is the Sugata. These three are the general titles. The following seven are the specific titles. Regarding "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna): "Knowledge" (vidyā) refers to wisdom.

The "Vehicles" (pāramitās) refer to the five perfections, such as giving (dāna) and so forth. "Perfection" (*pūrṇa*) means that by upholding the True Dharma, one is perfected in clarity (*vidyā-pūrṇa*);
by making offerings to several thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, one is perfected in practice (*caryā-pūrṇa*).

For being perfected in clarity, one receives the title of "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*); for being perfected in practice, one receives the title of "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*). This is the title of "Self-Awakened" (referring to merit and wisdom).

That which is called "endowed with feet" refers to the fruit of virtue—the fulfillment of merit and wisdom—just as a person who has feet is able to walk and stop. "The Well-Gone One (Sugata) and Knower of the World (Lokavid)" is a title for one who awakens others.

"Well" (Su) means capable; "Gone" (Gata) means having departed. "World" (Loka) refers to the three worlds: the world of the vessel, the world of sentient beings, and the world of wisdom and correct awakening.
The world of the vessel consists of mountains, forests, rivers, oceans, and so forth, which are like a vessel. As for the spirits... [and so on].

It contains sentient beings. Regarding the world of sentient beings: there are various categories such as those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, each possessing its own distinct emotional nature.
Regarding the world of the perfectly awakened ones: it is filled with the noble sages of the Three Vehicles, each possessing the correct path they have realized.
"Understanding" refers to liberation. As stated in the Great Sūtra regarding the lords of the three worlds, although each claims to have attained [their respective state],...
These are the gates of liberation; yet all are the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which is able to manifest appropriately through skillful means. This is also another epithet for the Tathāgata.
As for the "Unsurpassed One" (Anuttara-puruṣa), it refers to those from humans up to the gods, and from the gods down to the followers of the two vehicles.

From the followers of the two vehicles up to the bodhisattvas, and from the bodhisattvas up to the equal-enlightened ones (samyaksambuddha), each may regard themselves as superior, yet each has one who is above them.
Only the Buddha alone transcends both the mundane and the supramundane, and there is no one further above him.

This is also another designation for the "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat). Regarding the term "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi): "taming" (damya) refers to the process of training and cultivation; "tamer" (sārathi) refers to the driver.
This refers to "restraint" (*kōyū*). It is the noble title for a man or gentleman who is capable both of preaching and practicing [the Dharma].
All sentient beings fail to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), and thus they cycle through the six realms of existence without ceasing.

The Buddha preached the teachings of the Three Vehicles and nine divisions of scripture to regulate and restrain them, leading them from the state of ordinary beings to that of the sages, and from the small to the great, so that they may awaken to their original nature.
There is the Buddha-nature. Throughout the trichiliocosm, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is not a place where a Bodhisattva has sacrificed their body and life.
Were it not for one who is a Great Man capable of taming both self and others, who could possibly achieve this?
This is another epithet for the One of Perfect Knowledge (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*). As for the Teacher of Gods and Humans: all the gods within the three realms...
All others are disciples, while the Buddha alone is the Teacher, for he is uniquely capable of skillfully taming and guiding them. "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*).
Awakening oneself is the unsurpassed state; awakening others is being a "knower of the world who has gone to bliss.

When the practice of awakening is perfected, one is "endowed with knowledge and conduct. Because these three types of awakening are complete and all myriad virtues are fully possessed, he is thus titled [the Buddha].
The Buddha, the World-Honored One (Bhagavān), is so called because he has perfected these three types of awakening and is fully endowed with all myriad virtues;

thus, he is revered by all sentient and non-sentient beings, as well as by the three worlds of wisdom and perfect enlightenment. He is designated as "World-Honored" (Shizun) because he is the unsurpassed among men (Śāstṛ).

Speaking in terms of the fundamental *dharmakāya*, he is called a "Great Man" (*puruṣa*) because he is a tamer; speaking in terms of the adornment of myriad practices, he is called a "Teacher" by devas and humans.

Thus, regarding his attainment of Buddhahood through the transformation and teaching of both humans and devas, among these ten titles, none within the ten realms of existence—except for the Buddha himself—dare to assume them; from the devas down to the bodhisattvas, none are capable of bearing such names.

What was referred to above as "being protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" is this. What was referred to in the "Expedient Means" chapter as "accomplishing all profound and unprecedented dharmas" is this.
This bestows upon Śāriputra the prediction of the primary retribution (vipāka) based on cause and effect;

below, it bestows the prediction of the third [category], the environmental retribution (niśraya-vipāka). The section beginning with "The name of the land" introduces the subject; the section beginning with "That realm" provides the explanation.
The final two lines [of the preceding verse] refer to the adornment of the pure *nirmāṇakāya* (the primary retribution) of sentient beings.

The five lines beginning with "lapis lazuli" refer to the adornment of the pure *bhājanaloka* (the environmental retribution) of non-sentient things. The section beginning with "Tathāgata Padmaprabha" records the fourth turning of the wheel of Dharma;
that he teaches by means of the three vehicles is because, as stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter, all Buddhas appear... [in this manner].
Regarding the world of the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya), it is asked: Since the appearance of the Buddha Puṣparāja was not during an evil age, why did he also teach the three vehicles?
The answer is: It was due to his original vow. According to the *Mahākaruṇā-gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*, Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas;
on one occasion, when a brahmin begged for his eyes, he spat upon them and stepped over them. His body...
The son gave rise to anger and regressed to the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). He made a vow that on the day he attained Buddhahood, he would open the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

At the end of that *kalpa*, he was granted the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) as the fifth member of the retinue. This section contains the heading, the evidence, and the explanation. (The record states: "In the state of Chu, nothing was considered a treasure except for goodness;

this was taken as a treasure. The Sūtra regards the Bodhisattva as a great treasure; they are the same. Regarding "Those various [beings] below," many are counted as treasures. Regarding "If one desires [to attain] below," it is based on following and upholding [the teachings] as a treasure. Regarding "Not at the beginning below," virtue cultivated over a long time is the treasure. Regarding "In the absence of [conditions] below," it refers to planting the roots of virtue.)

[The Buddha] constantly acts for the benefit of those below. The Buddha praises the planting of merit as a treasure. One should always cultivate the treasure of wisdom. Being endowed with great supernormal powers is a treasure. Skillfully knowing [the path] is the efficacy of attaining the Buddha’s wisdom. To be upright and without guile, taking truth as one's treasure; to have firm resolve and mindfulness, untroubled by demons or heterodoxy—these are treasures.
Śāriputra, regarding the lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma, [the Buddha] bestows the prediction of his sixth dwelling in the world and its duration.

After twelve intermediate kalpas, the Tathāgata Puṣpārāma will pass away; [the Buddha] then bestows the seventh prediction concerning the time of his parinirvāṇa and the preaching of the Great [Dharma].

This is the prediction of the Bodhisattva’s transformation and attainment of Buddhahood. Śāriputra is the one who, following Huaguang, receives the prediction for the eighth [period] concerning the duration of the True and Semblance Dharma remaining in the world.
This marks the beginning of Śāriputra’s future attainment of Buddhahood through the Great Matter of Cause and Condition.
At the conclusion of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha bestowed individual predictions upon each member of the great assembly of devas and humans, and Śāriputra recorded them one by one.
This refers to what is called in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "The mind gave rise to great joy, for he knew within himself that he would become a Buddha.
The scriptural text extends from the point where the Buddha, after preaching the sutra, entered samādhi, emitted light, and caused the earth to tremble, up to this point.

This alone constitutes a definitive conclusion. One can thus believe that the words of the Buddhas—that they appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition—are not false.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Śāriputra, in a future age you shall attain Buddhahood as the Honored One of Universal Wisdom, named Flower Radiance (Puṣyarasmi), and you shall deliver immeasurable multitudes.
This verse is the text of the prediction of the second fruit and the ten titles.
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas, perfected the bodhisattva practices, and realized the supreme path through merits such as the ten powers—
this verse bestows the first introductory passage concerning the ground of the causal stage for those with two feet.
After immeasurable kalpas have passed, there will be a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha.
This verse marks the bestowal of the prediction upon the fifth retinue member.
The world shall be named Vimalaviśuddhāpagatakalmaṣā (Stainless, Pure, and Free from Defilement), where flowers, fruits, and seeds are always present.
This verse provides the textual passage concerning the third [aspect], the world of the secondary environment (*pratyaya-loka*).
"The bodhisattvas in that land are always firm in their resolve" (up to) "...the transformations of the Buddha Padmaprabha."
This is the commentary on the fifth verse of the *Śākyamuni-buddha-vaṃśa-anukrama-nirdeśa*, concerning the prediction regarding his retinue.
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory... [until] his lifespan will be eight minor kalpas.
This verse grants the sixth [point], the passage concerning the duration of the lifespan:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world... up to "...you should indeed rejoice.
This verse grants the eighth [point], the passage concerning the length of time the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma remain in the world. It briefly summarizes the fourth discourse.

The Dharma of the Three Vehicles. The seventh passage concerning the bestowal of the prediction of firm fulfillment (*kṣānti-pūrṇa-vyākaraṇa*) states: "The True Dharma (*saddharma*) possesses both teaching and practice; the realization of its fruit is not in vain.
The Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpa-dharma*) possesses teaching but lacks practice; it merely preserves the outward forms of the Triple Gem.
*Kalpa* means a period of time, just as in the Central Kingdom [China] a year is called a 'car' (*zài*) or a 'suì', whereas in the Western Regions [India], one speaks of 'years' (*nǐnsuì*)."

This constitutes the *kalpa* (the "Convenient Means" chapter states: "Among the assembly of śrāvakas, the Buddha declared me to be foremost; yet regarding my own wisdom, I am now in doubt and cannot fully comprehend it. It is precisely because his doubts were not yet resolved that he was addressed first among those of the highest grade.

It is precisely because his wisdom was foremost that he presented his understanding here first and attained the prediction [of enlightenment] beforehand. The "Highest Grade" chapter asks: "Is this the ultimate dharma? Or is this the path to be practiced?

Here, the Buddha first recounts for him the events at the sites of twenty trillion buddhas, thereby clarifying the path to be practiced. Subsequently, he grants him the prediction concerning the adornment of the kalpa and the land, thereby clarifying the ultimate dharma. The "Highest Grade" chapter says: "I pray you, utter the subtle and wondrous sound. At that time—)
He speaks according to reality; herein, the exposition and the prediction constitute the very subtle voice, which is speaking according to reality.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus... [up to] ...only now has he again turned the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths... [omitted] ...all dedicating it toward the Buddha-way."
"At that time," and so forth. The fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings are those enumerated in the Introduction Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

When the Great Assembly saw [the Buddha], Śāriputra himself described how he was revered by gods, humans, and others; the Buddha then conferred the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon him in the presence of the great assembly of gods and humans.
Thus, when the prediction was completed, the great assembly of gods and humans all rejoiced, made offerings, and celebrated with praise for this rare prediction.
This is the dedication of merit. In the first three requests made by Śāriputra, he said: "In this assembly, there are immeasurable multitudes who are able to revere and believe in this Dharma.
This refers to them. Each one removed their lower garment and, recounting the causes for their joy, offered worship.

Regarding the phrase "with superior robes" (the celestial lords of the desire and form realms offer divine, exquisite garments): when offerings are frequently described in terms of clothing, it indicates taking refuge.

Regarding the phrase "with flowers": this shows that the cause is identical to the fruit. (The celestial robes scattered [by the Bodhisattvas] revolving spontaneously in the void clarify the turning from the Small Vehicle toward the Great, and the transformation of the three vehicles into one.
The fact that the various celestial musical instruments all play simultaneously clarifies that both eye-and-form and ear-and-sound have all become the empty characteristic of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "and then" (*ji er zuo*): this praises the One Vehicle Dharma previously taught (referring to the *Upāya-paryāya*: "Having reflected on these matters, he then proceeded to Vārāṇasī," etc.). Regarding the phrase "now then" (*jin nai*): this rejoices in what is [taught] now.

This refers to the teaching of the One Vehicle Dharma (as seen in the *Upāya-paryāya* chapter: "Now I am joyful and fearless; among the bodhisattvas, I shall directly abandon the provisional means and teach only the Unsurpassed Way," etc.).
In the verse, the first four lines praise the past; the section beginning with "Now again" praises the present. Vārāṇasī was the place where the Hīnayāna was taught;

the five groups of disciples were those who attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle. "Arising and ceasing" refers to the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing, which differ from [the truth of] non-arising.
This gives rise to the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Regarding the statement that "this Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle":
it means that the present Mahāyāna is different from the former Hīnayāna; yet, the former Hīnayāna is precisely the present Mahāyāna.

This is why it is so exceedingly profound and subtle. There are few who are able to believe in it. It is because it is so profound and subtle that there are few who can believe; it is precisely because they believe...
It was few; therefore, we have often heard of its smallness, but were unable to hear of its greatness.
When the World-Honored One preached this Dharma, he spoke of those with great wisdom and resolute faith, such as Śāriputra, who has now received the prediction of his future Buddhahood.
Thus, although we ourselves lack such great wisdom, if we can merely rejoice in it, we too shall certainly attain Buddhahood within the three worlds.
He is the most honored and supreme. This corresponds to the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), where Mañjuśrī says:

"If there are those seeking the three vehicles who have doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them for them, so that they are exhausted without remainder. This refers to the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*).

"Then he provides the desk upon which the *Guangji* (Extensive Record) is laid out. From "The Buddha-way descends" onwards, he praises how there is reality within the provisional teachings of the past.
From "That which I have [attained]" onwards, he redirects the present Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...please explain the causes and conditions so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.

From the words "At that time" onwards, Śāriputra acts as a representative for his peers; he seeks to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for them, just as he himself has cleared away his doubts and received his prediction of enlightenment.
Therefore, he speaks on behalf of the twelve hundred people, initiating a series of various parables.

[This refers to the passage in the "Expedient Means" chapter where Śāriputra knows that the fourfold assembly harbors doubts while he himself has not yet fully understood them. Having received the Buddha’s confirmation and prediction above, his own personal doubts are now resolved. He requests again on behalf of the assembly, thereby completing the case of understanding the doubts of the fourfold assembly.

"World-Honored One, if it is thus" [and so forth] clarifies that there is no harm (it should be understood that there is both a proof and an explanation).
How much more so when the elder knows for himself [and so forth], concluding that it is entirely beneficial. From "The Buddha told Śāriputra" [and so forth], he praises his detailed explanation.

The parable clarifies the matter, and the response to the question is made with full awareness; hence it says, "Excellent," and so forth. The parable consists of five sections, and this section is the most important.
For the twelve hundred arhats had doubted that the Buddha’s prior teaching of the Dharma of the three vehicles was false, and they regretted that the nirvāṇa they had attained was illusory.
Now that the reason for this has been illustrated through the parable, and further clarified by comparing the earlier and later stages, [it serves to resolve their doubts].

I know that the reason the three vehicles were previously taught was to lead [beings] out of the burning house of the triple world, so that they might sit in the open air, escape suffering, preserve their own lives, and obtain a small measure of pleasure.
The reason the single vehicle is now taught is that only after escaping the suffering of the triple world can one ride the precious chariot and likewise preserve one's life. Thus...
To transform sentient beings is to benefit both self and others. Thus we know that the present teaching of the One Vehicle is precisely the fruition of why the Three Vehicles were taught in the past;
it is not that the present is real while the past was false. Seeing that the Buddha-dharma unfolds gradually, [the Buddha] does not bestow it recklessly.
This corresponds to the long passage in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, I distinguish and teach three," as well as the verse.
The text universally proclaims to the great assembly: "I shall teach and transform all bodhisattvas solely by means of the path of the One Vehicle;
there are no śrāvaka disciples.
[It continues: "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is likewise thus... even though he encounters great suffering, he does not regard it as an affliction."
This corresponds to the first section of the parable. From the passage "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata... onwards, the Buddha is equated with the elder;
he is the father of all the world, possessing virtue and being without fault. From the passage "In all... onwards, it clarifies that he is without fault.

This refers to the sentient beings of the hells and the three miserable realms, who possess the faults of fear and the perishing of the分段生死 (parīttābhisaṃskārika-jarāmaraṇa, or birth-and-death with distinct segments).

Among humans and devas, there are the faults of the five signs of decline appearing within their meritorious rewards, as well as the faults of various decays, afflictions, and anxieties such as poverty, distress, and separation from loved ones.

Although the noble ones of the Two Vehicles are free from the fault of birth-and-death with distinct segments, they still possess the transformation and death (vaipākika-jarāmaraṇa) arising from ignorance.
The darkness of death prevents one from opening up the vision of a Buddha’s knowledge. The Buddha, however, has forever exhausted all such faults without remainder.
Furthermore, as for the phrase "and fully accomplishes" below, this clarifies the possession of virtues;

that is, because he possesses real virtues, he has accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), great supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), and the power of great wisdom.

Because he possesses the virtue of power, he is fully endowed with the two perfections of skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*) of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
He is never weary; this is sympathetic joy (*muditā*). He constantly seeks virtuous deeds to benefit all beings; this is equanimity (*upekṣā*).

For if one does not experience great joy, one will become weary and fail to constantly seek virtuous deeds; likewise, if one does not exercise great equanimity [toward the welfare of others], one will not persevere.
Thus, although they seek virtuous deeds, they are unwilling to benefit all sentient beings and instead give rise [to rebirth] within the decayed and ancient fire-houses of the triple world.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In order to deliver sentient beings," it means that since the Buddha already possesses such virtue, he need not enter the triple world again;
for since his cultivation of virtue is already faultless, there is no further reason for him to enter the triple world, as he has severed all delusions. Now, there is none.

Having transcended all virtues, he nevertheless re-enters the burning house of the triple world. Because the Buddha himself is free from suffering, he brings sentient beings out of their suffering as well;
because he himself has attained realization, he desires to transform sentient beings so that they too may attain unsurpassed Bodhi.
It is for this reason that this one Buddha alone is able to act as the father of the sentient beings within the nine dharma-realms. Thus it is seen.
Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings," sentient beings are here correlated with the children within the burning house.

Although they are all sons of the Buddha, they have not yet emerged from the triple world (*tridhātu*) and thus experience little joy and much suffering. Birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth—everything that is born possesses these;

this collectively clarifies how the eight factors constitute suffering. Furthermore, from the section on the "five desires" (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) onwards, it specifically clarifies how the eight factors constitute suffering. [This] refers to seeing the triple world.
The severity of the circumstances of being burned and boiled in the burning house refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

These are the five coarse and inferior phenomena—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—obtained in the third section below. These five phenomena constitute the painful conditions of what sentient beings currently crave, pursue, and seek.
Karma belongs to the preceding cause. Furthermore, "below" refers to this craving, pursuit, and seeking; this is [the meaning of] "good."
The suffering of the five desires brings about the karma that invites present suffering as well as the fruits of future retribution, such as the hells;

therefore, it is said that one "currently undergoes manifold sufferings," and so forth. The above explains the four sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, encompassing the three periods of time.
Here, "present" refers to the current life, and "future" refers to after death; old age and sickness are included therein. If one is born in the heavens...
Regarding the "superior" [level]: this explains the four sufferings of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction. The text follows from the preceding:

it means that not only does one undergo the intense suffering of the hells and the three evil paths after death, but even if one possesses slight wholesome karma and is born among gods or humans, one still cannot avoid the sorrows of poverty and lack of wealth, destitution and lack of status, or hardship and lack of success.
Those who were once close relatives and friends, naturally loving and kind toward one another, now suffer the particular grief of separation.
Those who were once treacherous ministers, usurpers, or evil companions, naturally hostile, harmful, hateful, and suspicious, now suffer the particular affliction of being gathered together.

Thus, throughout the three periods of time, the causes and effects of the five realms of existence—whether good or evil—are all suffering. As for the state of being burned and boiled therein, how can it possibly be described?
The passage beginning with "In this way" concludes the general outline of suffering and clarifies that its subtle and manifold aspects are difficult to describe exhaustively.
The phrase "sentient beings are submerged within it" means that although the Buddha perceives this as suffering, sentient beings instead sink into it and regard it as pleasure.
The section beginning with "With joy" correctly explains their submersion within it.

The meaning of this fully concludes the preceding text. It states that the five desires and material gain are fundamentally realms of suffering, yet sentient beings regard them as sources of pleasure;
thus they give rise to joy and engage in play, greedily clinging to and pursuing them.

These are fundamentally states of mental anguish, yet because the nature of sentient beings fears that their greed will not be excessive or their seeking not skillful, they remain unaware of it. [This concerns] the three hells.
The path of rebirth is inevitably a bitter retribution; one ought to feel a chill in one's heart and stand in awe of it, yet instead people do not believe this.

They look only toward their lives before birth, having no leisure to consider what follows after death; thus they feel no alarm or dread. Whether in the heavens or among humans, poverty and distress abound.
Separation from the beloved and encountering the hated are, by their very nature, a mass of suffering; they are things that should be loathed and avoided.
Yet, one plants small roots of goodness as minor causes, seeking only the human body and celestial blessings, fearing only that these might not be obtained; thus, one does not give rise to revulsion.
Regarding these various kinds of suffering, all those who seek liberation ought to strive for it; yet sentient beings remain submerged and mired within them, and thus do not seek liberation.
Because of this delusion, they lack wisdom and therefore fail to perceive [the truth].
Because they fail to perceive it, they feel no alarm. Because they feel no alarm, they do not give rise to revulsion.
Because they do not give rise to revulsion, they do not seek liberation; instead, within this burning house of the triple world, they work as the sun rises and sink as the sun sets.
When the sun rises, they gallop eastward following their wholesome karma; when the sun sets, they flee westward following their unwholesome karma.

Changing heads and faces, they wander back and forth through the five destinies. Even for hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of kalpas, they fail to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Even when experiencing the great suffering of the Avīci Hell, they do not regard it as a calamity.

How is this different from your sons, whose bodies are being tormented by fire and whose pain is so acute that their hearts feel no aversion or distress, nor do they have the intention to seek escape?
Śāriputra, when the Buddha had seen this, he thought thus: [up to] "By what means can they understand the wisdom of the Buddha?
Regarding the phrase "Śāriputra, when the Buddha had seen this," it corresponds to the second section, the passage on the parable; the first seven lines constitute the reflection.
This means that the Buddha saw these sentient beings taking suffering for pleasure and considering them as if beyond salvation. Nevertheless, sentient beings are divided into...

His son, being truly ignorant, does not seek liberation for himself. Since I am his father and possess the perfect and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), how could I follow that ignorance and thus fall into unkindness by failing to fulfill the way of a father?
Therefore, it is said: "Then he had this thought," and so forth. This is why the Buddha clearly understands the capacities of sentient beings.
It was not that he did not accord with the Dharma, but rather that he necessarily sought to apply the Dharma according to the specific capacity of the recipient.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further provides the following [teaching], which corresponds to the second seven-day period of contemplation: namely, the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of happiness.

Although this is the duty that a Buddha, as a father, must fully fulfill toward those who follow the Way, the Buddha further reflects that while the Dharma is great, the capacities of beings are small; thus, it would ultimately be difficult to abandon skillful means in favor of the ultimate truth for the sake of all sentient beings.
This praises the qualities of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, powers, and fearlessness as being common to both sentient beings and Buddhas;
hence it says that "sentient beings cannot be equal [to them]. Below, the text raises a question to provide an explanation:

why is it that although these dharmas—such as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—are praised as being common to both sentient beings and Buddhas, sentient beings instead fail to attain liberation through them?
Because sentient beings have not yet escaped the karmic suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death, they are scorched by the burning house of the triple world.
Even if one were to grant them happiness, they would be unable to believe it; it is like a person in shackles who cannot suddenly be told of the glory of wearing embroidered robes.
Therefore, it is said, "How could they understand? and so forth. Although the Buddha [acts] for their sake...

A compassionate father cannot suddenly instruct his unworthy children; therefore, he gives rise to the following passage. First he extracts them from suffering, and only afterward does he bestow happiness.
This accords with the third sevenfold contemplation: it is the skillful means of concealing the ultimate truth while revealing the provisional.
The third section below clarifies the first phrase: "one should first extract the suffering and hardships of sentient beings. The fourth section clarifies the subsequent phrase:
"one later bestows the wisdom and bliss of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, causing them to sport therein."
"Śāriputra, it is like that elder... [up to] ...like those sons who, seeking ox-carts, emerged from the burning house.

This corresponds to the third section of the parable. In each section, the presentation of the metaphor followed by its application to the Dharma is intended to facilitate the easy understanding and liberation of the twelve hundred people.
The passage beginning with "Śāriputra, it is like that elder" cites the metaphorical text to clarify the commencement.

Thus, he conceals the reality (śūnyatā) and reveals the provisional (upāya). Thereafter, he bestows [the teaching] upon those of inferior capacity. This clarifies that at the end, one enters reality by means of the provisional.

The Tathāgata likewise bestows it upon those of inferior capacity; this accords with his concealment of reality. He does so solely through wisdom, which accords with his revelation of the provisional. [Question: Wisdom is reality, while skillful means (upāya) is the provisional.

The Sūtra states that wisdom and skillful means are both reality and the provisional, unfolding together. Why do you say in your commentary only "by means of the provisional"? [Answer: The Sūtra singles out the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) as reality. It begins with the Buddha himself...

The reality of enjoyment consists of both wisdom and skillful means acting as the provisional. This clarifies that when responding to capacities, the provisional is identical to the real; it clarifies that employing the provisional inherently contains the real. Otherwise, from what would the provisional arise, and to where would it return once extinguished? This is why this sutra clarifies that the provisional is not separate from the real.
As for the "three realms": the desire realm consists of the five destinies living in intermingled proximity;

the form realm consists of the four dhyānas; and the formless realm consists of the four emptinesses. Each has its own boundaries and categories. They are all called the "burning house" because they are all samsara.

This is the enumeration. (The section beginning with "To deliver" [拔濟下] follows: The sentient beings are equated with the sons of the elder; the teaching of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) is equated with the three carts outside the gate. The above provides a general summary of the two fruits—suffering and happiness—both within and without the triple world (*traidhātuka*). As for the following section...

A separate explanation of the cause of the *samudaya-satya*—the origin that brings about the fruits of suffering within the three realms: the five objects of desire, such as form and so forth, are like fires because attachment to them gives rise to craving.
This is why they are burned. Do not be greedy. These words of admonition and exhortation concern knowing suffering and abandoning its origin. Alas!
The five desires of the three realms are originally the fires of suffering that destroy life, yet sentient beings instead delight in sinking into them, playing with joy without fear.
This is because they regard the five desires, such as form and so forth, as subtle and exquisite, failing to realize they are coarse and debased.
The suffering of the fire of affliction. Now the Buddha exhorts you to recognize this suffering so that you may sever its origin (*samudaya*);

therefore he says, "You must not remain," and further, "Do not covet," and so forth. For from a single instance of covetousness arises craving and grasping (*upādāna*). Once craving and grasping exist, objects are divided into the favorable and the unfavorable.
When they are favorable, one flows along with them and forgets to return; this is truly the fire of suffering. When they are unfavorable, anger and delusion follow.
Thus life arises; it is especially a fire of suffering. Then the flames of the fuel of the three poisons will burn on without ceasing from birth to birth.
You must quickly descend into the triple world and instruct them to aspire toward cessation and cultivate the Path.

While one might perhaps speak with leniency regarding the suffering and its origin within the triple world when they do not yet realize it is fire, now that it has been clearly pointed out to you, it is as if fire is burning your eyebrows.
Since the urgency of burning one's head [to extinguish suffering] is paramount, it is said: "Quickly exit beyond the three realms.

Regarding the cessation and path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is no one to provide a guarantee; one might fear they are difficult to accomplish. Now that the Buddha exists, he acts as a guarantor for them.

Then one will emerge from the suffering within the triple world and attain the bliss beyond the triple world; thus, it shall not be in vain. The above constitutes the teaching on aspiring toward cessation (*nirodha*).
"You all should simply, in this present life... and so forth, constitutes the teaching on practicing the Path (*mārga*).
The Tathāgata, by means of such [teachings], brings them to completion. Although he possesses powers and fearlessnesses and the like, he does not employ them; rather, he relies solely upon wisdom.
Thus, it is in this manner that [the Buddha] rescues sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world.

Following the statement "He further spoke these words," the text clarifies the meaning of why the cessation and the path of the three vehicles constitute bliss, thereby explaining the significance of the words used to entice and advance them—all of which are praised by the Sage.
This refers to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and others, which cannot be praised by ordinary beings within the triple world.
This is a sigh of relief. "Sovereign and unbound" means not being fettered by the five desires, wealth, profit, or the various forms of suffering.
"Having nothing on which to rely or seek" means not relying on craving and pursuit to experience present sufferings.

"Riding upon these three vehicles" refers below to attaining the five untainted faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), and the four dhyānas.
By delighting in the eight meditative concentrations, the various liberations, and the samādhis, one will no longer subsequently undergo the sufferings of the hells, animals, or hungry ghosts.
To "attain immeasurable peace and happiness" means that one will likewise not experience the manifold sufferings of poverty,
distress, separation from the beloved, or encounter with the hated, whether among devas or humans.
Furthermore, the Buddha thus entices and leads [beings] toward the bliss of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) beyond the triple world.

Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings below [this level], he again clarifies for you that you should simply cultivate diligence and exert yourselves, leading them toward the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

By assigning the three vehicles (*triyāna*) to the three carts, he has explained the aforementioned Vehicle of the Hearers (*śrāvaka-yāna*). Internally possessing the nature of wisdom, they are endowed with vision.
The cause of the Way consists in hearing the Dharma from the Buddha and practicing it with diligent effort; this constitutes the conditions for attaining the cultivation of the Way.

To desire rapid descent is to say that haste prevents arrival; to seek [enlightenment] for oneself alone is not to act for the sake of others. This is why such a person belongs to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
This corresponds to the sheep-drawn carriage within the parable. Next, the phrase "If there are those of inferior [faculties]" and so forth explains the vehicle of the *pratyekabuddha*.
In Sanskrit, *pratyekabuddha* means "one who awakens through conditions" (*pratyaya-buddha*), and is also called "one who awakens alone" (*ekabuddha*).

A *pratyekabuddha* who appears in an age when a Buddha exists attains the fruit by hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination. A *pratyekabuddha* who appears in an age when no Buddha exists [attains it] by himself.

Having awakened to causes and conditions, one realizes the fruit. Now, to speak of "seeking the wisdom of spontaneity" (*svayambhū-jñāna*) and "delighting in solitary, sublime tranquility" refers to the designation for those who appear in an age without a Buddha.

(By "wisdom of spontaneity," it is meant that this wisdom exists spontaneously without depending on the instruction of a teacher; it is the knowledge of a *pratyekabuddha*. "Delighting in solitary, sublime tranquility" means not leading a following, but remaining alone and virtuous by oneself.)
This is the practice of the Pratyekabuddha. Because they profoundly understand the causes and conditions of all phenomena, they are given the name "those who appear in the world of a Buddha.

Therefore, the sutra first states phrases such as "hearing the Dharma from the Buddha," and subsequently states phrases such as "seeking spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). These two sets of phrases together enumerate the names of the two types of spiritual capacities (*indriya*).
Furthermore, according to another interpretation, "seeking spontaneous wisdom" means that their wisdom does not stop at that of the śrāvakas, but possesses internal knowledge within themselves.

It is simply a matter of nature. One who deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena will not have their resolve limited to that of the śrāvakas, who merely seek to swiftly exit the triple world and attain nirvāṇa for themselves.
Therefore, although compared to a bodhisattva it may seem small, compared to a śrāvaka it is vastly greater.

This is why the fruit is designated as the Middle Vehicle (*madhyayāna*), corresponding to the deer-cart within the parable. The subsequent phrase "if there is a lower [vehicle]" explains the aforementioned Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
"Diligently practicing with vigor" refers to the first five perfections (*pāramitā*), such as generosity (*dāna*). "Seeking all... refers to the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"All-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the Buddha-wisdom, and the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), which is spontaneous.
The wisdom of wondrous observation, the unlearned wisdom, and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done. Furthermore, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) transcends the pratyekabuddhas;
Buddha-wisdom transcends the bodhisattvas; spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) transcends the śrāvakas; and unlearned wisdom transcends devas and humans.
Only by possessing these four wisdoms can one first achieve the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the ten powers, and the four [fearlessnesses].
"Being without fear" refers to seeking the supreme; this is self-benefit. "Compassionately mindful of those below" refers to transforming those below; this is benefiting others.
"Sentient beings" are spoken of in terms of the three miserable realms (*trāya-patha*). Since the three miserable realms consist solely of suffering, it is called "peace and happiness.
Humans and devas have suffering and happiness in equal measure, hence it is called "benefit," meaning to remove their suffering and augment their happiness. "To deliver and liberate all" means...
This means that by means of the Bodhisattva vehicle, one delivers and liberates all those of the two vehicles.
Possessing this great mind of benefiting both self and others, it is unlike the small playthings of sheep and deer; rather, it is likened to the ox within the metaphor.

Because it is a vehicle (*yāna*), it is called the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*). The passage beginning with "The bodhisattva seeks this... explains the formation of the two characters for "Great Vehicle.
That which was previously termed the "Buddha-vehicle" is here called the "Great Vehicle" because the Buddha is the great fruit;
sentient beings are able to seek this great fruit and ride upon it, thereby delivering themselves and others. For this reason, it is also called the "Mahāsattva."

Regarding the Mahāyāna: [Question] Since the Mahāyāna is already present here and assigned to the ox-cart, why does the subsequent section state that they are "equally bestowed with the Mahāyāna"? Are there not two different kinds of Mahāyāna? [Answer] This refers to the differentiated Mahāyāna within the Three Vehicles prior to the forty years of the Buddha’s teaching.

The subsequent section refers to the non-differentiated Mahāyāna after those forty years, which is free from the distinctions of the three vehicles or the small and great. Thus, one should know that the Mahāyāna in this [first] section is the provisional teaching (*upāya*), while the Mahāyāna in the subsequent section is the ultimate teaching (*nītārtha*).

Although there are not two distinct natures, there is indeed a sequence of before and after. [Question] If this is so, then was the Mahāyāna prior to the forty years also the same as the Hīnayāna, and therefore false? [Answer] According to the analogy, outside the gate from the very beginning...

If there were no three vehicles, then this Mahāyāna here would seem to be empty. If we follow the *Upāya-paryāya* chapter: "Now, joyful and fearless, among all the bodhisattvas, I shall directly abandon the provisional means and preach only the unsurpassed path. When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma...

The net of doubt has been entirely removed. The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become buddhas. Furthermore, when Śāriputra described seeing the various bodhisattvas receive their predictions of buddhahood, yet noting that he and his peers were not included in this matter, it becomes clear that the Mahāyāna of this section and the Mahāyāna of the subsequent section are originally the One Vehicle;

they are not two different things at all. There is only a difference in the timing of their progress—whether sooner or later. Moreover, if one follows the later verse stating that although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means, all those beings they transform are bodhisattvas, then even the carts of the sheep, deer, and small oxen outside the gate are the Mahāyāna.
How could there be two? This fifth section, consisting of both the Dharma and the parable, uses comparisons to demonstrate that [the teaching] is not empty; it is precisely for this reason.
"Śāriputra, just as that elder [up to] 'is able to produce the foremost pure and wondrous joy.
This corresponds to the fourth section of the parable, clarifying that one ultimately enters the Real through the Expedient Means, attaining the wisdom-joy of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas.
"Śāriputra, just as that... and below introduces the simile; "The Tathāgata also likewise... and below provides the application (*yōjaka*).

Regarding the Dharma (from "If one sees the immeasurable" below): formerly, by means of expedient [teachings], there were those of the two or three vehicles. "By means of" refers to using the ninefold teachings as they were taught according to suitability during the first forty years of the Buddha's life as the gateway.

Through these, the capacities of the various followers of the two and three vehicles emerged from the perilous suffering of the triple world and attained the bliss of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) of the Lesser Vehicle—just as the sons safely emerged from the fire and reached a place of fearlessness. The passage "At that time, the Tathāgata... and so forth is a metaphor for the present teaching of the wondrous Dharma and entry into the reality (*tattva*).
Since the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha is vast and sentient beings are his own children, he does not begrudge [the truth] but treats them all equally.
It is for the sake of bestowing [the same gift]. It does not allow anyone to fall short; this explains the meaning of "bestowing equally.
For forty years prior, he alone permitted bodhisattvas to receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, while not permitting śrāvakas; this was to allow certain individuals to attain nirvāṇa alone.
Forty years later, he preached this sutra, permitting śrāvakas to likewise receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood alongside the bodhisattvas.
All these are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s own extinction. Regarding the phrase "these various sentient beings" below:

this restates those previously transformed who were led by skillful means. Regarding the phrase "all together with the Buddhas" below: this concludes the fulfillment of what was intended and the great matter.
"All are of one mark" refers to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle. "Of one kind" refers to the ultimate *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience).
"The foremost bliss" refers to attaining the finality of the fifth stage (*pañcamavihāra*), where the two types of death are forever extinguished and the lands and kalpas are adorned.
It is the wondrous bliss of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. In the past, Bodhisattvas attained the Buddha-vehicle; Pratyekabuddhas attained the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle;
and Arhats attained the Śrāvaka-vehicle. Thus, the single Buddha-knowledge and vision were differentiated into three aspects and three types.
Consequently, their bliss is also of three grades—limited and finite—and they do not attain the pure and wondrous [bliss].
First: "Śāriputra, just as that elder... [up to] ...teaches the three vehicles by differentiating them within the single Buddha-vehicle.

Śāriputra, from "just as that" onwards, the analogy is raised and applied to the Dharma; this is understandable. (This corresponds to the fifth section of the preceding analogy. Regarding what you may think of it:)

Question and Answer: To clarify that there is no falsehood. This is the fifth section of the current teaching; because it relies solely on the metaphorical illustration—which contains no falsehood—there is no need for question and answer. It simply states, "Śāriputra, just as those [in the parable]," and so forth, up to "then they [were saved].

This implies that since the Buddha knows the capacities of his audience, once they have understood the three points of the metaphor, they must necessarily understand the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Dharma.

Why is this so? [The following] provides the inquiry and explanation: namely, the initial teaching of the Three Vehicles was intended merely as a guidance and thus appears not to be the ultimate reality. Subsequently, he saves beings solely by means of the Mahāyāna, having never made such a prior promise. Thus...

It appears to be false. For what reason do you say there is no falsehood? One speaks of "falsehood" when that which does not exist is treated as existing—that is, to claim something can be granted while being unable to actually provide it.

Now, since the Buddha-Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power of wisdom, the fearlessnesses, and the treasury of all dharmas, he is not false; furthermore, he is able to bestow everything upon all beings.
It would not be false to say that [the Buddhas] do not begrudge the Mahāyāna Dharma to sentient beings;
rather, it is because the Dharma is vast while the faculties of sentient beings are small that the Buddhas can give it all, yet sentient beings cannot receive it all.

Therefore, at first they do not give it all, but later sentient beings are finally able to receive it all. Because there are the causes and conditions for sentient beings to receive it all, the Buddhas—

Employing the power of skillful means, [the Buddha] does not first bestow the Dharma of the One Vehicle in its entirety, but rather teaches it by distinguishing it into the three vehicles as a means of guidance.

In this way, the various causes, conditions, parables, expressions, skillful means, provisional wisdoms, and the teachings of the three vehicles previously explained are merely names that have not been fully bestowed; how could they be called false? This is because...
In the past, they did not receive it in its entirety, but now they have finally attained the definitive prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

How could this possibly be false? Why, then, would the twelve hundred arhats doubt that the Buddha’s previous teaching of the three vehicles was empty, or regret that the *nirvāṇa* they had realized was not true but illusory? Therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgata..."
There are immeasurable wisdoms and so forth.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"For example, there was an elder who had a large house (up to) where poisonous harms, fires, and various calamities were manifold."
This verse constitutes the first section of the parable. "For example, there was an elder" refers to the Buddha.

"He had a large house" and so forth extensively describes the state of suffering and its origin within the trichiliocosm of the three realms. A "house" (宅) means that which is relied upon or where one dwells;
it is what people rely on to settle their bodies. Because a house deteriorates over time, it is said to be "suddenly dilapidated. In summary, it is said:

Regarding the dwelling: to distinguish its components, a house consists of the hall (*táng*) and the quarters (*shè*). The hall is so called because it is "appropriate" (*dāng*); it is where one receives guests and engages in social exchange.
The quarters are so called because they are for "stopping" (*zhǐ*); they are where one’s person and family reside. That which leans against a wall is called a pillar (*zhù*).

That which obstructs [the structure] is called a foundation (*gēn*). That which runs horizontally is called a beam (*liáng*). That which runs vertically is called a ridgepole (*dòng*). The site of the rooms is called the foundation (*jī*). The steps and paving are called the stairs (*jié*). East and west...

It is said that the walls are the outer enclosures, while the front and back are the partitions (*bì*). Mud plaster is used to decorate the joints and crevices; thatched roofing is used to shield against sun and rain.
Those at the eaves are called rafters (*chuán*); those along the ridge are called *lǚ*. The fences surrounding the four sides are called perimeter barriers (*zhōuzhàng*).

Paths and alleys intersecting one another are called winding and crooked (*qūqū*). As for terms such as "lofty and dangerous," "collapsed and decayed," or "tilted and leaning," these clearly indicate a state of sudden ruin.
The shapes [of these birds] clarify how the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environmental retribution) of the three realms is as insubstantial as this.

The mention of "five hundred people" and so forth clarifies that where there is a world, there is the *sabhāga-vipāka* (the primary retribution) of sentient beings' karma. Regarding the "owls and hawks" below:
within the category of primary retribution, these are the retributions of animals. Owls and hawks harm those close to them; eagles and vultures feed on corpses; crows are the retribution for cruelty.

The magpie brings news of joy; the dove usurps the nest; the pigeon indulges in lust. Among the feathered multitudes of the animal realm, there are those who possess the three poisons to such an extent.
The *yuán* is the primordial; it is the largest of snakes. The *fú* is the retaliatory;
when touched, it retaliates by stinging the person; it is the largest of scorpions. The centipede is fierce and moves swiftly. The millipede—
*Lianxian* (dripping saliva) refers to running with sluggishness. *Shougong* (palace-keeper) is the *yantie* (gecko). It was raised in the Han palace;

its blood was taken using cinnabar (*dansha*) and applied between the eyebrows to prevent sexual misconduct. Therefore, it is called "palace-keeper. *Baiju* (hundred-footed) is the *xian* (millipede);
it is a many-legged insect. *You* is a large kind of rat; it is that which emerges from its burrow to devour mice. *Li* is a large kind of fox. [Year]...
Those who grow old and become seductive are like the *snīkṣa* mouse, a mouse with a sweet mouth that eats people without them feeling the pain.
Among the animals, there are those that are so light-footed, dull, and soft yet possess the three poisons to such an extent.
Below these are the various evil insects, meaning all manner of evil species; though their modes of flight differ, they are alike in their frantic, crosswise scurrying across decaying things.
It dwells within the center. Below are excrement and urine; the great and small excretions are so foul-smelling as to be unbearable.
Yet dung beetles and various insects consider them fragrant and delicious, gathering upon the overflowing impurities. Thus it is with the two organs of male and female.
Those who conceive thoughts of desire and pleasure are utterly deluded. The fox is full of doubt; the wolf is full of suspicion;
the jackal howls at night as a portentous omen; some take insects into their mouths to chew upon them; others tread upon excrement and urine with their feet.
The state of being "aw-cho" (齷齪) is extreme. To draw blood to the lips is called *tsai* (嚌); to bite through bone with the teeth is called *nieh* (齧).
This leads to insects being born that chew until almost nothing remains; thus, the corpse has been gnawed upon yet there is still a residue, hence it is called "lang-chi" (狼藉).
"Chi" (藉) means grass; it refers to the remnants left uneaten by a wolf scattered among the grass. When people of the world spread mats and set out seats, and arrange their cups...
The state of the scattered remains on the platter was truly loathsome. Consequently, a pack of dogs descended;

because these were the remnants of scattered flesh and bone, the dogs could not distinguish between themselves and others, eating them without relish as if they were discarded spittle, while scrambling and jostling amidst them.
To overturn with both feet and search about is called *bō* (搏); to gather and collect them into one place is called *zuò* (撮). *Bō* refers to the act of seizing and striking.
Because they cannot obtain what they grasp for, they become emaciated with hunger and seek food in terror. When they find something, they fight, claw, and tear at it while barking and howling.
To seize from the front is called "clawing" (cā); to pull from behind is called "tearing" (che). These describe the manner of their fighting.
Their snarling and barking describe the sound of their fighting. To snap at an object and die-fighting over it is called "snarling" (jianshi).
When they lose their belongings, they cry out and bark. These are among the hairy creatures of the animal realm, whether wild or domestic, who possess the three poisons;
such beings exist. "The terror within that house" below concludes the description of the animal realm and gives rise to the terrifying manifestations of the retribution of ghosts.
"They are everywhere" below clearly elucidates the retribution of ghosts. As the *Xijing Fu* (Rhapsody on the Western Capital) says:
