The mountain deity in the form of a tiger is called a *chī*; the house deity with a human body and a pig’s head is called a *mèi*. Transformations of wood and stone are called *wǎnglǎng*.
A *yakṣa* is said to be one who lives in suffering; they sustain their lives by devouring humans, living through such suffering.

Among the various categories of venomous insects and below—meaning all insects, birds, and beasts—though they are all inherently malevolent and poisonous, upon encountering a *yakṣa*, they become greedy for life and terrified.
Upon death, each likewise protects its own kind: those born from eggs protect what has been hatched with their claws;

those born from wombs conceal what they have produced within their bodies and call it "milk. When yakṣas come down in haste, they say: "Though he conceals it well, this [yakṣa] can forcibly seize it."
They seize [beings] to devour them; thus, once they are satiated, their malevolent intent becomes even more intense.
The sound of their quarreling and strife descends; it is precisely because their evil is so blazing. The *kumbhāṇḍas* are called "the fearsome"; they are the ghosts of impermanent death.
Some squat upon earthen mounds, while others traverse the void (a void being one or two feet above the ground). They fear neither the heavens within, roaming about with unrestrained license.
They frolic and play; they fear no one from without. They seize dogs by pinning them down, crying out with laughter as they take their pleasure. Their lack of restraint is extreme.
Among these ghostly realms, they obtain food through force and violence, unleashing the three poisons at will, their transformed appearances being utterly terrifying.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts below them who are hungry ghosts, unable to obtain food; they are tall, naked, and black, their forms being fearsome as they shriek and wail.
Seeking food, their voices are terrifying; with needle-throats and ox-heads, their appearances are terrifying; devouring humans and eating dogs, their mouths and tongues are terrifying;
cruel, perilous, and driven by hunger, their mental conduct is terrifying (driven by the urgency of hunger and thirst, they are thus explained as *preta* hungry ghosts who cannot obtain food).
Below the *yakṣa* and hungry ghost realms, there is a double summary of the two paths of ghosts and animals; that is, ghosts and animals. When satiated, they compete for food and engage in strife.

Or, when hungry, they cry out and run about, peering through the windows. This is a metaphor for how human beings, in every movement and stillness, are bound by the karma of the three poisons and cannot escape the triple world.
Their bodies and minds are oppressed until fire breaks out, resulting in rebirth in the lower hells.
Therefore, it is said: "Such various calamities as these," which appears below the section on the "decaying old house. This is intended to clarify the retribution of the hells; first—

Regarding those within the triple world of the great trichiliocosm who belong to the three miserable realms and eight difficulties—both the primary and secondary [environments]—the subsequent section on the "Elder" is appropriately intended for their rescue and relief.
That person has recently emerged; this is a metaphor for the Buddha having departed from the city of Gayā not long ago.

"He attains the realization of Perfect Enlightenment. [Question: "The previous statement used the term 'belonging to' (shǔ), while this one uses 'coming forth' (chū). If it belongs to something, it does not come forth; if it comes forth, it does not belong. How can these two be reconciled? [Answer: "If one says it 'belongs to,' then it has no concern with oneself, and thus there would be no reason to provide salvation.

If one says it 'comes forth,' then one is already being consumed by fire oneself; how then could one save others? This is used as a metaphor for the fact that all Buddhas originally abide in the stage of the causal ground (yīndì)."

All have made the vow to deliver all sentient beings as they would themselves; thus, the twelve classes of beings within the triple world are the property of the Buddha alone, and for this reason it is said they "belong" [to him].
However, if one does not first achieve Buddhahood oneself, then even if one wishes to follow them, there is no way to do so;
hence it is said they are "nearby but have yet to emerge. Below the section on the former residence, he describes their previous animal existences.
The two paths of ghosts and humans, both in their primary and secondary forms, are scorched by fire; this is precisely the hell realm.

Because the retributive suffering of hell is exclusively of the utmost gravity, it is said that "fire suddenly breaks out. Birth, old age, sickness, and death converge to form the *kalpa*-defilement (*kalpa-kaṣāya*);

hence, it is said that [the fire] arises "simultaneously on all four sides. Grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction subsequently boil and scorch them; hence, it is said that "its flames blaze together fiercely."

The rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars having already become utterly dilapidated, they shake, crack, and collapse when a fire breaks out (the above concerns the burning of the *nirmita-niśraya*, or external environment).

As for the various ghosts and spirits below (concerning the burning of the *sambhoga-niśraya*, or primary retribution), this refers to the various ghosts and animals who, at the initial outbreak of the fire, were heedless and frolicking;
now, being scorched by the flames, they raise their voices and cry out loudly, suffering the agony of singed heads and blistered foreheads.
As for the hawks, vultures, and various other birds, they are animals; as for the kumbhāṇḍas and others, they are malevolent spirits.
At first, when they were incubating, nursing, giving birth, or producing young, how much they cherished and protected them! As they came and went and roamed about, how much they enjoyed their play!
Now, however, they are frantic with terror and fear, unable to escape on their own. Even if they seek to rise a foot or two feet off the ground, they cannot do so. These are evil beasts.
The venomous insects, which at first ran about crosswise and in all directions, now all hide away in their burrows.
Their hiding in these holes was originally intended for survival, yet they did not expect to encounter the *piśāca* ghosts within the burrows who would maim and kill them;
thus, where there is no calamity from Heaven, there is misfortune from men. As for the jackals and their kind, which at first chewed, trampled, and bit others—
Regarding the corpses of men: who among them were heroes? Now they have already died before our eyes, and their corpses are further being devoured by predatory beasts.
Thus, the causal conditions of good and evil karma, and the resulting retributions of beauty and ugliness, are all clearly seen herein.
"Stinking smoke billows below" refers to insects such as centipedes that harbor venom; dwelling in dark places or behind walls, they believe they have found their proper abode.
Now, however, they are fanned and driven by stinking smoke billowing forth, scorched and roasted by the crackling flames, unable to find peace for themselves.
They can do nothing but struggle to escape from their burrows. Those who remain hidden in their burrows are at the mercy of the Piśācas;

those who emerge from their burrows find their hearts’ desire satisfied by the Kumbhāṇḍas. Thus, for those without merit, both staying and leaving result in injury; there is no place where they may find safety from death.

(Furthermore, regarding the various "lower" beings—referring to the evil ghosts who obtain food—they may drink and eat within their burrows or seek food outside them. Seeking survival amidst suffering, struggling to live amidst fire, they are nonetheless all but satiated ghosts.)
As for those who are hungry ghosts (*preta*), their heads are ablaze with fire and their bellies are tormented by hunger and thirst;

they run about in frantic distress, unable to look calmly in the four directions through windows and lattices as they did before. This is truly because of the sentient beings within the three realms and five destinies.

While alive, they indulge in the three poisons and commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct to gratify their momentary desires; upon death, they fall into the three miserable realms and undergo suffering for immeasurable kalpas.
As the Sūtra says: "These are all those who fall due to pure affliction and are scorched by the fires of karma.

Therefore, it is said: "Their dwelling is thus," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "poisonous harm below," it means that calamities and disasters are so numerous that they cannot be fully described; hence, it is said:
This is not a single [work]. If one does not interpret this text according to the three realms of existence (trāya), one will see only redundant and overflowing verbiage.

However, regarding the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma, when translated by a master of high skill who observes it with a clarified mind, it possesses systematic order and is entirely free of superfluous elements.
As for the commentaries and sub-commentaries of antiquity, they are often unclear and biased; their forced and artificial combinations are especially laughable.
At that time, the owner of the house stands outside the gate (until) he still continues to delight in and cling to his play without ceasing.

This is the second section of the allegorical text. Regarding "at that time, the owner of the house stands outside the gate," the word "near" (*jin*) from the previous section—referring to the person's recent departure—is used as a metaphor for the Buddha having newly sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), not long after emerging from the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Furthermore, regarding those who are said to have heard [the teaching]: these are the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi) who, at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, acted as Brahma kings, Śakras, and others who turned the wheel of the Dharma for the Buddhas.
(As the "Expedient Means" chapter states: "At that time, the various Brahma kings and the various Śakras, lords of the gods...")

The Four World-Protecting Kings, Maheśvara, and all the other hosts of devas joined their palms in reverence and paid homage, entreating me to turn the wheel of Dharma. I then reflected within myself: "If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings would remain submerged in suffering."

"...are unable to believe in these dharmas. As for the phrase "you, my sons, who previously engaged in play," etc., this clarifies that the twelve hundred arhats all previously received the Buddha’s teaching and gave rise to the Great Mind within the Dharma of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;
however, because they were obscured by ignorance, they kept their inner realization secret while outwardly appearing to come and frolic within the three realms. Having heard this, the elder...

"Below. One should insert the prose passage beginning with "The hands and body possess great strength," etc. "Just as [the father] below" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s desire to provide rescue through his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
"Exhorting and instructing" below is a metaphor for the Buddha’s desire to provide rescue through his power of wisdom (*jñāna*).

"Evil spirits" below provides a general description of the suffering of the three miserable realms (*trāya-patha*). "Venomous snakes" below provides a detailed explanation of the sequence of suffering within the three miserable realms (this section on "the difficulty of this suffering" concludes the argument).

The three miserable realms, with the hells being the most grave). "The sons," and so forth; one should expand upon the prose passage beginning with "Although the father felt compassion, he used kind words to entice and admonish them.
At that time, the elder had this thought (up to) reaching an open space, free from all suffering and hardship.

This verse from the third section illustrates the concealment of the ultimate truth (*tattva*) and the revelation of the provisional means (*upāya*). (Regarding the phrase "At that time" [ishi]: it is identical to the prose section. Regarding the phrase "The sons" [shoji]:

the prose states, "This house has already been consumed by a great fire; if I and my sons do not emerge in a timely manner, we shall surely be incinerated. The elder’s increasing distress arises because he fears being burned along with his sons. The six lines beginning with "Now this" [konsha] clarify the meaning of this increased distress:

that there is nothing in the house worth enjoying symbolizes that the five destinies within the trichiliocosm are all suffering; that the sons are immersed in play and sport symbolizes that sentient beings cling to suffering as pleasure; and their refusal to heed the instruction symbolizes their being harmed by the fire.)

This is an analogy for those who do not believe the Buddha’s words; they accumulate the causes of suffering and thereby invite its fruits. This is why the long prose section states that they "will surely be burned. The ten phrases beginning with "He then reflected" correspond to the long prose passage from "I shall now devise skillful means" up to "I will grant you whatever you desire," which stops at the phrase "according to your wishes.

The following section corresponds to the Buddha preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles according to the capacities and inclinations of those seeking the Small, Great, or Middle Vehicles, and the realization they thereby attain. The section beginning with "The sons" can be understood as it appears in the long prose.
"The elder sees his children emerge from the burning house... playing, joyful, and moving about freely without hindrance.
This verse constitutes the fourth section of the parable; it illustrates entering the ultimate through provisional means.

The passage beginning with "The elder sees his children" is a metaphor for the Buddha-father rejoicing because the children—the sentient beings—rejoice. The passage beginning with "These children" further clarifies the joy derived from the children's joy.
As for the father’s joy, it is because he considers that his son was conceived and born with great difficulty; furthermore, being young and ignorant, the child would not dare to commit evil.

This ignorance and lack of knowledge is the cause of suffering, while entering the perilous house is the fruit of suffering. "Many [lowly creatures]" correctly clarifies the danger of the house: the venomous insects represent the dangers of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*);
the *chimei* (goblins and specters) represent the dangers of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*); and the fierce fire represents [the dangers of the hell realm].

"The path of the hells is perilous" means that it slopes downward on all four sides; this refers to the three evil and dangerous paths, all of which possess the four sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
therefore, it is said they "arise together. "Yet these children... and so forth means that in the past, these children took suffering to be pleasure;
this is why the father is filled with anxiety for them. "I have already rescued them... and so forth refers to the present.
The sons, through the father’s employment of skillful means, are led to leave suffering and attain happiness;
thus, as a father, he does not fall into a lack of compassion. For this reason, he calls out to all people and concludes by saying: "I am now happy."

The passage beginning with "At that time, the sons... is a metaphor for the forty years prior, when, due to the person of expedient means, they originally sought the three vehicles—small, medium, and great.
The passage beginning with "The elder was immensely wealthy... is a metaphor for the forty years later, when the present sutra was preached to lead them into the ultimate reality.

(The four lines concerning the "storehouse" and so forth correctly illustrate his great wealth. The seventeen lines beginning with "He built various [mansions]" are a verse summarizing the prose section from "At that time, the elder gave each of his sons one great carriage" up to the text on "placing red pillows. There were eight great white oxen.)

The verse [lines] "駕以白牛" (yoked with white oxen) correspond to the prose from "何況諸子" (how much more so for the sons). The six subsequent lines of the verse correspond to the prose from "是時諸子" (at that time the sons... to "非本所望" (not what was originally expected).
"Śāriputra, I am also like this... up to "...these fires blaze fiercely without ceasing.
This verse corresponds to the first section of the doctrinal application. From "Śāriputra" onwards, the nine realms of sentient beings are divided into three categories of the world:

the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the world of receptacles (*bhājana-loka*), and the world of principles (*dharma-loka*). Each category has its own sages, yet the Buddha alone reigns supreme over all.
Among the holy ones, he is thus called "Venerable" and "Father. This corresponds to the prose passage beginning with "The Tathāgata is likewise," and so forth.
Regarding the section "All sentient beings," it corresponds to the prose passage beginning with "Seeing all sentient beings [afflicted] by birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.

(As all sentient beings are equally the children of the Buddha, why do they not become like the Buddha? Because they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and lack the heart of wisdom, they are unable to escape the burning house of the triple world. Regarding the section "Various sufferings," this is the main point.

The section beginning with "Like fire" clearly explains the meaning of being without peace. The passage beginning with "Constantly" correctly clarifies the reality of what is truly terrifying. (In this context, the reasons are explained extensively in prose; therefore, they are abbreviated here in verse.)

"The Tathāgata has already left the burning house of the triple world" (up to) "although he instructs and admonishes them, they do not believe or accept"—this verse corresponds to the second section of the Dharma discourse.
It explains and establishes the six lines of verse from the preceding section addressed to Śāriputra and others, clarifying the meaning of being both father and son.
Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata has already left," it refers to why the Buddha [acts as he does].
The Honored One is regarded as a father because he was the first to leave the burning house and dwell in tranquil seclusion within the forest wilds.

All sentient beings are considered the Buddha’s children because the entire trichiliocosm—the environmental support—and the twelve classes of beings—the primary retribution—are all the property of the Buddha. Since the former triple world has already become the Buddha’s...
There are. The Buddha has already transcended [the world]; the present triple realm belongs to sentient beings. Sentient beings, too, shall transcend it.
Those who have already transcended should function as fathers; those who have not yet transcended should be considered as sons.

Therefore, it is said that "the sentient beings therein" and so forth. Now, from the passage "here below," it refers to those who have not yet transcended the triple realm; hence, they suffer many afflictions.
[Question: It is difficult to understand. Since he has already transcended the three realms, he possesses abundant peace and happiness.
How could it be that while the father enjoys peace and happiness, the son remains in distress and difficulty, yet fails to receive rescue? Therefore, it says, "I alone," and so forth.

Although the subsequent teaching and admonition—referring to a father’s love for his son—is present, the son does not accord with the father’s wishes; this is because the Dharma is great while the capacity [of the recipient] is small. As stated previously...
The first eight lines correspond to the prose passage beginning with "When the Buddha saw this... and so forth.
The final six lines correspond to the prose passage beginning with "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further thought thus... and so forth.
Because their attachment to the defilements of various desires is profound, [there are those who attain] the state of a pratyekabuddha or non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.

This verse corresponds to the third section of the dharma-exposition. It explains the meaning of the ten phrases in the first section beginning with "deeply attached to worldly pleasures" and "lacking the mind of wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "to the various defilements of desire" and below, it follows the preceding text; that is to say, although they have been instructed and admonished...

As for those who do not believe, it is not that they dare to be faithless; rather, it is because they lack the mind of wisdom (*prajñācitta*), are deeply attached to the defilements of desire, and cling to suffering as being pleasure, and thus do not believe. For this reason, [the Buddha] employs expedient means (*upāya*);

that is to say, because they are so deeply attached to desire and lack faith, the Buddha does not teach them with the true wisdom of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), but rather with the provisional wisdom of expedient means (*upāyakauśalya*).

The teaching: it is by means of the One Vehicle that the three vehicles are expounded (the above clarifies that for those of dull faculties, the teaching is revealed as being capable of reaching them).
"Causing all sentient beings" and below clarifies the capacities to be reached, who, through the Buddha’s teaching, know suffering, sever the origin, aspire to cessation, and cultivate the path.
"These sons" and below generally clarifies the causal minds of the three vehicles. "Possessing the three insights" and below specifically clarifies the three vehicles.
The fruit and realization thereof.
"O Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings, that which I ought to accomplish until now is solely the wisdom of a Buddha.
This verse corresponds to the fourth section of the Dharma. From "O Śāriputra" onwards, it clarifies the manifestation of the capacity [to benefit] for the sake of sentient beings.
In this teaching, both the Dharma and its metaphors are for the sake of the One Vehicle; these metaphors refer to what the long prose section calls "I shall now further employ a parable.
The exposition of the Single Buddha Vehicle refers to what the long prose section calls "further clarifying this meaning."
If you can lower yourselves and exhort those who are the objects of your teaching so that they may believe the Buddha’s words, you will immediately attain the Buddha-way.
This is what is meant by the long passage stating, "All those with wisdom gain understanding through parables. The two phrases, "All shall equally...

explain the character "Buddha" (*buddha*) within the phrase "the teaching of the One Buddha Vehicle. The four phrases beginning with "This vehicle is subtle and wondrous... [explain the term "Vehicle"].
This explains the word "vehicle" (*yāna*) in the context of teaching the Single Buddha Vehicle. Regarding the phrase "that which the Buddhas find pleasing":
it means that because one has faith in and accepted the Buddha’s words, all Buddhas are delighted and grant their approval.

Because one has personally attained the Buddha Vehicle and is further able to awaken sentient beings, those beings praise and prostrate to them. Regarding the phrase "immeasurable billions": this refers to the Buddhas being pleased.
Above, it encompasses the ocean of fruition; below, by invoking the name and paying homage, it reaches down to the source of the cause.

This is why the Buddha-vehicle is said to be the most subtle, pure, and supreme, being fully endowed with immeasurable billions of powers, liberations, concentrations, wisdoms, and all other Buddha-dharmas.
These eight phrases explain and establish the two preceding phrases: "being unsurpassed among all worlds."

This clarifies the meaning of "Buddha" within the teaching of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). From the phrase "attaining such a vehicle" onwards, it further explains and establishes the two lines concerning how this vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme;
this clarifies the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*) within the teaching of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
That is to say, it causes the twelve hundred sons to attain this Mahāyāna, regardless of whether they are Bodhisattvas or Śrāvakas, so that all are immediately and equally [enlightened].
"Until reaching the site of enlightenment where one becomes a Buddha, there is no further detour.

Regarding the passage "For this reason," it means that because of these causes and conditions, whether they be bodhisattvas or śrāvakas, all shall attain Buddhahood; thus, one seeks throughout the ten directions with earnest scrutiny.
There is only the One Vehicle; there are no other two or three vehicles. It is only because of the Buddha’s skillful means that there appear to be two or three vehicles.
The passage beginning with "He told Śāriputra" serves as a general conclusion, summarizing the verses of the first, second, third, and fourth sections which establish the unity of the Dharma.
Regarding the previous statement that "all sentient beings are my children and I am their father":
the children refer to you twelve hundred people; the father refers to me, Śākyamuni. This concludes the first section.

(I am likewise the most honored among all sages, the father of the world, and all sentient beings are my children. From the passage "you have [suffered] through many kalpas" onwards, it clarifies that Śāriputra and the others [attained realization].
"Your righteousness" (the first phrase) clarifies the meaning of the Buddha as a father; this concludes the second section.
"Although I previously taught" (the second phrase) clarifies the meaning of the former teaching of the Three Vehicles; this concludes the third section.

"What should now be done" (the third phrase) clarifies the meaning of the present teaching of the One Vehicle; this concludes the fourth part of the current section. Each [phrase] corresponds [to its respective point].
This is evident. As for the fifth section, which does not employ verses to correlate the Dharma and its parables, it is because they all share the meaning of being non-false and non-delusive;
however, it is only upon reaching the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs that the teaching is fully articulated for the sake of the four great disciples.
"If there be a bodhisattva among this assembly... do not propagate [this] recklessly in whatever direction you travel.
These eight sections constitute the verses. Hereafter, I shall further explain this meaning through parables.
From here until the following section, these verses clarify that all that has been taught is for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas. This explains the above.
By this causal condition, if one seeks truthfully throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle (yāna) to be found, except for the meaning of the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*).

If there is a bodhisattva—this refers to one whose capacity (*indriya*) is great, and thus the Dharma is likewise great—because they listen with single-minded devotion amidst the assembly, there is nothing they encounter that is not the true wisdom-dharma of the Buddhas’ One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Although the Buddhas employ the provisional wisdom of skillful means, those sentient beings who are transformed by such means are also Great Vehicle bodhisattvas. This further clarifies [the point].
There is no other vehicle. If a person possesses small wisdom and is inferior, they claim that the Dharma is small;

this is because their own capacity is limited. This clarifies the exclusion of the Buddha’s skillful means. (Because their wisdom is small, they cling to the profound. Attachment belongs to the mind; desire belongs to the object. These are the worldly fruits of suffering arising from sense organs and objects. For the sake of such people, [the Buddha] acts as follows:

He observes those who are deeply attached to love and desire, taking suffering for pleasure. To them, he takes the reality-mark of the One Vehicle and explains it as the Truth of Suffering within the Three Vehicles. Thus, beings of small wisdom receive the Buddha’s teaching as it accords with their preferences.

In his heart, he was filled with joy and said, "I have attained what I have never attained before. The phrase "The Buddha spoke" refers to why it is said that he had attained what he had never attained before: because the Buddha’s teaching on the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is true and without deviation. "Without deviation" means it is not artificial.

These eight phrases constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) among the Four Noble Truths. If there are sentient beings who encounter these first eight phrases, they represent those of sharp faculties who, upon merely knowing the fruit of suffering, do not inquire further into its cause.

Conversely, if there are sentient beings of dull faculties, although they know that all pleasures are suffering, they still do not understand the root of that suffering; they remain deeply attached to the causes of suffering and cannot abandon them for even a moment, clinging instead to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

For the sake of such individuals, the Buddha employs the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*) and declares: "The cause of all sufferings does not have other dharmas as their basis; rather, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the fundamental cause. This is the instruction on the Path (*mārga*) that leads to liberation.
Regarding the extinction of craving, the following four lines concern the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). "Cessation" here carries the sense of "selective elimination.

Following the preceding text, it means that since craving is the root of suffering, if there are sentient beings who rely on the contemplation of the principle of quiescence (*śānta*) to selectively eliminate craving—the cause of suffering—then once that cause is exhausted, the various fruits of suffering will have no basis to rest upon. One should understand that the phrase "having no basis to rest upon" implies that while the afflictions (*kleśa*) still remain, the ultimate fruit has not yet been realized.

Upon reaching the fourth fruit, when the final three grades of afflictions of thought are completely severed, one begins to extinguish all suffering; this is called the third truth, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). To explain this Truth of Cessation, the following four lines [are taught].

The Truth of the Path (the Path consists of thirty-seven factors; all are capable of severing the bonds of suffering. When bonds are severed, it is called attaining liberation). "This person" and below:

this investigates the following of names (the preceding is the question; "but having severed false delusions" and below is the answer. In terms of the Dharma, it refers to the severance of *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*; in terms of analogy, it is like exiting the burning house and sitting in the open air. Calling this "attaining liberation" points to the provisional vehicle’s minor fruit). "In reality" and below:

this explains the discrepancy with the ultimate reality (in terms of the Dharma, the afflictions have not yet been severed at the level of ignorance, and the fruit has not reached its culmination at the stage of Buddhahood; in terms of analogy, it is like...).
"Remaining in the open air, he has not yet obtained the great cart of the white ox. When the Buddha says "has not yet obtained," it means that the three vehicles are unified into one.

This refers to the Buddha’s statement that this person has not yet attained actual extinction (*nirvāṇa*); it does not mean that they have nothing at all from what was previously taught in the Hīnayāna.
It simply means they have not yet attained the unsurpassed path to Buddhahood as taught here [in the Mahāyāna]. "My intention is not... refers to you.
The one thousand two hundred people, including Śāriputra and others, had realized the lesser fruits of the path;

though they considered themselves sufficient, their aspirations toward the Buddha remained unfulfilled, and thus they still felt as if they were not yet enough. This was because [the Buddha] did not wish for them to abandon their present greatness.
This is because they merely realized the small [vehicle] of the past. Regarding the passage "I am the Dharma King" and below: this follows from the preceding text.
It asks: since the Buddha’s intention was not to have them merely realize the small nirvana, why did he previously speak of the small [vehicle]?
Since the Buddha is the Dharma King of the three vehicles—small, one, and great—he possesses mastery over both the provisional and the real within the teachings of the small and the great.
The Sovereign One, in the past, gave rise to expedient means according to the capacities of beings;

he manifested the Great as Small to bring peace and security to sentient beings, so that they would not fall into the insecurity of the three evil realms due to their failure to believe in the Dharma. Now, because the capacities of beings have matured, he reveals the True Small as the Great.

To bring peace and security to sentient beings, so that they do not utter cries of lamentation and deeply reproach themselves, thinking, "How have I deceived myself and failed to find peace?"—therefore it is said, "to bring peace and security to sentient beings," and so forth. From the passage beginning "You, Śāriputra," onwards, he instructs the primary recipient:

when transmitting the Dharma while embodying the wondrous essence of the Buddha-mind, one must not lose the proper sequence of what precedes and follows. As for the "Dharma Seal" (dharmamudrā), this refers to the Buddha’s...
The Dharma King holds this seal of mastery over the provisional and the real, and over the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
With this seal, he certifies all sentient beings; he may transform the great into the small, or the small into the great. No celestial māras or non-Buddhist paths can alter or shift it.
"For the sake of benefiting those below" means that while previously he taught the benefits of the two vehicles of the Small Vehicle, now...
Regarding the statement that there is the benefit of the One Vehicle within the Great [Vehicle], the injunction "do not proclaim it recklessly in whatever region you travel" is a warning.
This means that for those who are ready [to receive the teaching], there is no lack of cause; the Buddha possesses benefits for both the Small and the Great Vehicles.
Whether you reside in a fixed location or travel on pilgrimage, do not treat all cases with indiscriminate ignorance. When the opportunity arises, you must not then recklessly proclaim it.

It is great. Yet, when the time for the ripening of the capacity [to receive it] arrives, it is falsely claimed to be small. If this is so, it is not only without benefit, but rather brings about harm.
If there are those who hear it, they should rejoice and receive it upon their heads. (Up to: Listen now again to the retribution for the sins of such a person.
This section repeatedly and clearly explains that wherever one travels, one must not propagate [this teaching] recklessly;
it is essential that it benefit others and cause them no harm. "If there are those who hear it" refers to the time of propagation:

if there are those who hear it, they first rejoice and subsequently receive it upon their heads. How could these be ordinary people? They must certainly be *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattvas.

This refers to a Bodhisattva who has regressed from the stage of non-retrogression. Regarding the phrase "if there is one who believes and accepts," this means that even if they do not accept it with the highest reverence (*mūrdha*), they are nonetheless able to believe and accept it;
such a person, though not yet a Bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression, is nevertheless one who has previously seen the Buddhas and heard the Dharma.
Such a person is one who is fully endowed with merit and wisdom (reverently making offerings, they are sufficient in merit; furthermore, hearing this Dharma, they are sufficient in wisdom).
The above has been stated provisionally regarding those who, upon hearing the Buddha appear before them, are able to believe and accept it. As for "if there is a person who can," below this means:
not only do they have crest-like faith in what the Buddha has taught, but if there is a person who can believe what you, Śāriputra, have said, such a person shall also see both me and you.
This is the mind with which the assembly of the Three Vehicles preaches the Dharma today. How could one fail to discern the capacity of the recipient and instead propagate it recklessly?

The reason stated below in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for insisting on selecting a capable and faithful recipient to transmit it is that this sutra was originally intended for those of profound wisdom who can hear the Buddha and the Dharma and possess the capacity for faith.
This is because it is not something spoken for those of deluded sentiments, confused principles, or shallow understanding who lack comprehension.
"All śrāvakas" and so forth means: why is it only for those of profound wisdom and not for those of shallow insight?

It is because the power of intellectual understanding possessed by all persons of the two vehicles cannot reach [this teaching]. "You, Śāriputra," and so forth means that although [the teaching] is suited to the capacity [of the listener],...
All those of the two vehicles are called "possessing wisdom," yet they must still rely on the power of faith to enter [the path], let alone others who lack wisdom and possess no such faith;
how could it be appropriate for them to transmit [this teaching]? Regarding the phrase "the remaining śrāvakas" and below:
this means that as for the remaining śrāvakas whom you were instructed not to transmit [it to], although they possess faith, they lack wisdom (they do not know).

The Dharma has no high or low; it is only the person who is honored. Therefore, one may be able to believe the Buddha’s words and accord with this sutra, yet be unable to believe your words, Śāriputra, and accord with this sutra.
Furthermore, "Śāriputra and those below" refers to the other śrāvakas.
The reason I do not believe your words is this: you consider yourself a Dharma-minister and compare me to a Dharma-king as you transmit the Dharma.
He will surely harbor pride and indolence, clinging to the view of self, thinking, "He is a disciple of that Buddha;
you are a disciple of that Buddha. Will he then practice patience over the long term, show respect to you, and seek the Dharma? This is another point.
As for the śrāvakas, even if they possess faith, they lack wisdom and thus cannot transmit [the teaching].
As for ordinary people of shallow understanding, you say that the rest of the śrāvakas—being members of the two monastic orders—are possessed of the view of self and thus cannot transmit it;
yet as for the other ordinary people, who are members of the two lay orders, they may not know what is good or evil and seem to be without the view of self—could they not transmit it?
However, the knowledge of ordinary people is extremely shallow, and the obstacles posed by the affairs of the five desires are particularly deep.
Although they do not harbor notions of "self" and "other," even upon hearing [this teaching], they find it difficult to understand; therefore, it is said that one must not preach it to them either.

As for the passage beginning with "If a person does not believe," this means that because both monastics and laypeople lack wisdom, you are all cautioned not to propagate it recklessly: for if ordinary people lack wisdom, they will not comprehend it.
If one does not understand, one will not have faith. If one does not have faith, slander will arise. When slander arises, the transgression is no small matter;
it is as if that person’s mind intends to sever the seed of Buddhahood for all the world.
The passage beginning with "or again, frowning" describes the physical appearance and mental state of one who severs the Buddha-seed; it means that such a person will surely be filled with sorrow.
It is manifested on your face. Day and night you wish to extinguish his teaching, yet you cannot do so; hence it is called "frowning. The impulse to annihilate him has taken root in your heart;
though you seek to disparage him at every turn, he appears difficult to move; hence it is called "doubt.

Although your intention in transmitting the Dharma is to deliver and liberate others, because you fail to discern the capacity of the recipient even once, there is thus only harm and no benefit. Therefore—
It says: "You should now listen to the account of this person’s retribution for their offenses. This clearly explains the retribution for offenses:

it means that you should not only listen to the retribution for those who slander the Dharma while the Buddha is in the world, but you must also listen to the retribution for those who slander the Dharma after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa;
therefore, it says, "You should now listen again. Regarding what was mentioned in the previous verse:
It is like the people of the three miserable realms; it is precisely because they do not believe in the Great Dharma that they have come to such states.
For this reason, the preceding section set forth analogies, while this section presents the actual teaching. Thus, the text is not established in vain.
When such a person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell... (until) they are born deaf and mute, their faculties incomplete.

This section implicitly includes the *preta* and *asura* realms; since *preta* are subsumed within the hell realm, and *asura* possess a small portion of celestial merit, they are not explicitly mentioned.
"When such a person’s life ends" refers to the retribution of the hells. Emerging from the hells...
Below: the retribution of animals. If one obtains the state of a human, it is the lower retribution of humans. The animal retribution is briefly explained as being of five types:
namely, dogs, jackals, camels, donkeys, and pythons. The human retribution is of two types: the retribution of karmic fruition, wherein the faculties are dull and inferior;
and the retribution of difficulty, wherein one never sees the lower realms.
"Constantly dwelling in hell as if visiting a garden" (up to) "do not preach this sutra among those without wisdom.
This section of the text appears to be a repetition, yet its meaning is actually distinct. Regarding the passage beginning with "Constantly dwelling in hell":

it means that due to the initial cause of slandering the Dharma, one falls into the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). As soon as these hardships are finished, one enters hell again. This refers to the retribution for evil deeds in hell.

The suffering is beyond words. Yet for these people, their karma is not of their own making; as they emerge and enter from time to time, they regard the hells as gardens, groves, and palaces, and thus it is said they "dwell there constantly.
In the other evil realms, such as those of the hungry ghosts, they do not depart morning or evening, and thus they are likened to a house or residence.
As for the animals—camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs—they come and go from time to time, and thus...
"Where the clouds travel. This clarifies that those who first emerge from the three miserable realms (*durgati*) to become human, and subsequently fall back down again, are as follows:

when they do emerge from the three miserable realms and later become human, they take afflictions such as deafness and blindness as their adornments, and thus do not realize their own ugliness; they take diseases such as dropsy as [their adornments].
As for clothing, one is not even aware of them upon their body throughout their entire life. Their bodies are constantly foul-smelling and base; this refers to those who slander the sutras.
They have fundamentally lacked the causes for seeing the Buddha or hearing the Dharma, yet they fail to reform and repent, remaining deeply attached to the view of self.

They cherish this inferior form; some people even loathe it. Failing to recognize their own ugliness and shame, they instead increase their anger. Humans and animals are of different species and ought not to mate in the wild.

Yet, when lustful thoughts blaze up, they do not choose their partners for the "clouds and rain" of union. This is attachment, which is greed; it increases anger, which is hatred; and it blazes with desire, which is delusion.
Possessing these three poisons, as soon as their human retribution is exhausted, they will once again fall [into lower realms].
One enters the three miserable realms. This is what is meant by "fully experiencing one kalpa"; when the kalpa ends, one is reborn again. How could there ever be an end to this?

Is it not thus that one constantly dwells in houses and frequents places of activity? Therefore, it is said, "those who slander this sutra," and so forth. From the phrase "for these reasons" onwards, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent section is introduced.
It means that the Buddha’s appearance in the world was originally for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings; his preaching of the Dharma was likewise for that purpose.
For the benefit of the world, you—Śāriputra and the others—did not discriminate between those who were suitable vessels and those who were not, recklessly transmitting this to unworthy recipients.
This caused ignorant and faithless sentient beings to slander the Dharma and mistakenly undergo such suffering. How could this have been the Buddha’s original intention?
Therefore, it is said: "I have thus spoken to you."
"If there are those of sharp faculties whose wisdom is clear and lucid... (up to) 'you should preach for them the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This section correctly teaches that one should preach for those who are the appropriate recipients (*yathābhavya*), explaining the meaning of why this sūtra was preached for the sake of benefiting the world.
It clarifies the passage concerning "those who hear it, rejoice in it, receive it upon their heads," and so forth. This consists of seventy-six phrases, divided into ten sections.
It is explained through the *pāramitās*. If there are those with sharp faculties and so forth, who possess wisdom when encountering the ten *pāramitās*, they are permitted to preach it;
their wisdom is clear and lucid, and this constitutes the cause for attaining this sutra. Those who have heard much and possess strong memory seek the conditions for this sutra.
As for "if a person has previously seen [the Buddha]" and so forth, when encountering the ten *pāramitās*, one who practices giving is permitted to preach it.

Furthermore, seeing the Buddha and planting roots of goodness is the giving of merit. To have a profound and firm mind is to not seek the minor fruits of humans or devas from the merit of one's giving;
this is what constitutes a "profound mind. As for the phrase "if a person is diligent," this refers to the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness is diligence in bestowing happiness. Not sparing one's own body or life is diligence in uprooting suffering. If a person is respectful...

"Et cetera" refers to the *dhyāna-pāramitā*. Having no divergent thoughts is mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*). Dwelling in mountains or marshes, away from the places of the foolish and worldly, is physical concentration (*kāya-samādhi*).
Furthermore, "Śāriputra and others" refers to the *upāya-pāramitā*, because they each attain their respective skillful means by abandoning evil and drawing near to the good.
"If one sees a son of the Buddha," and so forth, refers to the *śīla-pāramitā*.

Furthermore, upholding the precepts is like a precious pearl; it is the cause for the purification of the six sense faculties. Seeking Mahāyāna sūtras is the condition for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If a person is free from anger and the like, this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Being upright and gentle, one does not insult others.
Having compassion for all and revering all Buddhas, one does not insult people. Furthermore, regarding those who are "sons of the Buddha" and so forth:

This is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). Purifying the minds of the multitude is the self-benefit of wisdom. Using causes, conditions, and parables is the benefit for others through wisdom.
"If there is a bhikṣu," and so forth, refers to the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*). Seeking the Dharma for the sake of knowledge is the greatness of the power of faith.
That one's aspiration is great and not small is the greatness of the power of wisdom. "As when a person with a sincere mind," and so forth, refers to the perfection of vow (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
It is like honey. Seeking this sutra is the same as seeking the relics of the Buddha; regarding this sutra is equivalent to regarding the Buddha himself.

Do not seek other sutras. May your vows not be small. Never study heterodox texts; may you stay far from the deviant. As for addressing Śāriputra and the others: [it is because they are foremost among the disciples].
This connects the preceding section with the subsequent one. That is to say, by means of the ten *pāramitās*, the seeking of the Dharma is clarified;

that you are taught and explained [this] is the characteristic of a small portion within the many. The two characters "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "understanding" (*adhimukti*) serve as the foundation for the lower grade.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Four: The Parable of the Faith and Understanding.

"Faith" means having faith that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ various causes and conditions, parables, and skillful means in their discourse to preach the Dharma, all for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. (To have faith in the Dharma is to realize the convergence of the three vehicles into one. "Understanding" means...

One understands that all these teachings are intended solely for the transformation of bodhisattvas (if one understands this, then the provisional is realized as returning to the real). The Sūtra says:
"From of old we have truly been the sons of the Buddha"—this is self-confidence. It further says: "Yet we took pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma;
had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great, the Buddha would have taught us the Great Vehicle"—this is self-understanding.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding.

From the passage "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti" (extending to) "we now delight in speaking a parable to clarify this meaning," the section beginning with "At that time, the Venerable" refers to the parables spoken by the Buddha for the twelve hundred people in the preceding chapter; the scribe merely records [this here].
Four persons are set aside—namely, those who possess wisdom and understand through parables. Subhūti was foremost in understanding emptiness;
therefore, he was called "Life of Wisdom" (Hui-ming). Kātyāyana was foremost in elegant exposition and debate on the meaning [of the Dharma].
Kāśyapa, known as "Drinking Light," was foremost in dhūta practices. Maudgalyāyana, known as "The Clan of Mung Beans," was foremost in supernormal powers. Therefore...
All are designated by the title "Mahā" (摩訶), which means "Great. This refers to the four [disciples] who are the foremost among the great Arhats of the assembly of twelve hundred.
From the passage "What they heard from the Buddha" onwards, the text describes the two chapters on the Skillful Means and Parables.
Regarding the "Unprecedented Dharma," this refers specifically to Śāriputra, indicating that even as a Śrāvaka, he attained the same [realization] as a Bodhisattva.

[Sa]. He was granted the manifest prediction of attaining Buddhahood, including the adornments of the land and the duration of the kalpa of the One Vehicle, because it is a dharma never before encountered.
[Question: If this is so, then the author of the sutra records only the summary of the "Expedient Means" chapter and does not record the summary of the "Parable" chapter.

How can the commentary explain this as summarizing the texts of both chapters? [Answer: First, the single phrase "a dharma never before encountered" encompasses the entirety of both chapters. Second, since Śāriputra’s reception of the prediction occurs within the "Parable" chapter, there is no error in explaining the summary as encompassing the texts of both chapters. [He] gave rise to rare...
There are those of inferior capacity, such as Śāriputra and others, who were exclusively settled in the lesser fruits and had never previously resolved to attain Buddhahood.
Now, having received the Buddha’s teaching on these two chapters, they have been awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and they believe that their own minds can achieve Buddhahood.
They gave rise to great joy and realized the first stage (*bhūmi*). This constitutes the arousal of a rare mind and the act of leaping for joy.
From the passage "Immediately rising from their seats" onwards, the ritual of the six sense organs' joyful leaping is clearly elucidated.

From the passage "And addressed the Buddha, saying" onwards, four individuals of equal faith and understanding present their case together; hence the use of "we. Their years and virtue are both lofty, and thus they occupy [their positions].
"Monk," "Shou" (朽), and "Mai" (邁) are terms used to address those who are near death, incapable of further progress, or beyond the age of eighty and unable to fulfill their aspirations.
Regarding "self-attainment": within the sphere of the Buddha's realization, we consider ourselves as yet not having attained *nirvāṇa* without remainder;

thus, it seems as though the Buddha’s original vow remains unfulfilled for us. Yet, as beings caught in the cycle of birth and death, if we manage to escape the three types of suffering, we likewise consider ourselves to have already attained *nirvāṇa*. As the previous chapter states: "The Buddha taught the single principle of liberation; I..."

Others have likewise attained this Dharma and reached nirvana, yet they do not know the destination of its meaning; this correctly describes their state of mindfulness. Thus, we who are old and whose bodies are decayed have attained the lesser fruit of nirvana.

Thus, regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa, they would be incapable of it and unable to proceed toward the pursuit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. (This describes the *Madhyama-āgama* period among the five periods; it already encompasses the *Avataṃsaka* period. From the passage "In the past, the World-Honored One...
onwards, there is further a description of the teaching methods during the two periods of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Vaipulya* among the five periods.
During the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Vaipulya* periods, the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi was taught by the Buddha for the sake of the Bodhisattvas. Since...
"For a long time" refers to the thirty years during which the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the Vaipulya sutras were taught together.
"I was at the foot of the seat" means that while the Buddha was teaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* and Vaipulya sutras for those thirty years, I was also at the Buddha’s seat during that time.
The reason I did not further seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* was, first of all, because I was a person whose years had grown old and decrepit.
Their bodies were weary and exhausted. On one hand, they had attained *nirvāṇa* during the assembly at the *Āgama*;
however, by merely contemplating the three gates of liberation, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they found sufficient dharma-joy for their own personal enjoyment.

Consequently, regarding the Bodhisattva practices—such as the play of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and other such matters—their hearts felt no joy or delight. As stated above, "their years have all reached old age," referring to the span of their lifespans.
The former statement, "the body is weary and exhausted," refers to the physical form. The latter statement, "already having attained *nirvāṇa*," refers to the small fruit (*hīna-phala*).
This present statement, "emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)," refers to the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) possessed by the small fruit.

(In reality, these three dharmas—emptiness and the others—are possessed equally by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. This is evidenced by Śāriputra’s earlier remark, "We have entered the same *dharmatā* together," and by the *Zhao lun*, which states, "The three vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of nature and thereby attain the Way. Question: Since all three types of emptiness lead to the same entry [into reality], why is there a distinction?

"Why is it considered small? The answer is: "Because the transgression lies within a single thought-moment. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "All sentient beings are not called 'enlightened' because their thoughts have not yet been purified. What was mentioned above as "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" refers to the awakening of the fruit;
what is here referred to as "the Bodhisattva's dharma," etc., refers to the practice of the cause. Below, regarding "wandering in play":
This clearly elucidates the Dharma of the Bodhisattva. "Wandering" (*yóu*) means non-abiding; "sporting" (*xì*) means unreality; "spiritual" (*shén*) refers to the spirit;
and "penetration" (*tōng*) means that although one sports within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it does not obstruct the vital pulse of the sporting spirit in the present moment.
To cause all sentient beings to pass through to the other shore is the sublime function of this Bodhisattva-dharma.

"Working together to clarify [the matter] means having companions. At that time, the two messengers descend; they act according to the elder’s instructions. Regarding the title "like a father," what does this mean? It is because there are three reasons that establish the meaning of being "like a father. "I do not see any evil in you at all, as I do in others. This is the summary of the Chapter on Parables; I now guarantee this matter for you—it shall never be false. At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter (up to the point where it says) "the inferior mind was still not yet abandoned," this section serves as an analogy for the two periods of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.
It clarifies that although one does not seek the Great [Vehicle], one nonetheless partially realizes its greatness.

"Guest-worker" (*kèzuò*) and "slave" (*sīyǎng*) are terms of contempt used for both types of hired laborers. Today in Xin'an, when scolding children for being incompetent, one says, "guest-worker.

According to the *Wǔshí pànjiào* (Judgment of the Five Periods), twelve years for the *Āgama* period and eight years for the Vaipulya (*Fāngděng*) period constitute these twenty years.

"After this" means after the periods of the *Āgama* and Vaipulya; the Buddha, as the father, and the sentient beings, as the sons, finally came to understand and trust one another's minds. "Understanding" (*tǐ*) means that even if one were physically in their place, the father and son would be as one person. "Trust" (*xìn*)...

This is indeed so. To believe that the elder is truly like a father and oneself is truly like a son means that, since father and son already possess mutual trust, it is not difficult to enter [the house] as a son, nor is it difficult to leave as a hired laborer.

According to the reckoning of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, this is equivalent to the "removal of filth" in the Āgamas; for although the Dharma is great, the capacity of the practitioner is small. However, in reality he has not yet taken up residence in his son’s house; he still considers himself a hired laborer. "Being able to renounce" is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). This refers to what was stated in the preceding text: "Regarding the Buddha's transformation of bodhisattvas toward unexcelled bodhi (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they do not give rise to even a single thought of joy or aspiration. "For those of the two vehicles, it serves as the condition for attaining the Mahāyāna. Regarding "This is truly my son," the *Fahua yishu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), in the fourth section of the "Parable" chapter (*Upamā-parivarta*), states:

It is not said that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma through various causes, conditions, parables,
and skillful means for any purpose other than *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The passage "At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] the impoverished son," etc.,
concludes the section at the beginning of the chapter concerning the text on how immeasurable treasures are obtained without being sought.
“The World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder,” refers to the Tathāgata. “[Those who are] deluded, ignorant, and delighting in inferior dharmas” corresponds to the first section of the parable.
From “The World-Honored One, the great wealthy [elder]” onwards, the elder is used as an analogy for the Buddha; from “We” onwards...

"I liken myself to the impoverished son. From "The Tathāgata has always said" below, he explains the meaning of becoming a son, attributing it to the Buddha’s own words rather than daring to claim it for himself.

Suffering is manifold and its afflictions are heavy, yet one remains deluded and unaware of this because of a fondness for the lesser [vehicles]. The three types of suffering are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Because suffering is so abundant, there is feverish affliction; because of feverish affliction, there is delusion; because of delusion, there is ignorance.

This ignorance is precisely what constitutes *avidyā* (ignorance). Possessing this delusion of ignorance, one is thus confused regarding the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) that is inherently possessed by oneself.
Such knowledge and vision does not constitute being an outsider (*bāhyaka*), yet it results in clinging to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

How is this different from a destitute son who, out of fear, flees from his own biological father to go to a poor village? (According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vyākhyāyukti*, the three sufferings are identical to the three feelings. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, how should one contemplate the body upon which sentient beings of the three realms depend?

It should be viewed as a poisonous, inflamed abscess because it is accompanied by heavy afflictions (*dausthulya*). Regarding this very body, when a pleasant feeling arises, how should it be contemplated? It should be viewed as a poisonous, inflamed abscess that momentarily encounters a cool touch. Regarding this very body, when a painful feeling arises... )

How should one contemplate this? It is said: it is like a poisonous, inflamed boil touched by hot ashes; when a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant arises in this very body, how should one contemplate it? It is said: it is like a poisonous, inflamed boil that, apart from contacts such as cold or heat, remains inherently poisonous and hot by its own nature.

Thus the Blessed One said: "One should know that pleasant feeling is suffering because of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); painful feeling is suffering because of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is suffering because of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). This continues up to the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).

It is the foremost among pleasures. This is revealed by means of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*). How much more so for one afflicted by the three diseases of abscesses, scabs, and leprosy—only when one realizes that the third type of sensation, *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering inherent in conditioned formations), is like leprosy, does one attain *nirvāṇa*.
If one does not realize that the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is suffering, then the two sensations of suffering and pleasure will arise from it.
"Today the World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate [up to] that we shall have a share in the treasure-store of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
This corresponds to the second section of the parable. Regarding the word "today": it refers back to the previous section where we spoke of "past kalpas" due to the three types of suffering;
in reality, "today" indicates the time of the *Āgama* scriptures, not the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This refers to the time of the *āgama*, when the Buddha knew that we had endured much suffering in the past and were content with nothing more than the methods of the Lesser Vehicle for liberation from suffering. "Contemplation" refers to the preceding six consciousnesses and belongs to the category of cognition. "Elimination" has the meaning of cultivation and abandonment (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*). In the first chapter, the *Manobhūmi*, of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it asks: "How does birth arise? Because self-love (*ātmasneha*) has arisen without interval. Due to the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of beginningless attachment to conceptual proliferation, there are pure and impure karmas."

Because it has already been perfumed, that which serves as its substratum arises immediately from its own seeds within that very locus, through the dominant power of two kinds of causes. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Levels of Practice), fascicle 51, states:

"Moreover, for the practitioner of meditation, because the ālayavijñāna is the realm of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) designated by all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), it is now said to be 'cleansed. This refers to the practice of meditation whereby one cuts off the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the eighth consciousness;
it is merely like removing filth. We, the middle and lower [capacities], mean that we shall simply follow the Buddha’s teaching regarding the Dharma spoken by the Buddha.
By diligently cultivating the various contemplations of impurity, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, one indeed attains nirvana.
This is like that impoverished son who, by clearing away filth for the elder, receives the same daily wage as his master.

This is why the cultivation of the Path leads to the realization of cessation (*nirodha*). Having attained this—meaning having first reached nirvana—the mind is filled with great joy, and one privately thinks: "It is through cultivation that I have realized what has been attained."

It is vast; one does not know that it is still insufficient. It is said that within the Buddha-dharma, this is revealed as being distinct from the dharmas of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). "Do not speak of the six sense objects as being non-evil for us, for they are identical to perfect enlightenment. When the entrusted property is bestowed, one’s own karma has already truly made one a Mahāyāna son of the Buddha; there is no need to further seek its greatness.

He has no begrudging or sparing toward us. As for the reason below, it serves as an inquiry and explanation:
why was the Buddha previously suspected of being parsimonious, while we now realize he is not?

yet they had not yet realized the meaning that all three and one are equally devoid of falsehood.

This is because one was previously unaware of the three grades—superior, middling, and inferior.
Sentient beings are like grasses and trees; the Dharma taught by the Buddha is like clouds and rain.

Although these grasses and trees grow from small to large, the clouds and rain of the Buddha’s Dharma possess no distinction between provisional and ultimate, nor any sequence of before and after—it is simply of one single flavor.
How could one, because grasses and trees were small in the past and large now, conclude that the clouds and rain were first empty and later substantial? Therefore...
One knows that while clouds and rain do not distinguish between past and present, plants and trees naturally possess the distinction of being small first and large later.
This is why the Buddha, for the sake of his four great disciples and others, further expounded upon their faith and understanding regarding what had not yet been fully realized;
hence it is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter.

it causes those who are not yet settled to become settled. Regarding the teaching on abiding in ascetic practice and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): it causes those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa* to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Speaking in terms of the provisional teachings regarding the realization of the fruit: however, the arousal of the mind governs the stages of seeing, cultivation, and realization.

Seeing, cultivation, and realization collectively constitute the attainment of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is simply another name for liberation; therefore, the four phrases are defined as the virtue of liberation.
As for "the present world" and so forth, this refers to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. The *dharmakāya* pervades the three periods of time, and the three periods are collectively one.
"Truly knowing suchness"—that "I am all-equal" and so forth—is the virtue of *prajñā*. "All-knowing" does not mean knowing through partiality;
"all-seeing" does not mean seeing through pervasive wrong views. Furthermore, "all-knowing" means knowing through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), not through inference (*anumāna*);
"all-seeing" means seeing with the Buddha-eye, not seeing with the fleshly eyes of devas or humans. It is the knowledge of the Way—the path to unsurpassed *bodhi*—and...

It opens the mundane and supramundane paths; that is to say, it opens the path of the One Vehicle as well as the Three Vehicles. Furthermore, "opening" (kai) refers to initiating [a path], while "opening" also refers to clearing and smoothing [it].
To speak of the path means to explain its obstructions and unobstructedness, its dangers and ease, its suffering and joy, and its points of departure and arrival.
Without Prajñā, how could this be possible? "You gods and humans," and so forth, means that since the Buddha has already bestowed upon them their names...
Truly, with a great voice he summons the multitude; all sentient beings ought to listen to his command and seek the Dharma.
This metaphorically illustrates that the Buddha manifests his body like clouds, and it clarifies the single phrase:
"expounding all dharmas through wisdom and skillful means."
"At that time, the Tathāgata observes these sentient beings" (up to) "fully receiving nourishment and each attaining growth.

This passage combines the dharma and the metaphor to clarify that the preaching of the Dharma is like rain. Furthermore, it explains that the Dharma he preaches all reaches the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
From the words "At that time, the Tathāgata" onwards, the dharma is presented; following the preceding text, it means:
When the Buddha emitted this great sound, he surveyed with his Buddha-eye the assembly that had gathered like clouds upon hearing his summons.

Discerning the sharpness or dullness of their faculties and the progress or indolence of their natures, he assigned them offices according to what their faculties could bear and measured tasks against their capacities.
He then taught various dharmas—some threefold, some single, some small, and some great—so that none...

The assembly numbered in the hundreds of millions, all of whom attained the joy of the Dharma and its excellent benefits. The following passage clearly explains how these sentient beings obtained such benefit.
These benefits were both gradual and sudden. Regarding the distinction between the causes and effects of the three periods of time, and between the holy and the ordinary:

it is said that these sentient beings, for the most part, failed to hear the Dharma and consequently committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds. Thus, they were executed by others, and in their present lives, they found no peace or stability.
Upon death, one will fall into the three miserable realms; the spirits will seize and punish them, and they shall not be reborn in a favorable place.

Now, having once heard the Buddha-dharma, the principles of cause and effect are no longer obscure; by not committing evil in this life, one will enjoy peace and security in the present world, and after death, will be reborn among humans or devas.

Then they will be reborn in favorable realms. Such are those among the small roots, stems, branches, and leaves of sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma, obtain the wholesome benefit of the blessings and rewards of humans and devas.

Regarding the phrase "experiencing happiness through the Way" and so forth, this refers to those among the medium roots, stems, branches, and leaves of sentient beings who, while among humans and devas, [attain liberation] through the Way of the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
They receive the fruit of the bliss of the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and cessation (*nirvāṇa*), without losing sight of the cause.

Furthermore, they encounter the Buddhas and also hear the sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s six perfections (*pāramitā*) and ten thousand practices, thereby planting the causes for the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
Such is the case for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who hear the Dharma and obtain its excellent benefits. The phrase "having heard the Dharma" and so forth refers to these two [vehicles].

Once the practitioner has heard the Mahāyāna Dharma, they immediately distance themselves from the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), such that the various cycles of birth and death do not continue;
and they distance themselves from the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), so as not to obstruct right knowledge and vision. Thus, the *nirmāṇakāya* [operates] amidst immeasurable dharmas.
By relying on the power of one's own sovereign mastery, one may gradually enter the Great Path of the Buddha’s nirvana without remainder.
Such sentient beings—whether they be roots, stems, branches, or leaves—upon hearing the Dharma, obtain its excellent benefit.
Although there are differences between the minor fruits of humans and devas and the Great Path, they all equally receive the rain and clouds of the Buddha-Dharma.
By the power of this, one is able to advance step by step through each pool until reaching full completion and realization.
Is this not because all the teachings he expounded have reached the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)?

If this is so, how can it be said that what was previously attained as the "lesser fruit" was false, while what is now attained as the "One Vehicle" is only now true? This concludes the analogy from the passage beginning with "Like that great cloud," where the first two lines provide the comparison.
The passage beginning with "metaphors according to their capacity" and so forth; and the passage following "shrubs, trees, and forests" which says "all are made to rejoice" and so forth:

the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has a single characteristic and a single flavor (up to) his teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, which is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
"Thus, the Tathāgata... [and so forth]. This third section, which clarifies through both doctrine and parable, follows upon the preceding text.

It means that although the previous passage stated that in the past the Tathāgata taught the three vehicles—the small, the middle, and the great—according to what each was capable of, this does not preclude it from being the very same teaching of the single characteristic and single flavor given by the Tathāgata today. As for "the single characteristic," it is common to all Buddhas and sentient beings.
There is the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, the true reality of *tathatā*. This "one mark" therein accords with the preceding teaching on phenomena (*dharma*).
The Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena; this accords with the preceding analogy: although they are produced from the same earth, [they differ in their qualities].
Although the great trichiliocosm contains mountains, rivers, valleys, and gorges with diverse forms and appearances, they share the same characteristic of earth;
thus the treatise says: "The True Suchness of the mind is the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm. This is precisely that point.
"Of a single flavor" means that the teachings of the three vehicles and nine divisions spoken by the Buddha are all the same nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).

This is the flavor of the Dharma. This single flavor herein accords with the preceding Dharma. Furthermore, having thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena, he reveals to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom; this accords with the preceding metaphor:

just as when moistened by a single rain, the grasses and trees of the great trichiliocosm, though they possess different tastes—sour, bitter, salty, or pungent—what they receive from the divine rain is at first uniform.
First is the "sweet flavor. Thus, the Treatise says: "Because they are fundamentally equal and identical in their single awakening. This refers to the following:
by means of the three gates of liberation taught in the past within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it explains the single characteristic of the supreme One Vehicle of the present.
This means that what is now called the "one mark" (ekalakṣaṇa) of the Tathāgata’s teaching is precisely the same as the three marks previously mentioned, such as liberation (*vimukti*).
It is not that there is a separate, additional single mark apart from the three marks of the past. This is because the four great disciples in the *Śraddhāparivarta* state:
"They merely contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), yet their minds do not [enter] into the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas."

Joy and bliss. Now, it is clarified that emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are precisely the dharmas of the bodhisattva’s playful mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*).

Therefore, this is stated. Truly, because liberation is itself detachment, and detachment is itself quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), there are three names, yet in meaning they are actually of one single characteristic.
