At the end [of the passage], by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is explained as being of a single flavor, the ultimate finality.

Regarding the meaning: this is said in contrast to the initial period. Because the capacities of sentient beings at the beginning were small and unable to withstand the Great Dharma, the Buddha provisionally taught the true reality of the One Vehicle according to their needs as the three marks and three flavors.

Now that the conditions of their capacities have increased and matured, and the time for the Buddha’s ultimate nirvana has arrived, he cannot help but speak in accordance with the original intent of his enlightenment.

Therefore, the teachings on the three characteristics and three flavors of liberation and so forth, which were first expounded forty years ago at the beginning of the assembly, have all culminated in this single flavor of the ultimate *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience). As the previous sutra states:
"After a long time, O World-Honored One, you must surely speak the truth. And the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 575, says: "Mañjuśrī..."
Śrī. All the various Dharma-gates as I have taught are of one single flavor; that is to say, the flavor of detachment, the flavor of liberation, and the flavor of cessation.
Therein is no contradiction whatsoever. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "All sentient beings..."
All possess Buddha-nature; all are identical in the One Vehicle and one liberation, one cause and one fruit, and the same nectar of immortality.
All shall attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is called "one flavor.

The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that because those of the Two Vehicles do not sever and do not exhaust the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), they do not attain this one flavor. Now, this sutra desires to [make them] two...
The person on the vehicle, having severed the ground of the dwelling in ignorance until its ultimate end, attains the single flavor. Regarding the phrase "those who possess [inferiority]":
this means that although the Buddha’s Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor, there are sentient beings who hear the Buddha’s Dharma;
whether they maintain it in mind and recite it orally, or practice according to what has been taught, the merit obtained through these three karmas is entirely unconscious to them.

Know that these constitute a single characteristic and a single flavor. This Dharma of the Buddha is "one" because it accords with the capacities [of sentient beings], yet it is "different" because of those capacities.

Below, the text provides an inquiry to clarify this: why is it that while the Buddha-dharma is one, sentient beings—through the merit of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation of the three types of wisdom—are unaware that what they receive is both one and different? It is because only the Tathāgata [possesses] the supreme...

During the first seven weeks after his initial attainment of enlightenment, he employed the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) to contemplate and realize that although the dharmas of these sentient beings are fundamentally one, the seeds, characteristics, and essential natures (*svabhāva*) resulting from their various habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*) are not the same; thus, the merits obtained through their respective contemplation, cultivation, and practice each differ.
"Seeds" refers to the potentialities (*bīja*); "characteristics" refers to the specific manifestations (*ākāra*); and "essential nature" refers to the fundamental structure (*svarūpa*).
"Nature" (*xing*) refers to the nature of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*), as can be found in detail in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is one of the five specific object-oriented mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-caitta*) among the fifty-one mental concomitants. "Volition" (*cetanā*) is one of the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*) among the fifty-one mental concomitants.

To explain them in terms of the three types of action (*trividha-karman*), they both belong to the category of mental action (*manas-karman*); in reality, however, they pervade all eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). As for the character "cultivation" (*xiu*), it generally belongs to [the category of]...
The three karmas. This is why the functioning mind is identical [to that of a Buddha], despite the difference between them.

Because the Buddha alone has already transformed the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms, and because he has realized that the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses is one and only;

and because all sentient beings likewise possess this one-vehicle nature (*ekayānagotra*) of the self-witnessing portion of the eight consciousnesses. What is the matter? It concerns the five [factors] of the Small and Great [vehicles].
This refers to such matters as the objects of the truths and conditions. For example, sentient beings of lesser capacity contemplate, reflect upon, and cultivate the matters of humans and devas;

sentient beings of middling capacity contemplate, reflect upon, and cultivate the matters of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and sentient beings of superior capacity contemplate, reflect upon, and cultivate the matters of bodhisattvas.
This is what is meant. What is meant by "contemplation" and so forth? It means how one further advances to investigate and examine the meaning in greater detail.

That is to say, during the first seven days, the Buddha, having known the thoughts and the matters of practice and cultivation of sentient beings, further employed his wondrous wisdom during the second seven days to contemplate: "What are the causes and conditions for these sentient beings?"

Yet, how different are such acts of mindfulness, reflection, and cultivation! Those who practice mindfulness, reflection, and cultivation regarding the matters of the human and celestial vehicles possess the causal conditions for meritorious retribution.
Those who practice mindfulness, reflection, and cultivation regarding the matters of the two vehicles possess the causal conditions for fearing suffering and seeking happiness.
Those who practice mindfulness, reflection, and cultivation regarding the matters of the bodhisattva vehicle possess the causal conditions for benefiting oneself and others.

This is the condition (*pratyaya*). As for the question, "By means of what dharma does he recollect them? it means that during the third seven-day period, the Buddha again employed his sublime wisdom to reflect:

"Since these sentient beings possess such causes and conditions for recollection, reflection, and cultivation, by what dharma shall I provide for these sentient beings so that they may recollect, reflect, cultivate, and thereby attain their goal?"
What dharma constitutes the fruit? Sentient beings abide at a lower level; this clearly explains that by practicing correctly, one attains the fruit.

For those who contemplate, reflect upon, and cultivate the causes and conditions for meritorious retribution, the Buddha—using the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle according to what is appropriate—thoroughly and clearly elucidates it by manifesting the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, so that these sentient beings who contemplate, reflect upon, and cultivate may achieve their goal.
The practice of their profound resolve reaches its ultimate consummation, abiding in the fruit-stage of the Cakravartin kings, Śakra, and Brahmā.
For those who contemplate and cultivate the causes and conditions for leaving suffering and attaining happiness, the Buddha, through the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle,
exhaustively and clearly elucidates it according to what is appropriate, manifesting it as the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination in accordance with their thoughts.

He contemplates and cultivates sentient beings, enabling them to bring to ultimate fulfillment the practices of their profound resolve and to abide in the stages of the fruits of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha.
For those who contemplate and cultivate the causes and conditions for self-benefit and the benefit of others, the Buddha— through the true reality of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna)—
clearly and exhaustively reveals, according to what is appropriate, the dharmas such as the six perfections and the four means of integration.

Rather than contemplating and cultivating [the teachings] for sentient beings, one brings to ultimate fulfillment the practices of their profound resolve, abiding in the stages of the three levels of worthiness (*śaikṣa*), the ten stages of the sages (*ārya*), and the fruit of Buddhahood of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

"Only the Tathāgata" and so forth means that although sentient beings may attain Buddhahood and contemplate, reflect upon, and cultivate His Dharma, they remain in the various stages of the five vehicles; yet, each does not [attain it] by themselves.

Knowing that all these are differentiated from the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), yet each clings to them as being distinct, only the Buddha’s true wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) perceives and knows the merits attained by sentient beings at each stage;
it clearly understands the unimpeded dharma in which the original truth is one and three, and three and one. Within this, it is according to reality.
"Sees" means that it is not seen by the fleshly eyes of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) nor by the wisdom-eyes (*prajñā-cakṣus*) of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

This is because although these various eyes each attain a degree of clarity, they are all obstructed. As in the passage beginning with "like those grasses and trees," the text provides an analogy to conclude the section concerning sentient beings who hear the Tathāgata’s Dharma and so forth;
this refers to sentient beings of the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*) dwelling in their respective stages, each [not...].

They know for themselves the merit of the Buddha’s Single Vehicle (ekayāna), which is like grasses and trees that do not each know for themselves that they are receiving the single flavor of the clouds and rain from heaven, yet each abides according to its own superior, middling, or inferior nature.

This corresponds to the previous teaching on knowing the deep-seated inclinations and practices of all sentient beings with unimpeded penetration; it corresponds to the preceding metaphor of the various grasses and trees.

Each has its own distinctions. "The Tathāgata knows this" and below—this section cites the Dharma to conclude that only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings' lineages, characteristics, essences, and natures.

This means that although sentient beings are like grasses and trees, each unaware of the merits they have attained as superior, middling, or inferior natures, the Buddha knows from the very beginning that there is no [nature] above them.
The distinctions among the five grades—middle and lower—are solely the direct teaching of the One Vehicle, the true mark (*dharmatā*), the single flavor, and the nectar-like Dharma.
Regarding what is called "lower": previously, when the three marks were explained as being identical to the one mark, this was to clarify the awakening to the fruit of Bodhi.
Therefore, it is described as ultimately reaching all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), for all-encompassing wisdom is itself Bodhi. This...
Furthermore, explaining the single characteristic by means of the three characteristics clarifies the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is stated that ultimate nirvāṇa, characterized by eternal quiescence, ultimately returns to emptiness; for nirvāṇa is itself the virtue of cessation.

However, the fact that both the beginning and the end are expressed in terms of "ultimate" (niṣṭhā) serves to reveal that the bodhi of the two vehicles and their *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* are not ultimate.
Sentient beings of the nine dharma-realms may either fail to attain Buddhahood altogether, or if they do attain it, they do so only by achieving bodhi and nirvāṇa;
therefore, these terms are used interchangeably throughout. Question: Regarding the initial stage of the Hīnayāna...
Is this not a realization of emptiness? Why, then, do you now clarify the Mahāyāna by stating only that all things ultimately return to emptiness? Answer:

In the beginning, the Buddha, because his disciples were of small capacity, expounded the single characteristic as three characteristics—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
To speak of the characteristics of liberation, detachment, and cessation is merely to employ the discourse of "emptiness of persons. Now, as the Buddha preaches the Dharma, forty years have passed;
the time has come for the two vehicles to receive their predictions of enlightenment, and the time for the Buddha’s own parinirvāṇa has also arrived—this is called the ultimate finality.
Therefore, these three characteristics are shown to converge into a single characteristic, thereby clarifying the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Although there is a difference between the beginning and the end regarding the selflessness of persons and phenomena, the principle of emptiness realized therein is one and the same.
Therefore, it is said that they ultimately converge upon the mark of emptiness, which is eternally quiescent and extinguished.

This clearly reveals the essential intent of unifying the three vehicles into one and transforming the provisional into the real. Regarding the phrase "The Buddha, knowing this for himself," the character "this" (是) refers back to the aforementioned [emptiness].
The mark of quiescence means that the Buddha knows that from beginning to end, persons and dharmas are collectively one mark of empty quiescence;
thus he has certainly attained their ultimate destination. However, he did not speak of this at that time, but waited until forty years later to do so.
This is because although the Buddha knew the ultimate destination of all dharmas, he also knew the deep-seated inclinations and practices of all sentient beings.
Observing that the mind-kings and mental desires of sentient beings differ, he leads and protects them;

for this reason, he initiates the beginning [of his teaching] but does not immediately preach to those of the two vehicles that they should attain the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

"Leading" means leading the Dharma to accord with their capacities (*yathā-yogam*); "protecting" means protecting the Dharma, which is precisely how he protects their capacities. It is not that the Buddha initially has any stinginess.
In the end, I grant it to them; this results in the fault of false speech. From "You, Kāśyapa, etc. below, the first section is concluded.
You—Kāśyapa and the others—are equal to the remaining three great disciples, who are rare and few.
When I praised you four as being among the rare and few people in the world, it was because you were able to know me, Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

The Dharma of the three vehicles—small, intermediate, and great—which I have taught as appropriate for the past forty years, is precisely the Dharma of the single reality without the three vehicles that I now teach after these forty years; furthermore, you are able to believe and accept it.
To clarify this point below, I ask: why was it previously said that even if you were to speak of the Buddha’s merits for billions of kalpas, you could not exhaust them?
[The previous section] has ended. Why is it that you now further praise you all as being rare among men?

It is because the Buddhas of the ten directions and I, Śākyamuni World-Honored One, have preached the Dharma according to what is appropriate from beginning to end, and it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
It should be understood that the reference to "the words of the Buddha" or "the words of the Tathāgata" in the *Sūtra on the Universal Gateway* refers, for the time being, to Śākyamuni Buddha alone.
When it subsequently refers to "all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones," it indicates all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Regarding the statement that "teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand and difficult to know": this refers, for example, to how [Śākyamuni] initially taught the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) in accordance with the capacities of those with inferior faculties.
It was appropriate [to teach] by expounding the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Sentient beings understood only that there were three, not knowing that they were one;

this followed what was appropriate for those of lesser capacity, as it was difficult to understand and difficult to know. Now, at the conclusion, the three vehicles are unified. Following what is appropriate for those of great capacity, he expounds the one vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Sentient beings understand only that the present "one" is real and the former "three" were false; this follows what is appropriate for those of great capacity.
Furthermore, it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world... (omitted)... by means of various causes and conditions, he enables them to attain right view."
Regarding the section "Destroying Existence" (*bhavavidhvamsa*) below: the verse states, "The Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas... and thus he expounds them.

"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to ignorance, craving, grasping, and becoming, which are the causes of the world. "The world" (*loka*) refers to birth, old age, sickness, death, and the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), which are the fruits.

Since the Buddha has already destroyed existence (*bhava*), he should not undergo rebirth. That he now appears again is for the sake of acceding to the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, teaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles through various causes, conditions, and parables.

One should know that the destruction of existence is fundamental, true wisdom (*mūla-bhūta-tattvajñāna*), while his appearance is expedient, provisional wisdom (*upāya-kuśala-jñāna*). Because he possesses true wisdom, he is the King of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna-dharmarāja*).
It is not in vain because it possesses skillful means and wisdom; thus, it is not in vain as the Dharma-king of the Three Vehicles.
From the passage "The Tathāgata honors" onwards, it praises the teachings he has expounded, stating that they all reach the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
This means that although he employs reality as a skillful means to teach various dharmas, the teachings he expounds are all able to reach the state honored by the Tathāgata.
The ground of true wisdom is profound and remote; it is not something known by those of the Lesser Vehicle with their shallow intelligence.
From the passage "For a long time this essential [teaching] was kept silent" onwards, the verse describes how the Tathāgata perceives the ultimate destination of all phenomena.

That is to say, since the teachings he has already expounded are all capable of reaching this profound and remote ground of wisdom, why did he not teach this essential and subtle [truth] sooner? These...
This is the destination toward which the Dharma tends, for it is that which all Buddhas revere. Having remained silent for a long time, he waited for the right moment;

he did not intend to achieve realization quickly. "If one with wisdom hears this" and so forth—the verse also implies that one knows the conduct of the deep minds of all sentient beings and attains unimpeded mastery of their meaning. This means that since the Buddha does not begrudge the teaching of the Dharma...

Though one is urgent in wishing to save others, one does not strive to preach quickly because the practices of sentient beings' deep-seated minds involve few who possess wisdom and faith, while those who are ignorant and doubtful are many.
If one were to preach too hastily, they would not only fail to understand, but would also lose the opportunity forever, leading them to undergo endless suffering.
Thus, if one is too hasty, the benefit to sentient beings is slight, while the harm to sentient beings is great.

Because there is much [ignorance], it is said that "those without wisdom harbor doubt and regret," and so forth. Therefore, from the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa, below," it is meant that because there is such fear, one must quickly speak for the sake of harming sentient beings.
This is why the Dharma King, in teaching through others, accords with the capacity of sentient beings;
employing various causes and conditions, he speaks of the Small, Great, Three, and One Vehicles. Although this is called the use of expedient means (*upāya*), [it is for their benefit].
In reality, this means causing all beings to attain ultimate *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience). Therefore, it says "causing them to attain right view.

This verse, moreover, corresponds to the passage in the prose stating that one has "thoroughly exhausted and clearly understood all dharmas. The prose reads: "thoroughly exhausted and clearly understood."
This is called "teaching according to one's capacity. It is precisely because they teach according to capacity that sentient beings are able to fully comprehend.
The long passage refers to "all-encompassing wisdom," while this [text] refers to "various correct views. "Various" is equivalent to "all," and "correct view" is equivalent to "wisdom."
"Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud [which]... saturates the dry land so that medicinal herbs and trees all flourish.
This verse constitutes the first section of a single metaphor. In the prose (long-xing), the world’s grasses and trees are mentioned first, followed by the clouds and rain;

in the verse, this order is reversed. Furthermore, the imagery of the clouds and rain, through the addition or subtraction of characters, suffices to complete what was not fully expressed in the prose.
The water of a single flavor produced by those clouds [pervades] from the roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits to their luster and color.
This verse constitutes the second section of the extended prose, consisting solely of a single simile.
"Wherever the single rain falls, all things obtain freshness and luster; though the moisture is one, each grows lush and flourishing.
This verse corresponds to the third section of the long prose passage, which employs a single metaphor.
The Buddha likewise appears in the world... [omitted] ...all should come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One.
This verse combines the Dharma and the analogy to clarify the first section. From "The Buddha likewise" onwards, it first praises the reality of his greatness;
from "Great Sage" onwards, it subsequently praises the renown of his greatness. "I am the Tathāgata" refers to the foremost of the ten epithets. These two...

The "One Endowed with the Feet" (*pādavān*) refers to the second, third, and fourth of the Ten Epithets. Because he possesses both merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as his two feet: being endowed with the foot of merit, he is the Worthy of Offerings (*arhat*);

being endowed with the foot of wisdom, he is the Truly and Fully Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). Furthermore, the foot of wisdom is "clarity" (*vidyā*) and the foot of merit is "conduct" (*caraṇa*);

thus, it also encompasses the epithet "Endowed with Clarity and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*). Following the phrase "having emerged from the world," the verse [proceeds to] praise him as the "Well-Gone One" (*sugata*) and the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).
This is the fifth of the ten titles. "Like a great cloud" below praises the two epithets "Unsurpassed Being" and "Charioteer of Men," which are the sixth and seventh of the ten titles.

"The assembly of devas and humans" below praises the three epithets "Teacher of Devas and Humans," "Buddha," and "World-Honored One," which are the eighth, ninth, and tenth of the ten titles. The prose section provides the names first.
The subsequent section provides the actual explanation. In the verse, the reality is first indicated, and then explained through its names.
"I am the World-Honored One, whom none can equal" (up to) "just as those grasses and trees receive their natures differently."
This section consists of seventy-four lines. It is the second section, which explains the long prose through both textual exegesis and analogies.
The first thirty-six lines correspond to the passage from "At that time, the Tathāgata arose... to "...quickly attaining excellent benefit. Regarding the phrase "I am," etc.:
the Buddha is fundamentally without a self; he employs the term "self" in accordance with worldly convention, referring to himself as the sovereign of the nine dharma-realms and the three worlds.
All praise the Buddha as the Honored One, saying that none can equal him; this is for no other reason than that he is able to bring peace and security to sentient beings.
Though it was not necessary for him to appear in the world, he has manifested in the world to preach for the great assembly the pure Dharma of ambrosia, which is neither born nor extinguished.
This Dharma is of a single flavor; "below" refers to the pure Dharma of ambrosia, which, upon attaining this single flavor, leads to liberation.

This is the flavor of *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the phrase "with a single wondrous sound": although it is a single-flavored sound, it does not hinder beings from understanding it according to their respective categories;
hence it is called a "wondrous sound. This meaning refers to liberation and *nirvāṇa*.

One should know that the "wondrous sound" is the means of exposition (*nirdeśaka*), while "liberation" is that which is expounded (*nirdiṣṭa*). Regarding the phrase "constantly for the sake of the Mahāyāna," this provides further clarification.
This means that the Buddha did not merely expound this meaning at a single time;

rather, throughout forty years, although he taught the Dharma of the three vehicles and nine divisions, it was none other than constantly serving as the cause and condition for the Mahāyāna liberation and nirvāṇa, and never as the cause and condition for the Hīnayāna liberation and nirvāṇa. As I observe this...

"Cutting off all [attachments]" means that the reason the Buddha directly establishes the causes and conditions for the Mahāyāna is that, when the Buddha contemplates all sentient beings within the nine dharma-realms, he perceives them as universally equal and fully endowed with this essence of the One Vehicle Dharma;
therefore, he harbors no thoughts of partiality, attachment, or aversion. "I have no greedy clinging" means that the Buddha does not harbor greedy affection.

This refers to adhering to the Mahāyāna while dwelling therein. Furthermore, it is "without limitation or obstruction," meaning that the Buddha did not limit this great capacity by teaching it extensively for them, nor did he obstruct that lesser capacity by teaching it briefly for them; therefore, throughout forty years—
He constantly teaches the Dharma of the One Vehicle with impartiality for all sentient beings. As explained below regarding "for one person," this clarifies that [the teaching] is equal.
That is to say, just as the Buddha exhaustively explains the meaning for a single individual who is a suitable recipient, how could it be that many people do not hear it?
Therefore, it is said that it is likewise for the multitude. The above clarifies this.

"The Buddha’s mind for the sake of the multitude is universal. This explains that the Buddha constantly expounds the Dharma; furthermore, it clarifies that the Buddha’s mind for the sake of the multitude is uninterrupted by time.
That is to say, when the Buddha appears in the world, he always takes the expounding of the Dharma as his task, never having any other business whatsoever.
"Coming and going" refers to the fact that since the Buddha takes only the expounding of the Dharma as his task, whether he comes, goes, or sits...
While established in the four modes of deportment, there is nothing in which he does not preach the Dharma; never has it been seen that he ever grew weary or exhausted.

"To satisfy those below" means that the reason he is without weariness is none other than his desire to satisfy the sentient beings of the three worlds with the Dharma of the One Vehicle, just as the clouds and rain of heaven universally moisten the three types of grass and two types of trees. This...
The Buddha possesses no attachment and no obstructed views. Within the equality of the Dharma—regardless of whether one is noble or base—the capacities of beings are inherently unequal.
Among people there are the noble and the base; among ranks there are the high and the low;
regarding precepts there are those who uphold them and those who violate them; regarding deportment there is its possession or lack thereof; and regarding the vision of truth there is...
Regarding the heterodox and the orthodox, there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties and practices; however, the Buddha has no such likes or dislikes toward them.

He merely rains down the Dharma-rain equally, with a mind free from indolence and a body free from weariness. Thus, although the capacities [of sentient beings] may be unequal, the Buddha’s mind is consistently and never fails to be impartial.
This is as described in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" regarding the four great disciples.
The Master said: "The secret treasury of all Buddhas is the teaching of the actual reality solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas;
it was not for my sake that such essential passages as these were expounded. Therefore, I have repeated this earnestly to resolve his doubts. Now, within this there are five kinds of equality.
From the phrase "the Dharma is of one flavor" downward, it refers to the equality of the essence of the Dharma. I contemplate all...
"Below. The Buddha’s mind is impartial; he constantly acts for all who are below. The Buddha speaks of equality;
as he does for one person, so it is for many—equality between the few and the many. He constantly expounds the Dharma; this is equality through long-term practice.

At the end, take all those things that are unequal—noble and base, high and low—and reflect upon them once. One will see even more clearly that there is nowhere the Buddha does not act with impartiality.
The following thirty-two lines of verse summarize the prose section from "these sentient beings arise" up to "gradually attain entry into the Way.

Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings," this follows the preceding text; it means that because the Buddha-dharma is like rain from the clouds and never wearying, all sentient beings who hear the Buddha-dharma receive it according to their capacity and each comes to abide [in the truth].
Regarding the various stages (*bhūmi*): these stages are divided into five categories, hence the term "various. Alternatively, they are situated within the human and celestial realms.

First, there are the stages of the karmic rewards for humans and devas: among humans, the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) is the most noble; among the heavens, the kings Śakra and Brahmā are the most honored.
This explains the four phrases concerning nobility and meanness, high and low. [This] takes the Heaven of Śakra as the sovereign of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

They rank above the Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*) and below the Brahma Kings. This is because the Brahma Kings are the lords of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), while [the others] rank below Śakra and the gods of the Heaven of Empty Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Generally, those who are above are noble and those who are below are base;

their causes are all brought about by upholding the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), as well as being fully endowed with dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). As for the various kings, they range downward to include the Four Heavenly Kings (*cāturmahārājika*).
The "superior" refers to those such as the gods of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and the various minor regional kings (*kṣudra-rāja*) among humans.
Regarding the "lesser medicinal herbs," this corresponds to the preceding metaphor of small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves.
Although human and celestial kings are the most noble within the three realms, they still belong to the outflows (*āsrava*) of birth-and-death; nevertheless, all of them may [be included].
It relieves the suffering of beings and bestows happiness upon them; therefore, it is called "medicine. Because it is not merely a structural beam for the Buddha-dharma, it is compared to grass.

To "know the dharma of outflows" means to know the method of understanding suffering and severing its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*). This distinguishes it from what gods, humans, Śakra, and Brahmā do not know.
"To be able to attain Nirvāṇa" refers to those of the Lesser Vehicle who, having already understood suffering and severed [its origin]...
Because of this accumulation, one is able to attain *parinirvāṇa*. This phrase encompasses both the aspiration for cessation (*nirodha*) and the cultivation of the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*).

It distinguishes [the practitioner] from those in the realms of humans, devas, Śakra, and Brahmā, who still belong to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and do not attain *nirvāṇa*. Regarding "arising the six supernormal powers" (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*):

the six powers are the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna*). The three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*) are... [text continues].

These are the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): the clear knowledge of the divine eye, the clear knowledge of past lives, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. Question:

Since the three clear knowledges constitute half of the six supernormal powers, why are they established separately? Answer: The supernormal powers are categorized according to one's own realization, whereas the clear knowledges are categorized according to benefiting others.
This is detailed extensively according to the numerical categories of the Dharma. The above constitutes the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Śrāvaka-yāna.

Below follows the stage of the Pratyekabuddha-yāna. There are two types of *pratyekabuddhas*: first, the *pratyekabuddha* (solitary awakened one); second, the *pratyayabuddha* (awakened by conditions). Dwelling alone in mountain forests constitutes the ground for the solitary awakening of the *pratyekabuddha*.
Constantly practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) constitutes the craft for the solitary awakening of the *pratyekabuddha*. Herein, it is designated by...

Dwelling alone, they are bound as *pratyekabuddhas*; thus we know that [this category] includes both types of persons. Question: Why does the sutra not explicitly state that they emerge from among the *śrāvakas*?
Answer: There are those among the *śrāvakas* who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), whereas *pratyekabuddhas* appear in worlds where no Buddha exists.
Because many do not turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], it is said that "knowing the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)" refers to knowing those of the Śrāvaka vehicle;

this is because the term "untainted dharmas" encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles. The above has generally clarified that those of middling and inferior capacities all belong to the category of the Small Vehicle, and they all possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Regarding these "medicinal herbs," they correspond to the "middling roots" in the preceding analogy.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the central stalk" and continuing with "seeking the World-Honored One": this refers to those such as Śāriputra who turned their minds toward the Great Śrāvakas and desired to seek the station of a Buddha.
They declared, "Although I do not become a Buddha in the present life, I shall certainly become a Buddha in a future life."

Therefore, although they enter meditative concentration (samādhi) together with those of the two vehicles, they practice the concentration of diligence (*vīrya*) among the Bodhisattva’s six perfections, rather than the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Such individuals are the superior medicinal herbs among all medicinal herbs. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "all sons of the Buddha" and below:
"sons of the Buddha" refers to Bodhisattvas, for a Bodhisattva (*bodhisattva*) is cherished by the Buddhas.

They are called "sons" [of the Buddha]. There is a distinction between the three worthies (śrāvaka-ārya) and the four stages of preparatory practice (prayoga-mārga); therefore, they are referred to as "the various ranks.

Although they have not yet reached the stages (bhūmi), their minds are single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha-way. Though the Buddha-way is manifold, the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa-citta) are its foundation.

Therefore it is said that they constantly practice compassion. Although the Buddha has not yet granted them the prediction of their future buddhahood, they know for themselves that they will become buddhas;

they are certainly not subject to doubt or confusion by Māras, non-Buddhists, or those of the Hīnayāna. While they still abide on the stages prior to the bhūmis (*bhūmi-pūrva*), though they are greater than those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), they are still inferior to those on the bhūmis and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi-bhūmi*). They cannot be compared to medicinal herbs; therefore, it is called "This is named..."

He is a "small tree" [a Bodhisattva]. Regarding the phrase "dwelling securely in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)," this refers to Bodhisattvas on the stages from the Ground of Practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) up to the Ground of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*).
To say they "dwell securely in supernatural powers" means that their practice of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) is superior to that of ordinary beings.

To say they "turn the wheel of non-retrogression and deliver immeasurable billions of beings" means that they have transcended the mere certainty of knowing for themselves that they will become Buddhas; they have reached a state beyond doubt.
One should know that compared to the preceding medicinal herbs, they are called "trees"; compared to the small trees above them, they are called "great trees.
This combines with the previous metaphors of the great roots, great trunks, and so forth. Question: How are supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) distinguished from compassion (*karuṇā*)?
Answer: Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) merely bestows happiness; compassion (*karuṇā*) merely uproots suffering. Spiritual powers (*abhijñā*), however, do not stop at mere loving-kindness and compassion.

Even acts such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), and the ten non-virtuous actions—whenever they serve as a means to deliver sentient beings—a Bodhisattva can also settle their mind within them.

This is something that no Bodhisattva other than those on the stages (*bhūmi*) or those who are nearly perfected (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) is capable of. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says: "The powerful Māras of the ten directions..."
"O King, these are all bodhisattvas who dwell in the inconceivable liberation. Regarding the preceding metaphorical passage, it lacked two types:
the superior medicinal herbs and the small trees. Since these are present in this verse, it demonstrates that the medicinal herbs and trees each possess three grades:
superior, middling, and inferior. The six lines following "The Buddha’s impartiality" correspond to the long prose section concerning "that great cloud."

The passage "It rains upon all equally" concludes the analogy and its application to the Dharma, clarifying that equality resides in the Buddha while inequality resides in the capacities of sentient beings.

Thus, the Buddha’s Dharma is like rain from the clouds, possessing but a single flavor; yet when sentient beings receive it according to their faculties—like roots and stalks—their actual experience of it differs accordingly.
The Buddha uses this analogy as a skillful means to reveal and instruct [the disciples], [extending] until: "By practicing and training gradually, all shall surely attain Buddhahood.
This verse, which combines the Dharma and its analogy, constitutes the third section.

The first fourteen lines summarize the passage from "The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor" up to "by what dharma one attains what dharma," directly clarifying the explanation.
The first [section] concerns the meaning of the Buddha using the real as a provisional means. The Buddha brings down this analogy; this analogy is the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

"Skillful means" (*upāya*) refers to the opening instruction, which is provisional wisdom (*prajñā*). "Expounding" belongs to the aforementioned provisional wisdom. "One Dharma" refers to the real wisdom of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This means that by means of this chapter, the Buddha clarifies through analogy the various skillful means he employed for forty years prior.

Although the verbal expressions of the three vehicles and nine divisions, as well as the various provisional wisdoms, are numerous, there is not one that does not expound the single vehicle of the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the phrase "inferior to the Buddha’s wisdom," this means that from the past until now, the Dharma taught by the Buddha, when viewed from the perspective of you followers of the two vehicles, may indeed seem very extensive;
however, when compared to the Buddha’s own realized wisdom of realization (*pratyātma-jñāna*), it is but a small portion.

It is but a single drop within the ocean. This was likely said because the four great disciples might otherwise conclude that this single chapter constitutes the entirety of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable and boundless merit;
therefore, he spoke thus. When he said, "I rain down the rain of Dharma," it meant that before the Buddha he had declared that the Tathāgata’s merit could not be fully described.
That he now speaks of only a single drop is because the clouds of the Buddha-Dharma—
It rains. Although it is called but a single drop, it does not hinder this very drop from being able to fill the three worlds, because the one is immeasurable.
Regarding the phrase "the Dharma of a single flavor": although it fills the three worlds, it remains a single flavor.
It is indeed a single-flavored Dharma. However, it is practiced according to the capacity of sentient beings.
When the power of sentient beings is great, they are like the large trees in that forest of medicinal herbs, and the moisture they receive is also great.

When the power of sentient beings is small, they are like the small shrubs and grasses in that forest, and the benefit they receive is also small. Although there are differences of great and small, all of them obtain [the Dharma].
Through the rain of the Dharma, they gradually grow more lush and flourishing. How could one say that the rain of the Dharma of the past is different from the rain of the Dharma of the present?
Is it that the great tree of today is real while the small tree of the past was false?
The next thirty-two lines of verse praise the passage concerning sentient beings dwelling in various stages, beginning with their emergence and ending with their ultimate return to emptiness.
He then clearly elucidates the principle that all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time bring provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality.

Regarding the passage "The Dharma of all Buddhas," it refers to Śākyamuni Buddha alone; the reason he directly employs the rain of the single flavor to fill the world, causing all things—whether great or small—to gradually flourish and grow more excellent, is not because he acts with such intentional artifice, but rather because he accords with the [Dharma] of the ten directions.

This is the constant rule for all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Since all Buddhas constantly employ the Dharma of a single flavor to cause all worlds to universally attain fulfillment and gradually practice until they all realize the fruits of the Way, how could Śākyamuni be otherwise?
From the section on Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas below, the gradual cultivation is explained by means of this constant rule according to the Dharma.
The two lines, "All who practice attain the fruits of the Way," explain this through analogy, clarifying the meaning of gradual growth and flourishing according to the size [of the capacity].
One should know that in the preceding section, three types of medicinal herbs were listed: first, the small herb, which is a metaphor for the vehicle of humans and devas;

second, the medium herb, which is a metaphor for the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and third, the superior herb, which is a metaphor for those among the śrāvakas who have resolved upon the Great Mind.

The Mahāyāna. However, while there is the meaning of *śrāvaka*, there is no name of *śrāvaka*. This section combines the three types of medicinal herbs—the small, medium, and large—previously mentioned, treating them as a single category;
it is here that the name of *śrāvaka* is also included. "Dwelling in mountain forests" reveals that those of the Two Vehicles originally do not belong in the imperial court.
Regarding "abiding in their final body": although they have attained the fruit, their fetters have not yet been severed. Thus it is said:
Abiding thus, the fetters of existence have been extinguished; he shall not continue into future births. In contrast to the beginningless succession of taking up bodies, this birth is his final body.
Those who hear the Dharma and attain the fruit are said to have transformed from the states of kings, Śakras, or Brahmās, having previously existed within the realms of humans and devas.

Having heard the Dharma of the Truths and Conditions, they resided in temples and halls; yet, being enticed by worldly pleasures, although they knew suffering, they were unable to dwell in mountain forests to sever its accumulation.

Now that they have become Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, dwelling in mountain forests, they know suffering and have severed its accumulation, no longer undergoing the suffering of future existence, and have attained the realization of Nirvāṇa.

"Joy! Thus, the Dharma heard in the past has now yielded its fruit. Those who were formerly known as Wheel-turning Kings, Śakras, Brahmās, and so forth—those minor medicinal herbs—have each now attained growth and become middle- and superior-grade medicinal herbs.
From "If there are Bodhisattvas... below, it clarifies the meaning that the former small trees have now grown into middle-sized trees; it says, "Their wisdom is firm and stable."
Thus, one knows that it does not stop at what was stated above— merely focusing the mind on the Buddha-way and constantly practicing compassion—
but rather proceeds to "thoroughly comprehend the three realms and seek the Supreme Vehicle. This indicates that it does not stop at what was stated above—
merely knowing for oneself that one will certainly become a Buddha without doubt— but rather proceeds by means of this present thorough comprehension of the vastness of the three realms.
Compared to my previous self-understanding of attaining Buddhahood, it was narrow and limited;
therefore, herein, the principle is described as "seeking the Supreme Vehicle," and the metaphor corresponds to a small tree growing into a medium-sized tree.

According to the *Renwang jing*, this refers to Bodhisattvas who, through the ten wholesome deeds prior to the stage of "Cultivating Patience" (*śikṣā-akṣānti*), increase their practice and enter the three stages of the "Sages" (*tri-kalyāṇa*). Furthermore...
There are those who dwell in dhyāna; this means that by virtue of firm wisdom, they further abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Those who have attained the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) refers to those who, compared to the aforementioned abiders in supernormal faculties, further attain such power.

"Abiding" refers to the initial entry into the practice, while "attaining power" refers to its long-term maturation into functional utility. They hear that all phenomena are empty and their minds become vast.
This joy is known to be different from the joy of hearing that persons are empty.

To liberate countless sentient beings before oneself is known to be different from the liberation of beings through turning the non-retrogressive wheel; for even turning that wheel still involves the labor of verbal expression.

Light illuminates and thus knows; this is because it admits no sound. Therefore, within this context, compared to the preceding section’s metaphor, that which is called the "middle tree" has grown into a great tree.

This is different from the seeking of the Supreme Vehicle (Agryayāna), for while the latter merely seeks, the former has already grown and attained the ultimate. One should know that this is due to three [factors].

The "Stage of the Worthy" (*ārya-bhūmi*) increases until it reaches the "Tenth Stage. The above is a metaphor for the smallness and greatness of the capacities (*indriya*) and their respective gradual increases.
"Thus, Kāśyapa," and so forth below, is a metaphor for the Buddha’s body-cloud and Dharma-rain;

fundamentally, there is no distinction of small or great, nor of before or after—it is but a single flavor (*ekarasa*). Regarding "moistening the people and the flowers": "people" refers to the Dharma, and "flowers" is a metaphor; each attains [their own benefit].
"Accomplished reality" (*siddhatattva*) refers to the actual fruit. This term applies to both the Dharma and the metaphor.

It means that although the clouds and rain of the Buddha-Dharma are said to be no different, the capacities of those of the Small, Great, and Triple Vehicles do not, by means of this [Dharma], open the flower of their minds and bind the fruit of the Way in the same way;

rather, each accomplishes its own respective small or great [result]. Kāśyapa, you should know that the following six lines are a verse summarizing [the Buddha's thought] from "having known this" up to "arising."

This passage on the cessation of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) concludes the preceding two sections by clarifying the meaning of how the Buddha and all Buddhas employ provisional means to manifest the ultimate reality.

The phrase "by various causes and conditions" illuminates, in relation to what precedes, the single great cause and condition (*ekamahāprayojana*), and illuminates, in relation to what follows, the parable of the resting city (*tāḍāgaka*).
It illuminates all the sutras, encompassing everything taught during the forty years prior. Of these various...
Regarding "parables": examples such as the Udumbara flower, the burning house, and the medicinal herbs are all manifestations of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
They reveal the Buddha-way so that one may enter the ultimate reality by means of the provisional. As for the phrase "this is my skillful means," the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states:

"The merits attained by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas—their severance of the afflictions of the five stages and their liberation from the two kinds of birth-and-death—none can compare to [the merit of this]."
The Buddha said: "That which is called attaining *nirvāṇa* is entirely the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas.

This concludes the preceding section on how the Buddha uses these metaphors for the following fourteen lines. "All Buddhas are likewise" concludes the thirty-two lines concerning the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Now, the eight lines beginning with "I now [speak] for you all" are a verse summarizing the passage beginning with "You, Kāśyapa, are truly most rare."

Thus, the preceding section concludes and the subsequent one begins. This refers to how Kāśyapa and the others were most rare and extraordinary in their ability to believe in the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma according to what was appropriate for each.
Therefore, the Buddha now speaks to Kāśyapa and the others concerning the ultimate reality:
he clarifies that the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* previously realized by the assembly of śrāvakas is not, in fact, the Buddha’s *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Hence, it is said: "All..."
It is not extinction (*nirvāṇa*). You [should] descend [to this understanding]: since it is not the extinction of a Buddha, what dharma is it?
It is the small fruit of *nirvāṇa* practiced by you; it is the great cause for the path of a bodhisattva. Relying upon this great cause...
By practicing and studying gradually, one attains the great fruit of Buddhahood; it does not stop at merely attaining the small fruit of Arhatship. The Śrīmālādevī Sūtra states:
"Those who attain a partial nirvāṇa are said to be heading toward the realm of nirvāṇa.

It further states: "The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all enter the Mahāyāna. The Mahāyāna is precisely the Buddha-vehicle. Therefore, [the small vehicle is ultimately subsumed within the great].
The three vehicles are themselves the one vehicle. As for the one vehicle: it is the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*Bodhi* is itself *nirvāṇa*, and *nirvāṇa* is itself the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*, and so forth. This is as in the bestowal of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) in the lower fascicle.
Question: In this section, the dharma, the metaphor, and the words are redundant; how does this differ from the preceding section? Answer: It is with respect to...

Speaking in terms of the text: the preceding section emphasizes that what is received and what is inherited according to one's capacity differs for each; this section emphasizes the gradual increase and flourishing until each attains its own fruition.
Thus, the meaning of these passages is not the same. Speaking in terms of the doctrine: the preceding section clarifies that although they are one, they appear as different;
in the past, the provisional was not yet the real, and though the three vehicles each had their respective attainments, all were merely suited to their own limited capacities.
One must not generalize or overstate this. This section clarifies that although [the vehicles] are distinct, they are one; that the provisional is in fact the real.
The Three Vehicles are the steps toward the One Vehicle, for the Small can be increased until it becomes the Great. Thus, the three layers of both the Dharma and the parable all speak of "increasing.
This is how the meaning differs.
The Sixth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Prophecy" (*Vyākaraṇa*).

In the Sanskrit language, it is called *vyākaraṇa*; here it is translated as "Prophecy. To speak and bestow through the words of the Sage is called "bestowing" (*vyā*); to accord with the aspirations of the mind regarding the fruit is called "prophecy" (*karaṇa*).

First, Śāriputra requested that the causes and conditions be explained; the Buddha then expounded them through parables, all of which were intended collectively for the sake of the thousand [bodhisattvas].
Two hundred people attained understanding and received predictions [of their future enlightenment], yet only four actually attained full realization.
Therefore, I now alone first record the four great disciples, because these four great disciples have all already awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

As for the others, I shall wait until the conditions are ripe and my teaching is complete before bestowing predictions upon them. Regarding the fact that Kāśyapa is recorded first among the four great disciples, it is because of the Buddha-dharma...
Within this context, nothing is excluded from wisdom and practice. Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom;
Kāśyapa—translated here as "Shaker"—was foremost in ascetic practice (*dhūta*), and his seniority in the monastic community (*saṃgha-ratna*) was also the greatest.
Yet this prophecy was precisely for the sake of the śrāvakas, when the Buddha preached the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas.
This is the meaning of the mindfulness attained; it should be understood.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses (up to the point where it says), "even though there are Māras and the followers of Māra, they all protect the Buddha-dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses, addressing the bhikṣus:
"By my Buddha-eye... [as far as] ...the World-Honored One of Radiant Light; such were the matters."
"At that time" and below conclude the preceding section. "He addressed the assembly" and below is the formal bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon Kāśyapa. The verse above states:

"That which you all practice is the bodhisattva path. This refers to planting the roots of merit by reverently serving three hundred million *koṭis* of Buddhas, and planting the roots of wisdom by extensively proclaiming the Great Dharma;
this is precisely the gradual cultivation and study of the bodhisattva path, the foremost causal practice.
This is a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The preceding verse stated that they shall all attain Buddhahood; here it says they shall attain the name of the Buddha *Prabhāsa*.
This is the bestowal of the second fruit-prediction. The aforementioned [attainment] is equal to that of all Buddhas.

Regarding the ten titles of a Tathāgata, those who have not yet resolved for the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) are not granted them; however, for those who have already resolved their minds, these [titles] will certainly be theirs.
"He is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "the land named," this bestows the third and fourth prophecies concerning the *nirmita-bhoga* (dependent retribution).
This dependent retribution does not exceed the two polarities [of heaven and earth]. The "land" pertains to the realm of geography, while the "kalpa" pertains to the celestial realm of time.

As for "Light Virtue," it refers to the eternally quiescent *ābhāsvara* Pure Land. As for "Great Adornment," it refers to the land of adornment through actual retribution (*vipāka*). Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s lifespan," this bestows the... [fifth prophecy].

The fifth is the prediction concerning the primary retribution (*vipāka*). "The True Dharma" and below, it bestows the sixth prediction concerning the duration of the abiding of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma in the world.
"Below, the Perfectly Awakened One [bestows it] upon sentient beings. "The Realm of the Country" and below, explains the names of the country and the eon (*kalpa*). "Free from all... and below.
"Brilliantly Adorned. Below "Lapis Lazuli," it is said that his land is adorned with brilliance. Below "Bodhisattva," he is granted the prediction [of Buddhahood] as the seventh Dharma-kinsman.
Below "Without Māra," he is granted the prediction as the eighth Protector of the Dharma.

This means that although the Māras, gods, ministers, and subjects are among the inevitable numbers within the three realms, within the Buddha-dharma of Radiance, they do not perform the demonic deeds that harm the Buddha-dharma; for by means of light—
This clarifies that because the Buddha’s causal practices were vigorous, he was not defiled by Māra upon attaining the fruit; yet Māra also protects the Dharma.
Within the *Śāriputra-vyākaraṇa*, there is a prophecy of the transmission to Kātyāyanīputra, but no prophecy regarding Māra protecting the Buddha-dharma.

Each follows their respective vows and practices, mutually encompassing one another. Regarding the great cause and condition for Kaśyapa’s future attainment of Buddhahood, the Buddha [expounded] each and every...

He bestowed the prophecy upon him. Kāśyapa recorded each of these one by one. That a Śrāvaka should receive a prophecy of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood is truly like the Udumbara flower or the great treasure of the blue lotus;
it appears but once in a long while. The three subsequent sections of the record follow this same principle and require no further explanation.
Comparing the verses with the prose, the name of the land is missing: its name is Prabhāśrī, and the kalpa is named Mahāvyūha. Three.
The four sections are as follows; the remainder may be understood by analogy.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and the others [up to] spoke these verses with one voice:
"The Great Hero, the Fierce World-Honored One, the Dharma King of all Śākyas" (down to) "like one hungry who must be taught to eat.
At this point, the passage beginning with "At that time, Maudgalyāyana and the others were all struck with awe and trembling" describes their faith and understanding, with Subhūti taking the lead.
Kāśyapa was third. When it came to the description of the medicinal herbs and the bestowal of predictions, he found that in every instance he alone preceded Kāśyapa.
The three of them feared that the Buddha was pointing toward a single corner [of a square] while they wished to infer the remaining three corners for themselves;

thus, their minds were not at ease, and they were filled with such awe and trembling that they spoke the verses in unison, desiring the Buddha to personally proclaim their names and grant each of them his own prediction.
"Also. Below "The Great Hero" (Mahāvīra), it means that the Buddha is a singular hero of great valor, revered by the three worlds.
Among all the Śākya clans, he is the king who has shattered all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Therefore, he is able to take pity on us;
as stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter, that the twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas, and so forth up to the "Supernatural Powers" chapter.
"It is said that by gradually practicing and studying, all shall surely attain Buddhahood. This is precisely the voice granted to us, declaring that we shall become Buddhas.

"If [the Buddha] knows," and so forth, means that although we have heard this voice declaring our future Buddhahood, we have not yet received it as Śāriputra or Kāśyapa did—where the Buddha personally proclaimed their names and personally bestowed the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon them. "If the Buddha knows" [refers to this].
"We desire that the Buddha personally grant us a prediction of our deep resolve.
If he would look upon us with compassion and bestow such a prediction, it would be like sprinkling us with nectar (*amṛta*), removing our feverish afflictions and bringing us cooling relief.
As for 'nectar,' this refers to the supreme, pure Dharma of nectar; 'fever' refers to a heart of trepidation. This is because those of the Two Vehicles..."

Because they are not being scorched or boiled by the fires of the three realms, it speaks only of "removing heat. As follows from below, he again employs a metaphor to request his prediction [of enlightenment]:
coming from a land of famine, the hunger and starvation are extreme; this is a metaphor for the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Encountering the royal banquet, the joy and delight are profound;
this is a metaphor for the sound of the Buddha’s voice. Yet, with a mind of doubt and apprehension, one does not yet dare to eat.
The phrase "the man" is a metaphor for those who, though granted the Buddha’s voice, did not yet dare to believe it themselves.

The phrase "only upon receiving the king’s command did he dare to eat" is a metaphor for how one must receive the Buddha’s prediction before daring to accept the responsibility. The above constitutes the allegorical text.

The section beginning with "We... applies this to the Dharma; therein, "those of the Lesser Vehicle" corresponds to the starving country. The section beginning with "Not knowing... clarifies the faults of those of the Lesser Vehicle.

The fault lies in not knowing how one might attain Buddhahood. Although they hear [the teaching] below, because those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) would attain Buddhahood, it is like a hungry person encountering a king’s banquet;

their minds are filled with doubt and fear, so they do not dare to eat. If they were to receive [the prophecy of] Buddhahood below, it would be like following the king’s command and then daring to eat, feeling both satisfaction and joy. Those of the Lesser Vehicle do not believe in their own minds.
They shall become Buddhas; it is because they believe the Buddha’s words that it is thus. Alas!
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great disciples (and so forth), had delivered and liberated immeasurable bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, I now tell you: [the True Dharma shall remain for twenty small kalpas, and] the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty small kalpas."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus... [up to] "the semblance Dharma will also remain for twenty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
All the assembly of bhikṣus listened with single-minded attention (until) his land was adorned with immeasurable and incalculable [excellences].
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly (until) the Semblance Dharma shall also remain for forty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"This disciple of mine, Mahāmaudgalyāyana... (until) I shall now speak; listen well!"

Regarding all the great disciples who receive their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), although the adornments of their kalpas and lands differ from one another, they are none other than names bestowed based on their causal practices;

that is, the fruit is predicted by means of the name derived from the cause. For example, during Kāśyapa’s causal stage, he continued the light of Dīpaṃkara and anointed a Buddha image with purple-gold light;
thus, as an arhat he was named "Drinking Light" (Pītabhāsa), and upon becoming a Buddha, he was titled "Light-Radiance" (Prabhāsa). As for Śāriputra...
In the causal stage of Bodhi, his mind attained unimpededness. He remembered his births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; while in his mother’s womb, he knew emptiness and stillness.
As an Arhat, he was named Sudarśana (Good Vision) and also called Ākāśagotra (Born of Space). Because of being Sudarśana, when he became a Buddha, he was titled Lakṣaṇa (Marks);
because of being Ākāśagotra, he always dwelt in empty space when preaching the Dharma. During his causal stage, Candra-kumāra diligently swept [the grounds].
Regarding the Buddha-ground: when he was an arhat, he was named Wen-shi (Adorned with Patterns); upon attaining Buddhahood, he was titled Yánfú Jīnguāng (Jambū-golden Light).

Maudgalyāyana heard the causes and conditions during his causal stage and left the household life; as an arhat, he attained the foremost of supernatural powers. Upon attaining Buddhahood, he will be titled Duōmózhānxiāng (Tagara-fragrance).
This fragrance does not leave this place, yet it reaches that place; likewise, these supernatural powers do not abandon their causal basis, yet they manifest there.
The conditions have already been fulfilled; all effects do not contradict their causes, and their names accord with their reality.

Although this is the practice of śrāvakas, they are all bodhisattvas—they simply do not realize it themselves. Therefore, in the preceding verse, the Buddha first spoke to them to break down their attachment to causal practices, saying:
"That which you practice is the path of the bodhisattva. Subsequently, when he was about to bestow upon them the prediction of their fruit, he said:

Gradually practicing and studying, they shall all attain Buddhahood. Whether it be the size of their lands, the duration of their kalpas, the length of time their Dharma remains, or the number of their retinues—all these accord with their respective original vows; yet their merits neither increase nor decrease.
The final six lines concerning my disciples are for the sake of the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecy upon the Five Hundred Disciples."

Exegesis: The "I" and the following four phrases establish the foundation for the subsequent causes and conditions, while extensively explaining that the Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits.
This refers to the five hundred disciples whom the Buddha intended to bestow the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of their future Buddhahood;
it is because the Buddha had previously, in past lives, [established] the conditions for these five hundred people to attain Buddhahood.
It is because of causes and conditions.

In the seventh chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, titled "The Parable of the Phantom City," the term "phantom city" (*nirmita-nagara*) is contrasted with the "place of treasure" (*ratnasthāna*). "Phantom" (*nirmita*) means transformation; "city" (*nagara*) refers to a walled capital or fortress. First, the Buddha spoke of the fire...
The Parable of the House: Originally, [the Buddha] intended for twelve hundred people to simultaneously awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

however, only the four great disciples possessed faith and understanding, while the others were as if they had neither heard nor seen it. Therefore, the Buddha further spoke the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

Although this was for the sake of the four great disciples, it was intended to fully describe their merit, which could not be exhausted by that previous explanation. His true intention was indeed for twelve hundred...
Two hundred people attained simultaneous enlightenment regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and were all granted predictions [of their future Buddhahood].

As for the one thousand two hundred who did not attain enlightenment, it was because they heard that the Tathāgata is the King of All Dharmas, and that whatever he speaks—whether the three or the one, whether provisional or real—is entirely true and not false.
They thought to themselves: "Since both the three and the one, whether provisional or real, are all not false, then..."
The minor fruits we previously realized were not, in fact, anything other than the Great Vehicle of the present;
thus, we rested content at the "transformed city" (nirvāṇa) as if it were the "jeweled destination," refusing to advance further in our hope for a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).

For this reason, while the superior grade of prediction was granted to Kāśyapa, the other three great disciples must also seek the Buddha’s prediction, as they too constitute the twelve hundred [followers].
There were one hundred people who had been inspired [to seek awakening]. Now that they have been inspired to attain immovability (*āniñjya*),
the Buddha, having no choice, spoke of the causal conditions of his past lives to clarify how, in the past— prior to kalpas as numerous as motes of dust— he,
while serving as a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), once transformed twelve hundred people into Buddhas, just as a guide leads a multitude across five hundred treacherous and perilous passes.
[They traveled] for three hundred *yojanas* until they reached the place of treasure.
Once the śrāmaṇeras had each attained Buddhahood, they in turn delivered the twelve hundred people who were seeking the Lesser Fruit.

It was because those people whom he had brought along were weary and sought rest that, having no other choice, [the Buddha] established a conjured city beyond the three hundred *yojanas*. Now, these twelve hundred people have already attained it.
Regarding those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship yet still desire to be delivered through the Mahāyāna:
it is like the extinguishing of the conjured city and leading them beyond two hundred yojanas to the place of jewels, thereby fulfilling his original vow made when he was a śrāmaṇera under a Buddha.
Thus we know that the three vehicles of the past were not in vain. For example, it is like using a conjured city as a place of rest;

this can serve as a ground for advancing toward the treasure abode, and thus its name is not in vain. This does not mean that the conjured city itself is the non-falsity of the treasure abode of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle.
In this way, the teachings of the past took the One Vehicle as the cause, while now, by means of the two vehicles...
And having obtained the prediction of attaining Buddhahood as a condition, with past causes and present conditions, the matter admits of no further delay.
How could one persist in the citadel of the Two Vehicles—clinging to notions of non-transformation, of extinction, and of peace—and fail to press forward?
Therefore, it is called the "Parable of the Magic City" chapter; this is why these past-life causes and conditions must now be explained by the Buddha.
The merit of this is such that it cannot be fully described even by means of discourse. The text of the scripture, spanning the entire chapter, is divided into two major sections.
The first begins from the opening of the chapter with the Buddha’s address to the bhikṣus regarding the distant past, and extends until the sixteenth [section], where it says:
"I, Śākyamuni Buddha, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the Sahā world-system."
[The text] clarifies that the Buddha [taught] for the sake of the twelve hundred people who had previously planted the causes for the Mahāyāna in past lives,
and it reveals that the merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata are immeasurable and boundless. Next, it begins from the point where each of the bhikṣus and others says, "When we were śrāmaṇeras,
we each converted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," and so forth.

"This city is not real; it was merely conjured by me. This passage clarifies that for the sake of the twelve hundred people, the Buddha used the Śrāvaka Dharma as a "conjuration city" (nirmita-pura) to establish the conditions for the Mahāyāna of the present age, thereby manifesting the immeasurable and boundless merit of the Tathāgata’s skillful means and wisdom.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In the distant past... (up to) observing that long ago as if it were today.
From "The Buddha told" onwards, he introduces the kalpa of the past, generally clarifying the vastness and inconceivability of his previous lives.
From the passage beginning with "At that time" [it is stated that] the Buddha Jñānabala was Śākyamuni’s close relative in a previous life;

he possessed the ten titles, and there are the actual records of the adornments of his eon and land. Speaking in terms of the present, from the passage beginning with "O bhikṣus, that Buddha," it speaks in terms of after his parinirvāṇa, using a comparison to specifically clarify the inconceivability of his many past lives; therefore, it says, "extremely great and long."
"Far away. This is illustrated by the following passage, which uses a non-standard analogy to explain the text concerning how exceedingly long ago that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa.
It says: "If one were to grind all the soil of the great trichiliocosm into ink, the quantity of that ink would be immeasurable.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore," it means that the ink does not simply fall along with the earth, but rather falls further toward the east.
In the first thousand worlds, as soon as the first drop is cast, that drop is not very large; it is merely the size of a minute mote of dust.
Again, one passes over [the next] thousand worlds, which refers to casting the second drop of ink upon the ground as described above.
In this manner, one again passes over a thousand worlds for the second time, and then casts the third drop. Thus one proceeds.

Using ink from three points of the earth-realm (dharanī), one proceeds by multiplying this until reaching ten million points and so forth, continuing directly downward until the entire earth-realm is exhausted with ink.
By calculating the number of lands in this manner, the lands marked by the ink are infinite.

The phrase "In your case" (*yu ru*) introduces a question to clarify that [the lands] are innumerable; it means taking the ink from the aforementioned earth-realm to mark the lands being calculated, thereby...
"Could a master mathematician, together with his disciples, by calculating it, reach its limit and know its number?
"No, World-Honored One," they replied. "Truly so," [the Buddha said]. "They could not reach its limit and would not know its number.
O bhikṣus, this person is inferior; that is to say, even if one were to take all the dots and ink-marks passed over by this person..."
In a land where no ink has been applied, one takes all the dust with one's fingers and rubs it away until it is gone;
then, using that dust as a unit to calculate eons (*kalpa*), the number of eons exceeds even that count by many multiples.

The vastness of those eons is more than double what might be imagined—it is immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable) and inconceivable. From "I, as a Tathāgata" below, the section is concluded.
This explains that the Tathāgata’s merit of true wisdom is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable.
Yet, by the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, and true wisdom, the Buddha perceives this vast duration as if it were but a single day.
Thus, it is indeed true that Kāśyapa and the others could not exhaustively describe it even in immeasurable billions of kalpas. In the past...
Since the Buddha’s vision of kalpas is as clear as this, it further demonstrates that the bestowal of predictions regarding the future fruits for his great disciples is not in vain;
though the kalpas are long and the fruits distant, they will surely be realized.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I recall past lives through immeasurable and boundless kalpas... [until] penetrating immeasurable kalpas."

"I recall" introduces the verse as a general heading. "As a person" and so forth explains the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) through specific illustrations. "Beyond" and so forth explains the boundless (*ananta*).

"In this way" and so forth uses the analogy of particles to measure eons, explaining the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). "The Tathāgata’s unimpeded" and so forth concludes the section to manifest his virtues.
This refers to what is called "renouncing expedient means" in the *Upamāna-parivarta* (Chapter on Similes), which praises the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
