The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... [until] ...with single-minded devotion, palms joined, gazed up at the World-Honored One.

From "The Buddha told the bhikṣus" downwards, there is a general account of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū from his initial attainment of Buddhahood until his final parinirvāṇa and the duration of his lifespan.

Under the phrase "the original seat of that Buddha," there is a specific account of his beginning; that is to say, it describes the Great Penetration (Mahābhijñā) as the self-realization of a single Buddha.
Speaking in terms of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle, then beyond the limit of *Vīradhvaja* (the Buddha of the Past), the work was already completed and he was already a Buddha;

hence it says, "originally already. As for the phrase "about to attain" and below, this refers to speaking from the perspective of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time who manifest the Real as the Expedient;
thus, even at the present moment, at the gateway of the door, one still contemplates that the skillful means have not yet been attained. Therefore it says:
Regarding "the dharmas of all Buddhas" and so forth: the phrase "dharmas of all Buddhas" clarifies that these are not the dharmas of a single Buddha alone.
This refers, for example, to my own Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s contemplation during the first seven days immediately after his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.

The phrase "in this manner, for one small kalpa" below means that, generally speaking, from the very beginning of his Buddhahood, he contemplated for one small kalpa before sitting and preaching to all sentient beings.
Regarding the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment, fearing that sentient beings might not reach its depths, he contemplated for as long as ten minor kalpas,
yet still did not grasp the skillful means by which the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time reveal the reality as provisional.
Therefore, it is stated twice that "the dharmas of all Buddhas are equal. This refers to the contemplation of our Śākyamuni Buddha during his second seven-day period.
Since Śākyamuni lived for eighty years, the duration of his contemplation was expressed simply in terms of three weeks.
However, since the Wisdom Buddha has already lived for five hundred and forty million *nayuta* kalpas, [the calculation of time must differ].
Therefore, when contemplating this, it is expressed in terms of one minor kalpa up to ten minor kalpas.

At that time, descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he explained the ritual protocols for his original sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). This refers to the bodhimaṇḍa where the Buddha of Wisdom attained his original birth;
as for who prepared that bodhimaṇḍa, it was the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven prior to his sitting at the site of enlightenment.
He prepared his lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, one yojana in height. Therefore it is said, "First, for the sake of equality," and so forth.
Once the Buddha had prepared this seat, he addressed the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and uttered this prayer of aspiration:
The Buddha shall sit upon the seat I have prepared and attain enlightenment.
For it is the constant rule that the site where all Buddhas attain enlightenment must be prepared in advance by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Just as he sat down upon this seat—at the very moment the Buddha of Wisdom sat upright upon his throne—the Brahmā Kings of the Form Realm [arrived] at the seat.
From the beginning at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) until the end at his parinirvāṇa, [the Four Heavenly Kings] offered service solely by raining down celestial flowers;

the various devas of the Four Great Kings offered service solely by beating celestial drums; and the remaining six heavens, such as Yama and others, offered service solely by performing celestial music.
The above describes the ritual for the Buddha’s original sitting at the site of enlightenment.
Thus it is. From the passage "At that time, the bhikṣu Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū" onwards, it refers to the Buddha’s contemplation:

after ten intermediate kalpas had passed, he finally attained the skillful means of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time to adapt the Dharma to the capacities of sentient beings, opening up the ultimate reality as provisional expedients.
Consequently, all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time manifested their bodies before him and offered consolation.

This is illustrated by an analogy: it is just as when our Śākyamuni Buddha, during his third week of contemplation, reflected upon the skillful means employed by past Buddhas and thought, "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught through the three vehicles.

While he was engaged in this reflection, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before him, and their Brahma-voices offered him consolation and encouragement. Therefore, it is said that "this is the Dharma of all Buddhas."
The passage beginning with "Then [the Buddha] appeared before them" and so forth, although it recounts the events of the past Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,
actually clarifies the meaning of Śākyamuni Buddha’s own initial three-week period of contemplation described in the verses of the "Expedient Means" chapter.
It can be seen that our Śākyamuni Buddha was recollecting the Buddhas of the past; he was specifically recollecting this Greatly Penetrating and Victorious Wisdom Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū).
Since the Wisdom Buddha was already a close kinsman of Śākyamuni in a former life, his seven-times-three days of contemplation were also the family tradition handed down through generations.
The above has described the meaning of the Wisdom Buddha’s initial attainment of Buddhahood and his final entry into parinirvāṇa.
"Regarding the passage 'When that Buddha had not yet left home' and below: this is a retrospective narration of events from before the Buddha Jñāna had left his home.
It clarifies that our Śākyamuni Buddha, in past lives, served as one of twelve hundred people who sought the Great Dharma and planted the roots and source of great causes.
As for the sixteen sons, he mentions only the name of the first; this is to represent the whole by citing a single example. His father was named Jñānottara, and his son..."
It is said that "Jñānakūṭa" (Wisdom-Accumulation) corresponds in name to the awakening attained on the causal stage and the state of fruition.
Jñānakūṭa is none other than the one who will become a Buddha in the eastern land of Abhirati in a later age, named Akṣobhya (Unshakable).

The *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means) states that Śākyamuni once drew near to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; this refers precisely to those whom the Buddha himself attended.

This is a nearby location. That the princes abandoned what they held most precious to go to the Buddha is what is called "excellently continuing their father's will" and "excellently recounting his deeds"—they were those who achieved filial piety.
That the mothers wept as they saw them off was because they loved their sons while simultaneously being able to behold their lord so that he might accomplish the Way.
As for the mention of "the mothers," it clarifies that the sixteen princes were not born of a single mother.

Furthermore, when his ancestors, the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings, along with their high and low officials, all went to the Buddha, they saw that throughout the entire nation, regardless of rank, nobility, or status, everyone held the Way in equal esteem.
This was just like the ceremony when our Śākyamuni Buddha, Queen Yaśodharā, and King Śuddhodana together escorted Prince Rāhula into the homeless life. Having arrived...
[The phrase] "lowering the head and face" correctly clarifies the ritual of reverent salutation. The words of praise are fully contained within the verses.
They are expressed in verse as follows:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue... [omitted] ...therefore we all prostrate and take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One."

The six lines beginning with "Great majestic power" (*mahātejas*) correspond to the passage in the original verse concerning sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); this refers to the contemplation during the first seven days.
The eight lines beginning with "The World-Honored One is most rare" correspond to the passage concerning "one such minor kalpa" (*antarakalpa*);
this refers to the contemplation during the second seven days. The four lines beginning with "Now I see the World-Honored One" correspond to the passage concerning "passing ten minor kalpas."

This is the contemplation during the final third week. The fourteen phrases beginning with "Sentient beings are constantly suffering" are verses that correspond to the passage concerning the time before the Buddha left the household life.
The phrase "not knowing the path to the exhaustion of suffering" explains the meaning of being blind and without a guide.
The phrase "increasing the evil realms throughout the long night" explains the meaning of sentient beings being constantly afflicted by suffering.
Meaning: Now the Buddha has attained the most supreme text, clarifying the meaning of our having obtained excellent benefit and our great joy of celebration.
At that time, after the sixteen princes had praised the Buddha with verses, the devas and humans spoke further verses, saying:
"The Hero of the World, peerless, adorned by a hundred blessings" (up to) "shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.
From "At that time" downwards, those who abandon their treasures and go to the Buddha have this as their intention.

The eight lines from "The Hero of the World" downwards clarify that the Buddha possesses the two feet, the two benefits, and the three awakenings. The two lines from "If I" downwards clarify one's own...
The reason for seeking the Dharma is likewise the desire to equal the Buddha in attaining both the two benefits for oneself and for others.

The eight phrases following "World-Honored One" explain and establish the text regarding the "Hero of the World who has no equal," clarifying the meaning of "distinguishing and revealing so that they may attain this wisdom.
To know what sentient beings contemplate and how they act implies that their mental states and activities are not uniform.
Just as in the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, he also knows the practices of sentient beings according to their deep inclinations;

knowing their wisdom, power, and meritorious karma, there are thus differences in cause and effect. Furthermore, just as in the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, he has thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all dharmas, and demonstrates all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings.
"The World-Honored One, having fully known them," concludes that they have attained [the fruit].
This is the unsurpassed wisdom. Regarding the phrase "one who shall turn the unsurpassed wheel," it refers to making a vow to preach for the sake of the world while sitting cross-legged.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The Great Penetrating Wisdom-Victory Buddha [from]... filled the world, surpassing the radiance of all the devas."
At that time, from within five hundred million *koṭis* of lands in the eastern direction... [up to] he spoke these verses:
"Our various palaces... [up to] this great radiance shines everywhere throughout the ten directions."
At that time, [the beings from] five million billion lands... with one mind and in a single voice, praised him in verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter... we only pray that you will compassionately accept us."
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke these verses with one mind and a single voice:
"O Hero among Men, Honored One among the Two-legged, we pray that you will expound the Dharma; through the power of great compassion, deliver sentient beings from suffering."
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
The Buddha told the assembly: "When the Jñāna-Buddha first attained the Way, the earth shook throughout the ten directions.

In the midst of that land, light descended and illuminated the dark and obscure regions below, namely the space between the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), where the light of the sun and moon does not reach."
It is able to illuminate that which is obscured by evil calamities. That they all become brightly enlightened is due to the brightness brought about by the Buddha’s light.
As for the sentient beings therein who, upon seeing one another, all say, "We have suddenly come into existence": these beings in hell undergo extreme suffering as if in a long night;
though they dwell together in one place, they do not know one another. Once they are graced by the compassionate light of the Buddha, their [suffering] is suspended.
At this point of poignant realization, one finally attains the opening of the eye; thus, self and other see one another. One might doubt that sentient beings are newly born from within a cauldron.

Furthermore, below the boundaries of that land, light shines upward toward the higher realms. Although the Brahma heavens do not employ the light of the sun and moon, their bodily radiance likewise has its limits.
Because the Buddha’s light is both great and all-pervasive, it is said to surpass the radiance of all the devas. Thus it is.

Regarding the phrase "At that time, in the east," etc.: this specifically clarifies the auspicious movement in the eastern direction; the Buddha’s light was so preeminent that the devas were filled with doubt.
At that time, the various Brahmā deities descended and assembled to deliberate upon it. In the verse, the phrase "for the sake of the birth of the Great Virtuous One" and so forth [is used].
"He has just emerged from his doubt" means that when the various devas move or reside, each possesses a personal palace.
"Each with a robe-satchel and so forth" means that, being about to follow the light to behold its manifestations, they first prepare their ritual offerings.
"Going together toward the west," and so forth, means that because the Brahmā Heaven is in the east, they seek out the signs toward the west.
"Seeing Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū," and so forth, resolves their prior doubt; they know this is a Buddha appearing in the world, not a great deity being born.
"Immediately scattering heavenly flowers as high as Mount Sumeru" refers to [the flowers] reaching upward across five million *koṭis* of lands.

Thus it was said. To behold the abundance of the Brahmā heavens, and furthermore to make offerings to the Bodhi tree—not only to the Buddha, but also to his tree—is what is meant by "loving the person and extending that love to their belongings. Having made offerings of flowers, she then presented them to the palace;
first discarding the light, she then discarded the heavy, demonstrating that her heart of reverence was inexhaustible. [The Verse:]
"O World-Honored One, you are most rare and marvelous," and so forth, praises his compassionate mind; thus it says, "able to save," and so on.

"The Great Teacher of gods and humans," and so forth, praises his loving-kindness mind; thus it says, "universally [delivering all]," and so on. Regarding the phrase, "From where we have come," and so forth:
This clarifies the sincerity of their purpose in coming, showing that they do not cling to the bliss of meditative concentration.
When they say, "By the merit of our past lives," and so forth, they seek to have their sincerity examined so that their offerings may be accepted.

At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma, further explaining the reason for their long journey to make offerings, thus fulfilling the two-footed [Buddha].
This is for the benefit [of others]. At that time, the Buddha Jñāna’s silent assent was in accord with the Buddha’s own intention that the time had come to emit light and preach the Dharma;
though he did not speak, his mind granted the request. As it is said in the *Shishuo*: "The World-Honored One uses silence as a sign of consent.
Originally, the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment and had already attained Buddhahood, yet it was solely due to the reality of the One Vehicle.

The Bodhisattva held on too tightly; not only did the Buddhas fail to appear, but even his own sixteen princes who had been born to him did not draw near, let alone the Brahma Kings from five hundred million billion lands throughout the ten directions, all of whom came [to see him].
This is why it is said that he was "on the verge of attaining Bodhi. After he had completed ten minor kalpas of such contemplation—
Relaxing the ultimate for a moment, he reveals the provisional through the real.
Having attained the various Buddhas' skillful means for delivering sentient beings, the Prince arrives and Brahmā also arrives; only then is it said that one has attained Bodhi.
It can be seen that the phrase "attaining Bodhi" merely causes sentient beings to perceive the signs of becoming a Buddha. Such is the nature of skillful means and provisional wisdom.
This is its subtle excellence. Therefore, when all Buddhas attain enlightenment, they invariably intend first to preach the Three Vehicles.
This is because the pedagogical essence of the Sahā world is such that sentient beings find benefit in the faculty of hearing; they enter the path through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

For this reason, in the subsequent text, after the Buddha of Wisdom has received the invitations from the Brahmās of the ten directions, he likewise first turns the wheel of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
After turning the Wheel of Dharma, he then expounded the true reality (*tattva*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) to his sixteen princely sons.

Although this passage describes the events following Śākyamuni Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment and his journey to the Brahma heavens of the ten directions, it actually elucidates the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means):
"When I, Śākyamuni, first sat at the site of enlightenment, observed the tree, and walked in meditation, the Brahma kings entreated me to turn the Wheel of Dharma, and I turned it."
[The] ritual procedures. Although the texts for the nine directions below may have additions or omissions, they do not go beyond these; they can be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, the various bhikṣus [from] five hundred million lands in the southeast direction (up to) spoke these verses:
For what reason is this? (Up to: This is because many Buddhas appear in the world to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
At that time, five million *koṭis* of Brahma Kings (up to: offered these palaces, praying that [the Buddha] would graciously accept them.
At that time, the Brahma Kings, with single-minded devotion and in unison before the Buddha, spoke in verse:
"O Holy Lord, King of Devas... (omitted)... By virtue of our past merits and blessings, we have now encountered the World-Honored One."
The kalaviṅka is the bird of wondrous song. Even before this bird has emerged from its egg, it emits a subtle and exquisite sound that outshines all other birds;
the voices of all devas and humans cannot equal it. Only the voice of the Buddha surpasses it; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke these verses with one mind and a single voice:
"The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma, revealing the characteristics of all phenomena... [omitted] ...increasing those who possess patience and goodness."
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently gave his consent.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus from five hundred myriads of koṭis of lands in the southern direction [arrived] and spoke these verses:
"Our various palaces [have become radiant] because a Great Virtuous One has been born as a deva, or because a Buddha has appeared in the world.
At that time, five million billion Brahmā Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult to behold" (up to) "The World-Honored One possesses great compassion; we pray that you will graciously accept [this offering].
At that time, the Brahma Kings, having praised the Buddha with verses (up to) "with one mind and in unison, they recited in verse, saying:"
"We only pray that the Honored One among Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma... [until] you shall proclaim the profound and far-reaching sound.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent; it was likewise so for those from the southwest direction down to the nadir.
The phrase "up to and including" (*naijin*) is a term used for abbreviation by omission.
It means that one passes over the six directions—namely the southwest, west, northwest, north, northeast, and so forth—and thus abbreviates the textual descriptions of their manner of arrival.
At that time, from five million billion worlds in the zenith [up to] for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās, he spoke these verses:
"By what causes and conditions now [up to] have you been born as great virtuous devas? It is because a Buddha has appeared in the world."
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) with one mind and in a single voice, spoke in verse, saying:
"Excellent! To behold all Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world... (up to) may we all together attain the Buddha-way."
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) then spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma and beats the drum of the nectar-like Dharma... having practiced the Dharma for immeasurable eons."

The ceremonial protocols for the offerings from the ten directions are identical in all respects; however, in the enumeration of the *deva*, *nāga*, and *aṣṭakula* (eight classes of beings), the three divisions of *yakṣa*, *asura*, and *garuḍa* are both missing.
In the verses, the section beginning with "Excellent" (*sādhu*) praises the joy of beholding the Buddha’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

The section beginning with "Universal Wisdom" (*samantaprajñā*) praises the joy of hearing the Buddha’s great benevolence (*mahāmaitrī*). The section beginning with "In the past" (*purā*) [refers to] the east.
In the south, it is said that one hundred and eighty kalpas pass in vain without a Buddha appearing.
In the south, it is said that after passing one hundred and thirty kalpas, one now obtains a single vision [of a Buddha]. Reaching this point, it is stated:

"In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas," meaning that according to the depth or shallowness of the roots of goodness in each of the lands of the ten directions, there are varying amounts of time—whether long or short—in which one encounters a Buddha.
Regarding this inequality: from "The World-Honored One has not yet appeared" downward, it clarifies that because one does not see the Buddha, there are such evil fruits;
from "One has not heard from the Buddha" downward, it clarifies that because one does not hear the Dharma, there are such evil causes, whereby goodness is extinguished and evil increases.
From "The Buddha is for the sake of the world" downward, he concludes by returning to the praise: "Excellent is seeing [the Buddha]."

The scriptures of all Buddhas cause those who delight in perversity to return to the correct path and those who commit evil to follow the good; thus, the devas increase while the evil realms diminish.
We, the various palace lords below, seek to receive their reverent instructions and dedicate them toward our own benefit and the benefit of others.
We do not aspire for the minor fruits of humans or devas, but rather all vow to attain the Way of Buddhahood. Thus ends the hymn on beholding the Buddha.
The joyous celebration of making offerings. At that time, the five hundred youths likewise emulated the sixteen princes in requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

Following the section on the World-Honored One’s turning of the Wheel of Dharma, the text concludes with a dedication for universal wisdom and the honor of the Heavenly and Human Honored One, clarifying that through necessary wisdom one may provide the resources for the fulfillment of the two-footed.
"I only pray that you will accept my request" and below, it seeks your gracious compliance with the capacities and needs of beings.
This explains the Dharma that the Buddha practiced and studied over many kalpas, so that those who emulate and cultivate it may attain the fruit; this leads into the following passage.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... [up to] immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
"At that time" and below narrates the Buddhas who were invited. "Receiving from the ten directions" and below narrates the sentient beings who made the request.

"Immediately" and below correctly narrates the preaching of the Dharma in response to those capacities. Regarding the "three turnings": these are the three turnings of demonstrating the characteristics, exhorting to practice, and realizing the fruit.
Regarding the "twelve aspects": from the turning of demonstrating the characteristics, one comes to know that within the Four Noble Truths there is both the mundane and the transcendental.
The causes and effects pertaining to the gateway of the world are called the practice of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-caryā*).

Through the transformation of cultivation through exhortation, one attains the dharmas of the path of practice (*bhāvanā-mārga-caryā*), which consist of the realization that suffering and its origin are to be abandoned and the path and cessation are to be cultivated. Through the transformation of realization, one attains the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*):

the stage of the learner (*śaikṣa*) who investigates the truth and abandons delusions, and the stage of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) who has reached the ultimate truth and exhausted all delusions; these are called the practice of realizing the fruit (*phala-sākṣātkriyā-caryā*).
Therefore, each of the Four Truths undergoes three turnings, resulting in twelve aspects. As for the "Wheel of Dharma" (dharmacakra), the Buddha-dharma is like a chariot wheel;
it enters the hearts of sentient beings, turning them away from birth and death and establishing them in nirvana.
Regarding the passage "if a śramaṇa," etc., it means that although these Four Truths are but minor fruits, the Buddha contemplated them for ten minor kalpas before finally attaining them.
The Buddha manifests before them the teaching that reveals the provisional through the ultimate. Therefore, none—whether śramaṇas or others—are able to overturn it.
This is because although śramaṇas are Buddhist disciples who have left the household life, they do not even know it if it is not taught by the Buddha;

as for brahmins, who are ordinary householders, they have not even heard its name if they do not believe in the Buddha; and as for the devas, they are preoccupied with their own pleasures, while Māra seeks to destroy it.

The Dharma. Because Brahmā delights in meditative stillness (*dhyāna*), although each possesses a small measure of merit and wisdom, they are collectively categorized as belonging to the outflows (*āsrava*).
As for "the rest of the world," "the rest" refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas; these are termed the "world of wise and perfect awakening.
Although these all belong to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), they merely carry out their practices by receiving the Buddha’s command and do not dare to turn the wheel [of the Dharma] themselves.
It is said: "As for ritual, music, military expeditions, and punishments, they proceed from the Son of Heaven; the feudal lords dare not exercise them independently.

This makes it clear that the meaning of being able to exhaustively investigate [the truth] belongs only to Buddha after Buddha. To say "this is suffering" refers to the nature of oppression by suffering; this points to the body.
It shows that as long as there is a body, there is the oppression of suffering such as birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Body and mind are not pleasure; they are the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*). "Accumulation" refers to the nature of being summoned and experienced;

it indicates that the cause for the fruit of suffering is summoned and experienced by the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*), such as greed, anger, ignorance, and pride. This is what is meant by: "Knowing suffering, one should abandon its accumulation.

The above concerns the causes and effects of the mundane world. As for "the cessation of suffering" (*duḥkha-nirodha*): "cessation" refers to the quiescence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-nirodha*), which can be realized.

It is the nature (*dhātu*). Furthermore, the mention of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) indicates that within this body and mind, which are oppressed by suffering and affliction, there exists the very nature of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—namely, the unborn and undying. Regarding "the path to the cessation of suffering" (*mārga-nirodha*):

"path" refers to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*), the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which constitute the nature that can be cultivated. The mention of both the truths of suffering and cessation indicates...

Within this body and mind, which are oppressed by suffering, although the quiescent true nature of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is inherently present, it must be attained by cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
This is what is called "seeking cessation and cultivating the path," serving as the cause and fruit of the supramundane.
Among these three turnings, the first is the turning that demonstrates the characteristics; having completed this, one is fully exhorted to cultivate and realize [the truth].
Second, regarding the turning [of the wheel of Dharma]: thus, all four truths are expressed in terms of this suffering (*duḥkha*).

This is because the latter three truths—origination, cessation, and the path—are all first attained through the knowledge of suffering. Furthermore, "extensive exposition" below refers to expanding upon the teachings for the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna;

for the Pratyekabuddhas of the Madhyamayāna, it is taught as the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). This is done by extensively explaining suffering and its origination.
The gate of forward progression (*pravṛtti-mukha*) refers to [the chain] from ignorance as condition for volitional formations up to birth as condition for old age and death, and so forth.

The extensive cessation of the path constitutes the gate of retrogression (*nivṛtti-mukha*). It refers to the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Regarding "ignorance as condition for volitional formations":
The past two factors are the cause. "Non-existence" (wu) means "not. "Luminosity" (ming) refers to wisdom. "Activity" (xing) refers to deluded movement.

This means that all sentient beings, due to a lack of wisdom, within the ocean of the single true nature of suchness, neither know nor perceive themselves as being struck by the winds of the six sensory objects, thereby giving rise to a single moment of deluded movement. "Consciousness" (shi) has the meaning of discernment; it conditions delusion.
Because it moves, it discriminates. This is what is called the non-awakening of ignorance giving rise to the three subtle states.
"Name" refers to the four dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. These have no physical form or substance; they exist merely as designations.

"Form" refers to the union of the two drops—red and white—from the parents, which constitutes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and possesses physical characteristics. Consciousness serves as the primary condition, while the four great elements serve as its support.
As for "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa), it refers to the very first stage of entering the womb as a coagulated mass; at this point, the subtle five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are fully present.

Regarding "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases" (ṣaḍāyatana): this means that once the five aggregates are complete, the domains of the six faculties—such as the eyes and so forth—are established, and consciousness (vijñāna) thereby gains access to and exits from among them. Regarding "the six sense bases condition contact" (sparśa): this means that the faculties have been formed.

"Emerging from the womb" refers to the mutual contact with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). "Contact as a condition for sensation" means that when the faculties (*indriya*) contact their respective objects (*viṣaya*), one experiences them as favorable, unfavorable, or neutral, thereby giving rise to the three types of sensation:
suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. From consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to sensation (*vedanā*), these constitute the five present factors of the fruit;

that is to say, with the objective realm as a condition, the six coarse aggregates (*ṣaḍ-audārika*) are prolonged. "Sensation as a condition for craving" refers to the faculties and the mind... [the text continues].
One perceives the preceding object and gives rise to craving. "Craving conditions grasping" means that once the mind has developed attachment and delight, it necessarily desires to grasp and cling.

"Grasping conditions becoming" means that once grasping and clinging have arisen, afflictions and karma form heavy fetters, and one will inevitably undergo future existence through the causes and effects of good and evil.
These three [links] further serve as the causes for the three links of the present. "Becoming conditions birth":
This means that there exists this present cause and effect of good and evil; it refers to the body that will certainly be born within the three realms in the future.
Regarding "birth as the condition for old age, death, and so forth," it means that where there is birth, there must necessarily be the sufferings of old age, death, and so on.

These two, in turn, constitute the two resultant links of the future. Thus, these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) exist within a single moment as causes across the three periods of time.
The fruits arise through mutual dependent origination; they are induced and produced by one another's reliance and support, causing one to transmigrate through the three miserable realms;

therefore, they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*). However, in brief, these do not go beyond suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*). Those who are called followers of the Middle Vehicle (the *śrāvakas*) possess shallow wisdom;
they must first understand the fruit of suffering, such as birth and death, and only thereafter sever the afflictions of views and mental formations (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*).
This is the cause for their gathering; it proceeds from the traces back to the root. As for the capacity of the Pratyekabuddhas, their wisdom is more profound;
therefore, they trace back to and expand upon the most subtle ignorance within the causes for gathering. This proceeds from the root to explain the branches;
thus, for humans, the Middle Vehicle dharma consists of the twelve links of dependent origination. "When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease," and so forth.
That is to say, having arisen by being mutually induced by conditions, they likewise perish by being mutually induced by conditions. When the cause perishes, the effect is lost;

it is like when the skin no longer exists, the hair has nothing to which it can adhere. The above passage describes how the Buddha, having received the request, taught the dharmas of the small fruits of the Three Vehicles.
Below the section on "The Buddha among Gods and Humans," it clarifies that the number of those with the capacity to attain the Dharma is indeed as great as this. Truly...
This means he did not fail the request of the sixteen princes and Brahmā. "By not receiving anything" refers to being below all things;
that is, not being deluded by the six sense objects such as form, which constitute the dharmas of the flowing cycle of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).

"And regarding all outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to attaining the fruit of the path, which is the eternal tranquility of cessation (*nirodha*); this fruit possesses the three knowledges (*traividya*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*).

...and so forth. The above summarizes the benefits of the teaching given during the first assembly. From the second and third assemblies below, the benefits of the teachings given in numerous assemblies are summarized.
This clarifies that since the teaching has been given for a long time, the number of those transformed is extremely great and cannot be counted;
hence it says, "From this point onward," and so forth. Although this describes the activities of the Buddha of Wisdom (Jñāna-buddha) in preaching the Dharma, [it serves to illustrate the same].
In fact, this refers to the verses in the "Expedient Means" chapter which state: "I, Śākyamuni, went to Vārāṇasī and preached for the five bhikṣus;
this is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma," and so forth.
At that time, the sixteen princes [attained] the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"The sixteen at that time" refers to the sixteen princes; upon hearing the Dharma of the Four Truths and Dependent Origination, they immediately renounced their royal thrones in their youth to become monks.
According to the preceding verse on requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, it says: "Deliver me."
...and for all classes of sentient beings, [the Buddha] provides a detailed exposition so that they may attain this scriptural wisdom.
Thus, one knows that the preceding section concerns the deliverance of all sentient beings by providing a detailed exposition of the Dharma of the Truths and Conditions;
having enabled them to attain the wisdom of the Two Vehicles, this present section is the request for deliverance for ourselves, providing a detailed exposition...

It reveals the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, enabling one to attain the wisdom of the Mahāyāna. (The term "tongzi" [boy] refers to those who have not yet reached the age for capping or marriage. A *śrāmaṇera* is distinguished from a *bhikṣu*. According to the *Mingyi*:

*śrāmaṇera* means "ceasing [worldly defilement] and practicing kindness," signifying the cessation of worldly taints and the cultivation of compassion for all living beings. It is also called "diligent exhortation for men. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states that after receiving the ten precepts, one is named *śramaṇaka*, meaning "seeker of tranquility.

From seven to thirteen years of age, one is a *kākavāśika-śrāmaṇera* (crow-dispelling śrāmaṇera); from fourteen to nineteen, one is a *dharmārha-śrāmaṇera* (fit-for-the-dharma śrāmaṇera); and from twenty upwards, one is a *nāmamātra-śrāmaṇera* (nominal śrāmaṇera). Based on the following text, the present case should refer to the *dharmārha-śrāmaṇera*).

"Śrāmaṇera. The section beginning with "His faculties were... describes the planting of the causes for wisdom in former lives. The section beginning with "He had already previously... describes the planting of the causes for merit in former lives.

The section beginning with "Seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi... describes how, due to having planted the causes of merit and wisdom in former lives, he sought the Great Fruit immediately upon leaving the household life.
The above constitutes the narrative provided by the sūtra compiler. From the point where they "all addressed the Buddha" onwards is the Prince’s formal request for the Great Fruit;

As for the phrase "a great multitude," it is a metaphor for the twelve hundred people who previously resolved their minds for enlightenment during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, desiring to transcend the three realms and the two vehicles.
The Way is the precious place where one attains the Bodhi of Buddhahood. Regarding the mention of "a guide": he is wise and discerning, which qualifies him as a teacher;
he well understands what is open and what is obstructed, which enables him to lead. "Open" is a metaphor for Śākyamuni when he was a śrāmaṇera;
by the time he attained Buddhahood, he became the guide for all one thousand two hundred people. As for those whom he leads:
"The multitude" refers to the twelve hundred people who, within the three realms, were unable to cross over with diligence and sought to withdraw their great resolve.
From the words "They said to the Guide" onwards, the text correctly describes the meaning of this withdrawal: because they were utterly exhausted, their bodies could not advance further;
because they were terrified, they perceived the path as still far away. From the words "The Guide, seeing many [of them]" onwards, it is a metaphor for the Buddha seeing the twelve hundred.

"One hundred people fear the great. This means that outside the triple world, [the Buddha] manifests the *nirvāṇa* of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). "These [people] are to be pitied," and so forth, explains the formation of mindfulness.

"In a perilous path," and so forth, explains the abundance of various skillful means (*upāya*). The above uses the metaphor of the Buddha employing the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*) as skillful means.
"Announces to the multitude," and so forth, is a metaphor for the Buddha employing the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*) as skillful means.
Furthermore, there is the principle of *parinirvāṇa* and the emptiness of self (*ātman-śūnyatā*). Because it has no counterpart within the three realms, it is called "Great.

Because it wards off what is non-virtuous, stops deviance, and prevents further rebirth, it is metaphorically described as a city. It is the ground where those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) ought to abide.
Therefore it is said: "One may stop midway," and so forth. If one enters the lower [vehicle], this clearly explains acting according to one's inclination.

That is to say, first, there is nirvāṇa, which can be swiftly attained with peace and security; second, one may proceed further to reach the place of treasure. At that time, being utterly exhausted... [and so on].

This is a metaphor for the twelve hundred people who did not know that the provisional was the ground of reality; taking the small for the great cause, they considered what they had attained to be sufficient.

Therefore, they joyfully praised their birth in the final age, conceiving the thought that they had found peace and security. Above, it was said: "If one enters this city, one will quickly attain peace and security.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the guide," it follows that if one can proceed forward to the place of treasure, one may likewise attain it.

"Going to inspect" means knowing that the assembly has attained rest and is free from fatigue; this is a metaphor for the Buddha knowing that those of the Two Vehicles are no longer afflicted by the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*).
"Immediately extinguishing the conjured city" is a metaphor for now preaching the most ultimate reality for you all:
that none of the śrāvaka assembly have yet attained final nirvāṇa. The passage "speaking to the multitude" below is a metaphor for the fact that what you all practice is indeed Bodhi.

The path of the Bodhisattva: by gradually practicing and studying, all shall surely attain Buddhahood. "You who have gone and come" refers to having departed from the illusory city and returned to the place of treasure;
this is also a contemporary colloquialism. Since the small fruit is itself the great cause, it is said that the place of treasure is near.
"O monks, the Tathāgata is also like this... (down to) 'this city is not real; it is merely my own transformation.
O monks, [the passage] below joins with the preceding metaphor, beginning from "Suppose there were five hundred *yojanas*... up to the text that stops the journey across this difficult terrain.
This concludes the previous section. At that time, immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were transformed.
"Arising and extending into future ages, they are the śrāvaka disciples; they cease and submit to their tasks.
This means that just as the guide in the parable well knows the treacherous and evil paths, as well as the passages and obstructions, so too do the Buddhas within the Dharma.

Therefore it is said, "It is also thus," and so forth. Regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*): there are both the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformative). Hence it is called "all. These are the fruits of suffering. [The term] "afflictions" (*kleśa*)...

There is a distinction between the ignorance of views (*dṛṣṭi-avidyā*) and the ignorance of afflictions (*kleśa-avidyā*); these constitute the causes of suffering. The three paths of woe, such as the evil realms and the hells, are the places where one undergoes the fruits and causes of suffering.
They are "perilous difficulties" because the emptiness realized by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), once attained, prevents them from turning their minds toward unexcelled bodhi;
thus, for them, it constitutes a perilous difficulty. However, this is not the same as the future cessation of sense faculties and objects.
The birth-and-death of fragmented segments has its limits; therefore, it is called "long and distant.

Those who "should be removed" and those who "should be delivered" refers to the Buddha’s knowledge that among these beings in birth-and-death and affliction, there are those who should be removed and he removes them, and those who should be delivered and he delivers them.
From the words "If sentient beings merely hear... below, the meaning of those who should be removed and those who should be delivered is correctly elucidated, corresponding to the preceding metaphor.

Regarding the passage beginning with "He rouses the multitude" and ending with "giving rise to the thought of peace and security," and the section from "after my parinirvāṇa" up to "the skillful means by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma":
[I] submit that sentient beings hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*),
yet those who do not wish to see the Buddha or draw near to him do so because they fear that the path is long and suffering is protracted before its fulfillment.

"Knowing the inferior [capacities]" means that because the Buddha encounters these timid and inferior faculties, he teaches within the single vehicle (ekayāna) the characteristics of the Buddha the method of knowing suffering and abandoning its origin,
so that they may eliminate their suffering. "In order to bring them to rest" means that for those who seek to bring an end to their suffering,
the Buddha further teaches the cultivation of the path and the realization of cessation— the second, *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*— so that they may attain it.

"To ferry them across by means of bliss. The preceding section clarifies that for ordinary beings, one should explain that they ought to abandon the suffering of the three realms and ought to ferry themselves across to the bliss of the two vehicles.
If sentient beings abide in the two lower stages, one should explain that they ought to abandon the suffering of the two vehicles and ought to ferry themselves across to the bliss of the One Vehicle.
This corresponds to the preceding parable, from the passage "at that time the guide arose" up to "stopped."
This concludes the section on "Resting the Ears. It summarizes the preceding passage:
when the various bhikṣus perceived that the time for the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa had arrived, they rose and immediately accepted his instructions, bowing their heads to their desks.

Continuing from the preceding text, it means that if śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or sentient beings abide in the stage with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) according to the Buddha’s teaching, while in the second stage, the Buddha then acts for them.
The statement that "you have not yet accomplished what was to be done" and so forth means that you must eliminate ignorance and transform the suffering of birth and death.
The phrase "the lower state in which you dwell" means that you must be delivered by means of the bliss of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

"Not yet accomplished" refers to the non-fulfillment of the causes, such as the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the four means of attraction (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*), as well as the results, such as the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and the eighty minor characteristics (*aśītyanuvyañjana*). You...

"Abiding below" refers to the stage of having a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*). While it is close to the Buddha’s wisdom, one must not immediately grasp it as being identical to that wisdom.

Therefore, he instructs them to observe and deliberate that the nirvāṇa they have attained is not ultimate, but rather a skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddha—a teaching that differentiates the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) into three.
As in the passage "as that which is below," he cites the preceding metaphor by way of illustration.
He concludes with the two phrases beginning "In the One Buddha Vehicle. These are used as conclusions for all three cycles of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas... [until] shaking all things.

This verse summarizes five sections of the prose text where the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus concerning events from the distant past up to the point where the World-Honored One, having full knowledge, declared that he would turn the unsurpassed wheel. Each of these five sections consists of both prose and verse.
The same applies here. Of the twenty-two verses, the long prose consists of six verses; the remaining verses constitute the metrical gāthās.
While the long prose enumerates eight classes [of beings], it lacks the two classes of asuras and garuḍas; these are now supplemented by the verses.
"In the worlds of the eastern direction, five hundred trillion lands... [until] he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

This verse refers to the time when the Buddha told the bhikṣus that the Great Universal Wisdom-Victorious Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, arose [in resolve] until he compassionately expounded the Dharma practiced over immeasurable kalpas. This constitutes four sections.
This text consists of twelve lines of verse praising the eastern direction, four lines praising the remaining nine directions, and four lines praising the verses of the various sections.
The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom, having accepted the request of those people... [up to] ...cannot find its limit.

This verse covers the period from "At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the invitation of the Brahmā kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes" up to "incalculable [aeons]. This is the tenth section of the long prose passage.
According to the *Fengsu tongyi*, one hundred thousand is called a *yì* (億); ten *yì* is called a *zhào* (兆); ten *zhào* is called a *jīng* (京); ten *jīng* is called a *zǐ* (秭). Ten *zǐ*...
It says "kehe. "Kehe" is a general enumeration. The eight lines of verse praise the acceptance of the invitation and the preaching of the Hīnayāna Dharma;
the twelve lines of verse praise the attainment of the fruits by the great multitude who heard the Dharma.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras... (until) each attained perfect enlightenment.

This verse begins with the account of how all sixteen princes at that time left the household life as youths, and concludes with the sixteenth, our Śākyamuni Buddha, attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system.
Regarding the section on the cessation of bodhi, the text of the eleventh and twelfth sections comprises forty-two phrases in total.
The first four phrases praise the novice monk who, immediately upon leaving home, seeks the Mahāyāna Dharma.

The next four phrases praise the arousal of great vows, wishing that both oneself and others may equally attain Buddhahood, like one's original teacher. The following ten phrases praise the wisdom of the Buddha’s compliance.
Please explain "Great. One who knows the activities of the mind is a vessel for the Dharma that should receive the Mahāyāna.

Through causes, conditions, and parables, the means of deliverance and penetration each have their distinctions; yet, as that which is capable of discerning them, they do not, in total, transcend the single true characteristic of the mind.
As that which is discerned, although the subject and object are distinguished, the Bodhisattva path is one; therefore, it is called "the practice of the Bodhisattvas."

"Way. According to the present teaching of a single great period of a Buddha, the aforementioned eight phrases refer to the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* as constituting the Mahāyāna.
The latter two phrases refer to the harmonization of the former *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā*.

This constitutes the wondrous Dharma of the present age. The verses are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Next, four lines praise the Buddha of Wisdom entering meditative concentration and knowing those who do not believe;

this has its basis in the conditions of existence. Next, twelve lines praise the passage concerning the World-Honored One preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of twelve hundred people.
Finally, four lines praise the great capacity that is always shared with the Great Master.

The prose on "Birth" (the fourth section). The following four lines of verse praise those who preach the Mahāyāna, each attaining the great fruit throughout the ten directions simultaneously, thereby fulfilling the text concerning their original vows.

These four preceding sections of verse collectively summarize the twelve preceding sections of long prose, clarifying that Śākyamuni established the causes for the Mahāyāna in past lives for the sake of the twelve hundred people. (Question: The previous judgment was comprehensive...)

This chapter consists of two major sections. Each of these sections is further divided into twelve subsections. Why is this so? The answer is that the general meaning of this chapter centers directly upon the four characters "past-life causes and conditions" (*sukhāvatī-vyūha*);

therefore, the main body is judged to consist of two major sections: one major section narrating the causes (*hetu*) and one major section narrating the conditions (*pratyaya*). This is clear from the scriptural text. However, as the textual flow is extensive, it is difficult for people to understand it in detail; thus, each major section is further divided into several segments to facilitate comprehension.
"At that time, those who hear the Dharma shall each be in the presence of the various Buddhas... (up to) "...be careful not to harbor fear or dread.
This verse [summarizes] the prose section beginning from "O monks, when we were śrāmaṇeras...
up to "If such a person hears this, they will immediately believe and accept it. The text of the thirteenth and fourteenth sections begins from "At that time," below.
The verse on the past extends to the present fruit, showing that the cause is not obscured.

"Those who possess" and below refers to moving from the present verse to the future, entering the ultimate through the provisional. "I am" and below exhorts one not to forget the original cause. Therefore, and so forth...
"Exert yourselves to enter reality in the present; do not wait for the future through expedient means.
This means that since there are fundamental causes and conditions from the past, this is not a matter of acting ignorantly or falsely. "Now you...
and so forth means that all who possess a mind shall become Buddhas; it is not something beyond one's capacity.

For example, the verse beginning with "Just as on a perilous and evil road, remote and desolate, filled with many venomous beasts" (extending to) "...we shall together reach the place of treasure," corresponds to the prose section beginning with "Just as [a man] from five hundred *yojanas* away... and ending with the passage "I have manifested [this city] to stop them."
This long passage is divided into three sections. First, the teacher and disciples together seek the treasure-place in order to cross over dangerous evils.

Second, because the multitude fears [the journey], the teacher establishes a "transformed city" (nirmita-nagara). Third, when the teacher knows the multitude is at ease, he dissolves the transformation and exhorts them to return to the treasure.
The verses consist of forty-two lines; they correspond to those three sections. The first twelve lines correspond to the first section. For example:

"Below" refers to the perilous and evil nature of the path; it is a metaphor for the abundance of afflictions and sufferings within the three realms, and the lack of merit and wisdom among those of the Two Vehicles.

"Innumerable below" refers to the multitude of people capable of crossing the perilous path, as well as the vast distance of the perilous route to be traversed. "At that time" refers to the guide being endowed with meditative concentration.
Wisdom is able to rescue the multitude from peril and difficulty. The following twenty-four lines eulogize the second section.

"The multitude" and below refers to the fact that the assembly, due to sudden exhaustion, intends to retreat. "The guide" and below refers to the guide’s compassion for the multitude’s loss of the precious treasure.
"Immediately" and below refers to the guide’s skillful means, whereby he employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to conjure a city and adorns it.

The environment and its inhabitants are perfectly and vividly rendered as real. "Immediately he creates" below means that having manifested the city, he exhorts the multitude to enter it so they may cease their suffering and attain happiness;

this is a metaphor for the principle of self-emptiness beyond the three realms. Being endowed with the three insights, the six supernatural powers, meditative concentration, and liberation, one may sport therein.
"The people" below means that the multitude, not knowing it was not real, settled within the conjured city and [perceived it as] such.
This concludes the thought of having crossed over birth and death. The following ten lines constitute the verse for the third section.
From "The Guide" downward, it means that the Guide, knowing the assembly has attained slight rest, exhorts them to press forward and not remain fixated upon the conjured city.

From "I see" downward, it clarifies that the transformation was established as a skillful means because the multitude were weary and wished to retreat. From "You now" downward, it means that since you have attained coarse peace, you ought to...
Following with diligent application, one fulfills the initial resolve to reach the place of treasure.
I, likewise, act as a guide for all, leading them into the Buddha-wisdom.
This verse’s prose commentary states: "In the same way, the Tathāgata is also like this; now he acts as a great guide for you," and so forth. This final section combines the analogy with the Dharma.
From the words "I too" downwards, there is a four-line stanza regarding the time of the combination: "There was a single guide.
Because the Buddha is the guide for both the mundane and supramundane realms, it says "all. From the words "seeing all" downwards, [the analogy] is combined.
The four lines beginning with "Countless tens of millions of multitudes" describe descending midway on the path.

The four lines beginning with "All the people together were exhausted" explain that they were unable to descend. This clarifies that the Buddha saw those seeking the path to Bodhi abandoning it halfway through;
he said that the Buddha-way is long and distant, and can only be accomplished after enduring diligent suffering for a long time. Therefore, they were unable to cross over during the ocean of kalpas.

[The passage] "generating the Buddha" corresponds to [the verse] "being indolent and abandoning their initial resolve. Therefore, the following [passage] corresponds to the twelve lines beginning with "the Guide formed this thought.
The words "you, below" correspond to the four lines beginning with "having thus performed this transformation.

The words "once they know, below" correspond to the four lines beginning with "when all people have entered the city. The words "thereupon, below" correspond to "the Guide knowing that they had rested."

The lines beginning with "All Buddhas" correspond to the four lines starting with "I see that you are utterly exhausted. The lines beginning with "Now for" correspond to the two lines starting with "You now exert diligent effort.
This section of the verse consists of thirty lines in total. The first line says "I"; this "I" refers to Śākyamuni Buddha.
The subsequent mention of "all Buddhas" refers to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Seeing the three first and the one last shows that the provisional is the real;
this applies equally to Śākyamuni and all other Buddhas, for it is not a novel innovation. Question: Regarding the Buddha and the various Buddhas, why do they act as sentient beings?
Their minds have fully realized all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), and their bodies are fully endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Question: Is it only at the second stage that true cessation occurs? Answer: No; because it is possessed by all sentient beings and cannot be lacking, [it exists from the beginning].
