The eighth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples.
Regarding the term "five hundred": these are the great disciples among the twelve hundred followers.

Although the sūtra contains the expression "twelve hundred and five hundred," the title of this chapter specifically singles out "five hundred" because the remaining seven hundred must have been included within those five hundred.
Those who were first exhorted and inspired to resolve upon enlightenment are counted among the number of that teacher’s disciples; thus, the followers are included therein.

Therefore, in the sutra, the Buddha summarizes their total number as being one thousand two hundred arhats. They are all equally certified by the Buddha and originally possess no distinction of high or low.
Thus it is said: "I shall now, in the presence of these [disciples], grant them [the prediction] in successive order."
He bestowed upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Regarding their names, he first explained the origins of their initial resolve for enlightenment, saying:
"As for those five hundred arhats, such as Uruvilvā and the others...
and so on, up to: "Kāśyapa, you already know these five hundred masters; the remaining assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so. Thus spoke the Teacher.

The relative weight of these conditions can be thoroughly understood [as explained in the *Lengyan jing changshui jie*: "Regarding the one thousand two hundred and fifty people: first, Cunda and the other five were converted;

next, the three Kāśyapa brothers and their one thousand followers were converted; next, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with one hundred followers, were converted; next, the householder Yaśas and the other fifty were converted. Based on this, it is clearly seen that the remaining seven hundred were those who resolved their minds after being exhorted and transformed by the five hundred"].
Why does the record say "received" (*shòu*) rather than "bestowed" (*shòu*)? This is to manifest a mutual correspondence with the preceding characteristics.

Furthermore, at the end of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) granted to his four great disciples, it says: "My disciples, endowed with majestic virtue, numbering five hundred, shall all receive predictions.
Since it previously stated that they were "granted" [predictions], these individuals who have received them have merely accepted them.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "All Buddhas bring those with whom they have a karmic affinity to maturity without missing the proper time" (this sūtra brings twelve hundred to maturity).

"One hundred people attained Buddhahood; this is why it is said that the causal conditions were fulfilled once over. It is also said: "He bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattvas without missing the proper time" (this is why this sutra bestows predictions upon those of the three faculties according to their sequence, each at their respective time).

Question: According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, among the group of one thousand two hundred people, only five—namely the two Kāśyapas, Śāriputra, and others—took him as their teacher. How can you know [the truth] and yet say there were five hundred people?
"Is it the Master [who is at fault]? He replied: "One must understand that the chapter titles and the scriptural text correspond; one should grasp this through the meaning.

Since the chapter title says 'five hundred,' while the scriptural text gives specific names and records, yet does not list each name individually but speaks only in general terms of 'the five hundred arhats and so forth,' and since the scripture says 'one thousand two hundred,' which further contradicts the number in the chapter title—"

There is the fault of internal contradiction between earlier and later passages. To ensure the scriptural text remains free of such faults, one must understand that when it says "one thousand two hundred people," this refers to the five disciples including Śāriputra; those who received their predictions earlier are also included within that number.

When it says "five hundred," this refers to the five hundred people who were his peers in practice alongside Śāriputra and the others. Therefore, one should know that the remaining seven hundred are implied by the term "the rest."
There are one hundred [monks] in the ranks of the disciples; it is not that the scriptural text has omitted them—why such stubborn adherence to a fixed form? A question is asked:
Why does the scriptural text of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) not list each name individually? The answer is:

If the twelve hundred were to have their names listed one by one, even the paper for these seven fascicles of scripture would not suffice, let alone for the two thousand who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) to receive their prophecies hereafter.
Regarding the predictions for individuals and the six thousand people including the maternal aunt Yaśodharā, it would be difficult to record their names one by one as the paper would be insufficient.
Because the text of the sutra contains little paper while the number of those receiving predictions is great, the Buddha’s words employ brevity to encompass the vast;

speaking of immeasurable matters, it consists of barely sixty thousand words. This is truly a wondrous Dharma. Otherwise, the pages would be entirely filled with the detailed expansion of their bestowals.
The recording of personal names, as well as the descriptions of the adornments of the kalpa and the land, are identical throughout;

this only serves to cause those who read them in the final age to grow weary of their prolixity. At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra... [until] ...was able to know our profound minds and original vows.

Based on the precedent of the five men who received their predictions, when the five hundred arhats had heard the explanation of the causes and conditions, the Buddha should have immediately expounded the parable of the tied jewel to clarify their realization;
only thereafter would it have been appropriate for the Buddha to confirm and grant them their predictions. This would have been the proper sequence.
The present case is not like those precedents. The reason Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra alone is recorded first is that he was seen to be no mere disciple of inferior capacity, unlike Puṇṇa.
Below this, the scribe records the narrative; it describes how those suited to the teaching benefited from hearing the Dharma of the three turnings.

The preceding section concludes with the phrase "having heard these [teachings] from the Buddha," which summarizes the first cycle of the Dharma-discourse and concludes the text of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṭala*),
because that chapter extensively explains wisdom and expedient means as they accord with what is appropriate.

Furthermore, regarding the passage "I also heard [the Buddha] bestowing [predictions upon] all those of equal status," this summarizes the first cycle of the discourse on the parables, concluding with the four chapters on the Burning House, the Poor Son, and the Medicinal Herbs.
This is because these four parables are all intended to bestow predictions of enlightenment upon the great disciples.

Furthermore, regarding the passage "I also heard [of his deeds] in past lives," this summarizes the second cycle of the discourse on causes and conditions, concluding with the Parable of the Phantom City.
Regarding the text of this chapter: the matter of causes and conditions refers to the Buddha as a prince; the power of supernormal transformations refers to the Buddha as a guide.
As the Sūtra says: "One should employ great supernormal powers to manifest a great city. Sentient beings fear that the path to Buddhahood is too long and do not believe in the One Vehicle;
the Buddha is thus able to deliver them by means of a manifested city of lesser fruition, so that they do not lose their way.
Its greatness is such that sentient beings dwelling on the two stages conceive the notion of security. The Buddha is able to deliver them by means of the jewel of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

He does not exclude those of lesser capacity; hence it is called "sovereign supernormal power" (*vaśitā-abhijñā*). Regarding the passage "attained [the state] not yet descended," this describes the benefit of attaining the purification of the six sense faculties.

With a heart pure and leaping with joy, he purified the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), immediately rising from his seat, and so forth. He purified the physical faculty (*kāya-indriya*) by gazing [upon the Buddha].

Gazing upon the Honored Countenance and so forth, they purified their faculty of sight and formed this thought: having purified their faculty of the tongue, they remained silent with their mouths, for the tongue and mind were engaged in internal reflection.

As for the terms "approaching" and "retreating": "approaching" refers to advancing to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, moved by the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue, like a child approaching its mother;
"retreating" refers to withdrawing to stand to one side, out of awe for the Buddha’s majestic power, like a minister.
In their longing for the Master, they behold the Buddha’s compassionate majesty, which enables those who serve as his disciples to perfect the propriety of their every advance and retreat.
From the words “The World-Honored One was greatly amazed” onwards, the text describes the realization attained by the one suited to the teaching. The Buddha possesses the three virtues;

through the clarification of the hope for a prediction, he forms this thought—the meaning within that thought being the realization of the virtue of the Buddha’s Dharma-body. By means of the Buddha’s Dharma-body...
Because it is marvelous and rare in the world. "In accordance with the world" and so forth refers to awakening to the Buddha’s virtue of *prajñā*.
"Uprooting sentient beings" and so forth refers to awakening to the Buddha’s virtue of liberation (*vimukti*). "We [speak] regarding the Buddha" and below:

in contrast to the aforementioned Tathāgata, there are further immeasurable and boundless virtues; even if you were to speak of them for immeasurable billions of *kalpas*, [you could not exhaust them].
This is spoken exhaustively according to the capacities of those present. The intended meaning is as follows:

if Śāriputra’s wisdom, Kāśyapa’s asceticism, Subhūti’s understanding of emptiness, Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers, and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s skill in debate—each of whom is foremost in their respective field—were to describe the Dharma for themselves, they would say, "This is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One. This is illustrated by way of analogy.
The Dharma is said to be the unsurpassed treasury of jewels, obtained spontaneously without seeking; it is that which proclaims the merits of the Buddha.

Since it is said that even if one were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas, one could never exhaust it, how then could the wisdom and conduct of a single person like me, Pūrṇa, surpass those of the other five?
Therefore, we say that our understanding of the Buddha’s merits is equal [to theirs]. Only...
Regarding the passage "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, [descends]" and so forth: this means that the Buddha’s merits are so vast that I am truly unable to proclaim them;
yet my aspiration is profound, and the Buddha himself can know it. This describes the fulfillment of his vow and the bestowal of a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
Indeed, even before Pūrṇa had opened his mouth, the Buddha had already grasped his mind. Alas! Although Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra says that he cannot express the Buddha’s merits in words, yet...

To awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—could there be anything more excellent than this? To compare this with Shen Guang’s three prostrations at Shaolin, where he was said to have "attained the marrow," how could they differ?
It is only fitting that he was the first among the five hundred people to receive his prediction.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... (until) "gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva. From "at that time, the Buddha addressed...
onwards, the Buddha, acting as the appropriate recipient for the teaching (*dharmatā*), describes and confirms his profound mind and original vow. As for the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*):
it refers to deeply relying upon the traces of the śrāvaka’s minor fruits in order to skillfully transform immeasurable asaṃkhyeya [sentient beings].

This causes people to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. As for the "original vow," it means that he was originally a Mahāyāna bodhisattva endowed with the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*).
According to his lifespan, he made a vow to manifest as a śrāvaka in order to assist in proclaiming and spreading the Buddha’s Dharma transformation.
However, the Buddha must necessarily announce this to the assembly and confirm it, because the disciples see the Buddha appearing before them.
What is commonly praised as the foremost in preaching the Dharma for śrāvakas is but a limited trace;
it does not yet reveal the immeasurable foundation of his having practiced as a bodhisattva throughout many kalpas of the three periods of time, transforming beings and bringing them to buddhahood.
Therefore, it is said: "Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra? I have always praised him as being at the very bottom."

This clarifies the proximate traces perceived by the multitude. It also constantly praises their depth, meaning that when the Buddha praises the traces, he simultaneously praises their fundamental source.

Regarding "diligence and effort" (*vīrya*): this precisely sets forth the fundamental and proximate aspects commonly praised, thereby explaining and establishing the statement regarding the various merits.
"Diligence" (*vi*) means not coarse; "effort" (*īrya*) means not indolent. "Guarding and maintaining" means to lead [the mind] with one-pointedness...
Riding upon the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), he protects and sustains it within; this is called "aiding what is appropriate.

That is to say, by using the true reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) to assist the Buddha in proclaiming the truths and conditions of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) externally, he is thus able to bring joy to those among the fourfold assembly whose faculties are dull, catering to their inclinations.
Having heard his instructions and admonitions, they obtain benefit and rejoice. Regarding the phrase "fully explained" (具足解釋) below:

this means that although he conceals the reality and reveals the provisional for those of dull faculties on the outside, it does not preclude the fact that at the very moment of revealing the provisional, he has already fully explained the Buddha’s true Dharma—the real mark of the One Vehicle—within it for those of sharp faculties.
Therefore, he further caused those of equal spiritual practice (*brahmacarya*) to be like himself, so that they might provide great benefit.

From the passage "Since the time the Tathāgata passed away" onwards, it refers to Pūrṇa, whose original name was Huìběn (慧本), manifesting his traces in this world; relying on the Small Vehicle, he achieved greatness.

As for his eloquence and skill in debate, with the exception of the Buddha alone, there was no one else who could rival him. From the passage "You all must not say" onwards, it refers to the assembly.
One must not judge this merely by the Buddha’s ordinary, occasional praise;
one should know that Pūrṇa assisted me, Śākyamuni, in the Dharma of a single Buddha, and was foremost among the Saṃgha.
If this were so, how could his mind alone suffice to reveal its depth, and how could his vows alone suffice to reveal their foundation? In truth, it was before ninety billion Buddhas in the past.
It is likewise so; therefore, it says, "among those who preach the Dharma. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in all Buddhas" below:

the aforementioned "Buddha’s True Dharma" refers to the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This present reference to "the Dharma of emptiness preached by all Buddhas" refers to the Dharma of emptiness realized in common by the Small, Great, and Three Vehicles.
This Dharma of emptiness is, for instance, as found in the eight sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. The "True Dharma" is...
In the Vaipulya sūtras, when the three vehicles and the one vehicle have not yet been unified as provisional and real, there is a distinction between emptiness and the correct [teaching].

When the three vehicles and the one vehicle have already been unified as provisional and real, both emptiness and the correct [teaching] are called the "wondrous Dharma. Regarding "clearly understanding" (*liǎomiào*):

although the one vehicle and the empty dharma, as well as the three vehicles and the small vehicle, are equally realized and equally practiced, Pūrṇa clearly understood that the Small Vehicle is limited while the Great Vehicle is fundamentally great.
The provisional and the real, as well as the teachings and their essential substance, do not overlap.

"Thorough penetration" means to penetrate the emptiness of the three vehicles of the past—the shared realization of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and thereby reach the ultimate nirvana of the present Mahayana, characterized by eternal quiescence.
Ultimately, it returns to the emptiness of emptiness. The provisional and the ultimate meanings do not obstruct one another. Regarding the principle (*li*), there are the merits of self-benefit;

regarding the attainment of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there are the merits of benefiting others. The four analytical knowledges are those of phenomena (*dharma*), language (*nirukti*), meaning (*artha*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

All four are unimpeded regarding the Small and Great Vehicles, the provisional and the ultimate. If one follows the scriptural instructions, one should always be able to examine them with discernment.

The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are as follows: the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) is for the sake of preaching the Dharma with purity; the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is for the sake of being free from doubt;
the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) is for the sake of being without confusion; and the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is that which dwells therein.

"Endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva" and below refers to what is hidden within; "according to his lifespan" and below refers to what is manifested externally; "those Buddhas and the people of that time" and below refers to those ninety billion [Buddhas] of the past.
Those who were with the Buddha were all unable to know that Pūrṇa was originally a bodhisattva;
rather, they all took his outward manifestation to be that of a true śrāvaka. Since it was so for them, do not find it strange that the assembly before you now is likewise.
As for the passage beginning with "Pūrṇa," it means that Pūrṇa specifically used their ignorance as an opportunity to lead them toward the realization of the ultimate truth.

The provisional skillful means (*upāya*) are for the purpose of benefiting hundreds of thousands of sentient beings of the *Hīnayāna*, and furthermore, they transform those of the *Mahāyāna*, causing them to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in immeasurable numbers.
"Benefiting the lower" refers to the skillful means of opening up the provisional; "furthermore transforming the lower" refers to the skillful means of revealing the real;
"for the sake of purifying the Buddha-lands" refers to the skillful means of the provisional and the real according to the capacity of the audience. It is not [otherwise].
Only through the fulfillment of the person is one able to accomplish the adornment and purification of one’s own Buddha-field. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"A bodhisattva takes up a Buddha-field according to the beings he transforms. Thus, Puṇya-bhadra did not decline to spend immeasurable billions of kalpas.

Those who manifest as followers of the Hīnayāna are, in truth, those who secretly aspire to attain the Mahāyāna; they adorn themselves for the sake of their future attainment of Buddhahood, including the kalpa, the land, and the retinue.

From the passage beginning with "The bhikṣu Pūrṇa" onwards, it refers to those who, through the past and present, have initiated the profound mind and fundamental vows of the three periods of time for the future;
all such individuals are foremost persons. Regarding the "Seven Buddhas," formerly they were called the *Vipaśyin*... [text truncated].
Viśvabhū and Śikhin were the last three Buddhas among the thousand Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*.
Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni are the first four Buddhas among the thousand Buddhas of the present *Bhadrakalpa*.
Now, observing the text of the sutra, since it mentions "the seven Buddhas" and further says "now, before me," [it refers to these].
Furthermore, the phrase "among those of the Bhadrakalpa" and so forth indicates that Śākyamuni alone is taken as the present Buddha, while all others belong to the past.
Likewise, regarding the section on the future, one should understand that this refers to the future beyond the Bhadrakalpa;
it is just as when the twelve hundred arhats attain Buddhahood, Pūrṇa also acts as their protector and assistant.
He proclaims the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharma. As his disciples, how could the depth of their minds and the breadth of their vows ever be measured?
This is because there is nothing that does not seek the supreme above and transform those below. To purify the Buddha-land concludes the aspiration to seek the supreme;
to teach and transform sentient beings concludes the transformation of those below. Thus, these together form the whole.
This describes his causal practices. Below this, the prediction of his fruition is bestowed:
after immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he shall erect stupas made of the seven treasures that will fill his entire land.

"Passing through immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Since Pūrṇa had already sought [enlightenment] above and transformed beings below in this land for immeasurable billions of kalpas, he likewise attained Buddhahood directly in this very land;
thus, the fruit does not obscure the cause. "This land" refers to the Sahā world.
Therefore, in the subsequent chapter, when the exhortation to make vows and uphold the sutra occurs, figures such as Śāriputra and Pūrṇa are not seen.
Because Bodhisattvas such as Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra originally upheld this sutra in this land, they are called "Dharma-Illumination" (Dharmaprabha); this title accords with their actual merit.

The phrase "that Buddha" below provides a general record of the vastness of the buddha-field. The phrase "the seven treasures" below provides a specific record of the splendor and purity of the buddha-field.
The ground is level, being devoid of mountains, hills, valleys, or ravines; thus it is as clear and smooth as the palm of a hand.
Pure terraces and towers, by comparison with the celestial palaces, are thus filled and adorned. The above records the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment);

from "there are no evil realms" below, it records the *sattva-vipāka* (the sentient beings). There are no sentient beings of the female sex within the evil realms as their primary retribution (*sattva-vipāka*).

The pure attainment of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and radiant light constitutes the adornment of the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*) of sentient beings. The attainment of supernatural powers pertains to the faculty of mind (*manendriya*);

the emission of radiant light pertains to the faculty of body (*kāyendriya*). The passage beginning with "Aspiration and mindfulness" (*zhìniàn xià*) clarifies the source of the purity of the faculty of mind.

The passage beginning with "Universally" (*pǔjiē xià*) clarifies the source of the adornment of the faculty of body. The passage beginning with "The multitude of beings in that land" (*qí guó zhòngshēng xià*) clarifies the absence of lustful desire.
"Those who are benefited. All of the above concern the worldly retinue within the Buddha-field. "There are immeasurable [beings]" below refers to the prediction concerning the Dharma-retinue.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

These were presented as an introduction for Pūrṇa; although there is a sequence in their recording, all individuals are equally of the Mahāyāna.

The three turnings and the three faculties are nothing other than Dharma-gates. They were established simultaneously, yet appear in succession; fundamentally, there is no hierarchy between them. O Bhikṣus!
"Below. 'Buddha-son' refers to the Bodhisattva; here it refers to the Śrāvaka. 'The path they practice' refers to their profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).

'Skillfully learning expedient means' refers to their original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*). This means that although these Śrāvakas are now called 'Buddha-sons,' the path they themselves have practiced was originally the Mahāyāna, yet they manifested it as a small fruit.
Therefore, it is said they are 'skillfully learned. This does not hinder their ability to achieve greatness through the small."
Therefore, it cannot be conceived or deliberated upon. "Knowing the multitudes" and below clarifies the excellence of learning. There are five layers to this inconceivability:

namely, the reason why the sons of the Buddhas manifest the small while being the Great is that they first know the faculties, natures, and desires of sentient beings regarding the dharmas of the fruits of the small and the truths of the conditioned;
thus, [sentient beings] fear the Mahāyāna wisdom of attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, the [Buddhas...]
The Bodhisattva abandons the long for the short; though not acting as a Bodhisattva, he manifests as a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
This is the first instance of making the great appear as small, which constitutes an inconceivable attainment. From the words "By means of countless" [downward], he reiterates this point:
that while the various Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they employ countless skillful means, such that it is not merely how others perceive them.
Regarding those who are śrāvakas: they themselves also claim to be śrāvakas, yet they remain very far removed from the Buddha-way.

Because they ceaselessly deliver immeasurable people of small aspirations and great fear, all of whom achieve the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, this is called "the Great [Vehicle] manifesting as the Small.
This constitutes the second inconceivable attainment. Although their desires are small and they are indolent and inferior, [the teaching] is extended three times.
To clarify this: when one refers to the great as small and names it "small," these are all things that can be conceived. How then can you say they are inconceivable?

Although it is called "small" because it accords with the indolence of those who desire the small, this does not prevent indolence from being transformed into diligence, nor the small from becoming great;
gradually, it shall cause them to become Buddhas. This is done through indolence... [text ends].
This constitutes the third point: that through diligent effort, the inconceivable is accomplished. From "internally secret" (*neimi*) downwards, the fourth point clarifies this:
it means that while Bodhisattvas internally conceal the six perfections and myriad practices within their inner treasury, they externally manifest as Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles.

Because they appear only in outward form, they diminish the causes of suffering—namely greed and desire—and weary themselves of the fruits of suffering—namely birth and death; yet because of their internal state alone, [they do not abandon them].
In truth, one purifies one’s own buddha-field from within. To accomplish this inner state through outward appearance is inconceivable;
this is the fourth [point]. This has been shown in accordance with the conventional order. From "Showing the assembly" below, it is shown in reverse order. Regarding the "three poisons":
these refer to the three fundamental delusions of conduct—greed, anger, and ignorance—which cause people to fall into the evil realms; therefore, they are so called.

Poisonous views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). This is one of the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*); it refers specifically to the false view of venerating water and fire, performing sacrifices to heaven, and seeking blessings therein.
For example: Sundarananda was addicted to lust; Śāriputra harbored anger; Cūḍapanthaka was mired in ignorance;
Pilindavatsa was habituated to arrogance; and the three Kāśyapas venerated water and fire. All these were instances where the Buddha manifested [to transform them].

The disciples in the world are none other than manifestations of great power and skillful means, intended to deliver a certain class of stubborn and perverse sentient beings and cause them to return to the Buddha-way. Therefore it is said: "My disciples are such as these.

This takes the correct to demonstrate the false, and turns the contrary into the compliant, achieving what is inconceivable; this is the fifth point. From "If I were fully endowed" onwards, [the text] concludes the excellence of the feet.

Regarding the term "learning" (*śikṣā*): it is said that the skillful means of its manifestation are explained only briefly and not extensively, for fear that those who hear it might give rise to doubt.
Before praising Pūrṇa, the verse first praises the various great disciples because among the five hundred arhats there were members of the group of six bhikṣus.
Now, these thirty lines beginning with this Pūrṇa are distinct [from the preceding].
The verses [from] "Praising the Causal Practice of Pūrṇa" up to "Thereafter He Attains Buddhahood" consist of twenty-eight lines;
these separately praise the prediction of the fruition for Pūrṇa. Each may be understood by correlating it with the long prose version.

Within the section on the prediction of fruition, that which follows the long prose version praises the previous "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," wherein there is no teaching of the three vehicles. This chapter likewise contains no mention of a Saṃgha of the three vehicles. Thus, the Tathāgata...
It should be understood that in the "Chapter on Lifespan" there is no Buddha of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
At that time, the twelve hundred arhats (up to) all came to have the same name, namely, Samantaprabha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Kauṇḍinya, the bhikṣu shall see immeasurable Buddhas... you should proclaim [this] for them."

"At that time," and so forth. At the beginning of the first cycle of the Dharma-teaching, Kāśyapa and the other twelve hundred people heard the Buddha’s discourse on the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—after he emerged from meditative concentration;
yet they departed without knowing where this meaning was leading, much less hoping for a prediction of their own attainment of Buddhahood.
Even when the Buddha gave the parable, although they understood where the meaning was leading, they still remained seated, clinging to the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.

Because they were destined for the Mahāyāna, yet did not seek a prediction [of their future enlightenment], the Buddha, without being asked, spontaneously explained the causes and conditions in one full cycle.

He used the small fruit as a metaphor for the conjured city (*nirmita-nagara*) and the Mahāyāna as a metaphor for the place of jewels (*ratnasthāna*). This clarifies that it is not only the [four] truths and [twelve] links of dependent origination that are the causes for attaining Buddhahood;
he further demonstrates that even those with the three poisons possess the provisional means of the Bodhisattva vehicle, which is internally secret while externally manifest.
Only then did they come to understand the significance of "three first and one last," and "expedient means first and reality later.
Consequently, each formed a thought, wishing to receive, together with the great disciples, the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood. Thus it is said:
"We rejoice," and so forth. We rejoice because our minds are immediately illuminated by the *Upāya-parivarta* (Chapter on Expedient Means), giving rise to great joy.
It is said that they know for themselves that they shall become Buddhas. Ah! The teaching on causes and conditions has been completed in one cycle.
How great indeed is the merit of these twelve hundred people! From this, one can see the sequential order of the three cycles in the sūtra text; it was not established in vain.
"The Buddha knew these [people]" and so forth, correctly concludes that among the twelve hundred arhats mentioned in the *Upāya-paryāya*, all shall likewise become Buddhas.
Regarding this case: among the twelve hundred people, those for whom the prediction was first bestowed upon Cunda were as follows.
Cunda was a kinsman of the Buddha from his lay life and was the very first disciple to attain liberation at the Deer Park.

Following the five hundred arhats, the section formally concluding the bestowal of predictions upon the four great disciples begins: "My disciples, numbering five hundred, shall all receive their predictions."
According to the record, those five hundred people who shared the same name, Samantaprabha, were likewise Dharma-teachers;

they were alike in their understanding of the method for attaining Buddhahood through the three great kalpas and one birth, clarifying that while the fruit is manifest in humans, the cause must not be obscured.
Of the verses, the first twenty-four lines eulogize the adornment of the kalpa and the land of one individual, Kātyāyana; following Kātyāyana, the remaining lines eulogize the causes.

"Practicing. This section, "Constantly Emitting Great Radiance," praises the qualities of the fruition (*phala-guṇa*). There are five such qualities of fruition: first, radiance; second, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

third, renown; fourth, the respect of the multitude; and fifth, preaching the Dharma. Therefore, it says "is called" [below], meaning that because he possesses actual virtues, he is endowed with these beautiful names.
Regarding "his land" [below], this praises the purity of the *pariṇāmanika-dharmatā* (the environment) and the vigor of the spiritual retinue. "All ascend" [below].
To clarify: the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are immeasurable in number. To travel upon palatial towers and pavilions is identical to not leaving one’s door.

To present offerings to the Buddhas and return to one’s own land, traversing vast distances over the course of kalpas—such boundless matters being condensed into a mere moment—is identical to not stirring a single thought. This is not supernatural.

How could it be otherwise than through courageous penetration? This is truly because one has realized the Dharmakāya; thus, aeons as numerous as motes of dust are viewed as a mere snap of the fingers, and the lands of the ten directions are all contained within one's own mind.
This is not something seen by worldly eyes nor fathomed by the ordinary mind. [The following concerns] the Buddha’s lifespan.

There are four types of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*): first, the prediction that the Buddha possesses a full lifespan; second, the prediction regarding the True Dharma (*saddharma*); third, the prediction regarding the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*);

and fourth, the prediction regarding the Final Dharma (*paścimadharma*). These are recorded because the extinction of the Dharma causes grief among devas and humans, all of which are matters pertaining to the Final Dharma. Nevertheless, these all supplement what was not fully exhausted in the long version of the text.
Regarding the fourteen phrases in the middle section, starting from "those five hundred bhikṣus" and below, they follow the example of one person, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and apply universally.

The verse describes the adornment of the land during the kalpa of five hundred people; the final six lines, beginning with "Kāśyapa, you already know," follow the example of these five hundred to record the complete adornment of the lands during the kalpas of the remaining seven hundred people. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"One receives the prediction of enlightenment in one's presence, and one also receives the prediction in one's absence. This is precisely what is meant here. How marvelous is the scriptural text! How easy and concise it is!
At that time, the five hundred arhats (up to) were filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
This passage summarizes the meaning of the causal conditions from our past lives for myself and you all, concluding the text of the chapter on the Parable of the Phantom City.
Regarding the phrase "at that time" and below: whereas the preceding section listed the number as twelve hundred, here only five hundred people are mentioned.

As for the number "one thousand two hundred," if it includes the preceding [context], it encompasses the six individuals such as Śāriputra; if it includes the subsequent [context], it encompasses Ānanda and Rāhula.

Since the former have already been described as having attained realization, while the latter have not yet had their fundamental and derivative [stages] explained, the text speaks only of "five hundred" to distinguish them.
Nevertheless, throughout the entire passage, the emphasis lies on the single phrase of repenting one's transgressions and self-reproach. The world...
"Venerable One, we have always considered ourselves inferior. Relating our past delusions and present awakening, we establish this analogy:
we five hundred people have always failed to realize that spiritual capacity has both sudden and gradual aspects, and that the Dharma has neither small nor great dimensions.
We merely maintained the constant thought that the limited *nirvāṇa* with remainder attained by us was identical to the ultimate extinction realized by the Buddha."

To take the provisional as the ultimate was the reason for our former delusion. This precisely corresponds to the meaning of the "One Vehicle of Liberation" taught by the Buddha in the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*.

We too have attained this Dharma and reached Nirvāṇa; it is only now that we realize—referring to the passage below—that through the Buddha’s threefold exposition of the Dharma and its parables, our deafness and blindness have been opened and cleared away. Thus we know that what the Buddha previously [taught] was small, while what he [teaches] now is great. There is no [other].
It was not through gradual means but by the sudden [attainment] that he requested me to receive the prediction of his future Buddhahood; this is what constitutes his awakening today.
At the beginning of the Parable of the Burning House, the Buddha said, "All those who possess wisdom shall understand through parables.

Since you did not understand even then, you must have waited until the Buddha had preached the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* once more before finally realizing this—how could such a person be considered wise? Therefore, it is said:
Like those who lack wisdom, they now do not understand the direction of this meaning in the "Chapter on Expedient Means.
Previously it was said that they did not know; now it is said that they know. This shows that these five hundred people have finally attained true awakening.
The above clarifies the reason for their self-reproach; the following examines and clarifies their repentance, stating: "Therefore, before the Buddha, we said..."
We are wise ones; yet now we instead reproach ourselves as if we were ignorant. Why is this?

Since we, like Śāriputra and the others, have heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma through both the parable and the direct discourse for two weeks, we ought by now to have equally attained the Tathāgata’s wisdom and received the manifest prediction of our future attainment of the jewel of the noble path.
Yet we sit instead guarding the illusory city, and thus we have come to regard ourselves as small.
The wisdom that mounts it is its feet. The World-Honored One uses the following analogy to clarify the Dharma and reveal the distinction between delusion and awakening.
"There was a person"—referring to himself as one among those in the three realms of existence—accompanied by five hundred arhats as his close friends.

This refers to when the Buddha was a prince of the sixteen kings; being intoxicated with wine symbolizes that what he had realized was entirely free from outflows (anāsrava), yet still possessed of ignorance (avidyā). [This was said by] Master Baozhi.
The song says: "If one does not even partake of the rare delicacies of the joy of dhyāna, who could possibly drink the wine of ignorance?
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Only after the wine has been digested does one awaken. At this time, "official business" refers to public affairs; it refers to the sixteen śrāmaṇeras.
Diligently cultivate the six perfections and contemplate the swift attainment of Buddhahood; because this is for one’s own public business, it is said that "one should practice.

From the phrase "with priceless" [onward], it refers to the sixteen śrāmaṇeras who, with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle, spoke to the five hundred people—just as if one were to tie a *maṇi* jewel inside the soiled clothes of someone intoxicated with wine. The phrase "gave it to them and departed" is a metaphor for the sixteen bodhisattvas.
The śrāmaṇeras each went to attain perfect enlightenment in the ten directions. Regarding the passage "the man lay drunk": this metaphorically represents the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras.

Although each possessed the merit of ascending the Dharma-seat, because the five hundred people had not yet purified their ignorance, views, and afflictions (*kleśa*), they were unaware that they inherently possessed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the One Vehicle.
Having arisen, they wander below. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likened to one’s own country; the five realms of existence (*pañcagati*) are compared to other countries.

"For the sake of food and clothing" below is a metaphor for how these five hundred people, having become lost to what is originally possessed, have fallen into the five realms and cannot escape the food and clothing provided by the blessings and rewards of humans and devas.
They revere water and worship fire, observe the precepts of cattle and dogs, and strive with great effort to seek [their sustenance], which is exceedingly difficult.

This is difficult. The passage beginning with "If there were even a few of the lower grade" uses the metaphor of five hundred people who, having turned from external paths to the Buddha, are shown *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).
They sever their afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) and transcend the cycle of birth and death characterized by limited segments (*paricchinna-bhava*).

Yet, they do not realize that this is merely a small attainment, and instead consider themselves sufficient. The preceding section serves as a metaphor for past delusion; fortunately, they possess deep-seated, latent roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*).

The cause for mounting [the vehicle]. "Later, by a close friend" and below serves as a metaphor for the present awakening. It means that one relies on meeting the Buddha to fulfill the conditions for achieving the Mahāyāna.
"Later" refers to the discourse in this sutra occurring forty years hence. "Tut! is a sound of shouting to awaken someone. "Zai" is an auxiliary particle.
"Zhàngfū" (Great Man) is an honorific title for a man. "For what purpose? and below restates and rebukes the preceding text regarding [working] for food and clothing.

Thus, the text continues: it means that one need not undergo arduous seeking or falsely endure hardships for the sake of the blessings and rewards of humans and devas, nor for the minor fruits of the śrāvakas.

"I formerly desired to let [them know]" below refers to the matter of tying a priceless jewel within their robes, which I have indeed spoken of to you when I was among the sixteen [kings]. Regarding this—
"The year, month, and day" refers to the time when the Wisdom Buddha entered a quiet chamber in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.
What was previously described as "reposing in the five desires at will" is a metaphor for the enjoyment experienced upon the fruition of Buddhahood;

what is here described as "with priceless [jewels] and so forth" is a metaphor for when the Buddha, while on the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), formerly taught five hundred people to resolve their minds toward Great Awakening.
That which now exists as such means that the Dharma-nature, indicated by me in the past, is primordially present and has never been lost.

That you do not know it is because you are obstructed by ignorance (*avidyā*). Since fundamental awakening (*mūlajñāna*) is obscured by ignorance, even though one may attain a minor fruit, [one does not realize the ultimate].
To forget the Great Cause is to toil and suffer for the sake of mere livelihood; this is the height of delusion. You may now descend.
To realize the fruit by means of the cause is called "exchange" (*mào*); to achieve the great from the small is called "transformation" (*yì*).

Since the Great Cause already exists, you may now exchange that cause for the Great Fruit, manifesting bodies according to the various classes within the nine dharma-realms to encounter conditions and engage with sentient beings. Do not...
"Even though one gives to others, one has more than before, and there is no lack or deficiency. This corresponds to the Dharma.
"In the past, although I was deluded, I fortunately planted great causes"—this passage corresponds to the Dharma. "Now, the World-Honored One... and so on; this corresponds to the Dharma.

Although he has now attained awakening, he relies upon meeting the Buddha to fulfill the conditions for the great cause; this is the meaning of the passage [in the *Lotus Sūtra*]. He also fully understands the passage from the "Expedient Means" chapter:
"Though I speak of nirvāṇa, it is not yet the true extinction," and so forth. He likewise understands the passage from the "Parable of the Herbs" chapter:
"That which you practice is the bodhisattva path," and so forth. From the words "Because of this" onwards, he concludes by clarifying his state of exultation and joy at the beginning of the chapter.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"When we heard the voice of the unsurpassed, peaceful prediction [of our future enlightenment], we considered ourselves to have already attained fulfillment."
The verse establishes the analogy for the fundamental text:
"For example, a poor man goes to the house of a kinsman... up to "...indulging himself in the five desires.
This verse uses metaphors to clarify the Dharma, elucidating the texts concerning delusion and awakening.
We, too, are thus, O World-Honored One; throughout the long night [until now], our bodies and minds have been filled with universal joy.
The verse summarizes the meaning of the prose through a metaphorical analogy (as the verse and the prose differ slightly in wording, they are easy to understand when compared).
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Nine: Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula [stood] to one side, as they had wished.
"At that time" and below are the words of the sūtra’s narrator. "We each reflect upon ourselves" refers to the reflection arising at the time when our own sons received their predictions.
"Together we say" and below are the words of the two venerable ones;

it means that regarding this matter of attaining Buddhahood, although our present traces are those of those still in training (śaikṣa), our fundamental nature is that of the Mahāyāna, and we too shall likewise receive our predictions.

This is the division [of the teachings]. If it were said that among the five hundred people, he once taught Kāśyapa and others to transmit [the teachings], then although we are disciples of Śāriputra and Kauṣṭhila, we have studied nothing beyond the Hīnayāna Dharma.

As for matters such as the adornment of kalpas and lands, these are the great causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood; they must necessarily be recorded by the Buddha himself. Therefore, it is said:
"Only the Tathāgata is our refuge. Furthermore, we are the lowest among all, yet we are honored by our own names;
we are known and recognized by devas and humans, and you should grant us this record.

Because we share a kinship with the Buddha as members of his celestial family—one as the Buddha’s attendant to protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma, and one as the Buddha’s rightful heir to succeed him—"
To perpetuate the ancestral sacrifices, it is especially fitting to record this; hence it is said, "If the Buddha were to grant me [this], etc.
That "my vows are fulfilled" refers to the priority of the way of kinship. That "the expectations of the multitude are satisfied" means that the devas, humans, and asuras first rejoice.
At that time, those below the stage of learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) are what is meant by "the expectations of the multitude."
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "In a future age... [until] they shall all join in praising him and extolling his merit.
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I shall now speak within the Saṃgha concerning Ānanda, the upholder of the Dharma" (up to) "planting the causal conditions for the Buddha-way.

From this point downward, he first receives the prediction of his future fruit and title. Originally, Ānanda had long ago resolved upon the Great Mind; in his provisional manifestation, he served as an attendant.
Because he is foremost in extensive learning, he protects and upholds the treasury of the Dharma. His virtue of benevolence is like a mountain; his virtue of wisdom is like the ocean.

Since his fundamental essence and manifested traces are mutually unimpeded, he is called the "King of Sovereign Penetrations of Mountain and Ocean Wisdom. This title accords with his actual reality. Regarding the passage "should offer," it refers to the subsequent bestowal of the record of causal practice:
by making offerings to the Buddha, one fulfills the merit of the feet; by protecting the Dharma, one fulfills the wisdom of the feet. Because both are fulfilled, it is so.
"Subsequently attaining Bodhi" means that one's own three types of awakening are perfected. "Teaching and transforming others" means that the three types of awakening of others are perfected.

Because his merit is complete, his adornments are sublime and supreme; therefore, the land is named *Nityotthitadhvajāgra* (Ever-Erect Supreme Banner). Because his wisdom is complete, the teachings are thoroughly penetrating;
therefore, the eon is named *Ghoṣavyūhaparipūrṇa* (Pervasive Wondrous Sound). The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas is immeasurable as it elucidates the Dharmakāya.
Since Ānanda protected and upheld [the teachings] in their entirety, when he attained Buddhahood, his lifespan was long and the True and Semblance Dharma increased manifold;
he received the praise of all Buddhas. Thus, the fruit does not obscure the cause. In the verse, the causal practice is first praised. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Regarding the "one of great learning" (*bahuśruta*): this mind arises and ceases simultaneously with the mental attention based on hearing (*śrutamanasikāra*).
Because it arises bearing the causal imprint of that [hearing] and is able to maintain it through such perfuming (*vāsanā*), one is called a "holder of the Dharma.

Therefore, it is said: "I now declare among the Saṃgha that Ānanda is a holder of the Dharma. This is the title of the fruit mentioned later; the rest can be understood by referring to the long prose section.
At that time, among those in the assembly were bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds... (down to) "...because their original vows were such, they received this prediction.

Regarding the phrase "at that time" and below, this refers to what was praised when the Buddha first emerged from meditative concentration. "Those who have newly resolved their minds" refers to people who have just begun to generate the bodhicitta.
As for the phrase "all [of them] act thus," those who have first generated the mind of the Way do not yet possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) to a very great extent.
Therefore, because the original and manifested traces of the Bodhisattva and the Śrāvaka were not yet known, doubt was stirred.

Yet this [doubt] had to exist, for it was through this that the original and manifested traces of Ānanda could finally be unfolded. The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, addressed them with the passage beginning "O sons of good family.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* state that the Buddha first resolved to attain enlightenment in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha; however, the present sūtra states that he did so simultaneously with Ānanda under the Empty-King (Kṣemadatta) Buddha.

The resolve generated by the Buddha is spoken of according to the capacities of various beings. Truly, as with rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, those who have newly generated the resolve do not know the root of that resolve;
their delight in much hearing and their receiving of predictions are merely its traces and its aspirations. Therefore, from the passage "I have already...
onwards, it is said that diligence surpasses much hearing. As for the passage beginning "And Ānanda, you shall protect and uphold...", it refers to Ānanda...
It is difficult to regard the protection of the Dharma-treasury as mere diligence.

Whether slow or swift, noble or lowly, the Buddha and his attendant are, from the very first moment the Bodhicitta was generated, but a single thought-instant; there is no great difference in their status. Therefore it is said:
"Their original vows were thus," and so forth. The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-eight, states: "The Śrāvakas attain Anuttara..."
Regarding the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: since it is seen that śrāvakas possess the buddha-nature, even those who possess the buddha-nature may receive a prediction;
how much more so for those who have long since resolved their minds on bodhicitta. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
This refers to a manifested Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha) bestowing a prediction of enlightenment upon a śrāvaka;
it is not the Dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya). Ānanda personally heard this prediction bestowed before the Buddha’s very presence, and he spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and marvelous, causing me to recollect the past [and] protect and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas.

Ānanda lowered his face. "Are you not joyful that the Buddha has personally bestowed this prediction upon you? Why would he transmit it through another in succession? At that moment, he lowered his head.
"Examining this, the Buddha’s words to the bodhisattvas who have newly resolved [to attain enlightenment] are not false. A guest once asked me:
"Does the Buddha truly speak of events from many kalpas across the three periods of time? Is it real? I replied:

"Though the Buddha speaks spontaneously, he can cause those who hear and see him before him to feel as if they were face-to-face with him in person. For this reason, humans and devas believe in him with deep sincerity. The guest said:

If the Buddha were present now, I too would have left the household life. Therefore, in this passage, although the Buddha addresses those who have newly resolved their minds, Ānanda is able to recollect the Dharma-treasuries of all past Buddhas without obstruction and recognizes his own original vows;
all of this is due to the protection of the Buddha’s spiritual power and wisdom-power. As for the first four lines of the verse, they are as explained at length [in the preceding commentary].

The text is intelligible. Regarding the latter four lines: the first half clarifies the fundamental true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) of his original resolve to attain enlightenment together with the Buddha;

the second half clarifies the provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*) manifested in the trace-form of serving as an attendant. Thus, Ānanda alone embodies both the original and the trace, as well as the real and the provisional.

Having thus personally praised and clarified this, the two thousand [monks] subsequently received their predictions, and all those bodhisattvas who had newly resolved upon enlightenment finally closed their mouths in silence.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula... [until] ...he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son... [omitted] ...in order to seek the unsurpassed path."

Ānanda was preeminent in learning, while Rāhula was preeminent in secret practice (*guhyacaryā*). Because learning and practice support one another, the adornments of their respective lands are identical;

they differ only in the names of their fruits. The great vows of Bodhisattvas may involve wishing to serve as an attendant to protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma, or wishing to serve as a successor to offer sacrifices for the Buddha-way; these are all matters of secret practice. No one can know them, for only the Buddha can.
This is known. Thus, a verse says: "The secret practices of Rāhula, only I can witness and know them.

This refers to the time when the Buddha was making vows for the sake of the brahmin Ratnākara in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. At that time, there was a Śakra named Sudarśanapāda, who made a vow to always be a son of the Buddha wherever he may be.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of ocean-like wisdom; this is the seventh.
Jñānabhadra said: When a bodhisattva enters the future world, they observe and discern all kalpas, which are immeasurable and boundless.
They know in which kalpa there will be a Buddha and in which kalpa there will be no Buddha; in which kalpa how many Tathāgatas will appear in the world; what the name of each individual Tathāgata is;
in which world they will dwell; what the name of that world is; and how many sentient beings they will deliver.
He observes thus: "How long is his lifespan? He understands this completely throughout the limits of the future, yet he never reaches the end of it, nor does he ever grow weary of it.

This is why Śākyamuni bestowed the prophecy upon Rāhula; he knew that [Rāhula] would make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, all through the path of a son, practicing in secret.
Indeed, among all human affections, there is none more beloved than that for one's own child.
O son! When a son attains his father, what is there that he does not bring to its ultimate fulfillment? How much more so must this be true for the vows and practices of a Bodhisattva!

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that two thousand individuals, both those still training and those beyond training, were entirely equal in their mastery of both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma.
Then, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
These two thousand śrāvakas now stand before me (until) they gradually enter nirvāṇa.

These two thousand people were all disciples of Ānanda and Rāhula; their mental continuums (*manobhūmi*) are supple and pure, making them precisely the right vessels for awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and receiving their prediction [of enlightenment].
As the *Upāya-paryāya* chapter states: "If a person possesses a well-disposed and supple mind, they have all already become Buddhas."
This is the Way. Therefore, when the Buddha asked Ānanda whether he saw it or not, he did so to cause him to verify his prophecy; it was not bestowed in vain.
This concludes the Preface Chapter. Furthermore, there are two thousand persons, both those in training and those beyond training, according to the record.
At that time, two thousand persons—both those in training and those beyond training—hearing the Buddha’s bestowal of the prophecy, leaped for joy and spoke these verses:
“O World-Honored One, Lamp of Wisdom! Having heard the sound of the prophecy, our hearts are filled with joy, as if we were drenched by the sight of nectar.”
The Buddha’s wisdom is like a lamp; it can illuminate the realms of mind that the majestic radiance of the sun and moon cannot reach.
Hearing the soft and pure voice of his prediction of enlightenment, it was as if he had been sprinkled with ambrosia, and for this reason he rejoiced.
When Ānanda and Rāhula received their predictions above, my vow was fulfilled. This is what is meant by the fulfillment of all expectations.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Master.
Regarding the "Dharma-Master," "Dharma" refers to the wondrous Dharma that the mind itself is Buddha.

Taken narrowly, it encompasses the texts of the three assemblies and nine parables throughout the preceding and succeeding sections of this sutra; taken broadly, it encompasses the twelve [dharmas] expounded during the forty years prior to this.
Regarding the various sections of the sutras, because there is nothing that does not speak of this mind-dharma, the Master— namely, the twelve hundred arhats and the two thousand śrāvakas,
both those in training and those beyond training— will hear even a single verse or a single phrase, from the time the Buddha is present until after his parinirvāṇa.

With a single thought of sympathetic joy, one should know that all those who have received predictions in the past and future may, by means of the wondrous Dharma, serve as teachers and models for devas and humans;

these are of six kinds. However, the first three and a half fascicles of the sutra are Mahāyāna sūtras spoken for the sake of the śrāvakas, titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and are therefore called "Dharma. The latter three and a half fascicles of the sutra are the teachings for bodhisattvas.
Because they are protected and remembered by the Buddha, they are called "Teachers. Although the śrāvakas were originally bodhisattvas, the traces of their receiving predictions are recent.
If, after receiving their predictions, they were not taught the bodhisattva method of upholding this sutra, they would not receive the protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Therefore, from this chapter until the end of the sutra, it is all consistent with the Introductory Chapter.
This section enumerates the eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have long resided in this Sahā world;
they join in chorus and teach the method for those newly received predictions among the śrāvakas to become bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is called the "Dharma Master Chapter."

(Question: Regarding the śrāvakas who receive their prediction, at which stage among the bodhisattva grounds should they be situated? Answer: If one follows the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden [teaching], they should be situated in the seventh ground, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), or the eighth ground, the Acalā (Immovable), among the ten grounds. This is based on the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Laṅkāvatāra*.)

Because Bodhisattvas and Arhats alike [attain] the extinction of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*) within the seventh and eighth stages; and according to the original sūtra, all the śrāvakas who receive their predictions of enlightenment reside in the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). This is because the sūtra states: "You, Śāriputra, have entered by means of faith.

Based on this, since those śrāvakas who receive their predictions already abide in the stage of faith, the subsequent three and a half fascicles of the sūtra all teach the gradual and sudden perfection through the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksaṃbodhi*) for Bodhisattvas.

For example, the Dragon Girl did not traverse the stages but suddenly proceeded to the Stainless World (*Vimalā-loka*) in the south to achieve Perfect Enlightenment. As for Jñānakūṭa and Śāriputra, they initially both lacked faith, but later it is said that they "accepted it in silence with faith."

Therefore, this gradual faith is the very proof of the sudden teaching. If one were to maintain that by believing in one thing one believes in all, such that one would believe in the Perfect Teaching (Vairocana-yāna) through a gradual process, then even the assembly that emerged from the earth—including Maitreya, the World-Honored One who is to succeed him after one more birth—would still have things they could not believe.

This is because [Maitreya] raised an objection using the parable of the father being young and the son being old. Consequently, as the Buddha was about to preach the *Nirdeśa-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Lifespan), he repeatedly exhorted them, saying, "You all must believe and understand the true words of the Buddha.

Maitreya and the other bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, likewise replied three times: "We pray only that you will preach it; we shall believe and accept the Buddha’s words. Thus, immediately following the *Nirdeśa-parivarta*, the *Viniścaya-guṇa-parivarta* (The Chapter on Distinguishing Merit) was taught, distinguishing the stages from the position of self-confidence upward.

From the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha) back to the Bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain enlightenment, each and every one attains a portion of the ocean of merit within the nature of the Buddha-dharmakāya. According to the principle that "by believing in this one thing, one believes in all," this scripture serves as the national teaching.

In sum, the seven fascicles of text encompass both the fruit and the cause; they belong to the single character "faith" (*śraddhā*), for it is the gateway. Thus, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when the youth Sudhana, following the instructions of Maitreya, arrives at the country of Samantamukha and sees Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī extends his right hand from afar across one hundred and ten cities and touches Sudhana’s crown, saying:

"Good son, if you lack the root of faith, your mind will be inferior and filled with regret; your meritorious practices will be incomplete, and you will fall away from diligence regarding even a single root of goodness."

They give rise to attachment; they consider even minor virtues to be sufficient and are unable to initiate the practice of vows and aspirations. They are not sustained by spiritual friends, nor are they remembered by the Tathāgatas.

They are unable to fully comprehend suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such principles (*naya*), such Dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*), and such modes of conduct (*caryā*) and spheres (*viṣaya*). Whether it be through universal knowledge, various kinds of knowledge, exhaustive understanding, thorough comprehension, entry, or exposition, they remain incapable of doing so.

Whether it be through conceptual discrimination, realization, or protective attainment, none of these are capable [of encompassing it]. This correctly accords with the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*), the four stages of application (*prayoga*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) mentioned in the preceding sutra; all are subsumed within the single dharma-gate of the character "Faith" (*śraddhā*). Question: Why does the sutra not explicitly define the stages and positions?

Answer: Forty years ago, they were already recorded in other sutras. Therefore, it is said: "What was previously brought forth and internalized is what the Son knows. Thus, there is no need for further clarification, as it is inherently complete.

One should know that the Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages, as well as the Reward-Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*) and Transformation-Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), are those who sit within the three transformations of the Pure Land as described in the "Treasure Stupa Chapter" (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*). This is because both this Buddha and this land possess marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristics of gathering and dispersing. As for the Bodhisattva of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*), however, it is only...

The Dharma-Buddha protects and keeps [this teaching] in mind, for both that Buddha and his land are devoid of marks and devoid of accumulation or dispersal; it is precisely as described in the "Chapter on the Lifespan. Furthermore, regarding the method of teaching Bodhisattvas as disciples, one should follow the example of Śākyamuni when he served the rishis as a king.

Regarding the method of teaching Bodhisattvas as teachers who transmit the Dharma, one should follow the example of Śākyamuni when he used the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta to instruct the fourfold assembly of arrogant practitioners. Therefore, the latter three and a half fascicles of the sutra are judged to be the "Dharma for Teaching Bodhisattvas" protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
There is a profound purpose in this; let students reflect upon it.
At that time, the World-Honored One [bestowed] upon the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the phrase "at that time" and below: "thereby" (*yin*) means because, while within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja was named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana;
he had formerly practiced asceticism with diligent application for twelve thousand years and thereby attained [this state].
He attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms. When his body was burned, it was restored to its entirety; when his arms were set ablaze, they grew back again.
During the era of the Buddha Thunder-Sound Constellation-King Flower Wisdom (Ghoṣasvararāja-kusumajñāna), he was the prince of King Subhavyūha, named Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra.
Through my transformation by means of the Way, their parents heard the wondrous Dharma, left the household life, and realized the fruits of the path.
This truly constitutes a continuation of the merit of the "Opening, Showing, Awakening, and Entering" into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the great causal condition for a single matter.
For this reason, I have relied upon them to inform the eighty thousand great beings. These eighty thousand great beings are those enumerated at the beginning of the sutra; as previously stated...
In extolling their virtues, one should here follow the reflections of a bodhisattva who has newly resolved [to attain enlightenment]. One should assign names and bestow predictions accordingly;
yet, no such predictions are given here because these eighty thousand great beings each originally had their own respective Buddhas under whom they served.
In past kalpas, they all received great predictions and are now the elders who have long resided in this Sahā world; they are not [the recipients of my prediction].
Śākyamuni’s rightful successor is present here in this assembly; do not fail to assist in promoting the transformation of the Dharma. Therefore, I address him for this reason:
first, to testify that those who hear and uphold this sutra both before my passing and after my parinirvāṇa shall attain realization, even though the kalpas may be long and the fruition distant.

Vast and boundless. The words regarding the Buddha’s merit and wisdom are not empty. First, to ensure that one receives a prediction of enlightenment both in the present life and after death, one should make vows and uphold this sutra;
one ought to emulate the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja by burning the body or lighting the arm, undaunted by such hardships.
Second, it clarifies the origins and manifestations of the Buddha’s quest for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as well as the spiritual power and wisdom through which he spoke of them.

This is manifested through power, like a stupa emerging from the earth transforming the soil. In a mere instant, the Buddhas who are emanations from the ten directions are assembled to discourse upon the supreme practices for peace and bliss.
Sixty thousand bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, emerge as their retinue.

This great cause and condition of the one great matter, from its beginning to its ultimate end, would truly be difficult to believe were it not for the eighty thousand great beings who have newly attained the prediction of enlightenment.
[Commentary: There is a reason for this; therefore, by means of the single person, Bhaiṣajyarāja, [the Buddha] addresses the eighty thousand great beings.
From "Bhaiṣajyarāja, you see" below, the text of the preceding Introductory Chapter states that Mañjuśrī said: "All you people, you should now know: with palms joined and one-pointed minds, wait;
the Buddha shall rain down the Dharma-rain to satisfy those who seek the Way. This refers to the twelve hundred arhats and...

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 525, the Buddha himself explains that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) briefly consists of three types of knowledge.

Therefore, the Buddha knows that all phenomena are of one and the same characteristic—namely, the characteristic of quiescence.
For this reason, the Buddha is called "Omniscient regarding All Characteristics" (*sarvākārajñatā*), which encompasses the small, great, three, and one, as well as all modes of appearance.

Although the former sūtras were subtle, they still retained the traces of the three.

Regarding the vehicle (*yāna*): it has never been explicitly stated that there is only one reality. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is like the vanguard, while the *Nirvāṇa* is like the main army. Once the vanguard has defeated the enemy, the rear guard requires few more weapons.
