Citing evidence for the title: its actual meaning is recorded in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

When the Buddha made his vow before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha to attain Buddhahood within this defiled Sahā world, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha used the *puṇḍarīka* flower as a metaphor for the greatness of the Buddha’s compassionate vow.
Now that the Buddha has fulfilled the fruit of his vow to deliver sentient beings and attain Buddhahood, [the text continues] regarding what he was about to do in the past...
He manifested his parinirvāṇa and exhorted the assembly to make a vow to uphold this sūtra in this land so that the lineage of the Buddhas would not be severed.
Therefore, he caused the stupa to surge forth, transformed the earth, and gathered the Buddhas in order to entrust them with this sūtra.
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures (up to) where the various Buddhas who had manifested their bodies paid homage and made offerings.
Regarding the phrase "At that time" and below, the scribe of the sutra provides a ten-part description. First, he describes the height of the stupa:
one *yojana*, which is forty *li*. Five hundred *yojanas* would mean the stupa is twenty thousand *li* high. Regarding the phrase "length and breadth," he describes the [dimensions] of the stupa.
"Great. Two hundred and fifty *yojanas* would mean the stupa is ten thousand *li* in size.
The ground from which it emerges represents the eternally abiding mind-ground shared by the Buddha and sentient beings; it dwells within the emptiness of space.
This ground of the mind is formless and signless; it is the ultimate *nirvāṇa*, the state of eternal quiescence, which ultimately returns to the emptiness of emptiness.

Just as the worldly earth bears Mount Hua and Mount Yue without feeling heavy, and sustains the rivers and seas without overflowing, how could this supramundane ground of true emptiness not be able to support the two-thousand-li expanse and the ten-thousand-li height?

"Is it not a great stūpa of the seven treasures?"—this can be believed without doubt. From "various kinds" (*zhongzhong*) downward, there is a general description of the stūpa’s magnificent adornments.

From "five thousand" (*wǔqiān*) downward, there is a specific description of the adornments in seven items: first, railings; second, niches and chambers; third, banners and streamers; fourth, necklaces;
fifth, precious bells; sixth, incense; and seventh, pennants and canopies. All of these are made of the seven treasures.
This is a composite description. While the previous passage stated that the stūpa was five hundred *yojanas* high, it did not specify where its summit reached.

This passage states that its height reaches the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), from which we know that the distance from the summit of Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) to the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings is merely twenty thousand *li*.
Below the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*), there are three accounts describing the deities who made offerings to the stūpa.
The eight classes of beings, including the nāgas, are all those who draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, beneath the jeweled stūpa, the four assemblies did not merely see the stūpa with their eyes; they also heard a great sound issuing from within the stūpa, offering praise.
There were three aspects to this praise: first, the invocation of names; second, the extolling of virtues through the phrase "capable of," etc.; and third, impartiality.

There are several passages in the *Mahāmati* [Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra] that illuminate this: first, the passage in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya*) chapter concerning the self-realization of the unsurpassed path and the equality of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
second, the passage in the "Parable" (*Dṛṣṭānta*) chapter stating that for the sake of the śrāvakas, he preached the Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Now, from the "Expedient Means" chapter up to the "Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhi*) chapter, there are seven kinds of equality. Regarding these—

Regarding the Dharma, there is the equality of the provisional and the real, wherein three [teachings] precede and one follows. Regarding persons, there is the equality of the secret and the manifest, and the small and the great.

Regarding those who uphold and recite the sutra, there is the equality of merit between one who rejoices in even a single verse or a single thought-moment and one who explains the entire text in detail.
Regarding the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), there is no distinction based on the quantity [of practice]; all [are equal].
The equality of bestowing the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* refers to the equality of those previously mentioned.
Regarding the subsequent [category], there is the equality of manifesting the prediction for both enemies and kin, such as Devadatta and Yaśodharā.

Among the multitude who emerged from the earth, there is the equality of the one and the many. Regarding the lifespan of the Buddhas, there is the equality of the extension and contraction of the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Transformation-body.
...the equality [of all things]. Therefore it is said: "One who is able, by means of the great wisdom of equality, to preach for the great assembly," and so forth.
Third, from "In this way" onwards, this is the realization of reality; that is to say, the seven kinds of equality mentioned before and after are all true and not false.

From "At that time, the fourfold assembly" onwards, fifth, this describes the dharma-assembly obtaining the seal of praise through the voice emerging from within the stūpa—whether seeing or hearing it.
All were delighted that the Dharma they had received was true, yet they marveled at the miraculous occurrence of the stupa emerging from the earth. Therefore, it is said:

"They saw the great jeweled stupa," and so forth. Rising from their seats and descending [from the sky], six [verses] describe how, because the stupa remained suspended in the air, they all stood up, joined their palms, and withdrew to stand on one side; they likewise desired to ascend into the void. At that time, there was a Bodhisattva...
[Sa] (lower). Seventh, the description of those who are ready to receive the teaching (*pratibhānaka*). Desiring to remove the doubts of others and himself, he requests instruction from the Buddha.

The one ready to receive the teaching is named Mahāratnaprati-bhāna (Great Eloquence). Among the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there is the unhindered analytical knowledge of eloquence;

it is said that only one endowed with this analytical knowledge is able to preach without weariness. Furthermore, those who possess this eloquence number eighty thousand, who practice together with Bhaiṣajyarāja.

Among them was one person. Only one of superior capacity who clearly understood the maintenance of the sutra throughout the three periods of time, and who was no less venerable than King Bhaiṣajyarāja, was sufficient to serve as the cause for this chapter’s assembly of the ten directions and the three periods of time to receive the entrustment.

Only one endowed with great eloquence was sufficient to make the request. There are two meanings to "requesting": first, from "With what... below, it asks by what causes and conditions the jeweled stupa has emerged.

...and emerges from the ground. Second, again below: [The text] asks, "In general, as for those who build stūpas, if they do not enshrine the Buddha’s relics (śarīra), they then install various sūtras.
Since sūtras and relics are different things, how could they be spoken of together? Therefore, it says, "By what causes and conditions did the World-Honored One...

and so forth. At that time, the Buddha told [the assembly] below; this eighth section describes the Buddha’s response suited to the occasion, stating that within the stūpa there are neither relics nor...
The Sūtra states that this is the entire body of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who attained parinirvāṇa long ago in the past, and it is within his stūpa that the sound is produced.

This passage corresponds to the "Superior Grade" (śreṣṭha-pakṣa), for it contains the text stating that since the entire body of the Tathāgata is already present here, there is no need to further enshrine śarīra relics.
This first answers the second question. *Bodhisattvagatyupapatti-sūtra*, Chapter Two.
In the *Shēnshēnshělípǐn* (Chapter on the Relics of the Entire Body), it is stated regarding the Dharma of a single form:
"This great earth element is eighty-four trillion *li* thick. Beneath the earth is wind; beneath the wind is water; beneath the water is fire; and beneath the fire is sand."
There are diamond lands (*vajra-kṣetra*) within the sands, each eighty-four trillion *li* in thickness. The entire bodies of all Buddhas are contained within those diamond lands.

It continues, saying that there is a world called Dharmadundubhi, also eighty-four trillion *li* in thickness, where past billions of millions of Buddhas have all left behind their *śarīra*. I also possess the *śarīra* from that land.
It is neither one nor two; it does not abide in a single place, yet it is not that it does not abide.
It circulates and comes and goes, fully endowed with radiant marks, manifesting and teaching.

Thus we know that the entire-body śarīra of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna has all emerged from the earth within the Vajra-land and the Dharma-drum world. Following the descent of that Buddha, the first question is next answered.

Question: Regarding the causes and conditions for the arrival of the jeweled stupa, it is because during his causal stage, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna had previously made a great vow that even after attaining Buddhahood, although his body would remain within the stupa, he would also wish to hear this sutra and praise the virtues of the Buddha who preaches it.
Thus, the stupa surged forth to appear before him and serve as a witness; this should be understood as corresponding to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the highest grade.
The text protected since ancient times clarifies, from the passage "When that Buddha attained enlightenment" onwards, that the fruit of Muchika (Prabhūtaratna) is not obscured by its cause.
From the passage "That Buddha, by means of his spiritual power" onwards, it clarifies that the cause of Muchika constantly results in the fruit.

"Mahāpratibhāna, now, from 'Muchilo' [Mahāpratibhāna] downward, the meaning of the response is concluded by joining the feet. At that time, from 'Mahāpratibhāna' downward, nine sections describe the response following the request of the one capable of receiving it.
He requested to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; however, this request could not have been fulfilled without the empowerment of the Buddha's power.
Therefore, it says, 'By the supernatural power of the Tathāgata,' and so forth. From 'The Buddha said to Mahāpratibhāna' downward, ten sections describe the Buddha’s response."
Regarding "timely response" (dangji): it refers to the manifestation of the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, which serves to fulfill his profound and solemn vow.

That profound vow was that the Sambhogakāya Buddha who currently preaches the Dharma and the Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas who reside in various places throughout the ten directions must assemble together in one location;
only then did the Buddha Prabhūtaratna appear. This completes what was referred to as the "three [assemblies]" in the *Upāya-paryāya* chapter.

The statement that "the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions in all worlds is also thus," as well as the meaning of "fully opening, revealing, awakening, and leading sentient beings into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," refers to this.
Regarding the three periods of time: Prabhūtaratna belongs to the Buddhas of the past; Śākyamuni is the Buddha of the present;
and those such as Śāriputra who have received their predictions of enlightenment are called the Buddhas of the future. This is the division of Śākyamuni.
[This concerns] the body. For the sake of the Buddhas of the ten directions, that which constitutes the profound vow is this:

the Buddhas of the Reward and Transformation bodies throughout the three periods of time and ten directions must, together relying upon the upward-directed nature of the Dharma-body—which is equal and devoid of enmity or kinship—bestow the prediction of fruition upon those people who possess both enemies and kin.
From the passage "Mahāpratibhāna, my emanations... onwards, it refers to the deep and profound [vow] of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.

"May it be as you wish. Since your request is such as this, then the various Buddhas who are emanations of me, Śākyamuni, residing throughout the ten directions, should likewise assemble here. After Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, he said:
"I merely requested to see one Buddha of the past, yet I have now been granted the opportunity to see all the Buddhas of the present throughout the ten directions. Thus...
This is also our profound and earnest aspiration; therefore it is said, "We also aspire to equality.
At that time, the Buddha emitted two rays of light from his white tuft of hair (until) Buddhas and Tathāgatas filled the space therein.
"At that time," and so forth. The scribe’s narrative is arranged into ten sections.
First, it describes how Śākyamuni Buddha emitted light because he desired the emanation-buddhas of the ten directions to assemble;

he then beheld the lands and buddhas of the eastern direction, numbering as many as five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands. "In those various lands," and so forth, next describes the illumination and vision.

The adornment of the Buddha-land of the Nirmāṇakāya is purely pure and without defilement. From "Countless tens of millions" downwards, the third section describes the Dharma retinue of the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha as he perceives them;
these consist solely of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas and exclude the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna.
"Spreading everywhere below": Fourth, this describes the vision of the land’s environment and its inhabitants, all of which are encompassed by canopies made of precious jewels as curtains and nets.

"The Buddhas of that land below": Fifth, this describes the vision of the transformation-body Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) and bodhisattvas, all of whom take the preaching of the Dharma as their primary activity.
As the *Shangpin* (Chapter on the Superior) says: "In my thousands of millions of lands, I manifest a pure and solid body. In the [absence of...]"
"Measuring billions of kalpas, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings"—this is now further confirmed. "South, West, North, below":
these six lines describe one direction as an illustration for the remaining nine directions; hence it says, "the South, West, North, and so forth.

"At that time, the ten directions... and so on: these seven lines describe how the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions appear through the light, with principal and retinue in infinite layers.
All desire to come from their transformation bodies to the place of the reward-body Buddha in order to make offerings to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
"I shall now go" refers to the response; "should illuminate" refers to the past; "now should assemble" refers to the present; and "the time has arrived" refers to the future.

Below the section on Sahā, eight points describe how the various emanation Buddhas of the ten directions wish to come to this land, and by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the impure realm is suddenly transformed into a pure one.

There are ten sections concerning the transformation of the impure into the pure: first, transforming the ground into lapis lazuli; second, transforming it into jeweled trees; third, demarcating the paths with golden cords;
fourth, eliminating all signs such as villages and settlements; fifth, burning great precious incense; sixth, scattering celestial flowers upon the ground;
seventh, covering the area above with jeweled canopies; eighth, suspending various jeweled bells; ninth, leaving only this assembly behind; tenth, shifting [the assembly elsewhere].
The devas and humans are placed in other lands. The above constitutes the first transformation, the Land of Realized Reward Adorned with Virtue (*vipākavibhūṣita-kṣetra*).

Since this [land] is primordially pure, no further transformation is required; however, it is described as a "transformation" for the sake of those who have newly received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Therefore, within the text concerning the transformation:
It does not mention the absence of hells and the like because those who have newly attained the prediction of enlightenment have, at the outset, not yet awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus they perceive the pure as impure, just as Vimalakīrti and Śāriputra perceived it.
Now that they have awakened, they perceive the impure as pure, just as the Brahma King Śaṅkhakeśa perceived it. At this time, above all the Buddhas...
9. It is recorded that the emanated Buddhas of the ten directions each arrived at their lands of recompense with their respective attendants;
beneath jeweled trees and upon lion thrones, they sat cross-legged, each having a specific place assigned to them. Thus it continues in succession downward. 10.
It is recorded that although the transformed lands of the ten directions are vast and immense, they cannot accommodate even a single portion of the emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha, let alone—
It can accommodate the nine other directions’ emanations; this shows the multiplicity of Śākyamuni Buddha’s responsive transformations.

This serves as the basis for the second and third transformations of the land described in the subsequent text. Each is accompanied by attendants, which provides the precedent for the dispatching of messengers to inquire after his well-being in the later sections.
If we, as human beings, can read and recite this sutra, there is no need to perform meditative visualization; we shall immediately behold the great trichiliocosm.
In this world, there is not a single moment or a single speck of dust that is not the Buddha. At that time, Śākyamuni descended;
that is to say, Śākyamuni Buddha desired to fully accommodate the remaining emanation-buddhas of the nine directions.

Subsequently, beyond the Flower-Treasury World-System (Kusumagarbha-lokadhātu) of the Sahā trichiliocosm, he further transformed the realm where ordinary beings and sages cohabit into a land of reality.
This refers to the adornment of the Buddha’s land of retribution. Therefore, it says, "In each of the eight directions, there is further transformation," and so forth.

Since it is precisely through this transformation that the ordinary becomes the holy and the defiled becomes pure, when compared with the passage describing the initial transformation—which states that there are no hells and so on—it can be seen that within the Buddha’s land of actual retribution and adornment, the six classes of ordinary beings and their defilements have never existed from the beginning. This is also indicated by the passage beginning with "lapis lazuli."
This can be understood from the text regarding the first transformation. Mucilinda means "Stone Mountain," and Mahāmucilinda means "Great Stone Mountain.
The Cakravāḍa Mountains also have large and small varieties; those that encircle the small chiliocosm and the great trichiliocosm are all composed of iron.
Sumeru is called "Wondrous High" (Miaogao); it is composed of the seven treasures. This applies generally.

Regarding "the lower": this refers to the fact that there are no mountains or seas to separate it. This Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages shares the same adornments as the aforementioned Land of True Reward and Adornment;
thus, they together constitute a single pure land endowed with adornments.

Śākyamuni Buddha, for the sake of all Buddhas who will come in the future, [descends] thirdly to the outside of the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages, where he transforms the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*).

The remaining lands constitute the land of true retribution (*sambhoga-kāya*). They are the seats where the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) of Śākyamuni sit as Buddhas in other countries during future ages.
Therefore, it says, "Furthermore, in each of the eight directions, he again transforms," and so forth.

At that time, the passage beginning with "In the eastern direction" concludes the description of the second transformed land, which accommodates all the transformation bodies divided from Śākyamuni’s own eastern quarter. As...
This concludes the sequential explanation of how, through three successive transformations, the pure lands are made to accommodate all the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni throughout the ten directions.
At that time, in each direction, during the second and third transformations of the lands, it is stated that there are two hundred million *koṭis* and so forth;
now, combining these two instances of two hundred million *koṭis*, it is said to be four hundred million *koṭis*.
This is also due to the Buddha. The sutra text transforms the land a second time to accommodate the emanations from the ten directions.

Regarding the third transformation of the land, since it states it is "for the Buddhas to sit upon in the future," and "future" refers to the future [time], it thus accommodates the emanations of the three periods of time.

This meaning expresses that [the land] is vertically exhaustive across the three temporal limits and horizontally pervasive throughout the ten directions; all of this is due to the Buddha and the assembly.
Birth and so forth are all manifestations of the eternally abiding true mind. As the Sūtra says:
"Your body and your mind, the mountains and rivers of the non-Buddhists, space, and the great earth—all are objects manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind.
When the Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he contemplated for twenty-one days; it was precisely because he contemplated that sentient beings had reached this state.
Yet there were sentient beings who, though possessing eyes, did not see; and though possessing ears, did not hear.

When it was said that forty years had passed, and this sutra was finally preached, the Dharma-rain fell in three stages, moistening and opening the way for the deaf and the blind, so that each received a prediction of enlightenment. It is within this chapter that this occurs.
The transformation of the lands and the gathering of Buddhas are none other than the clear demonstration, revelation, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
To see that my Śākyamuni Buddha alone has such a multitude of emanations, such vast lands, and such sovereign spiritual powers—
this may be called seeing the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) only with eyes, and hearing it only with ears.
One has now heard the voice of Samantabhadra. Yet, because this is merely the initial attainment, one cannot yet escape the initial drying up of karmic habits;

thus, one still perceives the presence of lands and further transformations, as if Buddhas were coming from without. Even when it was recorded that Ti-p'o-ye-shou and others, along with the dragon girl, would attain Buddhahood upon standing on the earth, those who newly received these predictions each made vows to propagate the sutras and attained the superior practice of peace and bliss. As for the old...
The assembly of those to be converted all surged forth from the earth, realizing their own long-lasting lifespan.

Thus, the Buddha of the pure *dharmakāya* is entirely devoid of any visible marks of self or other; the land of eternal quiescent radiance is such that it undergoes three transformations yet remains unchanging.
Only then did they realize that those who read, recite, accept, and uphold this sutra possess pure wisdom.
The wondrous perfection: its essence is eternally empty and tranquil, yet it possesses the infinite merits of a Buddha. Therefore, after discussing the span of his life, his merits are distinguished;
there are differences such as rejoicing for a single thought-moment and the purification of the six sense faculties.

By citing the story of Nityapradīpta, he confirms the vastness of upholding the sutra during the causal stage, while manifesting supernatural powers as a trace of his activity. Finally, he entrusts the teaching upon the fruition stage.

This is the great enterprise of the Dharma; it is the single great causal event of the Buddhas alone. Having investigated its beginning and end to their ultimate conclusion, there is finally no further residue remaining.
This sutra is the grand compendium of all Buddhas. Question: In the "Introductory Chapter," the emission of light is said to be from between the eyebrows;
why does the present text simply say "a single ray from the white tuft"? Answer: The space between the eyebrows symbolizes the state beyond fixed positions (*amūla*).
Because the śrāvakas regard *nirvāṇa with remainder* as the ultimate reality, their attachment is refuted by means of the "state of non-existence" (*amūla*).
Now, since all these śrāvakas have become bodhisattvas, both their bodies and their lands are nothing other than a single ray of light from the *ūrṇā*.

Therefore, one need not inquire whether there were eyebrows or not between them. Question: Since all the devas and humans were already relocated within the three transformations of the land, why does it say that "precious celestial flowers are spread everywhere upon its ground"?
Answer: These precious flowers resemble celestial flowers; they do not necessarily have to be those scattered by the various heavens.
Alternatively, these may be Mahāyāna bodhisattvas acting as devas and humans, rather than ordinary beings who could simply be relocated.
As for this, does not this sutra say: "Only the assembly of this gathering is wicked"? How could there be no devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings within this assembly?
Question: The Buddha’s mind is compassionate toward all places; why then do you speak of moving [the assembly] away from the devas and humans? Answer:

Because the Buddha’s prediction concerning the dragon girl regarding Devadatta was an event unlike any other, and fearing that the obstructions of gods and humans were so deep that they would find it difficult to believe, might give rise to slander and fall into suffering, he temporarily set it aside.
It was only upon reaching the "Chapter on Spiritual Powers" that he allowed them to hear the name of her land, Saha.
The Buddha’s name is Śākyamuni, and the Sūtra’s name is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. It is by planting roots of goodness therein that one is transferred [to a pure land];
this is precisely what constitutes the Great Compassion of the Buddha. Question: How can a single entity manifest immeasurable bodies? Answer:
For three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the Buddha cultivated the practices of a Bodhisattva among the twelve classes of sentient beings through the power of his great vows, assuming immeasurable bodies.
Upon attaining Buddhahood, all those bodies from his previous various forms became Buddha-bodies;
thus, his bodies are as numerous as his vows. How much more so for a single thought-moment within our dreams, which can still manifest the infinite...

Regarding the scope of the Buddha’s realm: the Buddha is the Most Honored One of Great Enlightenment. For him, the power of his spiritual penetrations and the power of his wisdom are such that the one is immeasurable and the immeasurable is one;
this is simply the natural order of things and is not to be wondered at. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest immeasurable worlds and unspeakably many varieties of Buddha-bodies."
This sufficiently proves that [the Buddha] manifests as emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Furthermore, it says:

"All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the various adornments and countless ornaments of immeasurable worlds. This sufficiently proves the transformation of the pure land. Question:
Why must the transformation of the land and the assembly of Buddhas necessarily await the appearance of the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna? Answer: Prabhū... [text continues]
The Jewel Buddha appears. One sees that the Buddhas of the past do not perish; though they have entered parinirvāṇa within their stupas, they manifest by sharing their seats.
One sees that the Buddhas of the present are not born. By making vows to uphold this sutra, one sees those who have newly received predictions of future Buddhahood;

although the kalpas may be long and the fruition distant, by upholding this sutra even once, one immediately realizes the principle of non-arising and non-perishing, becoming equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
What is meant by "all have already attained the Buddha-way" is that there is no further need for them to attain it. Question:

Regarding the assembly of emanated bodies and the transformation of the pure lands, these are merely vast and profound words; most people do not see them. Are they actual realities, or are they illusory arts? Answer:
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, these are all composed of the actual virtues of the category of wisdom associated with the eight consciousnesses;
they are not illusory phenomena. The treatise states: "Although these four categories of wisdom are all universally capable of taking all phenomena as their objects, their functions differ."
This refers to the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśajñāna), which manifests the signs of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) and its pure land, and maintains untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*).

The Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) manifests the signs of the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and its pure land. The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) is able to manifest the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and its land.

These points accord with the descriptions of the bodies and lands in the *Sūtra on the Distinction of Phenomena* (*Dharmadharmatāvibhaṅga-sūtra*), without the slightest discrepancy. As for the Wisdom of Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*)...
Chapter: Examining the capacities and faults of oneself and others, raining down the great rain of Dharma, shattering the net of doubts, and bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
This corresponds to the section on the division of the body and the transformation of the pure land in the *Sūtrasaṃuccaya*, following the sixteen subsequent chapters of the sūtra.
They are identical and without difference. When one examines the sutras through the lens of the treatises, they are all the true principles and phenomena of the supramundane;

how could they be mere fabrications? It is only that our own bodies and worlds are both the perceived and perceiving aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*) transformed by the eight consciousnesses.

We give rise to the two attachments of self and dharmas, and from beginning to end, we are merely bound and constrained by karma, unable to effect transformation. Whenever we encounter the words of the Buddha, they are all...

They falsely label it as illusory and vain. They do not realize that since the Buddhas are able to transform consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), all manifestations are not afflictions (*kleśa*), but are entirely in accord with the wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the treatise states: "Such a Dharma-body has three distinct aspects.

First is the Svabhāvakāya (Self-nature Body), which refers to the true, pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Tathāgatas; it is free from characteristics, quiescent, and transcends [conceptualization]."
All conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are endowed with boundless, true, and eternal merits;
they are the equal, ultimate nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), and are also called the *dharmakāya*, because it is the locus upon which the dharmas of great merit depend.

Compassion and benevolence...

"Yue" (To allow). Regarding her social interactions with others: her will and intent were harmonious and elegant. Regarding her natural endowment and refined appearance: although this describes the virtues of the Dragon Girl, it actually clarifies the ritual conduct of those who uphold this sutra.

One sees that although the Dragon Girl was young in years, she was no different from Śākyamuni Buddha in having accumulated merit and virtue over immeasurable kalpas. He failed to realize that this was the wondrous function of a Bodhisattva: for the sake of indolent sentient beings, she manifested the attainment of Buddhahood after a long duration; for the sake of diligent sentient beings, she taught that one can achieve Buddhahood instantaneously. If this is so, how could one know that Śākyamuni [was not already a Buddha] in other worlds?

Encountering those who practice with diligence is not the same as the Dragon Girl’s demonstration of instantaneous attainment. As for the manifestation [of this], it is said in the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) that when Kāśyapa Buddha was a bhikṣu, Śākyamuni Buddha was a louse and Devadatta was a flea; they lived within the bhikṣu’s robes, causing him distress. The bhikṣu made an agreement, saying:

"Whenever I am engaged in my duties, you may jump about and bite as you please, but when I enter meditative concentration, I pray that you both will cease. The louse followed this instruction, but the flea alone violated the agreement. Because the bhikṣu could not attain concentration, he burned his robes with fire, whereby both the flea and the louse perished.

The bodies of the flea and the louse were like a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), their smallness and size being exactly comparable. Within the ocean of kalpas, the Buddha sacrificed his life in this manner to transform a class of sentient beings who were fleas and lice. Thus it is said.
The reason Mañjuśrī did not answer before the discourse was concluded is that he had the dragon girl as his witness. As for the verse stating "profoundly penetrating," etc.:
the dragon girl represents the state of an animal, which is the aspect of transgression (*āpatti*); awakening to the fruit of Bodhi is the aspect of merit (*puṇya*).

To be able to believe that the dragon girl can attain Buddhahood is to profoundly penetrate the fact that transgression and merit are one and the same in their true reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, the nature of luminosity pervades...

"It illuminates the ten directions. This refers to the capacity for realization (*pramāṇa*), thereby manifesting the virtue of *prajñā*. "Subtle and wondrous" and below refer to that which is realized, thereby manifesting the virtue of the *dharmakāya*.

Liberation and Virtue: Because the Dharma-body is subtle, it is that which devas and humans revere; because the Reward-body is wondrous, it is that which dragons and spirits honor;

thus, you are not a vessel for the Dharma. Moreover, the Buddha-way is remote and vast, requiring many kalpas to traverse.

Only after the accumulation of complete practice is this finally accomplished. This is based on such statements as "the Buddha-way is vast and remote," which suffice to explain how one can attain unsurpassed bodhi.

since neither conditioned nor unconditioned phenomena function [as inherently existent], how could supramundane phenomena function as real entities, or mundane phenomena as unreal ones?

This is because both the mundane and the supramundane, whether existent or non-existent, real or unreal, are all identical with the true nature of reality (*tathatā*). This verse, when viewed in light of the extensive prose, explains that all phenomena are the true nature of reality.

"Furthermore, one does not engage in the two phrases, nor does one differentiate," etc., means that since the true reality (*dharmatā*) realized within the inner mind is already non-engaging, how could one possibly differentiate external characteristics such as "male" or "female"?

The above clarifies the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which is emptiness within existence. From "cannot be obtained" onwards, it clarifies the contemplation of the conventional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), which is existence within emptiness. That is to say:

Although internally one does not differentiate the true nature (*dharmatā*), and externally one does not differentiate male or female, yet one does not fail to attain—nor remain ignorant of or blind to—the dharmas of superior, middling, or inferior;
conditioned or unconditioned; real or unreal; male or female, and so forth—and thus fall into annihilationism.
This verse summarizes the single phrase "non-differentiation" from the long prose passage: "The Bodhisattva, regarding the sphere of principle and practice..."
Therefore, it says, "This is then," and so forth.
All dharmas are empty and non-existent... (up to) "...this is called the place frequented by the wise.
This separate verse concerns the practice of proximity. From "All" onwards, the verse summarizes the long prose on contemplating all dharmas as empty according to reality.

[The verse speaks of] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the nature of non-existence like space. Question: Since the prose section mentions "suchness" (*tathatā*) as the true characteristic (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), why is it not mentioned in the verse?
Answer: The true characteristic is precisely the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Therefore, the single line in the verse stating that "emptiness has nothing [to be grasped]" fully encompasses both the true characteristic and the characteristic of space. This is because ordinary beings...
Generally, one perceives all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), as being real, yet fails to perceive their primordial reality—the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When a sage realizes the principle that all phenomena are empty, this is called the "mark of reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); thus, the aggregates and all other phenomena are entirely empty and illusory.
This is why the sage and the ordinary person, the ultimate and the conventional, and principle and phenomenon, are of one essence while differing in function. There is nothing permanent.
"Abiding. The prose contains no such text, nor does it mention arising or ceasing. The verse completes what the prose lacks: "The prose does not arise; the prose does not cease.
From the phrase "This is called the wise one" onwards, the verse concludes the text.
[The practitioner] engages in inverted conceptualization regarding the existence and non-existence of all phenomena (up to: remaining as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
Regarding the phrase "reiterating the practice of conduct and its basis" (*caryā-vihāra-anuvāda*), it refers to the statement that these arise from the proximity of inversion.
Now, concerning the expression "reiterating the practice of conduct and its basis," it is because there is a distinction between the two bases of conduct. In these two bases—

The principle (*li*) and the practice (*xing*) are identical. Therefore, the Translator [Xuanzang] treats them as "principle-practice" (*li-xing*) in the prose, while the Verse [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] treats them as "practice-principle" (*xing-li*).

This is because while the realization of principle is one, its manifestations are myriad; and because in the case of "practice-principle," there is the phrase "even when practicing, one does not act, for there is no discrimination."
The verse states that those who are free from inversion certainly do not engage in conceptual discrimination;
whereas those who possess inversion do discriminate among phenomena as existent or non-existent, right or wrong, real or unreal, arising or ceasing.

As for the subsequent section, it means that once a holder of the sutra knows that those with inversion discriminate among phenomena, they should then practice restraint in mountain forests and secluded places.

With a mind free from inversion and non-conceptualization, cause them to abide securely within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle, as immovable as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains. A monk asked Yunmen: "When not a single thought arises, what then?"
The Gate says: "Mount Sumeru. This is it.
To contemplate that all phenomena are non-existent (up to) being eternally abiding in a single characteristic is called the "near practice" (*upaniṣad*).

Regarding the three verses on the practice of the locus: "contemplating all [phenomena]" and below means that the practice of the locus is not merely contemplating the one [characteristic] through the near practice.
All phenomena are empty and non-existent. Thus, one practices the practice of engagement. Furthermore, one contemplates that all phenomena are entirely non-existent, like space.

Regarding the phrase "there is no solidity," it means that not only is there no permanence in the practice of engagement with the immediate object, but even in the practice of engagement itself, all phenomena lack solidity. One should know this to be non-existent.
"Solidity" (*sāratā*) is itself "non-permanence" (*a-nityatā*); these terms differ in expression but are identical in meaning.

"Not arising below" means that it is not only in the principle of the proximate realm that there is no arising or ceasing; even in the principle of the sphere of activity (*gocara*), there is likewise no production, movement, or regression.
"Abiding permanently in a single aspect" means that it is not only in the principle of the sphere of activity that one dwells immovably, like Mount Sumeru, but also in the proximate realm.
Regarding the principle of abiding: by observing all phenomena, one does not give rise to arising, movement, or regression;

thus, the true reality (*dharmatā*) realized within the inner mind is also eternally abiding in a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that what was previously stated as "immovable like Mount Sumeru" and what is now stated as "eternally abiding in a single characteristic" clarify the point through both dharma and metaphor respectively.
"If there be any bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa... is able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in future ages.

This passage concludes the response to Mañjuśrī. Regarding the words "If there be any" and so forth: this refers to those who uphold the sutra in future ages. They should enter into practice according to the sutra;
they should perform what ought to be performed and draw near to what ought to be drawn near. Thus, their minds will not be timid and their spirits will not be weak.
The term "Bodhisattva" (菩薩) sometimes appears below [the title], while above it says "bhikṣu. Here, "Bodhisattva" refers to the bhikṣu who upholds the sūtra during the final age;

such a person is indeed a bodhisattva. Therefore, at times he enters into stillness to rectify his thoughts and discriminative perceptions, and in accordance with the principles explained in the sūtra, he contemplates the phenomena of the aggregates and other mundane and supramundane dharmas.

First, one attains its foundation, which is self-benefit. Following the section on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is said that having already attained self-benefit, one must further benefit others by elucidating the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for kings and others.

Regarding the section on Mañjuśrī, physical conduct is proximate [to the teaching] as one of the four types of practice; since one has already previously been cautioned not to associate with kings, princes, and so forth.

Regarding the current statement, "for the sake of kings and others," this means that one should not personally associate with them; however, if they come for the sake of the Dharma, then it is permissible to associate with them.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata... [up to] ...he shall provide explanations so that they may attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, from "Mañjuśrī, below" onwards, the "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō) are introduced. For those who preach the sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, "correcting one's speech" refers to the words spoken before a gathering;
"proclaiming with the mouth" refers to the words used when reading the sutra for one's own practice.
"...below. This means that whether one speaks or reads, one must not attribute faults to the person or to the sūtras;
thus, one’s speech will be peaceful and joyful. Furthermore, 'nor disparaging those below' refers specifically to those who can be faulted.
As for 'other Dharma masters,' this refers to those who proclaim other sūtras, as well as others who do not proclaim other sūtras."

I have heard that what distinguishes [this master] from other Dharma masters and others is this: when his name is invoked to speak of his faults, the person feels apprehensive and does not advance toward the Great Vehicle;
yet when his name is invoked to praise his virtues, the person remains content with their lowly state and does not abandon the Small Vehicle.
Therefore, one must never speak of his transgressions, nor should one disparage him as being inferior; indeed, it is not merely that one should not do so.
One does not utter words regarding the beauty or ugliness of physical forms with the mouth, nor does one harbor matters of resentment or suspicion within the mind.

Because these various mental states will inevitably be manifested through speech, one must cultivate them well. The phrase "should abide in the practice of peaceful conduct" at the end of the section clarifies the benefits of right verbal karma;
that is to say, by not giving rise to resentment or suspicion in the mind, one ensures that listeners do not feel opposition.
The intention is this: because one does not manifest beauty or ugliness in speech, even when questioned about a minor matter, one is not hindered from answering with the Great [Truth].
This enables both the questioner and the listener to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma for peace and security... (up to) it cannot be fully exhausted even by means of calculation or parable."
"Bodhisattvas always delight in what is lowly" means that for a bodhisattva to preach the Dharma with ease, they must first possess the requisites for such ease.
There are four: first, the ground; second, a seat; third, bathing the body; and fourth, fresh, clean clothing. The body is internal, while the ground and so forth are external;
therefore, it is said that both the internal and external are pure, and so on. "If there is a bhikṣu... and so forth means that because of the presence of [these] comforts...
Because of the equipment of joy, one attains the assembly of peace and happiness. There are nine such assemblies; four consist of the bhikṣus and so forth, and five consist of kings and so forth.
"By means of the subtle and wondrous" refers to the fact that by possessing this assembly of peace and happiness, one accomplishes the benefit of peace and happiness. There are three such benefits:

first, the meaning is wondrous and the countenance is harmonious, thereby benefiting those who observe and listen; second, one answers according to the difficulty [of the question], thereby benefiting those who inquire.
"Please. Third, [the teaching] unfolds the provisional to manifest the ultimate, thereby benefiting those of gradual and sudden capacities.

This means that by employing the provisional distinctions of the small, medium, and great three vehicles—such as through causes and conditions—one answers difficult questions and enables others to resolve their minds toward the Great Vehicle.

Through the gradual leading to the sudden, and the provisional leading to the ultimate, one increases their capacity for entry into the Buddha-way of the One Vehicle. "Eliminating indolent sentiments," and so forth, refers to the desire to achieve accomplishment.
Regarding the benefits of peace and happiness: one must eliminate the mind that lacks peace and happiness and follow instead the mind of peace and happiness.

Minds such as laziness are what must be eliminated; the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is what one must follow. "Day and night" refers to preaching the Dharma through the mind of loving-kindness, thereby attaining great benefit and great happiness.
There are five aspects of peace and happiness: first, preaching without interruption day and night; second, employing analogies...
1. Teaching immeasurably; 2. Teaching so as to bring joy to all three [types of beings]; 3. Teaching without expectation of the four requisites; 4.

Teaching with the aspiration that oneself and the assembly may together attain the path to Buddhahood—this phrase is the most important. Therefore it says, "This is indeed a great benefit," and so forth. Question:
Above it was said, "by means of causes, conditions, and parables," and here again it says, "by means of various causes, conditions, and parables. Is this not redundant? Answer:

Regarding the passage "For the sake of the three vehicles above," he spoke by means of expedient means (*upāya*) in gradual stages. Regarding the passage "For the sake of this one vehicle," he spoke by means of the unsurpassed path (*anuttara-mārga*).

While the conditions, metaphors, and names are the same, their meanings differ. From the words "When I have entered parinirvāṇa" onwards, he provides a concluding response for those who are suited to the teaching;
that is to say, if those who preach the Dharma in the final age can speak as described above, they will not only avoid bringing harm upon themselves, but will furthermore possess merit.
Virtue is inexhaustible. There is no inferiority of mind. This means that the one who preaches the Dharma dwells in peace and security, such that external insults do not reach them.
There are five [qualities]: first, freedom from sorrow; second, freedom from verbal abuse; third, freedom from fear; fourth, freedom from weapons and staves; fifth, freedom from expulsion.
All of these arise because the preacher of the Dharma has no envy or affliction in their heart and abides in the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, it is said: "Abiding securely," and so forth. From "The wise one" downward, he is endowed with merit.
Furthermore, from "Mañjuśrī" up to "venerating, honoring, respecting, and praising the Sūtra."
Furthermore, from "Mañjuśrī, below" onwards, the text introduces the upholder of this sutra who, at the time when the Dharma is about to perish, desires that it not perish.

This first rectifies his intention (*manas-karma*). Although there are many ways in which the mental faculty may be improper, the four factors of envy (*īrṣyā*), jealousy (*mātsarya*), flattery (*śāṭhya*), and deception (*māyā*) are the most serious.
Therefore, it says: "Do not harbor envy and so forth. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Envy refers to being preoccupied with one's own reputation."
*Śāṭhya* (deceit) means to deceive others by acting with crooked compliance and manifesting artificial expedients in order to win over their favor.
*Māyā* (guile) has the nature of being crafty and fraudulent; its function is to provide a wrong livelihood.

In the treatises (*śāstra*), envy and jealousy are treated as a single dharma, whereas in the sūtras they are taught as two distinct dharmas. This is because the sūtras were spoken for the sake of bodhisattvas who uphold the sūtras, while the treatises... [are for others].
This describes the mental factors (*caitta*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and is therefore slightly different [from the preceding]. "Nor does he harbor malice below" (*na cāpy adho*):

although this appears to be a separate statement, it is actually a phrase intended as an explanatory conclusion. This is because *īrṣyā* (envy) involves frequent disparagement and abuse, whereas *mātsarya* (jealousy) involves seeking out others' faults.
"If a bhikṣu... below refers precisely to those who possess the three vehicles—small, medium, and great—in their full extent. "He shall not obtain... below is the explanation.

This constitutes flattery. Therefore, one must admonish and encourage others not to cause them distress by speaking with sycophancy, saying, "You are very far from the Way and will ultimately never attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)," thereby causing them to give rise to doubt and regret.

This is because those of the Hīnayāna originally fear that the Buddha-way is too long and arduous, requiring the endurance of great toil for a long time before it can be accomplished; thus, even if one now complies with them through such indirect means...
That [statement] may appear to be flattery, but in reality it is a phrase intended to vex the opponent.
As for the following passage, although it interrogates and explains his flattery, its true purpose is to convey a sense of contemptuous derision; thus it says, "You are negligent," and so forth.

Furthermore, the subsequent section should not be interpreted as establishing his deceit (*śāṭhya*), because deceit involves much conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and gives rise to contention and strife. The above constitutes the exhortation.
The meaning of "admonishing not to bring about lack of peace and happiness" will be explained below. This is the meaning of the instruction to attain peace and happiness;
each point is the reverse of the preceding text. That is to say: because of being free from envy, one gives rise to the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings and pities them;
because of being free from jealousy, one gives rise to the thought of a compassionate father toward all Tathāgatas and respects them; because of being free from flattery...
Therefore, regarding Bodhisattvas on the three stages of the *pūrvayoga* (the stages prior to the grounds), one should regard them as the Great Teacher and learn from them;
regarding the great Bodhisattvas of the grounds throughout the ten directions, one should always pay them respectful homage with a profound mind. Question: Who would dare to envy the Buddha?
Yet, you instruct us to regard the Tathāgata as a compassionate father so that we do not envy him. Answer: This refers to the six teachers in that land.
Devaputra: This is true of the various Confucian scholars of the Tang and Song dynasties in this land. [The opponent] says: "They were all manifestations. [The master] says:

"Generally, when Bodhisattvas possess the ignorance that obscures the transition between lives (ganyin wuming) and have not yet attained awakening, they truly give rise to jealousy. However, once they have attained awakening..."
This refers to manifestation. Because it is non-deceptive, one preaches the Dharma equally to all sentient beings;

one does not speak extensively for those who are attached, nor speak sparingly for those who are otherwise. Therefore, it says, "because of conforming to the Dharma," which means conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

"Because there is fundamentally no [basis for] much love or hatred. From the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī," below, he concludes the preceding text, forming the third practice among the four dharmas.
This means that because I do not insult others, others will not come to trouble or disturb me.
From the passage beginning with "Obtaining what is good," it means that not only do they not trouble me, but on the contrary, they become my fellow students and brothers.
[This] is practice. Furthermore, one attains [the status of] a teacher. "Having heard" and below refers to those who are disciples today;

on another day, they will in turn become teachers of others through the wondrous Dharma. This is what is meant by the elephant king walking and the elephant cub following, or one lamp extinguishing while another lamp continues.
Thus the True Dharma abides long in the world, and this is how the seeds of the Triple Gem [are preserved].
This shall not be interrupted or extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, one should abandon jealousy, anger, and pride... [until] being honored by immeasurable multitudes."
The four lines beginning with "If one desires... are the verse summary (*uddāna*). The sixteen lines beginning with "Not slighting...

are the verse commentary (*bhāṣya*). "Not slighting others" comments on non-envy. "Nor engaging in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma" comments on non-deception. "Not causing others to doubt" follows below.
The verse "not being sycophantic" corresponds to the section beginning with "These are the sons of the Buddha. The verse "compassion" corresponds to the section beginning with "not being envious.
The verse "three perceptions" corresponds to the section beginning with "shattering. The verse "preaching the Dharma with equanimity" corresponds to the third section.

The two preceding sections and this current section provide a detailed explanation of "donning the Tathāgata’s robe" and "sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat"; the following section provides a detailed explanation of "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber."
Furthermore, from "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" (up to) "because they are protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī," the term "the final dharma-ending age" (*paścima-kāla*) refers to the very beginning of the degeneration of the Dharma, specifically the time when the Buddha-dharma is about to perish at the end of the final age. From the phrase "Among householders," the fourth practice is introduced. In...
"Householders" refers to upāsakas and others; "those who have left the home life" refers to bhikṣus and others.
Although these four assemblies of monastics and laypeople possess the internal protection of the Buddha-dharma, they have not yet attained the Great Nirvāṇa of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Therefore, one should give rise to great compassion for them and contemplate bestowing happiness upon them. If one is not a bodhisattva, one should observe the precept of not associating with those [who lack such intent].

Regarding the eight types of persons who, although possessing the Buddha-nature, have not yet fully prepared the external protection of the Buddha-dharma, and who still harbor much greed and lack faith in the Triple Gem—thus destined to fall into the three miserable realms—it is for these people that one gives rise to great compassion, intending to extract them from their suffering.
The phrase "should act as follows" explains the greatness of this compassion; it means that one should keep in mind the fourfold assembly of both monastics and laypeople.
Furthermore, there are those who are not bodhisattvas, or those with much false wisdom, or those holding high positions, whose conduct throughout their lives is fraught with great faults.
They have lost the wondrous Dharma taught by all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time through skillful means according to what is appropriate;
they do not hear it, do not know it, and are not awakened to it, thereby lacking the penetration of the fundamental nature (*svabhāva*). Moreover,
To lose one's sense of shame and fall into arrogance and conceit; to neither inquire, nor believe, nor understand;
and thus to be deficient in receiving the lineage of the teacher—these failings constitute what is called "great suffering," while mindfulness of them constitutes what is called "great compassion.
An elder of the Chan school asked a practitioner, "What thing in the world is most painful? He replied, "The Avīci Hell."
Regarding hell: [The Master] took up the robe of a former Chan practitioner and said, "No. To not clarify the Great Matter beneath the seams of this robe—this is what constitutes great suffering.
This is it. Although such a person does not descend [into hell], it refers to the fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople, as well as those who are not Bodhisattvas;
even if they have lost the opportunity to hear or inquire about this sutra due to a lack of intent, those who uphold the sutra must not [be so].
Because they possess a mind, they are not yet delivered. Even if one cannot deliver them while in the causal stage, one must certainly make a vow to do so upon reaching the fruit.

When attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wherever those beings may be among the four modes of birth and nine classes of existence, I shall, by means of my spiritual and intellectual powers, universally manifest form-bodies to transform them according to their kind, striving to lead them to attain [enlightenment].
Abiding within this sublime Dharma, one knows by hearing and understands through inquiry. That which is a great loss in the present will surely become a great gain in the future.
This gain is the reason for the existence of great bliss, and that which leads [others] is the means by which great compassion is perfected.
Therefore, it is said: "Lead them so that they may attain [it]," etc. The section beginning with Mañjuśrī concludes [the discourse].
"Arising before and following after" refers to those who preach the sutras in the final age;

if they can practice this fourth great compassionate deed, they will not only be free from faults, but will also receive protection, offerings, and respectful salutations from both within and without.
"Below, like space" means that it is not only humans who show reverence, but all the devas of the three realms also come to attend and follow them because of the Dharma. If one is...
"Below" means that the various devas do not merely attend upon him when he speaks;

even when he does not preach the sutras, they constantly remain by his side day and night, fearing that someone might come to pose difficult questions. The reason for this is that both during speech and silence, he remains in accord with the wondrous Dharma.
"Below" serves as an interrogative and explanatory phrase, meaning: why is it that he attains [this state] whether speaking or remaining silent?
The devas and nāgas provide protection because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Where the sutra is, the Buddha is; where the Buddha is, the devas and others cannot fail to come.

Since the Buddhas and devas protect and mind this sutra, they must necessarily protect and mind the person who expounds it. This serves as the foundation for the following section, corresponding to the Dharma Master.
This chapter of the sutra is the secret treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
It is protected by the World-Honored Buddhas and has never been revealed since ancient times—such is the text.
One should know that the passage "dwelling in the stage of patience" and so forth refers to donning the robe of the Tathāgata. This is the observation of the proximate state.

The phrase "all dharmas are empty, their true marks being such as they are" refers to illuminating the sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat and the manifestation by the Buddha of his body of pure radiance.
This section on great compassion refers to entering the Tathāgata’s chamber.

The concluding text regarding the four practices states that whenever one speaks so as to be heard and accepted by humans and devas, this illuminates the Buddha-way realized through the power of the mind of diligence.
This is the ornamentation of transformation. Mañjuśrī shall [from the Lotus Sūtra] expound it for you all.
From "Mañjuśrī" downward, he clarifies the basis for the parables presented in the preceding section, stating that this sūtra is immeasurable.
Those whose names are difficult to hear within this realm are protected by the spiritual power of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
That you have now been able to see them in person and maintain their recitation is brought about by the Buddhas' four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
This is what is meant by my attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: wherever one may be, through spiritual power and wisdom-power, I shall lead them so that they may dwell therein.
This is within the Dharma. As for the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī, it is like," there are three sections illustrating that not even a single word can be heard in immeasurable lands.
First, the king possesses great power and is able to subdue small kingdoms that do not obey his commands.
Second, from the section beginning with "The king sees his army" onwards, the king rejoices in those who have merit in the campaign and bestows rewards according to their achievements.
There are six items of reward: first, fields and houses; second, cities and towns; third, clothing and utensils; fourth, rare jewels;

fifth, elephants, horses, and carriages; sixth, slaves and subjects. This is a metaphor for the various sūtras taught by the Buddha during the forty years prior [to his final teaching], according to what was appropriate for each individual's capacity.
"Third, only the bright jewel from the topknot" refers to the king possessing a supreme treasure which he kept...
The crown of the head is not included in the list of rewards. If this treasure of the state were granted as a single reward, it would cause the king’s retinue to be struck with astonishment.
This is a metaphor for how, forty years ago, although Śāriputra and others harbored doubts, they were saved by means of the teaching of the Hīnayāna.
The Buddha likewise does not preach this sutra. From the passage "Mañjuśrī, as for the Tathāgata" downward, this is the first section of the analogy corresponding to the Dharma.

Here, the Buddha is equated with the noble king; meditative concentration and wisdom are equated with his majestic power. His attainment of the land of the dharma-nature and his sovereignty over the three realms correspond to his subduing of all kingdoms.
The fact that various māras do not submit corresponds to the disobedience of minor kings. The battle waged by the generals of the worthy and holy ones corresponds to the conflict [with those rebels].
He assembled various kinds of troops and went forth to wage war. "Various kinds of troops" refers to elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. Regarding the "Buddhas and noble generals":
in the Hīnayāna, those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) and above are called "noble" (*bhadra*), while *arhats* are called "sages" (*ārya*).

In the Mahāyāna, those at the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration are called "noble," while those on the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are called "sages. As for those of lesser merit below [these], this corresponds to the metaphors within the Dharma.

Next is the section concerning the period prior to forty years [after the Buddha's enlightenment]. This refers to when the Buddha, rejoicing that those who practiced the three vehicles—both the Small and the Great—had achieved merit in their cultivation, preached the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-dharma*).
If these are correlated with the king’s rewards: first, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) corresponds to fields and houses; second, liberation (*vimukti*) corresponds to clothing and utensils;
third, the five untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) correspond to precious jewels; and fourth, the five untainted powers (*anāsrava-bala*) correspond to... [the remaining reward].

The elephants, horses, chariots, and mounts represent the five kinds of Dharma-wealth: namely, mindfulness, diligence, intention, concentration, and the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), along with the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
These, together with the servants and the populace, constitute the six gifts of *nirvāṇa*, which correspond to the city.

As for the statement that he did not preach [the lower teachings], this corresponds to the third section of the analogy: it means that during the forty years prior [to his final teaching], the Buddha did not preach because he feared their capacities were too small.
This sutra is like a king who, fearing that his retinue would be startled or alarmed, does not bestow the crest-jewel—the supreme treasure of the state.

The passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī is like a wheel-turning monarch" serves as a metaphor; how much more so for those who obtain a vision of it, or receive, uphold, read, and recite even a single verse?
This means that the king did not previously grant the crest-jewel as a reward because the merit of the military host was small and insufficient [to warrant such a gift].
He granted it. Later, seeing that among the multitude of soldiers there were those who had achieved great merit, his heart was filled with exceeding joy.

There are three types: first, the intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*); second, the kalpa of formation and destruction (*saṃvarta-vivartakalpa*); and third, the great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). Furthermore, the intermediate kalpa is of three kinds:

first, the kalpa of decrease (*apahāra-kalpa*); second, the kalpa of increase (*vivardhana-kalpa*); and third, the kalpa of both increase and decrease (*vivartasaṃvarta-kalpa*). As for "decrease," it refers to the period when the human lifespan decreases from an immeasurable number of years down to ten years.

As for "increase," it refers to the period when the human lifespan increases from ten years up to eighty thousand years. As for "both increase and decrease," it refers to the period when the human lifespan...
From ten years of age, it increases to eighty thousand years; then, from eighty thousand years, it decreases back to ten years.
Within this process, eighteen such cycles of decrease and increase constitute twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*). Twenty intermediate kalpas pass while the world is being formed;
having been formed for twenty intermediate kalpas, it remains stable. These together are called the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*). Twenty intermediate kalpas pass [while it remains].
When the world is destroyed, it remains empty for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*). This combined period is termed the *saṃvartakalpa* (the kalpa of destruction).
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: "As thus described, each of the four periods—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—consists of twenty intermediate kalpas;

According to the treatise, the intermediate great kalpas (mahākalpa) can be understood; however, the exposition of minor kalpas (antarakalpa) has not yet been seen.

Within each minor kalpa, the human lifespan increases from ten years up to eighty thousand years, and then decreases again from eighty thousand years back down to ten years.
Thus, fifty small kalpas—the passage of the aforementioned fifty cycles of increase and decrease—are subsumed within a single moment.
