Except for those who have previously studied the Hīnayāna, even they may now hear this sutra; thus it fulfills their great capacity and allows them to see the Buddha.
This is the wondrous function of subsuming the great within the small and uniting the small into the great.

Therefore, the Buddha is also well-versed in the matters of the great Bodhisattvas, not being hindered by considerations of sequence or priority, smallness or greatness, newness or antiquity, or proximity or distance. Hence it is said: "At that time..."
"Venerable praise, etc.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and eight thousand [others] (up to) joined their palms in worship and inquired after the Tathāgata’s well-being.
Regarding the phrase "at that time," according to the *Huayan Shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), Maitreya is fully called Maitreyī; this is translated as "The Compassionate One" (Cishi).
This is his family name. There are three causes for it: first, in a past kalpa, he encountered the Tathāgata Mahāmaitreya and vowed to share the same name;

second, he attained the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind; third, while his mother was pregnant with him, she possessed a compassionate mind. Therefore, he is named Ajita, meaning "Incapable of Being Conquered.
This is because, from birth, he was endowed with the marks and signs of excellence and merit such that no one could surpass him. Thus...
The World-Honored One Śākyamuni bestowed a prophecy upon the Future Buddha Maitreya, who is in the stage of a *upapadya-bodhisattva* (the position immediately preceding Buddhahood).

Furthermore, the "eight thousand [bodhisattvas]" and those below them are all bodhisattvas in the stage of *upapadya*; they are so numerous that they all simultaneously form this thought. The passage beginning with "We... explains the formation of this thought.

The preceding section clarified how one can rejoice in the distant original capacity (*dūrabhava-śakti*) while remaining close to its traces; this section clarifies how the immediate traces are suddenly abandoned while forgetting the distant original capacity.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
"The great assembly of immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas (up to) from where have they come?"

"At that time" and below narrates how the interlocutor possesses the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), whereby he knows that the assembly shares his own doubt. "And wishing to" and below means:
if the assembly doubts while he himself does not, he may provide a decision; if he himself doubts while the assembly does not, they may be consulted.
Now, since both he and the assembly doubt, he speaks a verse to question the Buddha. This serves as the inquiry corresponding to the second section mentioned previously.
"Immeasurable" (wúliàng) below refers to the assembly that has gathered. "In the past" (xī suǒ) below means they were originally not acquainted with one another;
therefore, they requested the Buddha to explain their place of origin and the causes and conditions for their arrival. These two phrases are repeated as a question.

Regarding the second section, since it states that they had previously all been dwelling in the void of the lower realms within this Sahā world, why did the *adhikārika* (the primary audience) not perceive or know this, such that they asked again?
Answer: First, the second section is a narrative arrangement by the compiler of the sutra and is not the word of the Buddha.
Second, since there are distinctions among the three thousandfold great chiliocosms within the Sahā world, it was unknown which specific Sahā world’s lower realm [the interlocutor] resided in;

therefore, he demonstrated his forgetfulness of the chapters and verses in order to seek an explanation of their general meaning. "A massive body" refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). "Wisdom," etc., refers to the... [text ends].

The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Its resolve is profound. The Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This verse refers to the passage concerning how the bodies of all bodhisattvas are golden in color and so forth.
Because these three bodies and three virtues are fully possessed, sentient beings delight in beholding them and inquire about the direction from which they have come.
Even the retinues led by each of these bodhisattvas cannot be fully known.
This concludes the third section of the prose commentary, which asks about the total number of teachers and disciples; the verse summary below states that their numbers are immeasurable.

Therefore, the Ganges sands are not used to clarify the number. The sixteen lines beginning with "There are great bodhisattvas" separately eulogize the number of *śata* (hundreds) for both teacher and disciples.
The eight lines beginning with "Ten million nayutas" separately eulogize the number of *koti* (billions) for both teacher and disciples.
The four lines beginning with "single and without retinue" specifically praise those who are solitary and without followers; they are also immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable.
In the prose section, the counts of *śata* (hundred) and *koṭi* (ten million) proceed from many to few, yet the single count alone exceeds the counts of *śata* and *koṭi*.
Within these verses, it is precisely the counts of *śata* and *koṭi* that lead [the assembly], while those with fewer followers follow.
It is also more numerous than the multitude of those who lead assemblies. Thus, below, the conclusion states that both the number and the magnitude are difficult to calculate.
These bodhisattvas of great majesty and vigor (until) all emerge from within.
This illuminates the fourth section of the prose commentary. According to the following verse, this is an inquiry into the four meanings of the causal conditions of the root and its branches.
The phrase "these various" [etc. refers back to the aforementioned number, indicating the assembly that possesses majestic power and is endowed with diligence.
Diligence (*vīrya*) is one of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); it is the cause for accomplishing the Buddha-way. The phrase "who acts as" [etc.]—*śu* meaning "who" or "what"—refers to...

This assembly of those with the majestic power of diligence—what Buddha served as their teacher and transmitter, preaching the Dharma to instruct and transform them so that they accomplished the path of Buddhahood?
Because his preaching of the Dharma and instruction constitute the totality of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), he serves as the condition for those who are diligent.
From whom did they descend? This asks from which Buddha they first attained the mind [of awakening], the very root of becoming a Buddha; this is stated in terms of self-awakening (*svabodha*).
What Buddha-dharma is extolled? What sūtras are received and practiced? What path of the Buddha is cultivated?
These are spoken of collectively in terms of self-awakening and awakening others, serving as the final stage for attaining Buddhahood. Thus concludes the section below.

This means that such causes and conditions—the essence and the details of the various great Bodhisattvas, their spiritual power and wisdom—do not come from elsewhere; rather, they arise from the four [reliances].
He then split the earth and emerged; this was a most marvelous thing. [The interlocutor] asked: "Where did you see those bodhisattvas who possess the power of divine wisdom and diligence?
He replied: "During that time, for fifty intermediate kalpas, I circumambulated and praised all the Buddhas of the three times and ten directions, and paid my respects to my original teacher.
How could this have been possible without the power of diligence, divine wisdom, and spiritual insight?"
"World-Honored One, since I first came [to this assembly], I have never before seen such a thing" (up to) "I only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the multitude.

This verse corresponds to the fifth section of the prose commentary. From the words "World-Honored One" onwards, the interlocutor states that from the time he followed the Buddha until now, he has never witnessed an event where such a great multitude emerged from the earth.
From the words "I pray that you will explain" onwards, he requests [the teaching] as to whence [they have come].
The first phrase refers to the name of the land from which [the Buddha] has come, as well as the name of that land being requested. "I have always... and so forth means:

the reason for requesting the name of the land is that, although he himself has traveled through various lands, he has never before seen such an assembly; therefore, [he speaks] within this great assembly.
"I do not know even one person. Suddenly, he descended from the ground and requested: "By what causes and conditions have you gathered this single phrase?
Since I do not know even that one person, I pray you will explain the causes and conditions for your sudden emergence from the earth.
This is what is called abandoning what one has practiced and recited, falling into forgetfulness and lack of proficiency; it is termed "seeking fame."
Why is this so? In the "Dharma Master" chapter (*Fashipin*), the Buddha has already granted that those who uphold this sutra in the final age shall share a lodging and be covered by his robes;

he further permits the dispatch of transformed beings from the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of supernatural beings to serve as the audience, ensuring they do not oppose the speaker’s intention.
Furthermore, in the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter (*Baota pin*), he convenes the Buddhas of the three periods and the ten directions to testify that [the Dharma master] shares a lodging with Śākyamuni.

By observing how he protected and remembered them, one can infer by analogy that the multitude now emerging from the earth are likewise manifestations sent by the Buddha to testify that he upheld this sutra throughout three incalculable eons, thereby personally realizing the pure and radiant Dharmakāya.
This was done to avoid contradicting the inclinations of the listeners. Why, then, seek further explanations regarding the land and the name?
What Maitreya has spoken is what is called "losing the text. Thus far, he has requested a resolution for the doubts of a single individual suited to the occasion.
From "Now, this [passage] below" onward, on behalf of the assembly of eight thousand [bodhisattvas] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he requests a resolution of their doubts.

This concludes the proof for the fifth matter seen within the light during the Introduction Chapter (*nidāna-parivarta*), namely the passage concerning the various causes and conditions and various resolute understandings (*adhimukti*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Regarding the transformation of the lands in the *Ratnakoṭa-parivarta*, it transforms only the eight directions; however, regarding the two directions of above and below, it has never been stated.

[The section on] "Transformation. Now, as the various bodhisattvas surge forth from below, the gods in the void proclaim in a loud voice during the subsequent "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra-parivarta);

this refers to the "upper direction," whereby the ten directions are complete. This single phrase concerning the causal conditions of the beginning and end herein serves as a concluding proof for the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta), stating:
"Such are the causes, such are the conditions, and such is the ultimate equality of the beginning and end."
Thus, one knows that sound is taught through its causes, conditions, origins, and ends.
Were it not for the Compassionate Honored One, who is in his final birth before Buddhahood, manifesting doubt, how could the chapters and verses on the Buddha’s lifespan be thoroughly mastered?
Furthermore, this is the Great Hall of Compassion established by Maitreya for those who uphold the sutras in the final age.
"At that time, the various Buddhas who are emanations of Śākyamuni... (down to) "...you yourselves shall hear it through this.

From "At that time" downward, the emanated bodies are introduced. From "Those Buddhas" downward, the attendants of the emanated Buddhas likewise raise questions of doubt, just as Maitreya and the others did.
This is what is meant by the successive layers of principal and retinue, proclaiming in unison throughout the ten directions. [End of] Testimony.
The preceding verse states that those present at this great assembly all desire to know this matter. From the passage beginning "At that time, the Buddhas...

it is meant that since there are questions and answers concerning the Buddhas of the future and the present, one must wait to hear them. Alas! As for the number of the manifested bodies of the Buddhas, how many are they?
As for the three transformations of the land, how vast is their extent? May the Buddha’s single voice pervade everywhere, so that the members of this Dharma assembly may attain [understanding].
I have heard that what is called the "perfect voice" resounds clearly and pervasively, encompassing the ten lands all at once. How profound is this!

Contemplate it so as to bring about such realization. This account of Maitreya’s prediction of his succession appears in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* (Zhong Ahan Jing) within the Northern Canon, in the case of the "Sheng" (聖) volume.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha—[omitted]—desiring to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"You should practice with diligence and single-mindedness; I wish to explain this matter. [Omitted] You all should listen with one-pointed attention."

"At that time" and below: the Buddha praised his skillful ability to inquire about the Great Matter (*mahā-kṛtya*). The preceding verse spoke of the "causes and conditions of the beginning and the end," while here it is called the "Great Matter.
This clearly discusses the orthodox teaching of how all Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the single Great Matter of causes and conditions;
how could one hastily conclude this as belonging to the section on the propagation of the Dharma (*parīndanā*)? "You all" and below: this refers to armor and mail.
The *Jinglü Yishu* (Commentary on the Rituals) states: "To call armor 'jia' (armour) is to say it is like the shell of a tortoise. A *zhou* (helmet) refers to the *dōumóu* (cuirass).
This means that when Maitreya and others ask about matters of such great significance, they must employ the *pāramitā* of diligence (*vīrya*) as their armor and cuirass;
thus, their resolve becomes firm, stable, and unshakable. This is because Maitreya [is...]
Within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, because their minds were constantly harboring indolence, he exhorted them with this.
"The Tathāgata now wishes to descend" refers generally to the entire section; since everything revealed in this sutra is the wisdom of all Buddhas, it says so.
"The sovereign power of all Buddhas descends" specifically refers to the two chapters on the Lifespan and the Distinction of Merits, as...
The "Chapter on the Lifespan" [demonstrates that] the distant is the near, and this is that; showing oneself is showing others.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Analysis of Merits," those who attain merit upon hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan do so entirely through the power of the sovereign spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*) of all Buddhas.
From the passage "The Lions among Buddhas" downward, the two chapters on "Subduing by Spiritual Power" and "Entrustment" state that [the teaching] has thus emerged.
His broad and long tongue reaches up to the Brahma-world; he emits light from his pores that universally illumines lands as numerous as motes of dust for a full hundred thousand years.

Only then does he retract it, and with a single snap of his fingers or a cough, he stretches out one arm and hand to stroke the crowns of the heads of immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattvas, entrusting them with this sutra. Such rapid manifestations are all the lion-like displays of the Buddhas.

By the power of the divine spirits. Regarding the passage "The majestic might of all Buddhas subdues [them]" below, this refers to the two chapters on the merits of the Dharma-preacher and the Ever-Not-Light (Sadāparibhūta).

In the Chapter on the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent (Nityodyukta) is presented as the primary recipient of the teaching (*dharmika*), demonstrating that one who acts as a Dharma-preacher must always be diligent and courageous regarding this sutra. In the Chapter on the Ever-Not-Light, it is Mahāsthāmaprāpta who is addressed.
The Bodhisattva acts as the appropriate recipient. He manifests as a Dharma-preacher so that he may not disparage those with overweening pride, thereby attaining great power.
In this context, if one does not point to the preceding and succeeding chapters, then the wisdom and spiritual powers of all Buddhas would have no basis;
even if many [passages] were combined, they would all be forced interpretations. Within the verses:
"Should exert diligence below" praises the wisdom of all Buddhas. "You now [should] below" praises the sovereign supernormal powers of all Buddhas.
Those of the Two Vehicles cannot truly know this sutra through the power of faith alone; those on the Ten Stages cannot explain it extensively without the endurance of the stage of patience.

Now, Maitreya and others occupy the rank of the position immediately preceding Buddhahood (the Stage of Rebirth); they have transcended the stages of the Two Vehicles and abide in the state of Equal Enlightenment (Sambodhi). Beyond...

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Thus it is said: "Emerging from the power of faith, one abides in the excellence of patience. From "I now" [onward], there is a verse on the lions' playful strides (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) of all Buddhas.

From "that which is obtained" [onward], there is a verse on the majestic ferocity of all Buddhas. Question: Why does this not include the *Anumodanāpuṇyaskandha-parivarta* (Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing)? Answer:

Because it is subsumed within the *Dharmabhāṇakaguṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Qualities of the Dharma-preacher). This section is specifically [treated here] because the matter under discussion is of great significance.
Exert yourselves with diligence. The following section synthesizes the provisional and the ultimate (honji-suijaku). It is as if answering a question.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken these verses, [from "until"] wishing to restate this meaning, spoke further in verse:
"Ānanda, you should know... [down to] "...I have been teaching these multitudes since long ago.

Here, from "At that time" downward, he grants the answer appropriate to the occasion. From "Ānanda" downward, in response to the question, he cites the phrase "these beings of great majesty and virtue" from the interrogative section to acknowledge its cause.
From "I, at... downward, he responds to the two preceding phrases: "Who was it that preached the Dharma for them? and so forth.

This answers the inquiry regarding the conditions [for his awakening]. "Taming those below" and so forth answers the preceding question of "from whom did he first resolve his mind," thereby answering the basis of his self-awakening.
Herein, the word "I" corresponds to the "who" in the question; it refers to me, Śākyamuni Buddha, who tamed this assembly and resolved his mind.
"These bodhisattvas below" and so forth answers the preceding two phrases concerning the source from which he made his vow.

Answering the question of their place of origin: following the phrase "in all the sūtras," one responds to the three preceding phrases concerning the "proclamation of which Buddha-dharma" to answer the conclusion of "awakening others.
This means that this assembly is proficient in all the various sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
The section beginning with "contemplating" explains how they have attained such proficiency; this answers the two points: from where they come and by what causes and conditions they have gathered.
Having asked this, [the Buddha] states from "Ajita" downward that he clarifies the meaning of dwelling in the space of the lower realms. He says:

"As for your question regarding those who constantly travel through various lands yet have not seen this assembly—it is because this assembly does not delight in being among the many or in having much to say;
they always delight in quietude and practice with unceasing diligence. For this reason, you have never been able to see them. Furthermore, it does not mean that they do not descend.
"As for your question regarding those among this assembly whom you do not recognize: it is because this assembly does not abide by relying upon humans or devas from the very beginning;
therefore, you are unable to recognize them. This is truly because this assembly is diligent, whereas Maitreya is indolent."
This assembly has mastered the recitation and study [of the scriptures], whereas Maitreya has abandoned them and allowed them to be forgotten.
This assembly does not rely on humans or devas, while Maitreya favors the noble clans; since their paths diverge in every respect, how could he recognize them?

In the passage beginning with "Constantly delighting in the lower," it clarifies that they do not rely on humans or devas because the wisdom of humans and devas is shallow and their obstructions are deep, whereas this assembly delights in profound wisdom.
This is an obstacle. Furthermore, in the section "Also constantly" (*yì cháng xià*), it clarifies the meaning of which Buddha’s Dharma is being extolled and which Buddha’s path is being cultivated.

It shows that this assembly does not merely delight in the Dharma and path of our single Buddha, Śākyamuni, but also constantly delights in practicing the Dharma and paths of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
In the section "With single-minded diligence" (*yī xīn jīngjìn xià*), it clarifies the causes and conditions for the gathering.
This means that this assembly has gathered for this specific cause and condition: namely, to seek the unsurpassed wisdom of Buddhahood.
In the verse, "Ajita, you should descend," the first line restates and answers the cause. "All are those transformed by me" answers the condition.
"Causing them to resolve upon the Great Vehicle mind" answers the basis of self-awakening. From "These [beings]" onwards...
The verse answers the two lines regarding "who preached the Dharma for him. The section beginning with "relying upon" (依止) answers the question of his place of origin.
The *Ratnastūpa-parivarta* describes the gathering of the emanated Buddhas; the *Adhimuktyāparivarta* describes the assembly of kinsmen, kings, ministers, and others;
and within this, the passage "This is my son, born from me" refers to the subsequent *Parīndanā-parivarta*.
The passage beginning with "Illuminating all my houses and people, I entrust them all to you" is the prose response.

The verse that follows clarifies that such a multitude has never been seen before. The passage beginning with "In this way" is the prose response praising which Buddha’s Dharma and practicing which Buddha’s Way.
The verse response states that one delights in the Dharma of all Buddhas and practices one's own Way.
The phrase "the Dharma-Buddha and the various Buddhas" refers to their mutual discourse. Regarding "day and night," the verse answers by asking through what causes and conditions they assemble.

Regarding "in the Sahā world," the verse answers by clarifying that the multitude does not recognize even a single person. The long prose passage answers by stating that they do not rely upon humans or devas;
the verse answers by stating that they dwell in the space below. These meanings are interwoven. Regarding "vow and mindfulness," etc. [the following follows].
The verse-response clarifies why this assembly wishes to dwell in the lower regions:
for their own benefit, it facilitates the two perfections of diligence and wisdom, which are firm and stable; for the benefit of others, it facilitates fearlessness in preaching the Dharma.
The phrase "I [attain enlightenment] below" serves as the basis for the subsequent section. The long prose states: "I attain bodhi in the Sahā world. One Sahā.
Regarding the vastness of this trichiliocosm, the Buddha, with his body that pervades the entire dharma-realm, manifested the assembly emerging from the earth;
as his fundamental essence and its traces corresponded, there appeared to be no obstruction. Thus, the verse further speaks of attaining perfect enlightenment at Gayā.
Gayā is a city within Jambudvīpa; its location is the nearest and accessible to human beings.

The time during which the Wheel of Dharma was turned was the shortest, yet it could be known by people. However, the multitude who emerged [from the earth] possessed such magnificent virtue and were so numerous that Maitreya and others had never before seen or recognized them.
Now, it is said that they were those who, through his teaching, resolved their minds on enlightenment and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, and that they shall all attain Buddhahood.
Thus, their original nature and their manifested traces are truly beyond comparison. Regarding these Maitreya and others...
The reason for raising the doubt that the father is younger and the son is older in the following section is that the prose and the verse differ;
there is a specific purpose for this. From "I now" onwards is the exhortation to believe, meaning that all the answers provided above to your questions are the Buddha’s true words.
Maitreya and others should believe this. From the passage in the "Expedient Means" chapter, "I have come from afar;

the suffering of birth and death has been forever exhausted," down to the "Life Span" chapter, one should consult the text. Previously it was said that he was transformed [by the Buddha] at Gayā, a place near [his enlightenment];
here it is said that he has been transformed since time immemorial. This is because the recent trace does not differ from the distant origin. Thus, the multitude for a long time...
This constitutes a new transformation; it is even more difficult for Maitreya and others to believe.

This does not mean that the Buddha’s Dharma-body has a long lifespan while his manifested Reward-body and Transformation-bodies have short lifespans—how could humans know this? How marvelous are the sacred scriptures!
How could they be easily understood?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) having heard this matter, likewise did not give rise to doubt.
"At that time" and below serves as the responsive reception of the preceding text, giving rise to a sense of wonder and questioning: "How could it be in a short time?

This receives the four lines from the preceding verse beginning with "I [taught] at the city of Gayā. "Taught and transformed" and below receives the line from the preceding verse: "Thereupon he taught and transformed."
These four lines serve as the basis for the inquiry. Following "Then [he] said" (即白下), he describes his thoughts of doubt and wonder, submitting them to the Buddha.

He says that when the Buddha was a prince, having departed from the palace of the Śākyas, the place where he renounced worldly life and attained the fruit [of enlightenment] was not far from the city of Kapilavastu;
it was very near. From "From this time onwards" (從是下), it means from the time he attained the Way until the present day, only [a short time has passed].
"More than forty years"—at that time, [the Buddha] was still very young. How is it that, during this short period in his later years, he was able to perform such great deeds of a Buddha?

How could he, by means of the power and merit of a Buddha, have taught and transformed such immeasurable multitudes who emerged from the earth, so that they were destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? This is truly worthy of doubt.
[The term] "the Buddha’s power" (*buddha-anubhāva*) refers to the force of the majestic and great might of all the aforementioned Buddhas.

"The Buddha’s merit" (*buddha-guṇa*) refers to the wisdom, mastery, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of all the aforementioned Buddhas. From the words "O World-Honored One, this great [assembly]" below, the author clarifies the magnitude of the matter:
that is to say, this great assembly is incalculably infinite; it is not something that could be contained within the vicinity of the city of Gayā. From the words "These [beings]" below...
This clarifies the excellence of his virtue. It means that these multitudes of śrāvakas have, in fact, planted roots of merit under immeasurable other Buddhas throughout long-distant kalpas;
they are not those who could have been converted by Śākyamuni Buddha during his forty years of teaching.
To now claim that these multitudes of śrāvakas, who planted merit under other Buddhas long ago, were instead converted since the Buddha attained enlightenment is [an error].
Unless one were to seek to seize the property of others, this would constitute a deceptive statement; therefore, it is all the more strange. Who in the world could believe it? Thus it is said:
"World-Honored One, matters such as these are difficult for the world to believe. In response to the above, [the Buddha said]: "I now speak words of truth;
you should all believe them with a single mind. This is illustrated by the following analogy: just as one who dwells near the earth for a short time can achieve greatness.

The matter is indeed suspicious. That someone under a hundred years of age should, through the metaphor of a multitude of virtues flourishing, achieve [enlightenment] in a short time at a proximate stage, is all the more strange.

While it might not seem so suspicious for an old man to point to a youth as his father—given that there are sons born of paternal uncles in the world—it is different when he says, "He gave birth to us";
this refers to one's own biological parent, not comparable to a son of a paternal uncle. Therefore...

"It is difficult to believe. "The Buddha is also like this," and so forth, which applies the Dharma to the analogy. "Not long after attaining the Way," which corresponds to his physical beauty, black hair, and age of twenty-five.
"And this great assembly," and so forth, which corresponds to the people. "Having already [practiced] for immeasurable... and so forth.
Combining these years: in the analogy, it simply says "possessing years"; in the Dharma, there are many who possess virtues. "As a Buddha" below refers to possessing the virtue of diligence.
"A good person" below refers to possessing the virtue of meditative concentration. "Attaining the great" below refers to possessing the virtues of supernormal powers and precepts.
"Skilled at" below refers to possessing the virtues of wisdom and eloquence, including the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth. All these virtues are complete.
Today the World-Honored One descended and, citing what was above, pointed to a hundred-year-old man and said, "This is my son.
This refers to those rare jewels among men who have possessed virtue throughout distant kalpas;

today, they are pointed out as those who, since the Buddha attained the Way, have been transformed, awakened their minds, and realized the fruits of the path. In truth, the fundamental and the manifested traces do not meet; therefore, I [am] further...
Pūrṇa and the others said: “World-Honored One, it has not been long since you attained the Way, yet you have already been able to perform such a great meritorious deed.

This is as difficult for the world to believe as an old man having a young son. Although we are of low station—claiming that we are the Buddha’s disciples—and although we trust the Buddha and propagate his skillful means, saying that he possesses true wisdom and supernatural powers, we ourselves can only inspire faith in others [to this extent].”
Nowadays, those who have newly resolved their minds to seek awakening live after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; they may not necessarily believe this and might instead slander it.
"Only thus," and so forth, means that the Buddha can resolve the doubts of the great assembly present before him, and he does not worry about the lack of faith among people of future generations.
Question: In the parable, the young man points to the old man, and the old man points to the young man.
"Father! In the Dharma, it is appropriate only for the younger to point to the elder; it is not appropriate for the elder to point to the younger. Why is this? Answer:
"The text should have contained this [clarification], but the translator overlooked it. However, the meaning directly emphasizes that the father is young and the son is old on one side;

therefore, it is not appropriate for the elder to point to the younger. Question: "In which part of the scripture is there seen an instance where an elder recognizes a younger person as his father? Answer: "In the first [section] above."
When he emerged from the earth, he completed his prostrations and praises to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions; only then did he alone pay his respects to Śākyamuni.
This was an instance where the elder recognized the younger. At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

1. Upon hearing of his father’s death, his heart was filled with grief; 2. He reflected that while his father was alive, he could have been saved;

3. He realized that now, alone and exposed, he had no one to rely upon; 4. Overcome by sorrowful emotion, he attained an awakening; 5. He came to know that the color, fragrance, and flavor of the medicine were excellent; 6. By taking the medicine, his illness was cured.

In this same way, when these sentient beings hear such words, they conceive a sense of its rarity, harbor deep affection and longing, and thirst for the Buddha, thereby planting the seeds of liberation.

To uphold, read, and recite this sutra is to obtain the roots of goodness for revealing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The passage beginning with "His father" serves as a metaphor:
once one has obtained this sutra and awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one perceives that one's own *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding and indestructible;
this is what is meant by "his father returning. Therefore, it says, "causing all to... and so forth.
"What do you think, sons of good family? [down to] "those who speak of me as having the fault of falsehood according to the Dharma.

From "Sons of good family" onwards, there is a question and answer. By means of the analogy that there is no falsehood, it illustrates that the Dharma is without falsehood; therefore it says, "The Buddha said, 'I too,' etc.
This refers to the secret, remote origin of the Dharmakāya, concluding that it is imperishable. "For the sake of sentient beings" and so forth refers to... [the section concerning] the Dharmakāya.

The manifestations and transformations of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, through their supernatural powers, do not perish though they manifest as if perishing; this concludes the section on non-arising. Furthermore, there is no "inferior" [view].
This concludes the passage stating that the dharmas of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are likewise uniform. At the beginning, Maitreya and others say:

"Matters such as these are difficult for the world to believe. Moreover, they consider that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, bodhisattvas who have newly resolved upon enlightenment might give rise to [views that] destroy...

Because the causes and conditions of dharmic offenses and karma are thus layered and manifold, this text repeatedly provides a comparative reckoning so that one may know that the truth is sincere and not false.
This is why the merits of those who hear this chapter are distinguished as being of the lower grade.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"From the time I attained Buddhahood until now, throughout the number of kalpas that have passed, [I have remained here] and only now do I emerge to preach the Dharma."
"At that time," and so forth, consists of eight sections in long prose. The first section contains the words of a sincere request for the teaching to be expounded;
as it follows the standard format, it lacks verses. Consequently, the versification begins from the second section.

However, the verse for the second section consists of only one line, because the long prose emphasizes solely that since my actual attainment of Buddhahood has been immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas [of eons].
The analogy of the kalpas being as numerous as motes of dust does not go beyond illustrating the preceding passage; therefore, it is not versified.

Thus, the phrase "Since I attained Buddhahood" and so forth refers to the constant teaching mentioned below, which is a verse summarizing the third section of the preceding text concerning how he has constantly remained in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma since that time. The phrase "In order to deliver" and so forth summarizes...
Regarding the passage "In the interval between these, I spoke of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others," it actually refers to the subsequent verse:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood has been for as long as this. The phrase "I am always... serves to clarify that since the Buddha is eternally non-extinguished.
When he had not yet descended into the royal palace, for what reason was he not seen? First, it was because the Buddha’s supernormal power prevented them from seeing him;

second, it was because sentient beings were obstructed by their own inverted views. Therefore it is said: "Though near, etc. Following this, [the text says] "The multitude saw him descending," and so forth.
It is said that because sentient beings do not perceive that the Dharma-body is of the same essence as the Buddha, they do not realize it is indestructible even when near them;

rather, they see only the appearance and disappearance of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) Buddha and thus offer worship to the śarīra. With hearts full of longing, straightforwardness, and gentleness, they pray only to behold the Buddha, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
Consequently, they cause the Buddha and the Saṃgha to appear together at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where he preaches that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding.
Yet they are not extinguished. This verse was spoken for the sake of such persons, in the passage beginning, "I left home at a young age," and so forth.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that when the Buddha Candanaguhya of the past was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he beheld the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception with his divine eye.
There was a person destined for deliverance who, however, required eighty-four thousand kalpas to pass before descending into the human realm; only then would it be the appropriate time.

For this reason, although the Buddha of the Sandalwood Cave manifested his passing through skillful means, he concealed his body through the power of meditative concentration, awaiting the completion of that person’s kalpa before descending to the world to preach the Dharma and bestow a prophecy. At that time, there was only him...

This refers to the fact that some people see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, while others neither hear nor see it. "By means of skillful means" and below is a double conclusion regarding both manifestation and cessation;
all are skillful means. "In other lands" and below is a verse summarizing the passage concerning the hundreds of thousands [of lands] and so forth.
"You all" and below means that the Buddha was originally preaching the Dharma in other lands, yet you did not hear it, and thus you [conclude that he has entered parinirvāṇa].
When a Buddha passes into extinction, people fail to realize that for those whose suffering and affliction are profound, the Buddha does not manifest his responsive transformation body;
yet when they develop a thirst of longing and reverence, the Dharma-body emerges once more to preach the Dharma. This section praises the appearance of the Buddhas in the world.
By the power of secret supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), there are passages concerning birth and non-birth;
such supernormal powers have been attained through long-term cultivation of practice over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

This verse’s fourth section concerns the Buddhas’ parinirvāṇa not being imminent. Regarding the passage stating that although they have passed into extinction, they do not actually pass away due to the power of secret supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), the single line concerning these supernormal faculties serves as a conclusion to the preceding section on "the various powers of supernormal faculties" and so forth.
Now, as for the judgment of this fourth section, it is based on the prose of the fourth section concerning what the Tathāgata has said.
The manifestation of the sutras and the exposition of the affairs of one's own and others' bodies all belong to the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*).

Therefore, these are used as terms to indicate the Dharma. However, the passage "always dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and other abodes" is a verse summarizing the fourth section concerning the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñānadarśana*), for such knowledge and vision as they truly are is precisely the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because he knows and sees reality as it is, and because the Dharma-body alone pervades all places, he is eternally present on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and in other abodes.
This is why the long passage states that "the characteristics of the triple world have no birth-and-death, whether in decline or emergence," and so forth.

Thus, the old editions state: "The Buddha is fundamentally not extinguished. This is an abbreviated explanation; the present extensive commentary provides the full interpretation. As for what is seen...

The verse text should be expanded into prose. Regarding the passage "sentient beings," it means that although the Buddha does not pass into extinction, from the perspective of sentient beings, he appears to pass away.
This is based on the prose commentary’s statement: "Because sentient beings possess various natures, etc.

It is solely because sentient beings have various inclinations, desires, conducts, perceptions, and erroneous discriminations that they perceive the exhaustion of the eon within the non-extinguishing *dharmakāya*.
"Even when burned by fire," and so forth. "My this [abode]" refers to the non-extinction of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment).

The long verse explains that because the Tathāgata clearly perceives that there are no various inclinations, desires, conducts, conceptions, or erroneous discriminations, he attains the peace and security of the Pure Land of *Śāntaprabhāsa* (Quiescent Light).

"Heavenly beings and humans," and so forth, refers to the non-extinction of the *sambhoga-vipāka* (the physical body). "Gardens and groves," and so forth, further clarifies the non-extinction of the *niśraya-vipāka*.

"Regarding the phrase 'the state of light': this clarifies the state in which the primary retribution does not perish. Regarding the phrase 'I am pure': this concludes the clarification that the Buddha-land, both its environment and its inhabitants, does not perish.
As for those sentient beings who, despite their environments and primary retributions being consumed by fire, still possess sorrow and suffering, these are sentient beings with transgressions;
they have been brought about by the conditions of their own evil karma, and thus for many kalpas they have not heard the names of the Triple Gem."
This verse [describes] those of meager merit who have not planted roots of goodness, and so forth. From "All those who...
onwards, it concludes by clarifying that the devas and humans who dwell in the Pure Land following the Buddha either enjoy themselves among jeweled trees or strike drums while scattering flowers.
Within the midst of the kalpa’s conflagration, one who perceives that which does not perish is one who has cultivated merit within the three realms of existence;
thus, with a harmonious and upright mind, they behold the Buddha and hear his Dharma.

This is forever distinct from those of meager virtue who, for many kalpas, have not even heard the names of the Triple Gem. At times, [the teaching] descends further to clarify that it resides herein.

In preaching the Dharma, there are differences of length and brevity. This refers to the fact that for those disciples whose roots of goodness are extremely deep and ancient, he preaches the distant origin of the Dharma-body; hence it is said that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable.

This corresponds to the passage in the long version beginning with, "Since I attained Buddhahood, it has been a very long time," and so forth. From "After a long time" downwards, it refers to those whose roots of goodness are slight.
Those who have recently attained realization speak of the recent traces of the manifested transformation; thus it is said, "It is difficult to encounter a Buddha.
This refers to the long passage beginning with, "Some see the Buddha, while others do not," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "My wisdom is inferior" and below:

the former speaks of the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*), while this speaks of the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*). As for "the light of wisdom": through supernatural power, one manifests the affairs of one's own and others' bodies; through wisdom, [one realizes the truth].
This is because it explains the matters concerning one's own body and the bodies of others. The preceding verse describes the lifespan of the Dharmakāya as not being shallow.
Following the section on "lifespan," the verse describes the lifespan of the Nirmāṇakāya (the retribution body) as being inexhaustible. This corresponds to the long prose passage which states:
"The lifespan accomplished when I originally practiced the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted. Therefore, it says, "having cultivated for a long time," and so forth.
"You who possess wisdom... shall enter the unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body.
[The text continues: "You all, descend. This is the fifth section of the long prose. It means: "You, Maitreya and others, are all people of wisdom.

Having heard that the Buddha’s three bodies—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body—and their lifespans, whether remote in origin or proximate in manifestation, are all divine..."

This is the universal skillful means. Do not harbor doubts regarding these beings—whether they are sons or fathers, young or old—and do not entertain the lack of faith that the attainment of the Way is near or that its accomplishment is vast.
You should sever these [doubts] so that they are forever exhausted without remainder; then you will know that the Buddha’s words are true and not false.
This is like the physician’s purgative. Although this generally summarizes the sixth, seventh, and eighth [sections].
The passage consisting of the three sections that serve as metaphors for the Dharma actually clarifies the first line [of the verse].

That is to say, the reason for teaching you all to believe that the Buddha’s words are real and not false is that, just as a skilled physician, wishing to save a mad son who has lost his mind, speaks of death;

so too does the Buddha speak of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) while he is actually present to save those suffering from various afflictions. From "Because it is permanent" (*yǒngcháng xià*) onwards, it refers to the Buddha.
Why is it that while actually remaining present, he speaks of extinction? It is because sentient beings, seeing the Buddha as eternally abiding, harbor arrogance and negligence;
they become attached to desire when born, and fall into evil states when they die. Therefore, although the Buddha does not truly pass away, he manifests the appearance of extinction.
Having completed the verses for this chapter, the following section beginning with "I am always... serves as the introduction to the next chapter, meaning: "Therefore, I am born."

As for saying "extinction" and then again saying "arising": it is because, in my ordinary observations, I know that among sentient beings there are those who practice the Path and those who do not, and they cannot all attain awakening simultaneously.
Therefore, regarding those who practice the Path, I speak of the Buddha’s remote origin and long life-span.
To those who do not practice the Way, he says that the Buddha’s traces are near and his lifespan is short;
this is because he teaches various dharmas according to the capacity of sentient beings to be saved. He constantly reflects within himself:
"Although for forty years I have taught various dharmas of arising and ceasing and instability, I must nevertheless constantly form this intention: by what dharma shall I [lead these beings]?"
Whether they have already practiced the Way or not, all sentient beings shall attain a uniform entry into the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom,
thereby establishing the great cause and swiftly accomplishing the Buddha-body, thereby realizing the great fruit. Now, as this sutra is preached up to the section on the Buddha’s lifespan,
both the new followers such as Maitreya and Śāriputra, as well as the ancient assembly who emerged from the earth, shall all attain [this realization].

One will swiftly accomplish the Buddha-body and unsurpassed wisdom. It becomes even more evident here that there are no three faculties of capacity, no three vehicles of Dharma, and no three bodies of the Buddha.
The Seventeenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "Distinguishing Merit. Regarding the "distinction of merit":
this refers to the members of the great assembly hearing that the Buddha’s Dharma-body and lifespan are long-lasting, whereby each individually realizes the Buddha’s merit within their own minds;
that is to say, they attain entry into unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly accomplish the Buddha-body.
For instance, there are those who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and those who have attained the gates of *dhāraṇī* and so forth;

yet the Buddha assigns them their respective portions and distinguishes them, so that they may know that although the birth of the Buddha and the Dharma-body are of one essence, there are ten thousand differences in their realization and enjoyment according to the depth or shallowness of their capacities. It is like the single moon in the sky, which appears divided according to the waters.

Because its form and shadow [are thus manifested], it is called the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits. This, too, is sustained by the empowerment of the sovereign supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of all Buddhas.
Otherwise, how could the span of their life be discussed within such a short time, while their power and virtue pervade the entire great assembly?
Would this not be a swift accomplishment? It perfectly illuminates the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, wherein the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless.
It is the merit of incalculable *asaṃkhyeya*.
At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha’s discourse on the lifespan [up to] the mind of *samyaksaṃbodhi*.
From this point downward, the scribe of the scripture provides a narrative account, describing how they attained the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha and swiftly accomplished the Buddha-body.

"At that time" and below: the Buddha summons those who are the appropriate recipients (*yathābhavya*) to distinguish their merits; this serves as a general summary of the teachings expounded in the "Superior Grade" (*uttama-kula*).

"Six hundred" and below: a specific enumeration of the number of those who have attained these merits. Among these individuals who have attained merit, there are distinctions between the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) in terms of their general and particular aspects;
as for their stages, they comprise the three types of bodhisattvas, the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*), and the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*).

Regarding the grades of many lifetimes: suppose there were a single Gaṅgā River forty *li* in length, containing an incalculable number of grains of sand; how much more so for the sands of six hundred and eighty million *nayuta* Gaṅgā Rivers!

Even if all those Buddhas were to know their number—one grain of sand corresponding to one person—and there were such a multitude of beings who, upon hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan, attained the merit of the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). According to this standard...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is for those who have attained the merit of the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*) and the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
This is because the *Śūraṅgama’s* Dharma-patience of Non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is listed after the three gradual sequences (*tri-sukha-anupūrva*) and before the stage of Dry Wisdom.

According to the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is for those who have attained the merit of the two stages: the seventh, the Far-reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), and the eighth, the Immovable (*acalā*). This is because...

The Five Patiences of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*—namely, the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—follows after the patiences of subduing, faith, and compliance, and precedes the patience of quiescent extinction.
Thus, that sūtra states: "The bodhisattva of the patience of non-arising is one who is far removed from [the three poisons] and possesses immovable contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*), and so forth.
According to this fundamental sūtra, these are spoken of in terms of sentient beings. Although "sentient beings" is a general designation for the nine dharma-realms, it actually refers to—

It is so named because they have never before attained Buddhahood. If one speaks according to the preceding verse regarding the entry into supreme wisdom and the swift accomplishment of the Buddha-body, then these six million eight hundred thousand sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all possess the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun*).

They realize everything in a single realization; thus, even while remaining within the stage of Dry Wisdom (*gan-hui*) or the Ten Faiths (*shi-xin*), it does not hinder their being subsumed within the [ten stages of the Bodhisattva path].

The realization of the stages (*bhūmi*) is not contradictory in either of the two sūtras; however, they differ in their instructional approach to the sequence of stages. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* is definitive in this regard.

If explained in terms of the six sense faculties, this "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) encompasses all six faculties, for every faculty and every object is the non-arising of the Dharma-body. One should accept this principle of non-arising within the mind.

Therefore, it is said "again, there are a thousandfold more" below; this means there are a thousand times more Bodhisattvas than those [already mentioned] numbering six hundred and eighty million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands.
A Bodhisattva is a name for one who is about to become a Buddha but has not yet attained Buddhahood.
This refers to those capable of attaining merit. "To hear and maintain" (*śrutadhara*) below clarifies what is attained. "Hearing" (*śruta*) refers to the faculty of the ear;

"maintaining" (*dhara*) refers to upholding. *Dhāraṇī* is translated as "total retention. This means that within the faculty of the ear, one hears the principle of the Dharma-body’s non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which can encompass all phenomena and uphold immeasurable meanings. Because there is both hearing and maintaining, it is so called.

Section on the Gate. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Then your dharma-body would be identical to annihilation; who then would cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
This refers to it. Regarding its stage, this is one who has attained the merit of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), because within the character *chi* (to hold/maintain) lies the meaning of "abiding.
These two preceding items constitute the "self-awakening" among the three types of awakening; both are reckoned according to the *saṃkhyeya*.
This is a numerical calculation. From here below, ten types [of worlds] are enumerated based on the counting of particles (*rajas*). Within the first category, there is again a "lower" type:
a single world, which is one Jambudvīpa among the four great continents. However, a world is formed from subtle particles;
when these particles are multiplied by various numbers, they exceed even the multitude of sands numbering a thousand times six million eight hundred thousand and so forth.

"Attaining the eloquence of joyful speech" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) refers to this assembly of beings who, upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, attain the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) among the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
In terms of the six sense faculties, this refers to the faculty of the tongue, because eloquence belongs to the faculty of the tongue.
In terms of the stages of practice, these are those who have attained the merit of the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*), for eloquence pertains only to [this level].

Because the tongue is able to act, there is next the "lower" [stage], which refers to the six sense organs. Regarding the sequence of the mental faculty (*manas*), this pertains to those who have attained the merit of the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) and the four preparatory practices (*catvāraḥ prayogāḥ*). "Revolution" (*khu-an*) carries the meaning of dedication;

the mind can revolve throughout the ten directions and silently encompass the three periods of time. Its swiftness is such that in the space of a single bowing and rising, it traverses the four seas. This...
Among the three types of awakening, it is the self-awakening that partially realizes the Dharma-body and awakens others.
Furthermore, below this, one thousand Sumerus, suns, moons, four continents, and even Brahma-worlds are called a small chiliocosm; a thousand times a small chiliocosm [is a medium chiliocosm].
This is called a medium chiliocosm. A thousand times a medium chiliocosm is called a trichiliocosm (a three-thousandfold great chiliocosm).
If one were to take the atoms of a great chiliocosm and divide them into groups, they would exceed even twice the number of atoms in a single world-system.
"Capable of transforming the lower" means that this great multitude, upon hearing of the Buddha's lifespan, attains the merit of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) among the ten stages.
This is because they experience joy at being non-retrogressive—that is, never again falling back into the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Regarding "turning [the wheel]": it means that having personally attained non-retrogression, one further turns the Dharma-wheel of the stage of non-retrogression for others.
This refers only to those who have eight births remaining; among these, there are those who should attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after ten births. The above is the sequential description.

In all cases, it proceeds from the few to the many; this clarifies that the increasing numbers are inconceivable. Furthermore, there is a "lower" [category] of two thousand, which refers to what is called a medium chiliocosm; this proceeds from the many to the few, clarifying that the decreasing numbers are inconceivable.
Seeing those who have attained the great fruit, their assemblies are relatively small. "Able to turn downward" means that these numerous multitudes hear of the Buddha’s lifespan.
This refers to the attainment of the merit of the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*) among the ten stages.

Because in the second stage, the perfection of the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is particularly complete for oneself—such that the defilement of breaking precepts is first rendered pure—and because one is able to turn the wheel of the pure Dharma for others;
herein, it should be understood that one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after nine more births. In all cases, this is not explicitly stated.

[This is] for fear that the text would become overly verbose and lose its elegance. "Furthermore, there are five [levels]" below refers to what is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), consisting of one thousand Mount Sumerus, suns, moons, four continents, and Brahma worlds.

"In eight births one shall attain" below means that when these sentient beings hear of the Buddha’s lifespan, they shall attain the third stage, the Luminous Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), among the ten stages.

This is also a matter of merit. Since the third stage, the Radiant (*Prabhākari*), still differs from the ultimate stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) by eight positions, there should be seven, six, or five births remaining before attaining Bodhi at this point below.
In terms of stages, these should include the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages. Regarding the atoms of the world-systems, one should also state their quantity. [The text] connects...

Regarding the passage concerning the "four sets of four continents" and so forth, although the sequence of initial formation is established, the Buddha did not explicitly state it because, in some cases,

there may be eight births prior and four births subsequent, while the intermediate stage itself possesses seven, six, or five births— corresponding to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages respectively.
First, it may be that those who attained merit at that time were not meant to be born [in this world], and thus the numerical sequence of their lands was omitted from the beginning or end.
Second, it may be that the Buddha’s speech was so skillful that he intended for one point to be repeated three times. Third, it may be that the translators abbreviated the text;
seeing its interwoven complexity, they avoided making the phrasing overly rigid. Sixth, there is again the term "below," which refers to...

There are as many as the atoms of four sets of four continents. Regarding "four births shall attain," this refers to these multitudes of atoms who, upon hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan, shall attain the merit of the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Going) stage within the ten bhūmis.
"Seven" further has a lower [count], referring to the atoms of three sets of four continents. "Three births shall attain" refers to these many multitudes.
Hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan, one attains the merit of the eighth stage, the Immovable Bhūmi (*acalā-bhūmi*), among the ten stages.

"Eight" further has a lower meaning, referring to the number of dust motes in two sets of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*). "In three births, one shall attain" refers to those who possess this number of dust motes;
by hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan, they attain the merit of the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there is a lower level, which refers to the multitude of atoms within a single set of four continents:
Pūrvavideha (East Godānīya), Aparagodānīya (West Godānīya), Uttarakuru (North Kuru), and Jambudvīpa (South Jambudvīpa), together with one Mount Sumeru and one sun and moon.

This refers to one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*). "One birth shall attain the lower" means that these multitudes of beings, upon hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan, will attain the merit of the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), within the ten stages.

Because the Cloud of Dharma stage is still separated from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) by only one birth, there is yet another "lower" category; it is not called "one world system," but rather "eight worlds."
This refers to sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms within eight *Jambudvīpa* worlds. Question:
Are not eight *Jambudvīpa* worlds the same as two sets of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*)? Answer:

Because the breadth and narrowness of the four continents are unequal, it is expressed by saying "eight *Jambudvīpa* worlds. This is what is seen by the Buddha-eye and known by the Buddha-mind; it is not...
The comparison of what may be disregarded is precise to the very last detail; these are words of true knowledge and true vision. All are set forth below:

it is said that if there are such beings among the masses who hear of the Buddha’s lifespan, they shall, by their initial resolve, immediately attain the merits of the stages from the Ten Grounds up to the stage of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). As the Sūtra says: "At the moment of the initial resolve, one immediately encompasses..."
This refers to the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment through the five stages. This vision is for sentient beings of great capacity who realize it directly and instantaneously;

their initial awakening (śikṣā-bodhi) accords with their original awakening (prakṛti-bodhi). This corresponds to the preceding verse regarding the attainment of the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom and the swift accomplishment of the Buddha-body.
