This did not merely involve the vastness of the horizontal and vertical realms, but also spanned a duration of many years. Therefore, it says, "for a full hundred thousand [years]."

[The interlocutor] asks: "If the Buddha’s lifespan is limited to eighty years, how can it be said at another time that it is a full hundred thousand years? [The Master] answers: "It is like the dream of the yellow millet;

within a single dream, the entirety of one's life's affairs is completed. How much more so with the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), which can condense the long into the short and unify duration and brevity—how could this be conceivable by the intellect?
Thereafter, [the text] proceeds to describe the Buddha and his emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*), manifesting their physical forms."

This refers to supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). It means "to gather" or "to withdraw. In contrast to the word "emerging" (*niḥsṛta*) used previously regarding the emergence of the broad and long tongue, here it refers to the sound of the coughing and the withdrawal of the tongue-phase;
the sound as it enters the mouth descends together with the Buddha and all his emanated Buddhas at the very moment the tongue-phase first emerges.
Each hand forms a mudrā; thus, when the tongue is now retracted, the mudrās are released, and the index fingers of both hands snap to produce sound.
"These two below" refers to the power of the marks of sound, which likewise pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
Viewed in this way, beyond the three transformed pure lands, there still remain the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions. How insignificant [is this world]!
Sentient beings cling to what they possess as their own and desire to be greater than others; how narrow-minded they are!
Thus, the creator of characters used "stinking" (*chòu*) to represent self-aggrandizement. The earth is fundamentally below; there are two conditions for an earthquake:

first, seeing that the insentient vessel-world is falsely bound, and now desiring to manifest the truth and return to the source, it therefore shakes; second, desiring to transform the sentient beings outside the [current] lands through the three transformations.

Seeing my Sahā world, including its principal and attendant beings, as well as its physical and spiritual environments, as constituting a single realm, he causes those who have made vows to go to other worlds where those who uphold this sutra have passed away;
therefore, he causes the earth to quake. Regarding the phrase "the sentient beings therein" and so forth:

it means that those sentient beings of the ten directions were initially obstructed by the two hindrances of afflictions and dharmas; although they are identical to the Buddha and his manifested emanations, [they remain obscured].

There are those who possess eyes yet do not see; now, through the Buddha’s power of spiritual penetration, their deafness and blindness are shattered, and they behold the manifold bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions—both principal and attendant—accomplished through the Buddha’s power of vows, as well as the singular body of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, past and present, accomplished through the Buddha’s power of wisdom.
This is what is meant by "responding to conditions and meeting with sentient beings without exception. And...

"Constantly dwelling upon this seat of enlightenment" describes, within the context of the Three Jewels as a single essence, the Buddha Jewel in which the Dharma-body and its physical environment are clearly distinguished.
"With the vision below" refers to the Sangha Jewel within the Three Jewels as a single essence, who never depart from the Buddha’s side.
"Having already seen below," one should understand that the multitudes in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are likewise [of this nature].
When the earth was previously transformed, the devas and humans who were moved and repositioned, as well as the five thousand arrogant members of the assembly who withdrew from their seats—
initially hindered by the obstacle of conceit (*adhimāna*)— were unable to perceive the wondrous realm of this Dharma assembly.
As stated in the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*, by means of various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), those beings with perverted views, though [physically] near, [are rendered distant].

They did not see [him]. Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Lifespan," it is already recorded that while the Buddha was in the causal stage as the Bodhisattva Constantly-Not-Light (Sadāparibhūta), he did not harbor resentment toward those with overweening pride;
how much less, now that he has attained the fruit of Buddhahood, would he allow them to withdraw from their seats or be removed?
Would he not ultimately cause them to see him? Therefore, by means of his supernormal powers, he bestowed his grace so that they might see him. —The Chapter on the Lifespan.

This means causing them to give rise to yearning and, through the transformation of their minds, to aspire [to the Dharma]. At that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Vulture Peak Mountain.
As for those who have withdrawn from their seats and been repositioned, they have no intention of seeking jewels; yet they arrive spontaneously.
Therefore it is said: "All were filled with great joy," and so forth. Immediately, the various devas descended, enumerating the multitudes from the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Furthermore, by virtue of the power of the devas, they were able to hear the names of the Dharma-body Triple Gem—the environment and its inhabitants—within this land.
...and the name of the Dharma-treasure. "Beyond this" (passing below) teaches the knowledge of the names of the environment (*āśraya*) of this land.
"Within this" (in the midst) teaches the knowledge of the name of the Dharma-lord (*dharmanāyaka*), who is the primary retribution (*sambhoga*) of this land.

"Now for" (now acting as) teaches the knowledge of the names of the sutras spoken by the Dharma-lord for the sake of his Dharma-ministers. This is for the purpose of [the prophecy] given to Śāriputra during the *Upamā-parivarta*.
The five phrases beginning with "The śrāvakas preach Mahāyāna sūtras" correspond to one another. The passage "You all... below instructs them to rejoice in that Dharma;

the passage "You should also go down... instructs them to make offerings to those Buddhas. These are all instructions from the devas, serving as a conclusion and proof for the case presented in the "Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta," where at that time I extensively dispatched devas, nāgas, and others to assemble the audience for hearing the Dharma. This is the section concerning Maitreya.
This refers to the Buddha’s renown pervading the ten directions, extensively benefiting sentient beings.

The passage beginning with "Those various [beings]" describes how the sentient beings of that land follow the mandate of their Lord to pay homage and practice mindfulness of the Buddha. The passage beginning with "By means of various...
describes how they follow the mandate of their Lord to offer worship, thereby manifesting their profound faith and understanding. As Maitreya said: "All are endowed with roots of goodness."

This refers to assisting the unsurpassed mind. As for the various items scattered below, their manifestation through the transformation of the Dharma by the mind is what is moved by the Buddha and his manifested Buddhas, who take great compassion as their chamber and gentleness and patience as their robe.
Therefore, all the scattered objects combined to form a precious canopy that covered and sheltered the Buddha above.

At that time, from the ten directions below, the first Buddha had already transformed his pure land three times, yet many humans and devas still remained to be relocated. Now that there was space to accommodate those who were to be moved from their seats, [the assembly gathered].
Upon seeing, hearing, and paying homage, those who were retreating advance, yet that which was moved and placed remains fundamentally unmoved;
thus, the worlds of the ten directions are pervasively unimpeded, as if they were a single Buddha-land.

My Buddha, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, and the emanation Buddhas have fulfilled their vows, such that the three bodies—the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa—are perfectly one and the same. This applies to both the lands of ordinary beings and sages, as well as the lands of skillful means.
The *sambhogakāya* realm (*shibao tu*) is identical to the *dharmadhātu-prabhāsvara* (*jiguang*). No distinct forms or characteristics of self and other can be perceived therein.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If one wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, one should purify the mind so that it is like empty space;

by remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and all grasping, the mind will encounter no obstruction wherever it is directed. Master Dushun’s verse says: "If a person wishes to realize true emptiness..."
This is the principle: the True Suchness within the body extends universally without; sentient and insentient beings share a single essence.
Everywhere is identical to the True Dharma-realm—all this refers to this meaning. When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reaches this point, the Buddha’s spiritual power manifests here:
there is not even a space the size of a needle-point that is not filled by the Buddha’s Dharma-body, and there is not even a pore the size of a speck of dust that is not his Pure Land.
"Perfectly so. To know this and to see this is called the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
How could such a marvelous thing exist within the teachings of a single great period? I believe that the Lotus Sūtra is truly the king among all sūtras."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, headed by Upariṣṭha, [up to] the point where it says, "the various Buddhas entered parinirvāṇa here.
Regarding the phrase "at that time," the previous section on supernatural power states:

"Regarding Mañjuśrī and others," this refers to the eighty thousand great beings such as Mañjuśrī, each of whom had their own respective Buddhas to serve in past kalpas, and each of whom received teachings from those former Buddhas.
Regarding these entrustments: for instance, Mañjuśrī was a disciple of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, and Bhaiṣajyarāja was a disciple of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa;
both have records of such entrustments. Neither were they disciples converted by Śākyamuni, but rather venerable elders who had long resided in this realm.
Therefore, he manifested supernatural powers, for none but such elders would be sufficient [for this task].

[The Buddha] testified. This section entrusts [the teaching] through the power of wisdom, addressing Bodhisattva Shangxing and others because Shangxing and his peers were the direct disciples personally transformed by Śākyamuni Buddha; the Sūtra is not something that can be entrusted to those who are not dharma-heirs.
"By the spiritual power of all Buddhas" below [the previous section] cites the greatness of the aforementioned spiritual powers.
"If I, by means of this" below refers to the profound power of the merit and wisdom of this sutra.
"In brief" below means that since the vast spiritual powers manifested above cannot fully encompass the entrustment of this sutra, one should condense the extensive into the essential and concise.

This clarifies it. "All dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata" refers to the mind-dharma of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the single great cause and condition (ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya) in which such marks, nature, substance, function, causes, conditions, fruits, retributions, beginning, end, and ultimate reality are all equal.
"All sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata" refers to the light from between his eyebrows illuminating the east.

He manifested the transformation of the earth into a stūpa, brought forth the Many-Treasures Buddha, assembled the emanated bodies, and caused the assembly to dwell in the air. He caused the multitude to surge forth from the ground;
sixty minor kalpas passed as if they were half a day. Furthermore, he enabled those with superior faculties to perceive both the signs of sound and form.
The unification of all realms into one is precisely the power of the Buddha’s mind of the Great Cause and Condition (mahā-kārya-hetu-pratyaya) and his knowledge-and-vision.

That which is called "the treasury of all the Tathāgata’s secret essentials" refers to the teaching that bestows the prediction of manifest enlightenment upon those of the Two Vehicles, declaring that the minor fruits previously attained were not ultimate.
Furthermore, it is taught that all śrāvakas maintain a hidden inner reality while manifesting outwardly as teachers of Devadatta and even as dragon girls.
Attaining Buddhahood: The Tathāgata has long since realized the Way, and his lifespan is boundless;

all of this is the essential core of the Buddha’s mind of the one great matter, the cause and condition for [the liberation of] beings. Regarding "all the most profound matters of the Tathāgata," this refers to the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, when he was one of the sixteen princes, and the time of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna (King of Constant Light), when he was the bhikṣu Never-Disparaging; in both cases, it is the same.
The "Great Matter" (mahā-vastu) refers to the mind and its activities as known and seen by the Buddha. All of these are contained herein;

that is to say, what has been expounded above is all recorded within these seven volumes of the expressive text (*vyañjana*), proclaimed and clearly explained without the slightest concealment or omission.

Therefore, [the passage] beginning with "You all, below" exhorts those who are the primary audience to become six kinds of Dharma-preachers and to cultivate this according to the Dharma within their own minds.
[The passage] beginning with "In whatever land, below" exhorts those who are the primary audience to become six kinds of Dharma-preachers and to reverently uphold those who possess the Dharma.
One should revere places where the Dharma resides; in all such cases, one ought to erect a stūpa to manifest this honor. There are seven categories of locations where a sūtra scroll may be kept:
first, a garden; second, a grove; third, a tree; fourth, a monastic dwelling; fifth, a lay residence; sixth, a hall or palace; and seventh, mountain valleys or wildernesses.
Below, the text provides an inquiry and explanation as to why both persons and locations should be honored with the erection of stūpas and offerings. This is because...

The place is itself the site of enlightenment; that person is himself the Buddha. To attain Buddhahood at the site of enlightenment, to turn the wheel of Dharma, and to enter parinirvāṇa—these constitute the Great Matters.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers... [until] their limit cannot be found."
This verse consists of three sections. The first two sections state: "The Buddhas," and so forth;

this means that the Buddhas abide because they rescue the world, and their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) manifest because they delight beings. The section beginning with "The mark of the tongue" correctly clarifies the characteristics of the immeasurable supernormal powers.
The section beginning with "For the sake of" correctly clarifies the delighting of beings; that is, it is because they delight those who seek the Buddha-way.
Born with a tongue only a few inches long, yet reaching as far as the Brahma-world, and with a body sixteen feet tall that emits countless rays of light—all these are rare wonders in the world.
The above verses praise the divine power of the physical marks; now follows the section on the Buddhas’ voices and coughs.
"The sound of verses and marks of supernatural power" refers to the sound produced by the mouth and fingers, which is heard throughout immeasurable lands in the ten directions.
"The sixfold earthquake" signifies the joy of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas such as Ūrdhvaṃgama, who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, are able to uphold this sutra;
it manifests these sounds, marks, and immeasurable supernatural powers. "Entrustment" (referring to the section below) means that all Buddhas...
The reason for manifesting immeasurable supernatural powers is twofold: first, to entrust this sutra; second, to praise those who uphold it.
Even if one were to praise the merit of such a person with supernatural power for immeasurable kalpas, it could never be fully exhausted.
The passage beginning with "This person" clarifies why he grants such great supernatural power and praises them for many kalpas.
As for "inexhaustible": because the merit of one who upholds this sutra is boundless and infinite, like the empty space of the ten directions.
One who can uphold this sutra has already seen me; [up to: they shall have no doubt whatsoever.

This verse constitutes the third section. The first six lines, beginning with "One who can uphold [this sutra]," mean that the upholder of the sutra, upon seeing the sutra, sees all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions, as well as the bodhisattvas whom those Buddhas have taught and transformed.

The next eight lines, beginning with "Furthermore, one who can uphold [this sutra]," mean that the upholder of the sutra does not merely see the Buddhas and bodhisattvas; rather, it causes [them] throughout the ten directions...

All Buddhas of the three periods of time give rise to joy. Furthermore, before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, one immediately beholds them and makes offerings to them.

Regarding the ten phrases concerning the Buddhas sitting beneath their trees: it means that the upholder of this sutra does not merely behold the Buddhas and make offerings to them so as to cause the Buddhas to rejoice;
rather, it refers to the secret and essential dharmas obtained by the Buddhas within the bodhisattva assemblies.
One will also personally realize this before long, thereby attaining self-awakening.

Furthermore, regarding all the teachings and their meanings, as well as the names and terminology spoken by the Buddhas, one will joyfully and eloquently expound them, thereby perfecting the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
This brings about the inexhaustible benefit of awakening others; like the wind in the sky, nothing can obstruct it. Regarding the Tathāgata...
The following ten phrases refer to the fact that the holder of this sutra attains the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), which are as unimpeded as the wind.

Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, regarding all the sutras spoken by the Buddha—the origins of their causal conditions and the sequential chapters and verses—they can explain them all according to their meaning without exception, and they are all in accordance with the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, like the radiance of the sun and moon, they are able to extinguish the [afflictions] of sentient beings.

Throughout the darkness of the long night, whether in motion or stillness, he teaches immeasurable bodhisattvas to ultimately abide in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), so that they may achieve the perfection of self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of practice.
Therefore, from the words "The wise one" (*yasya jñānam*) onwards, the preceding meanings are summarized to encourage its upholding.
This concludes the prose and verse text of the "Chapter on the Perfect Jewel Stūpa."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-two: Entrustment (*Parīndanā-parivarta*).
According to ancient commentaries, to speak with earnest exhortation is called "entrusting" (*zhù*); to commit a matter to another’s care is called "charging" (*lèi*).
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma-seat... [up to] "...then one has repaid the kindness of all Buddhas."

Regarding the phrase "At that time" and so forth: in the preceding chapter, the Buddha manifested supernatural powers while seated in order to cause five thousand of those of superior grade who had risen from their seats to return, and to move the assembly to the three transformed pure lands.
In this chapter, he manifests them again because he entrusts this sutra to them, placing great weight upon its transmission and reception.
Rising from the Dharma seat, he stepped outside the stupa and stood there, manifesting his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). As for why these powers are said to be "great":

it is because when he transformed the pure land in three ways and caused the vast multitude to emerge, the Buddha, with a single hand, simultaneously touched the crowns of every head without omitting a single person.
Thus, one truly believes in the greatness of the Buddha’s power. This is for my sake, as stated in the Parable Chapter.
"He possesses physical strength"—this is so. The above constitutes the narrative arrangement by the scribe.

As for the conclusion and verification of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Preacher," it serves as the case of the Tathāgata stroking his head with his hand; thus, the following section contains the Buddha’s earnest exhortation, forming the entrustment to Jñānabala.
Furthermore, the conclusion and verification of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Preacher" serves as the case of being dispatched by the Tathāgata to perform the work of a Tathāgata; that is to say:
The Buddha has spent many kalpas in the practice of austerities and encountered great difficulty in attaining the Dharma.
That he now entrusts it to you so easily is solely because he desires you to propagate it with a single mind and increase its benefits,
so that sentient beings of the末代 (final age) do not let time and kalpas pass in vain, nor falsely create obstacles for themselves regarding the great causal conditions of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore it is said: "You all should with one mind propagate [this teaching]," and so forth. Thus, from the third *samādhi* downwards, the first [instruction] is to cause propagation and increase;
its meaning emphasizes benefiting others. The second and third instructions concern entrustment (*parindanā*); their meaning emphasizes benefiting oneself while also benefiting others.
Below this, the text provides an inquiry for clarification: that is to say, why is it that the Buddha, through many kalpas of arduous cultivation, [attained what is] extremely difficult?
Having attained this Dharma, why is it that he does not begrudge it, but instead causes you all to propagate it widely?
It is because the Buddha possesses great compassion and lacks even the slightest stinginess; furthermore, he does not fear that others will easily become Buddhas by following his example.
This passage clarifies that the Buddha has compassion and no parsimony, and because he does not fear that others will equal him, he is able to bestow [the Dharma] upon the multitude.

It gives rise to the three kinds of wisdom that constitute Buddhahood. Regarding "the wisdom of the Buddha": "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*). It is simply to awaken to the fact that one's own mind is the Buddha;

this is self-awakening (*sva-bodha*), which is the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Regarding "the wisdom of the Tathāgata": "Tathā" refers to original awakening, true suchness (*tathatā*);
"gata" refers to coming forth from original awakening, true suchness, to deliver sentient beings. This is awakening others (*para-bodha*).
...is also the wisdom of the provisional contemplation (*prajñā*). As for "natural wisdom," "self" refers to self-mastery (*svatantra*), while "natural" refers to spontaneity (*t'ien-jan*).
This is because it is feared that sentient beings do not know that they are originally the Buddha’s self-mastered and spontaneous nature.

They would otherwise stubbornly cling to the necessity of proceeding from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to the provisional, giving rise to a great compassion based on attachment and views, thereby forming the four marks of selfhood (*ātman*). Therefore, after [the sections on] emptiness and the provisional, the Buddha and... are clarified.

Sentient beings, in their totality, possess a single mind that does not depend on cultivation. Although they engage in the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), they are fundamentally and spontaneously sovereign.

This is the perfection of awakening and practice, which is the wisdom of the Middle Way Contemplation (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*). The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata is all... concludes this.
The Buddha possesses compassion and is without stinginess; he is able to bestow the three types of wisdom and serves as the great benefactor for sentient beings of the nine realms.
You all should likewise descend and entrust this to the bodhisattvas. Having become children of the Buddha, you should learn from the Buddha’s compassion and lack of stinginess.
In future ages, you should descend and teach others how to emulate the Buddha in bestowing wisdom upon sentient beings through provisional contemplation. For...
He causes that person to descend [to a lower level] and teaches the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of both the Buddha and sentient beings;

the wisdom of the contemplation of natural gnosis (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is contained therein. The above constitutes the teaching for those of great capacity, wherein the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is expounded.
If there are sentient beings of lesser capacity, he should teach them by making the One Vehicle appear as the Three Vehicles. You...
To conclude: Bodhisattvas such as those mentioned above need only follow the Buddha’s teachings; this itself constitutes repaying the Buddha’s kindness, and there is no need for any other pursuit.
The case concerning the entrustment within the jeweled stupa is hereby completed.
At that time, the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas (up to) replied, "So be it, World-Honored One; we pray you have no concern.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas of the lower and upper grades made vows, desiring only to personally attain the true, pure Great Dharma.
Because their minds were predominantly focused on self-benefit, the Buddha, in this chapter, bestowed his supernatural power upon them and stroked the crowns of their heads.

Thereafter, he earnestly exhorted them to disseminate [the teaching] with single-minded devotion so that it might widely increase and flourish; this was because his desire to benefit others was profound.

Having heard that the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings had achieved the benefit of both self and others, the great beings were filled with joy throughout their bodies, and their hearts became even more respectful. Furthermore, they issued words of filial obedience, repeating them again and again.

Thus it is said: "As commanded by the World-Honored One," and so forth. This concludes the section on how the vows of the Bodhisattvas from other directions—more numerous than the sands of eight Ganges Rivers—are fulfilled through this local upholding of the sutra.
"At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... (up to) "...all were greatly rejoiced upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken.

This section from "At that time" onwards means that once the cause and condition for the one great matter of the Buddhas' appearance in the world has been entrusted, the emanation Buddhas previously assembled must each return to their own original lands. The section beginning with "Dharmakara" refers to the former fiefdom.
Regarding the door of that stūpa: when asked why it was not also commanded to return to the lower realms, he replied:

"I still wish to leave behind evidence for the request of King Flower Constellation (Dharmodgata) regarding the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga*; to instruct Wonderful Sound (Gandharvasvara) to come and see Mañjuśrī;

to receive the portion of the necklace from Avalokiteśvara; and to establish the field of merit for Akṣayamati. Thus, having completed the circulation of the main section, the supplementary branches now flow forth."
There are six chapters in total. The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga* is placed at the beginning because Bhaiṣajyarāja upholds this sutra and is beloved by all sentient beings;

it demonstrates his lack of惜惜 (parsimony/regard for self) in burning his body and setting his arm on fire, as well as the causes for the "Dharma-preacher" chapter and the vows made in the "Upholding" chapter.
For Bhaiṣajyarāja to uphold the sutra in this land is indeed a difficult task. In...
The sounds from other directions were not yet sublime; therefore, it was followed by the "Chapter on the Coming and Going of Sublime Sounds.
Therein, one beholds the eighty quadrillion nayutas of beings as they follow the patterns of circling and returning, revolving throughout the worlds.

Although it is wondrous for others, it circulates within one's own person; yet for oneself alone, it is not so. Because of this mastery, it is followed by the "Universal Gate Chapter" of Avalokiteśvara.

One sees that the sixty thousand assemblies, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, led by Śikhin and others, who each desired to attain the True, Pure Great Dharma, were none other than engaged in the karma of the Universal Gate’s mastery. Thus, it flows and circulates until it reaches the mastery of the Universal Gate.
Thus, it may be said that all dharmas are subsumed and immeasurable meanings are upheld; therefore, it is followed by the "Dhāraṇī Chapter.

Because *dhāraṇī* means "total retention," when the teaching circulates to this stage of total retention, it above accords with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and below accords with the shared essence, compassion, and yearning of sentient beings in the six realms, thereby adorning the wondrous enlightenment.

The conduct of King Śubhavyūha has reached its ultimate point; it is exhaustive and there is nothing further to add. Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Original Deeds of King Śubhavyūha.
King Śubhavyūha represents the fruit of Buddhahood, while Samantabhadra’s exhortation represents the cause of Buddhahood.
To clarify that the cause of this sutra encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause, none surpasses what is contained herein.

Having established the four virtues and perfected the myriad practices externally, he did not abandon the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, but came to sport within this Sahā world;
therefore, it concludes with the "Chapter on the Universal Worthy’s Exhortation. Thus ends [the scripture].
These six chapters constitute a separate circulation of the text in sequential order. They secretly reveal that this sutra is the King of Medicines for delivering sentient beings from suffering.
Furthermore, from the "Dharma Master" chapter through to the "Entrustment" chapter, they are nothing other than the teachings for bodhisattvas that are protected and remembered by the Buddha.
Nevertheless, these six chapters each form a distinct branch within the original scripture.
This clarifies the single practice; hence it is called the "Distinct Section on the Circulation.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," the twenty-third:
the sentient beings of this Sahā world suffer from many and heavy illnesses. When a bodhisattva obtains this sutra...

He is the King of Medicines and a skilled physician for the world. He enables the cold to obtain fire, the naked to obtain clothing, merchants to find their masters, and children to find their mothers;
he provides boats for those crossing, lamps for those in darkness, treasures for the poor, and kings for the people.
Thus, he is called the "King of Medicines. Furthermore, he must be able to endure the illnesses of sentient beings, sharing in their sorrows and afflictions without ever retreating.

Breath (*āśvāsa*) serves as the fundamental subject; therefore, it is called the "Fundamental Matter" (*vastu-vibhanga*). According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, his own account of the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*) is based on this cause:
from his being a skilled physician in the world throughout beginningless kalpas, up to his discernment of the causes of flavors, the Buddha certified him by naming him Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King).
According to the original sūtra, his former name was Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (All-Living-Beings-Delight-to-Behold).

Because he diligently practiced this sūtra under the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he obtained the medicine of the *sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Bodies); therefore, he is named Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King).

Furthermore, regarding the "former life" (*pūrvayoga*), it refers to the events after he had attained the samādhi: his body was burned and then regenerated, and he offered his arms as an offering by fire.

One should know that because the restoration of the arm is something that was originally possessed, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* speaks only of obtaining the medicines for curing diseases of the mundane and supramundane realms;

what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* teaches, however, is the Great Medicine among the medicines of the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane. Each of these two sutras describes a distinct matter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying: [omitted] "...and by singing praises of the Buddha as an act of worship.
Regarding the passage from "At that time" downward, it refers to the specific capacity of the audience:

although this Sahā world is a world of the five turbidities and an evil age feared and dreaded by all people, why is it that the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja alone made a vow to travel to this land? What was his past practice?
Furthermore, regarding the passage "The World-Honored One is the King of Medicine" and below:
it means that the reason the King of Medicine is able to traverse the Sahā world today is necessarily because he was able to undergo and practice difficult asceticism over many kalpas.

I pray that you will explain a small portion from within this vast majority, so that the assemblies of devas, nāgas, and others may hear it and give rise to joy, emulating his example in their conduct as they uphold this sutra.
At that time, from "The Buddha said" onwards, [the text] first recounts the name of the Buddha whom Bhaiṣajyarāja originally served, along with his ten titles.
From "That Buddha" onwards, it recounts the great number of the assembly of disciples of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

From "The Buddha’s lifespan" onwards, it means that although there are distinctions of rank between the Buddha and the assembly, their lifespans and physical characteristics are equal. From "In that land" onwards, it means that the buddha-field is purely pure and its adornments are magnificent.
"Under one tree" refers to the place where the assemblies of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sit; it is at a distance from that [tree] equal to the full range of an arrow's flight.
One should know that since the lifespans of those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are long, their bodies are also massive;
thus, this "range of an arrow" is not as short as the current measurements of a hundred or eighty paces. (Quoted from the *Mingyi yinyi*).

Jiashan says: "The range of one arrow is two *li*. Others say it is taken as one hundred and fifty paces, or one hundred and thirty paces, or one hundred and twenty paces, etc., upon the various jeweled terraces.

Regarding the phrase "upon the terraces," this means that not only do the assemblies of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sit there, but furthermore, ten billion devas perform celestial music, song, and dance as an offering.
This is for the sake of nourishment.
At that time, that Buddha, for the sake of the one named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (All-Beings-Delight-to-Behold), [and so forth] spoke these verses to his father:
"Great King, you should now know: I am now traveling to that place [and so forth] to relinquish this beloved body."
Having spoken these verses, he addressed his father, saying: [up to] joining his ten fingers and toes, he praised the Buddha with a verse:
"Your countenance is most wondrous and marvelous; its radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have previously made offerings to you, and now I come again to behold you in person."
At that time, while the World-Honored One was still in the world, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana [appeared].
At that time, under the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa, all humans and devas attained what they had never experienced before.

This entire section narrates the past kalpa of the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana. Because he obtained this *Bhaiṣajyarāja* (Medicine King) sūtra, there occurred the account of his burning of the body and its subsequent regeneration, as well as the original story of his offering of his arm and its restoration. Since these events constitute a single case that must not be severed, they are treated as one section.
From the words "At that time" onwards, it narrates how the Buddha Vimalaprabha preached the sublime Dharma for the sake of Priyadarśana and the assembly.
The following section describes how Priyadarśana alone practiced according to his words, engaged in ascetic disciplines for a long period, and thereby realized the *dharmakāya*.
This is because the *sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* is itself the *dharmakāya*;
the *dharmakāya* acts as the manifestor, while all physical forms (*rūpakāya*) are its reflections within the *dharmakāya*, serving as that which is manifested. However...
The Dharma-body is the form-body; the form-body is the Dharma-body. They appear as many while being one, and though many, they are one.

This is the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; hence it is called "samādhi. Regarding the phrase "having attained this," it means that because the cause has been realized, the fruit is accordingly fulfilled.
"Immediately [the text] says 'below. Since the fruit has already been attained through mindfulness, one should repay its grace; thus it says 'immediately below.

Within *samādhi*, one is able to manifest all forms (*rūpa*), because flowers and incense both belong to the category of form-dharmas. Regarding the phrase 'this incense below,' it means that the incense is small in quantity but heavy in value.
According to the *Mingyi* (Explanations of Names and Meanings), one thousand two hundred grains of millet weigh twelve *zhū*. Thus, six *zhū*..."
This is the count of six hundred grains of millet. Descending from samādhi, he reflected upon what had been manifested within that samādhi; it belonged to his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
Generally, any Mahāsattva who has attained the Dharma-body is capable of personally and independently desiring to burn their own body as a Dharma-offering.
He immediately took and ingested them, desiring to transform his impure physical substance into a fragrant body. *Candana* refers to ox-head *candana*;
its meaning is translated as "medicine-giver. *Guggulu* is resinous incense; *dūrva* is grass-fragrance; *pippalī* is clove; and *agaru* is aloeswood.
The *Nāmasaṃgīti* states: "Agaru," which is translated here as "sandalwood. It originates from the banks of Lake Anavatapta and is called "Lotus-Treasury" (*padmagarbha*).
It is about the size of a sesame seed pellet, yet its fragrance pervades the entire Jambudvīpa realm.
"Resinous incense" (*jiaoxiang*) refers to the class of pine incense. Furthermore, regarding "drinking": since they take fragrances as food, they further take oils as drink to sustain the fire.

The *Yì* (Book of Changes) emphasizes this. "Filling a thousand [vessels]" refers to food, drink, and fragrant oils; it means that by desiring these to endure for a long time, one ensures they remain purely fragrant without impurity, so that their radiance may last far into the future.
Regarding "applying fragrant oil to the body," it means causing the entire body to take on the form of a single wax torch.

Regarding "by means of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*)," it refers to burning the body as an offering to the Buddha; one aspect is the power of supernormal faculties, and the other is the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Because of this power, one attains a radiance that is both great and universal.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The various Buddhas therein" and ending with "none can compare to making offerings with one's own body," this clarifies that bodily offering is true diligence;
therefore, it is called the "true Dharma-offering. If one compares such offerings made through supernatural powers with other material gifts, all the latter are...
It does not equal it. Good son, this is called "extolling the supremacy of the gift of Dharma. It is superior to the gift of material wealth.
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Vows and Practices (*Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*), there are seven kinds of Dharma-offering: first, practicing according to what one teaches.
Second, benefiting sentient beings; third, gathering in sentient beings; fourth, undergoing suffering on behalf of sentient beings; fifth, diligently cultivating roots of goodness;
sixth, never abandoning the bodhisattva’s activities; seventh, never being separated from the bodhicitta. This is the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana.
In a single movement, all seven practices are fully realized. "His body burns downward" refers to the body that is being consumed;

it perishes in accordance with the exhaustion of the power of the fragrant oil he has applied. "All sentient beings" and so forth means that within this samādhi, one can manifest all manner of bodies;
therefore, even when life ends, one is reborn. Regarding "Pure Virtue" (*Jingde*) and so forth, the Jin translation previously states "suddenly."
However, he was born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Later, it says he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*); this was to conform to his birth by transformation.
Following the previous passage stating that there were no women in that land, he then spoke in verse to recount past events.
Seeing that the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana was originally a prince, he spoke these verses to attribute the merits of his former deeds to the Buddha.

This is the Dharma. Translated during the Jin Dynasty. Following the verses, there is a passage in which the Father King praises his son’s aspiration and desires to go together with him to the Buddha;
with this inclusion, the meaning is further complete. Regarding "attaining understanding" and below: all sentient beings refers to the twelve classes of living beings.

Their languages are truly difficult to fully understand, yet [the Bodhisattva] joyfully perceives them. Now, speech is the sound of the mind. Having attained [this realization regarding] the twelve classes...

When one gives rise to the mind [of awakening], one attains its *dhāraṇī*. The passage beginning with "Furthermore, having heard" means that after attaining the *dhāraṇī*, one hears this sutra again, consisting of such a number of verses.
According to the *Mingyi* (Explanations of Names and Meanings), *nayuta* is called *gou*.

This is based on the numerical system of the *Suanjing* (Arithmetic Classic), which lists ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand, hundred million (*billion*), *zhao*, *jing*, *zi*, *gai*, *rang*, *gou*, *jian*, *zheng*, and *zai*; thus, *gou* is [the term for *nayuta*].

The seventh number among the ten is *zhì* (兆). The *Fengsu tong* states: "A thousand produces ten thousand; ten thousand produces a hundred million (*yì*); a hundred million produces a billion (*zhì*); a billion produces a *jīng* (京);
a *jīng* produces a *zǐ* (秭); a *zǐ* produces a *gāi* (垓); a *gāi* produces a *rǎng* (攘); a *rǎng* produces a *gōu* (溝); a *gōu* produces a *jiàn* (澗); a *jiàn* produces a *zhèng* (正);
and a *zhèng* produces a *zài* (載). Furthermore, there are four ways of reckoning a *yì*: first, one hundred thousand is taken as a *yì*; second, one million is taken as a *yì*.
One *billion* (*yi*). Third, one *billion* is ten million (*chī wàn*). Fourth, one *billion* is ten thousand times ten thousand (*wàn wàn*).
Now, following "eight hundred thousand million billion" (*qiān wàn yì*), it further says "nayuta. This clarifies that all four types of *billion* are complete;
thus, after the term *billion*, it is annotated as *nayuta* (translated here as *gōu*). As for *vighana* and so forth, they appear among the sixty great numbers in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.
It constitutes the sixteenth, eighteenth, and twentieth [sections].

"Great King, I shall now descend" means that since that Buddha is currently present and his Dharma is widely available, one must not fail to extend offerings to him in order to repay his profound kindness.
Following the words "Having spoken thus, he descended," the text describes the protocol for inviting the Buddha, which differs from ordinary travel by water or land.

Furthermore, from "Going down below" onwards, it describes the etiquette for seeing the Buddha and the words of praise for the Buddha, which accord with the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
"His countenance is most wonderful" praises the Buddha’s Reward-body; "His radiance illuminates the ten directions" praises the Buddha’s Dharma-body.

"I have previously made offerings to him" speaks of past causes; "Now I again come to behold him personally" speaks of repaying the original source. This is the *Sukhādarśana-gāthā* (Verses on Seeing with Joy).
Having finished the praise, he asked the Buddha why he still remained in the world; this meant that he himself would be reborn once more, thereby celebrating the Buddha’s eternal abiding.
At that time, beneath the sun and moon, it was said that while the Buddha’s Dharma-body is indeed eternally abiding, his response to conditions has its limits.
Therefore, he ordered the preparation of the requisites for *nirvāṇa* to await the time of his final passing. Furthermore, he issued a general decree.
"Entrusting the family business of the Buddha-dharma" does not mean that there are persons or dharmas apart from it.

Furthermore, "separately entrusting the family business of the Buddha-dharma" does not mean that there are the land of dependent retribution (niṣyanda-phala) or the sentient beings of primary retribution (vipāka-phala). "All that [I possess]" and so forth refers to the entrustment of affairs for the future.
Thus, it concludes the previous case regarding the arrival at the time of extinction.

This sufficiently demonstrates that although Bhaiṣajyarāja made a vow to uphold the sutra during the "Chapter on the Encouragement to Uphold," there was no one else to whom the Buddha entrusted [the teaching].
This is because Bhaiṣajyarāja was originally a disciple of the Buddha Śubhavyūha and had previously received the entrustment from that Buddha; it merely serves to corroborate his Dharma.
Although he possessed supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he was unable to hand over his family estate. The passage beginning with "At that time" shows that he conformed to worldly filial piety;

being unable to forget his human emotions, he was moved by profound grief. The section beginning with "Thereupon" shows that he followed the instructions of the entrustment, cremated his body, erected a stūpa, and extensively enabled sentient beings to cultivate merit.
Regarding the phrase "this shore of the sandalwood ocean": it is because this [shore] is more valuable when compared to that [other shore].

"[Stacked]" (the character 積) has the pronunciation *zì*. This refers to placing sandalwood on the ground. "Furthermore, he thought to himself" (*fù zì niàn xià*) means that what had been done above was insufficient for his aspiration;
he further desired to burn his own arm as a ritual offering (*dharmapūjā*). "He then spoke" (*biàn yǔ xià*) refers first to settling the assembly.

"One should contemplate with a single mind" (*dāng yīxīn niàn*) means that the great multitude should unite into a single mind; it is not permissible for each individual to harbor their own separate thoughts. This is truly because of the people.
The mind is like water; thoughts are like waves. When mind and thought are unified, it is like waves subsiding and the water becoming still.
To behold one’s own arm being burned without alarm or fear is the primary foundation for attaining *samādhi*.

After these words were spoken, [the Buddha] explained that burning one’s arm for a long duration causes one to gain benefit. There are two kinds of benefits. "Causing countless... and so forth refers to the first: causing one to seek...
Those of the Hīnayāna and ordinary people alike have all resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*). All are caused to descend;
the second [point] causes them, by means of the former, to unify their mental reflections. Now they all attain this samādhi.

At that time, from "all the bodhisattvas" onwards, the great assembly manifests as if sharing in sorrow and affliction, thereby initiating the vow of Priyadarśana. At that time, from "all [beings]" onwards, is the vow of Priyadarśana.
That his arm was restored even before it had completely perished means that the physical body cannot resist the Dharma-body;
this demonstrates that this sutra is as effective as the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja). Therefore, it says, "May my two arms be restored as they were.

From this point downward, it describes how the body is burned and then regenerated, and how the arm is lost and then restored; all of these arise from sincere resolve, not from a desire for ostentation, curiosity, or the display of wonders.
This would be to delude the masses. Therefore, it moved heaven and earth, and the falling of flower-blossoms was a auspicious response.
Although this recounts the original deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is truly intended for those who uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa to take as their model.
Since the Buddha passed away, who has practiced such diligence? Only the Second Patriarch, Master Daokai, who stood in the snow and severed his arm.
It is as if one were able to perceive it clearly.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña (up to) "...even a single four-line verse, its merit is the greatest.

From "The Buddha told" onwards, [the text] connects the past with the present, enabling one to see that *Priyadarśana* and *Bhaiṣajyarāja* are different names for the same person at different times; they are originally one and the same.
There is but one person. Regarding the passage beginning with "The bodies he has sacrificed," since those already mentioned serve as examples for those not yet mentioned, there are still many more.

From the passage beginning with "Sudhana, if after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa," it means that if there should be someone who resolves their mind to seek the great Dharma-body of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even if they do not burn their entire body like Priyadarśana or sacrifice both arms, they are nonetheless able—within [the Dharma]...

Within the physical body (*rūpakāya*), even if one offers a mere small portion of a single finger of the hand or foot as an offering to a Buddha stūpa, this person surpasses the merit of giving external wealth such as kingdoms and cities.
This is because they have sacrificed the present, difficult-to-renounce physical body for the sake of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which has not yet been seen.
"If there were another person," and so forth, means that even if there were someone else...
If a person does not originally seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, but merely seeks the blessings and rewards of humans and devas,
and further cannot burn their body or arms, nor their hands, feet, or fingers, yet fills a great trichiliocosm with jewels to make offerings to the four noble ones—
the merit obtained thereby is still not as great as that of one who merely receives and upholds a single four-line verse of this sutra. Why is this?
This sutra elucidates the Dharma-body; those who can uphold it shall hear the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Yet there are those who seek the blessings and rewards of gods and humans, thereby depleting their bodies and wealth—seeking to abandon suffering through further suffering—and thus benefit neither the Dharma-body nor the form-body.
They cannot be compared for a moment to Medicine King Bodhisattva; they recklessly injure the physical body bequeathed by their parents.
Truly, this is to be pitied.
Suvarṇapuṣpa, it is like all the streams, rivers, and great rivers... (up to) the merit obtained is likewise immeasurable.
This entire section clarifies the previous section concerning the past kalpa of Priyadarśana; as for why he is now named Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is because he has attained—

This is the Sūtra of the Medicine King. Therefore, ten similes were previously used to illustrate that this sūtra is a king, and twelve similes were subsequently used to illustrate that this sūtra is medicine.

From the passage beginning with "Sudhana-rāja," as follows, it continues from the preceding text to explain that [the merit of] burning one's body, arms, or fingers, or filling the great trichiliocosm with jewels to make offerings to the four holy ones, is all not equal to bestowing [this sūtra].
Regarding the fact that one who upholds even a single four-line verse of this sutra obtains greater merit:
it is because this sutra, when compared with all other profound and great sutras spoken by the Buddhas, is like the deep and vast flow of a great river among all streams.
This sutra is like the ocean; it is the foremost in its profound depth and vastness.
This is because among the teachings of all the sutras, there are the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Within these three vehicles, the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles are shallow and small, while the Bodhisattva vehicle is profound and great. This is a relative profundity.
Great! This sutra is the foremost and most profound and vast. This sutra is profound and vast because it does not speak of three [vehicles], but speaks only of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
That it does not speak of three does not mean that it eliminates the three vehicles;
rather, it is because the three vehicles are nothing other than what has been differentiated from the One Vehicle. That it speaks only of the One Vehicle is as follows:

It is not that there is a separate One Vehicle apart from the Three Vehicles; rather, it is precisely by synthesizing the Three Vehicles previously taught that this present One Vehicle is established.
It is like the currents of rivers and streams, which are not divisions of the ocean, yet upon reaching their ultimate end, they all return to the ocean.
For this reason, this sutra is used as a metaphor; among all profound and great sutras, it is the foremost.
...its profundity and greatness. Furthermore, regarding the profound and great nature of the various sutras:
do the various sutras not state that all sentient beings have been Buddha from the beginning? Do they not state that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature?
Although it is said thus, those of the two vehicles truly do not know that they have been Buddha from the beginning. What kind of Buddha would they have become? All [remain as they are].

There is the Buddha-nature. Where does this Buddha-nature reside? Now, this sutra bestows upon Śāriputra and twelve thousand others the explicit prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of their attainment of Buddhahood.

Thus, there exists for each the name [of the Buddha they will become], the kalpa and land in which they will dwell, the adornments [of that realm], the assembly of Dharma-disciples, the lifespan, and the duration for which the True and Semblance Dharma will remain in the world. Yet, as for whom these predictions are being turned toward—[the text continues] thus, all...

Regarding the principle that all sentient beings have been Buddha from the very beginning as explained throughout the preceding sutras, it is only upon reaching this sutra that one truly knows and truly sees it through the bestowal of the Jewel. Is this not like the currents of rivers and streams returning to the ocean?
When we proceed to discuss the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," it is said that the eyes, ears, and so forth, born of one's parents, are constant; one need only maintain them.

This sutra is thus entirely pure. Furthermore, it is known that what was previously taught in all the sutras—that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature—is not found elsewhere, but resides directly within the six sense organs, such as the eyes and ears, which were born of our parents and are part of our ordinary experience.
These very six sense organs cause the jeweled stupa to emerge, transform into a pure land, assemble the emanated bodies [of the Buddha], and manifest forth.
The assembly of śrāvakas remains empty at the place where they gather for many kalpas or even half a day; yet, because it was personally known and personally seen by me, it must be true.
Is it not the case that while the currents of rivers and streams are deep and vast, once they reach the ocean, they become the foremost in depth and magnitude?
So too, although this single four-line verse may be called a mere small portion, it is like drinking from the great ocean.
With a single scoop of water, one drinks up the flavors of all the streams, rivers, and great rivers of the four continents without leaving a single drop behind.
Thus, just as the ocean is the foremost in depth and magnitude and reigns over the hundred rivers, this sutra is the foremost in depth and magnitude and reigns over all other sutras.
This concludes the initial section using the metaphor of depth and magnitude. Furthermore—
As with the earth-mountain below, the second uses the high mountain as a metaphor. The "earth-mountain" refers to ordinary mountains composed of earth and stone.

Regarding the "black mountains," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are three tiers of black mountains surrounding the four continents; the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains surround the small chiliocosm;

and the Great Iron Ring Mountains surround the medium chiliocosm and the great trichiliocosm. As for the "ten precious mountains": [they are as follows:]... (The list of ten precious mountains follows).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: First, the Snowy Mountains; second, the Fragrant Mountains; third, Mount Kailāsa; fourth, Mount Ṛṣigiri (the Mountain of Seers and Sages);

fifth, Mount Yugandhara (translated as "Double Support"); sixth, Mount Aśvakarṇa (the Horse-Ear Mountain); seventh, Mount Nimindhara (translated as "Supporting the Edge," being the edge of the seven golden mountains);
eighth, Mount Cakravāḍa (Master Ying says this is the "Wheel-Encircling Mountain"); ninth, Mount Īśādhara; tenth, [Mount Vinataka].

Mount Sumeru (wherein each of the various mountains has its own height, yet Sumeru is the foremost in height; this serves as a metaphor for how this sutra is superior among all sutras, as should be understood). The preceding section uses the oceans and mountains to serve as metaphors for those things formed from earth.
Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "like the multitude of stars," the third and fourth sections use those things formed as images in the heavens as metaphors;
these illustrate that within their respective spheres of radiance, each has its own preeminence. This is because the moon is able to...
It illuminates the night; its brilliance surpasses that of the myriad stars. This sutra illuminates the long night of ignorance, surpassing all other sutras.
Just as the sun can illuminate the day and its light dispel all darkness, this sutra destroys the darkness of all unwholesome states.

It differs from other sutras in that while other sutras require arduous cultivation and realization to dispel darkness, this sutra does not depend on cultivation or realization; one need only know how to raise it up.
Lowering their heads, they have all already attained Buddhahood. Thus, all evil karma and darkness—when brought forth—are entirely transformed into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, as in the passage beginning with "Just as a minor king," the fifth, sixth, and seventh [analogies] employ the most honored among the Three Talents of Heaven, Earth, and Man as metaphors;
these illustrate that this sutra is supreme, its sovereign, and its father, respectively. All are ranked in order.

First. The seven types mentioned above use the six mundane realms of ordinary beings as metaphors to illustrate the unsurpassed meaning of this sutra, because each of these metaphors emphasizes the sense of being unsurpassed.

Furthermore, from "all ordinary beings" downward, the eighth, ninth, and tenth sections employ the four supramundane noble ones as metaphors to illustrate the perfectly equal meaning of this sutra, because...
This is because each metaphor primarily emphasizes the meaning of "perfectly awakened" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).

However, the eighth metaphor not only illustrates the sutra itself, but also serves as the foremost illustration for those who uphold the sutra. From the words "O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, below this sutra...

onwards, the twelve metaphors illustrate the meaning of "perfectly awakened" in this sutra, as each metaphor primarily emphasizes the meaning of "perfectly awakened. Regarding the phrase "capable of saving," it refers to the sutra.
It possesses the meaning of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and therefore is able to save people and cause them to uproot their suffering and affliction.

When the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are once opened, even the suffering and affliction of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*) are all extinguished; thus, it is said to be "able to bring great benefit.

This refers to the sutra possessing the meaning of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), which fulfills one's vows and has the sense of bestowing happiness. When the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are once opened—
Whatever class of beings one dwells among and whatever karmic actions one performs, all have their fundamental basis for fulfilling one’s wishes. The above constitutes the Dharma.

As in the twelve lines following the "Coolness" section, these metaphors are employed to manifest and fulfill those wishes, possessing the power to enable people to escape suffering and affliction—just as [the metaphors of] the thirsty, the cold, the naked, the merchant’s son, the crossing, the illness, the darkness, and the poor person or trader.
The terms "vessel" (*bhājana*) and so forth collectively clarify the meaning of "sickness" and the meaning of "affliction," all of which possess the sense of "desire.

This is like a pond, fire, clothing, a merchant leader, a mother, a ship, a physician, a lamp, a jewel, a king, and a torch, which collectively clarify the meaning of "medicine" and possess the capacity to save;
all must be filled. The passage beginning with "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* likewise... uses the dharma to correspond to the metaphor. If a person...
"Having heard [this]" and below, it illuminates the six kinds of Dharma-preachers and the ten kinds of offerings to encourage their practice.
The frequent mention of lamps is because they are the specific medicine for curing the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*). *Campaka* refers to the golden flower.
It is also called *huáng huā* (yellow flower). *Suman* is translated as "flower that skillfully gathers the mind.
*Pārala* is translated as "reborn flower," because it grows during the rainy season; it is also called "summer-born flower," because there is much rain during the summer.
*Navamālikā* is translated as "miscellaneous flower. *Mallikā* is translated as "jasmine flower" (*nài huā*) or "garland," for its flowers can be made into garlands.
Therefore, when one infuses sesame seeds with flowers and takes the oil to light a lamp, it not only provides illumination but also possesses a great fragrance.
Śrīgarbha, if there should be anyone who hears [this] (up to: in wisdom and meditative concentration, none can equal you).
The preceding section clarified that this entire sutra constitutes the Medicine King, and that the merit of one who receives and upholds it is immeasurable.
This section clarifies that the merit of merely upholding the single chapter on the Medicine King is no different from that of receiving and upholding the entire sutra.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Sudhana," which refers to a single chapter: whether it be a man or a woman, speaking from the perspective of the Buddha being present—
Furthermore, if there are women who merely hear [this teaching], men will immediately gain merit;
however, women must receive and uphold it before they can avoid taking female form in future lives. Thus, one can see that the male body is more noble than the female.
As for the passage beginning "If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa," this refers specifically to women after the Buddha’s passing who practice the entirety of what has been taught.
The reason for this is that, among those excluded from the three evil realms, women suffer the most;
thus, it further demonstrates that those who are not women possess even more abundant merit. When compared with birth in the Pure Land, this sutra is the cause for attaining birth there.
In the Sanskrit language, Amitābha means "Immeasurable Life" (Wuliangshou); this is what is attained through this sutra.
This is the land of fruition. One does not descend [to lower realms] again, for there is no defilement of the three poisons or the great and small *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).

Having attained the stage of a Bodhisattva, one possesses the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). The reason why it is said that "seven million" and so forth are the number of Buddhas seen through clear vision is that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are not limited by the measure of the six sense faculties and the six sense objects. At this time, the various Buddhas... [descend].
Praising the practice of the cause: you have now been able to descend [into it]. Praising the awakening that is the fruit: both cause and fruit are vast;
therefore, you are protected by the spiritual power of many Buddhas. Thus, all those of the three vehicles cannot equal you in concentration and wisdom.
O Rājāgraputra, this bodhisattva accomplishes such [deeds] (up to) benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.

Regarding the section below, "O Rājāgraputra," it means that in the preceding passage, when comparing the merit of one who upholds a single chapter with that of one who upholds an entire section, it is because the power of the merit and wisdom of this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja is so great. Therefore...
If a person merely hears the "Chapter on the Former Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" and praises a single word of its excellence,
that person’s body and speech will emit fragrance in the present life, and they shall obtain merit equal to one who upholds this entire chapter.
For this reason, below the section on Sukhāvatīvyūha, the preceding nineteen chapters were entrusted to those previously dwelling in the Sahā world, such as Upariṣṭa.
Because [the Buddha] is equal to the bodhisattvas, he entrusts this chapter to those who are the appropriate recipients.

Regarding "evil Māras" (*ā-māra*), it would be more consistent to include the characters "without" (*wú*) and "do not let" (*líng*) at the beginning; otherwise, it would be equally consistent to delete the characters "sever" (*duàn*) and "cut off" (*jué*).
The following section serves as a corroborative inquiry, demonstrating that this sutra is an effective medicinal dharma. *Zhīyīn* explains this sutra as...
The same applies to Bhaiṣajyarāja. From "Sudhana, if you... onwards, it concludes the clarification: those who receive and uphold [this teaching] shall obtain the Dharma-medicine;
they are thus not far from being Dharma-kings. Therefore, those who strive for the Buddha-way should revere those who uphold this sutra, and thereby they may obtain its Dharma-medicine.
From "When he had spoken these words... onwards, it concludes the testimony: one hears a single exposition in the presence [of the Buddha].
This chapter is the attainment of the medicine of the Dharma; this medicine is named the *dhāraṇī* that understands the speech of all sentient beings.

From the passage "The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna descended" onwards is the concluding praise. Because the one who is suited to the occasion has obtained his request, we know that the Buddha did not entrust this sutra to Bhaiṣajyarāja and the others; its merit is thus great.
