Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Written by Ruyū, Abbot of Kongō-ji Temple in Mino, Hokuō:
The Twenty-fourth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.

Regarding "Gadgadasvara," according to the sūtra, this refers to [the bodhisattva] who, during the causal stage, offered one hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments to the Buddha Ghoṣadatta. Furthermore—
Eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven treasures were obtained as a result;

through these, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies According to Type by Means of the Sublime Dharma, which enables him to travel back and forth throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Because he was named for his mastery of this sutra, it is called the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara."
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the light of the mark of a great man (up to) the white tuft of hair, which shone universally throughout that land.
From this point downward, the text will describe the Buddha whom Gadgadasvara originally served; first, it describes the illuminating light of Śākyamuni, which issues forth from two places:

the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head and the space between the eyebrows. This light symbolizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which exists within the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* of all Buddhas.

Regarding the body: first, it possesses the mark of the invisible crown of the head. One must not, because the bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in that land are large, disparage the small bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in this land by conceiving thoughts of inferiority. Why is this?
If one considers the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) of the Buddhas to possess marks, then the bodies of the Bodhisattvas in that land are forty-two thousand [yojanas] in height.
A *yojana* is already vastly larger than the six-foot body of a Buddha in our own land;
how much more so is the body of the Buddha in that country, which is six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas* tall? Thus, it would be difficult for them to see one another.

However, if one contemplates the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of that land through the formless *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas, then although their bodies are long and large, they are entirely illuminated [by wisdom].
Within the Buddha-light of my land, there is a reason why the emission of light is necessarily called the "marks of a Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* (the cranial protuberance), the *Buddhadhyānasamādhisāgara-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s skull bone is perfectly round, like two joined fists;
its color is pure white, and it possesses five great Brahma-marks. At the time of his birth, both Māyā and her sister [Mahāprajāpatī]...

None of these were seen. Instead, five marks of Brahmā appeared, emitting light that illuminated the Brahma-world and extended further upward through immeasurable worlds, manifesting as cloud-pavilions within the realm of all Buddhas—places unseen even by Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
His hair was one zhang, two chi, and five cun long, the color of deep blue lapis lazuli; it curled upward at the crown of his head, forming spirals like conch shells.

Therefore, he is also called "Spiral-Haired" (*śikhin*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "He carries all sentient beings upon his head, having perfected the fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) on his crown.

Furthermore, the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara Sūtra* describes the white hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows as having the outline of various wheels, measuring five feet in length, appearing like tubes of lapis lazuli or crystal beads, manifesting immeasurable hundreds [of rays].
There are ten million colors. Regarding the initial birth, the taking of a consort, the renunciation, and the attainment of the Way, each manifests in different durations.
As for "shining everywhere" below: in the beginning of the sutra, the light shines upon the eastern direction, merely described as eighteen thousand worlds;

now it is said to shine everywhere upon hundreds of eight hundred thousand *koṭis* of *nayutas* of worlds, equal to the sands of the Ganges. Thus, from the beginning to the end of this Dharma assembly, there is a distinction between the distant and the near.

They are distinct. In total, there is a single, eternally quiescent mind-light that does not depart from [the realms of] sentient beings and Buddhas alike; it manifests principle according to phenomena, yet in reality, there is no smallness or greatness.
"Beyond these numbers" refers to the Buddha-land of Pure Light Adornment, which still lies outside hundreds of thousands of worlds and so forth.
This reveals that the light of our Buddha is vast and inconceivable. [This describes] the land and the Buddha.
"All are pure by name" means that, in terms of both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*), they are all the pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Next there is a mark of greatness called 'The Cloud Universally Illuminating All Abiding in the Oceans of Worlds.'"
He emits precious light that fills all of space and the dharma-realm.

Within it, he universally manifests pure and wondrous sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), as well as the adorned physical forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, such that those who behold them attain the state of "seeing nothing.
This is what is meant. Regarding the passage "Śākyamuni [descends]": although the lands of those Buddhas are vast and numerous, the light of our Buddha [pervades them all].
It illuminates everywhere.
At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment (up to) "the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom.
From the words "At that time" downward, it describes the countless Buddha-lands of Universal Pure Light Adornment; therefore, it says "all. There is one...
"Below" means that in all those lands, there is a body of wondrous sound for each according to their capacity. "Having long since" refers to the perfection of merit;
"and all" refers to the perfection of wisdom. "Attaining the Wondrous Banner" refers to the samādhis resulting from the dual perfection of merit and wisdom, which are reckoned as sixteen kinds.
As the text itself contains sixteen sections, they shall be explained accordingly so that [the reader] may see them.
The reality of samādhi is not as [you] have described. Here, you are merely explaining the literal meaning of the characters, which has no bearing on the actual significance.
"In this way" and below refers to these sixteen samādhis as the primary ones; since there are many other samādhis besides them, the word "etc.
(*ādi*) is used. For a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, every movement, stillness, and action is nothing other than samādhi, and nothing other than its name.
Because he upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Śākyamuni Buddha’s light shines down upon him. This means that Gadgadasvara understands the original intent behind my Buddha’s emission of light;
he immediately addresses his own Buddha, expressing his desire to come to this land to make offerings to the Buddha and to see the assembly of Mañjuśrī and others, for whom he requests [permission].
At that time, from the passage "Pure Flower" (*Vimalaprabha*) onwards, that Buddha earnestly exhorts Gadgadasvara not to disparage this land.

Regarding the "receptacle world and its inhabitants" (*bhājanaloka-sattvaloka*): because [the inhabitants] give rise to thoughts of inferiority, in order to conform to the forms of this land, Wonderful Sound must transform and manifest a small body;

this is because he first formed the perception of himself as inferior. From the words "Good son" onwards, there is a separate explanation that one must not disparage the receptacle world and its inhabitants of this land.
Below the section on the Buddha’s body, there is a separate explanation stating that one should not disparage the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of this land.

However, below the section on your own body, he uses that [other land] to manifest this one, so that you may see that the bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the lands of the ten directions—possessing their true majesty and the radiance of their merit—are all far superior to those in this land.
As the Sūtra says: "Because they were short and small in stature, they looked down upon others. How could this apply to the inhabitants of our land?
As for the retribution of foulness and evil, the primary retribution is lowly and inferior. Do Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all plant causes for being despised?

It is nothing other than a manifestation in accordance with the capacities [of sentient beings]; how could one give rise to thoughts of inferiority? Therefore it is said: "For this reason, you go," etc.

The Jin translation says: "The Buddha-lands are fundamentally empty; it is the sins and blessings of sentient beings that currently appear as different. This is correct. Below, regarding "Wondrous Sound" (Ghoṣadatta), it should...

The "occasion" refers to having already abandoned the pure to approach the defiled; fundamentally relying on the power of the Buddha, why would these small and great realms not be mutually integrated and encompassed?
Why would they consent to alter their forms and change their natures, giving rise to thoughts of inferiority? Therefore it is said:
"I now go to the Sahā world, all of which is equal."
"Then, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat... (up to) "...with *candana* and *vaiḍūrya* gems, and using *kiṃśuka* jewels for its pedestal.

This section describes the arrival of Gadgadasvara and explains the first samādhi, the "Exquisite Banner Mark" (*Sudarśana-dhvaja-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*). Here, "exquisite" (*sudarśana*) refers to the wondrous mind;
the "banner" (*dhvaja*) possesses the function of subduing the heterodox and supporting the orthodox, and it is represented by the lotus flower as its mark. Regarding this—
This is the preliminary section, marking the manner of entering samādhi. It clarifies that Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) meets our Śākyamuni through the Dharma-body.
This is what the Chan school refers to as "not permitting night travel; arriving early at the break of dawn. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva, while in one buddha-land, hears the Dharma and receives it into memory; yet his body does not move, by the power of samādhi."
Within unspeakably many assemblies of Buddhas, he manifests his body everywhere; yet he does not divide his body, nor does he emerge from meditative concentration.
In each instance, he produces unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodies through samādhi.
In this manner, throughout all kalpas, they are inexhaustible. This refers to the "Samādhi of the Sublime Banner Mark" mentioned below.

Power: because it can render the distant near. Beyond those worlds as numerous as the sands of eight hundred and ten million *nayutas* of *ganges* rivers, not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak, he manifested a precious lotus flower.
As for the mention of eighty-four thousand [petals] of the lotus: first, this expands the capacity of the single mind, corresponding to the Dharma-gates and afflictions.
The first [point] prefigures that the assembly of Dharma followers from whom the Sublime Sound (Ghoṣadatta) comes will be as numerous as this.
Below, in the section on Jambudvīpa, it describes the characteristics of its flowers: the Jāmbūnada tree has a vast canopy that covers all of Jambudvīpa;
wherever a drop of its water falls upon the earth, the soil turns into red gold, such that no other gold can compare to it. The *kiṃśuka* flower is said to resemble the beak of a parrot.
Its precious color resembles that [of the sun]. Because this sutra is titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara manifested this sign beforehand.
Upon seeing the title "Lotus" (*puṇḍarīka*), one should not regard it as the ordinary red or white lotuses found in the mundane world.

This was indeed a miraculous response in the form of a precious lotus flower. Therefore, in the subsequent section, Mañjuśrī asks by what causes and conditions this omen has appeared, and the Buddha answers that it is for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sūtra; there is a profound reason for this.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince (up to: "also wishing to make offerings and listen to the Lotus Sūtra")—although this section consists of questions and answers regarding the meaning of the preceding section, it is in fact the *Sūkṣmadhvaja-lakṣaṇa-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Subtle Banner Sign), which demonstrates the second *Lotus Samādhi*.
Mañjuśrī, the teacher of all Buddhas, demonstrates being one who asks while appearing not to know; this clarifies [the nature of his inquiry].
As for the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, it can only be brought to ultimate completion by one who grasps its essential fundamental wisdom.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "that bodhisattva has come so that I may behold him."
This section constitutes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. By means of this exchange of questions and answers, it demonstrates the third, the *Vimala-guṇa-samādhi*.

"Purity" refers to the merit of the pure *dharmakāya*; that is to say, within the pure *dharmakāya*, one possesses the merits of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, including their physical forms, dimensions, and dignified deportment.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī," the question concerning the planting of the roots of goodness is intended to...

This reveals the pure *dharmakāya* as the root of all wholesome qualities. Question: Those who cultivate merit wish to reveal that practice arises from the pure *dharmakāya*, thereby first accomplishing merit.

As for the phrase "and yet able to," it seeks to reveal that because the pure *dharmakāya* is the source of all wholesome qualities, one is first able to make the distant near and the non-existent existent, manifesting many thousands of millions [of forms].
The Lotus Flower represents great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). Regarding the passage "What samādhi does he practice? and below:

Mañjuśrī asks for the name of the samādhi to demonstrate that he intends to enter the reality of "Pure Virtue" (*viśuddhaguṇa*) by following its name, thereby practicing so that those of like sound may respond to one another and those of like breath may seek one another;
only thus can one perceive the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as the retribution of Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*). By means of this—
The physical appearance, dimensions, dignified deportment, and movements belong to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) as a result of karmic retribution. "I only pray...

and so forth refers to the *dharmakāya* of the emanation body of Samantabhadra’s wondrous voice; unless one is empowered by the Buddha's power, one cannot perceive it. As an ancient master’s verse says:
Within the shadows of variegated clouds, an immortal appears, holding a red silk fan to shield his face. You must fix your gaze upon the immortal;
do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand. Now, Mañjuśrī seeks to see the wondrous color and form of the Buddha—this is very much like wanting to see the fan held in the immortal’s hand.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [down to] Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, desired to see your body.

At this point, Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to manifest a sign. Since the Buddha did not personally command him, but instead deferred to the venerable Prabhūtaratna Buddha, this demonstrates the fourth samādhi, the "Play of the Constellation King. This is because Prabhūtaratna was an ancient patriarch of the past.
Because the Dharma King has come to sport in this land, at that time, from beneath the earth, [a voice was heard].
All the Buddha-lands of Pure Radiance Adornment are distant from this Sahā world by as many worlds as there are grains of sand in one hundred and eight million *nayuta* of Ganges Rivers.
Although Gadgadasvara had entered meditative concentration there, he was summoned from that place by this single sound.
"How easy and near it is for him to come! Were it not for the divine power of the *Rājavikrīḍita-samādhi*, how could he do so?
How marvelous is its meaning!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land.
The phrase "At that time" and below indicates the fifth, the objectless samādhi (*anālambana-samādhi*).

This means that although he passes away from that land because the conditions for the Buddha-dharma there are temporarily absent, he arrives in this land by establishing the power of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).
Together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, he came forth and, prostrating his head at [the Buddha's] feet, offered him a jeweled necklace.

This section demonstrates the sixth, the Wisdom-Seal Samādhi (*jñāna-mudrā-samādhi*). "Wisdom" refers to the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, as well as the Buddha’s Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
"Seal" (*mudrā*) means that the wisdoms of the Buddha and the bodhisattva mutually certify one another, such that they cannot be altered.
"Unchanging" (Easily): This refers to the fact that the number of people who arrived, as determined by the seals below, does not differ from the number of flowers manifested previously.
"The path traversed": This describes the three auspicious signs of their arrival: first, the earth shook in six ways; second, precious flowers rained down from the heavens;
third, celestial music played spontaneously. "These Bodhisattvas": This determines their physical characteristics and sizes, of which there are eight types. The first is the eye.
1. Blue like a lotus. 2. Two faces, more perfectly round than the full moon. 3. A golden-colored body. 4. Fully adorned with ornaments. 5. Abundant majesty and virtue. 6. Radiant light. 7.
Complete with the [major] marks. 8. A firm and solid body. "Entering the seven lower [realms]" seals and determines the deportment of *vīrya* (diligence).
"Arriving at this [state]" seals and determines the deportment of *śamatha* (calm abiding). "With price" seals and determines the offering.
Regarding the words "approaching and prostrating to me": all such seals of wisdom (jñāna-mudrā) are analogous to worldly phenomena;
they all occur spontaneously and without being sought. Therefore, they are called samādhi.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...are you dwelling in peace, with few afflictions, and enduring well?

From the words "addressed" downwards, although the wondrous voice transmits the greetings of the Buddha of that land to my Buddha, it is in fact a manifestation of the seventh samādhi, the "Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings. These words of greeting are all from this land.
Because the wondrous voice can understand the speech of all sentient beings: "few illnesses" is a question concerning the body; "few afflictions" is a question concerning the mind.

Regarding "your daily activities," this extends the inquiry as to whether the body is free from illness. Regarding "worldly affairs," this extends the inquiry as to whether the mind is free from affliction.
The above inquiries concern the teacher who is capable of transforming others. "Not many [disturbances]" and so forth inquire into the suitability of those to be transformed. Capable...

"Not possessing the great or small latent afflictions" refers to the question concerning the mundane affairs of sentient beings. "Not lacking filial piety or submissiveness" refers to the question concerning the supramundane affairs of sentient beings.
"Able to subdue" refers to the question concerning whether there are obstacles from Māras in the true and mundane practices of sentient beings;
all these questions concern Buddhas of the present life. "Long since passed into extinction" refers to the question concerning the past.
Regarding the matter of the Buddha’s coming and going, and following the section on "inquiries," there is also an inquiry into the matters of the body and mind of the past Buddhas.
How could the Buddha of that land not know the matters concerning the body and mind of this land’s Buddha, as well as those of Prabhūtaratna?

This does not exceed the distinction between host and guest, nor the etiquette of the world; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is no different from worldly dharmas. [End of] the inquiry regarding Gadgadasvara’s previous departure.
The Buddha of that land—there was no such question in that Buddha’s assembly. Why, then, is it said here that the Buddha of that land inquires after [the World-Honored One’s] welfare?

Answer: Seeking this through the logic of the text, there ought to have been such a passage previously; however, the translator feared prolixity and thus omitted it from the earlier version, while now making it manifest alone.
Question: When Gadgadasvara inquires after [the Buddha’s] welfare, why does the Buddha not respond? Answer: It is logically required that he should; yet even this was omitted by the translator.
[This passage] is detailed and elegant.
"World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna... therefore I have come here.

From "World-Honored One" downwards, this is the initial intention of Gadgadasvara: his original purpose in coming to this land was to make offerings to the Three Jewels currently present and to pay homage.

After the Buddha had departed, seeing that the jeweled stupa was already closed, he therefore requested the Buddha on his behalf to reveal the eighth samādhi he had attained, "The Collection of All Merits," as well as to demonstrate the meaning of circulating and returning while upholding the sūtra.
This was because seeking to see many Buddhas constitutes the "collection of all merits" and accords with the worldly principle of social reciprocity. At that time, Many Treasures...

The Buddha did not open the stupa; he merely praised those who were virtuous, meaning that if one simply maintains the original intention, all merit is already accumulated, and there is no necessity to further desire to see my body. Therefore, he said, "You are able to make offerings," and so forth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: [down to] "hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.
At this point, Mañjuśrī beholds the lotus and raises three questions. The first question concerns what roots of virtue were planted.
He possesses great supernormal powers. Second, he asks what samādhi [the Buddha] practices, desiring to emulate and cultivate it himself.

Third, he seeks the Buddha’s empowerment of spiritual power so that he may perceive the physical appearance, stature, majestic demeanor, and movements of [Gadgadasvara]. Upon Gadgadasvara’s arrival, he directly fulfills the third request;
however, as the first two requests have not yet been concluded, Puṣpadatta further requests to see where Gadgadasvara has gone.

He has attained the ninth pure samādhi. Because he formerly made offerings of music and precious bowls to the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Voice King as causes and conditions for purity, he is now born in the land of the Buddha Pure-Flower-Abiding-King-Wisdom and has attained supernatural powers such as manifesting flowers;
this is because they are the retributive fruits of that purity.
"Kusumaśrī, you see only that the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara (up to) transforms into a female body to preach this sutra.
This section demonstrates the tenth [power], the Samādhi of the Play of Supernatural Powers (*ṛddhivikrīḍita*).

Because manifesting various bodies is entirely the play of supernatural powers, the passage beginning with "Kusumaśrī, you see only... means that Kusumaśrī sees only that Gadgadasvara is able to manifest as a bodhisattva.
The body of Śakra. Yet they do not know that he is able to manifest his body and preach the Dharma within all various classes of beings.

Or, by manifesting as lower [beings], it explains the manifestation of various bodies. As for the mention of Brahmā of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the omission of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is because the latter lacks material substance;
thus, when speaking of manifesting form, the Formless is also included. Śakra is of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); he is sovereign over the fifth [level] of the Desire Realm.
"Deva" refers to Mahesvara, the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm, which includes the two heavens of Yama and Tushita.
Regarding the "Great General of the Devas," the definition of the name states that according to the Tiantai interpretation, Sanjaya-Saumya is the Great General of the Heavenly Armies.
He has eight arms, rides upon a peacock, holds a rooster, carries a rattle-drum, and grasps a red banner; he commands thirty-eight divisions.
He travels through the world to reward the virtuous and punish the wicked; thus he is called the Great General of Heaven, Vaiśravaṇa.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, his fame for merit and learning spreads in all four directions, and he is the Heavenly King of the North. He governs the three heavens beginning with the East.
Regarding the Cakravartin kings, there are distinctions based on gold, silver, copper, and iron. As for the various minor kings, this excludes the four [great kings].
A Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*); all others are minor kings. A Bodhisattva is able to manifest in any of these forms. "Elder" (*śreṣṭhin*):

the *Fengsu Tong* (Compendium of Customs) states that one who is advanced in years and mature in virtue, and who serves as a leader among people. "Householder" (*gṛhapati*): the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that one who delights in discussing profound names and terms and dwells in purity.
"Official" (*rājan*): on a large scale, this refers to a prime minister; on a small scale, it refers to a district magistrate. "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*)—it is said: [text continues]
"Purified conduct" (*śīla-caryā*) is also called "the ordinary person on the path of hair" (*mārga-keśa-bāla-pṛthagjana*). The above all refers to manifesting in the body of a male.

From "or manifesting as a bhikṣu" onwards, it is explained by referring to both males and females together; this is because bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās constitute the female bodies among the fourfold assembly.
From "or manifesting as the wife of an elder" onwards, the Sanskrit term is *vṛṣalī*, which here means "wife."

A wife speaks to her husband; a woman speaks to a man. As for boys and girls who have not yet entered into the way of husband and wife, they may manifest as devas or nāgas—these are the eight classes [of supernatural beings].
Question: Previously, you enumerated the various devas; why do you repeat them here? Answer: The previous ones were the lords of the three realms, and thus each was listed by name individually.
These eight classes, however, would have no sovereign or governing authority if there were no devas; therefore, they are not [redundantly] included.

Regarding the phrase "a certain person": because those above reside in the realm of present bliss, while all those below reside in the realms of suffering of the three miserable paths, it does not say "present body," but simply states that they are all able to provide salvation.
Regarding the passage from "even unto the king" downwards, it should be translated as "assuming the bodies of present elders, women, and so forth.
The reason for placing this at the end is that although the status of kings, palace ladies, and the like is noble, their husbands [are not necessarily so].

The pleasures of women may be lacking; since their suffering is second only to that of the three miserable realms, no mention is made of the wondrous sounds [of the heavens] or what Dharma they preach.
Instead, this sutra is mentioned twice. This sutra refers precisely to this very scripture, for it was expounded by a Mahāsattva of the Dharmakāya.
Within the ten dharma realms, every movement and every stillness is the wondrous Dharma.
Thus it is that the power of the great supernatural penetrations and wisdom of the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue (Flower Virtue is the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound) is such as this.

This section demonstrates the eleventh samādhi, the Torch of Wisdom (*prajñā-ulkā*). Because it illuminates the Sahā world and other realms with manifold wisdom, it carries the meaning of a "torch of wisdom.
From the passage beginning "Huade [Flower Virtue] is Miaoyin [Wonderful Sound]" onwards, it follows from the preceding section.

This refers to the *Avataṃsaka* and other such scriptures. One knows only that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*) can protect sentient beings such as the Brahmā kings of the Sahā world by manifesting various bodies and preaching his sublime Dharma;

yet one does not yet know that within the Land of Universal Pure Light Adornment (*Sarvavyūhaprabhāsaviśuddha*), his spiritual wisdom and transformations likewise exist simultaneously in each respective place, without any distinction.
This refers to what has been diminished and extinguished. Regarding the passage "this bodhisattva, by means of various [powers]," etc.,
it means that although Huade (Flower-Virtue) knew that Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) manifested the wisdom of various Brahma kings and others,
illuminating both this and that land so that each Brahma king could attain what was to be known, he still did not know that spirit.
The transformations of wisdom simultaneously respond throughout the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions; it is likewise so.
This is truly because the Bodhisattva Miaoyin (Gandhahastin), through the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, has realized the Dharmakāya.
Since the Dharmakāya pervades all places, he is able to respond to each [being] simultaneously, yet people find this difficult to fathom. (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Ten Unimpeded [Knowledges]).
The chapter states: "A Bodhisattva, within a single body, manifests bodies throughout all worlds;
with a single voice, they manifest the diverse sounds and languages of all worlds, causing all sentient beings to each attain understanding. This refers to that.

From "If one should respond" onwards, the preceding section described the manifestation of the six ordinary bodies; here, it reiterates the capacity of the audience to whom these teachings are addressed, explaining the mundane vehicles of humans and devas. Five.

The precepts are the wondrous Dharma of the ten wholesome paths. This passage describes how the four bodies of the sages manifest in order to respond to and teach according to the capacity [of beings].
It explains the wondrous Dharmas of the supramundane—namely, the Small, Middle, Great, Sudden, and Perfect vehicles.

For those who wish to attain the Small Vehicle, the Dharmakāya responds to their capacity by manifesting in the form of a śrāvaka and preaching the Dharma of the Four Truths. For those who wish to attain the Middle Vehicle, the Dharmakāya...
The Dharma-body responds to capacities by manifesting in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preaching the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

For those who wish to attain the Mahāyāna, the Dharma-body responds to capacities by manifesting in the form of a Bodhisattva on the stages of the Three Worthies and Ten Grounds and preaching the Dharma of the Six Pāramitās.
For those who wish to attain the Supreme One Vehicle—becoming Buddhas instantaneously without traversing the gradual stages—it is the Dharma-body [that responds].
He responds to the capacities of beings by manifesting in the forms of Reward-Buddhas and Transformation-Buddhas to preach the Dharma of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth.

Whether in this land or other lands, throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he simultaneously and universally responds; there is nowhere where it is not thus.
Therefore, it is said, "In such various ways," and so on. The above clarifies that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound has realized the merit of the Prajñā of the Dharmakāya, and so forth.

Below, it clarifies the attainment of the virtue of liberation. This means that for those who should be delivered through *nirvāṇa* not merely by manifesting their bodies in the world, the Bodhisattva likewise manifests birth and subsequent extinction within the *dharmakāya*, which is neither born nor extinguished.
The section beginning with "Huade Miaoyin" (Flower Virtue and Wondrous Sound) concludes the preceding text.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "is able to thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
This section demonstrates the twelfth, the King of Adornments Samādhi (*vyūharāja-samādhi*). All physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) are what is manifested;

these are the six classes of ordinary beings and the four classes of noble ones. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is that which manifests them, yet it does not rise from its seat, nor does the body [move].
This is the locus of movement. The Dharma-body is the sovereign of all form-bodies, and all form-bodies are the adornments of the Dharma-body;
therefore, this dialogue is named the "Adornment King Samādhi. Although it responds to Huade (Flower Virtue), [it does so by means of this samādhi].
He also answered Mañjuśrī regarding which samādhi he practices, saying, "I pray that you will tell us the name of that samādhi.
When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being spoken, [the assembly] also attained this samādhi as well as dhāraṇīs.
Although this passage describes how the great assemblies of the two lands heard the Dharma and attained benefits, it actually demonstrates the thirteenth samādhi, the "Pure Radiance" (Vimalaprabhā).
Abiding in the *dharmakāya* is called "pure," while universally illuminating others is called "radiance.
Now, by the single utterance of the deity Subhavyūha’s wisdom, all people immediately attain the same realization; is this not precisely the samādhi and the *dhāraṇī*? Thus, both are concluded.
When Mañjuśrī had finished speaking, [the assembly] said, "We, too, wish to diligently practice this.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara (up to the point where he) produced hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of musical performances.

This demonstrates the fourteenth samādhi, the "Pure Treasury. His return to his native land symbolizes that all manifestations of physical bodies and spiritual wisdom are stored within the ocean-like treasury of the pure Dharma-realm body. Question:
Since Miaoyin (Gandhahastin) is simultaneously present in this land, that land, and worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, how is it so?
I trouble you again with this inquiry. In response: Generally speaking, all great Bodhisattvas necessarily possess the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) manifests in accordance with the ten realms of existence; it may be large or small. The *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) appears to come and go.
The *dharmakāya* (dharma body), however, pervades all places; it neither goes nor does not go, and it neither comes nor does not come. —Miaoyin.
That which manifests according to the various types of beings throughout this land, other lands, and the sands of the ten directions is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
That which comes and goes between these [lands] is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).
Having returned to his own country, [the Buddha] together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*).
Although this passage describes the words of returning to one's life, it actually demonstrates the fifteenth unique samādhi (*āveṇika-samādhi*).

This is because the words of returning to one's life do not describe the benefits obtained by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The reason for this is twofold: first, [it is because... (text fragment).
Those who ride in these vehicles have all already received the prediction of the Mahāyāna; there is none among them who is not a bodhisattva.

This clarifies that the coming and going of Gadgadasvara, as well as his wisdom and supernormal powers, are entirely methods for teaching bodhisattvas and are not shared with any of those of the two vehicles.
How profound and mysterious is the meaning of this sūtra!
When this "Chapter on the Coming and Going of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, the Bodhisattva Śrīgarbha attained the Lotus Samādhi.

Although this serves as a general conclusion for the chapter as a whole, it actually demonstrates the attainment of the *ṣoḍaśākāra-dharmadhātu-parivarta-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Sixteenth-Day Rotation).
Although the Sahā world was separated from the Buddha-land of Universal Pure Light Adornment by a distance as vast as hundreds of eight million billion nayutas of Ganges-sands of Buddha-worlds,
the voice of the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound traveled back and forth between them.
Because it is but a single day, if people are able to attain the wondrous meaning of this chapter, it is just like the sun completing one circuit of the heavens in a single day;
those with eyes and feet must wait for this before their endeavors reach fulfillment.

Therefore, to describe the benefits gained, it is stated that forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), clarifying the retributive body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Bodhisattva.
Day. Although there is coming and going, the heaven of the Dharma-body has never known birth or extinction. Such is the essential nature and characteristics of the Lotus Samādhi;
therefore, Puṣpadatta asked about this and likewise realized it. (Question: Since the benefits previously attained were already described, why are they recounted again here?)

Answer: The preceding passage described the bodhisattvas of the two lands; this passage describes the devaputras and those who are the primary audience (*adhimukta*). This is intended to reveal that the names of the samādhis differ.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-five, "The Universal Gate of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara," it is said:
"Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is also called Bodhisattva Avalokitasvara. The *Cien Zhuan* (Biography of Ci'en) states: "In the Sanskrit language, [it is] Āryāvalokiteśvara..."

*Va-ro* (Vairocana) means "Observation" (*guan*). *I-shi-va-ra* (Īśvara) means "Sovereign" (*zizai*). In reality, "Observation" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) which is the subjective faculty of cognition;
it is the True Observation, the Pure Observation, the Observation of Vast Wisdom, the Observation of Compassion, and the Observation of Loving-kindness.
"World-Sound" (*Shìyīn*) refers to the perceived-object part (*nimitta-bhāga*), namely the sounds of worldly suffering and affliction, such as the seven calamities and the two types of seeking.
"Voice" (Śabda) is the title [of the chapter]. This names the chapter after a person; "Universal Gate" (Samantamukha) names the chapter after the Dharma.

That is to say, with a single body and mind, one universally responds to the thirty-two Dharma-gates. Naming the chapter after a person clarifies that when a Bodhisattva attains this sutra, their compassion (*karuṇā*) can extract them from suffering.
Naming the chapter after the Dharma clarifies that when a Bodhisattva attains this sutra, their loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can bestow happiness. In total, these do not go beyond the primary point.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* sets forth two kinds of extraordinary merit. In that [sutra], the practitioner himself declares his realization of perfect penetration;

here, the Buddha recounts the three kinds of reality of perfect penetration to answer the needs of the specific audience according to the sequence of compassion. Each scripture thus serves its own distinct purpose.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (down to) "immediately observing his voice, all attained liberation.
Regarding the passage from "At that time" onwards: the questioner is necessarily Akṣayamati because he is the one suited to the occasion.

This indicates that while the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara (Wondrous Sound) traveled back and forth and maintained the sūtra through his faculty of the body (*kāya-indriya*), his mental faculty (*manas*) still possessed limits; thus, by coming here, his intention regarding those lands was exhausted.

The intent of revolving between these two lands is exhausted; therefore, in the superior grade, the Buddha’s praise of Wonderful Sound speaks only of his supernatural powers and wisdom being undiminished, but does not say that his physical body is undiminished. As for Avalokiteśvara, who maintains this sutra through the faculty of hearing:
Without the need for the labor of coming and going, the Ear-Gate Universal Illumination Samādhi harmonizes above and responds below;

thus, the intentions of both parties are inexhaustible. Therefore, the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña cautioned Gadgadasvara not to disparage this land by conceiving thoughts of inferiority, for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest their bodies in accordance with the world, and though they may appear lowly, [they are in truth supreme].
Although small, its supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom, as well as its mastery over transformations, exceed those of the worlds of the ten directions;

therefore, the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is appropriate for this occasion. According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, regarding the relative merits of the six sense faculties, only the faculty of mind is perfectly pervasive (*paripūrṇa*), being similar to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*).
However, the mind depends upon the five preceding sensory objects and thus possesses arising and ceasing; it does not equal the ear.
The roots, arising and ceasing, are both perfectly transcended by the eternal reality. This is why Ajita (Akṣayamati) still inquires of Avalokiteśvara.
As for the passage beginning with "And so it was," this follows the preceding chapter as a question. It asks:

since the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara (Miaoyin) received his name through the causes and conditions of offering music and a bowl, by what causes and conditions did the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara receive his name?
It is by virtue of this condition that he is so named. This is because, in the mundane world, the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) each have their respective counterparts:
visual observation belongs to the eye organ and should correspond to the object of form; sound is the object of hearing and should correspond to the ear organ.

Now, regarding Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, since his practice of "observation" is said to be through the ear organ, it appears to contradict the conventional relationship between the sense organs and their objects in the world. Therefore, it is asked: "By what cause [is this]?"
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddha told [them] below": it explains why the Bodhisattva is named Avalokiteśvara (Guan-shih-yin).

This is not like the worldly sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), which are characterized by the attachment to delusion and the emission of light, where each organ derives its name from its respective object.

Rather, because he has transcended the sense organs and their objects, he takes as his contemplation the *bodhicitta* inherently possessed by all Buddhas and sentient beings; therefore, if there are those in the three [realms], such as the immeasurable hells...
Sentient beings suffering on their journey, upon hearing the name at once and reciting it in unison, will have their voices heard by the Bodhisattva through his perfect observation;
without missing a moment, they shall all simultaneously attain liberation. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

First, because I do not observe my own voice (meaning that a Bodhisattva does not use the observing wisdom of their own capacity to observe the sounds of the names invoked by those immeasurable sentient beings suffering in pain;

if one observes only the sensory object of the sound, the Bodhisattva themselves is already stuck in deluded manifestation—how then could they deliver others? Moreover, if one uses observation to observe the observer, one can only observe the first;

it is difficult to observe the second, so how could one fully liberate them from their suffering?). Because the observer is not observed (meaning that if the observing wisdom does not observe the sound of the invoked name, then what is there to observe?).

By turning back the observing wisdom that contemplates, and reflecting upon one's own non-observing Avalokiteśvara-contemplation, both subject and object become empty. [Thus one] causes those sentient beings suffering in the ten directions [to attain liberation].

They contemplate their voices and all attain liberation (meaning that because both the wisdom of the Bodhisattva who contemplates and the object contemplated are empty, those suffering are led to contemplate the sounds of the names of the Noble Ones).

All shall attain liberation from the suffering and afflictions of the three miserable realms. This is like a king possessing virtue, upon whom the people rely; or like a mother possessing compassion, upon whom her children depend. Although the king and the mother have no partiality toward their subjects and children, if those subjects and children, when facing hardship, are able to invoke the names of the king and the mother, then all their calamities will naturally be resolved.

The word "contemplation" (*guan*) in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is spoken from the perspective of the capacity of the practitioner (*ji*), whereas the word "contemplation" in this sutra is spoken from the perspective of the response (*ying*).
The former is like describing a prescription for medicine; the latter is like describing its efficacy. If these two meanings are not understood together, [the distinction will not be clear].

The meaning is difficult to comprehend and resolve. This is answered by revealing the perfect reality through the power to liberate one from the sufferings of the three miserable realms, such as hell.
"If there be anyone who holds the name of this Avalokiteśvara... (up to)... for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara."
This section reveals the perfect reality by means of liberation from the suffering of the three calamities.

It is for the sake of the meaning of "perfection" that when one person utters the name, all people are delivered from disaster. "If there should be... and so forth means: if there should be someone who single-mindedly upholds the holy name.
It seems there will certainly be no fire disasters. Even if one were to encounter them by chance, the fire would be unable to burn them.
Generally, all things and people are inevitably consumed when meeting fire; that it does not burn now demonstrates the majestic power of the Bodhisattva.
Therefore, it says, "By this, the Bodhisattvas... The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Second, the revolving of knowledge and vision," and so forth (*Wenling’s Commentary* says:).

The four great elements of the internal and external are constantly interacting and influencing one another. Since seeing and cognition belong to the element of fire, when the activity of seeing interacts with it, one perceives a fierce fire. Interpreting this based on that [preceding] explanation, it means that because the Bodhisattva possesses these virtues, those who recite and uphold [the teaching] are enabled to escape suffering;

it is not for no reason. The subsequent sections may all be understood by analogy. However, the preceding section serves as proof for the principle that "once one faculty returns to its source," and thus speaks only of the hearing of the fundamental faculty. This present section serves as proof for the principle that the six faculties achieve liberation.

Therefore, it is spoken of in terms of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "vision" (*darśana*). This is because "knowledge" pertains to the four faculties beginning with the body, while "vision" pertains to the eye faculty.

If there is danger from great water, following the preceding text, it says that by the power of the Bodhisattva, one is not only able to escape the peril of fire; even if one encounters the peril of water, by merely once invoking the name of the Sage, [one shall be saved].
They are immediately carried into shallow waters, where they are easy to rescue. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Third, the hearing and listening revolve back...

(The Wēnlíng commentary says: "Hearing and listening belong to water; therefore, when the karma of hearing engages, waves and billows appear"). "If there are hundreds or thousands" refers to the great number of people.
"In order to seek" refers to entering the sea because of seeking the seven treasures. Although those who seek treasures are many, it is not necessarily the case that all [will succeed].
Encountering the peril of wind, it is therefore said: "Suppose that... Water is originally black in color; thus, the seawater is deep and vast, and its wind is black.
Two ships sailing together are called a *fang*. A *rākṣasa* is a female ghost (*nārī-ḍākinī*) who devours humans; because there are many such ghosts, they have formed a kingdom.
If there is anyone among them who recites the name of a Sage, even if they are but one person among many, all shall see [the protection].

They are spared from harm; this further demonstrates the great majesty and power of the Bodhisattva. From this point downward, including the preceding section, he answers the questions of those present according to their capacities.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Fourth, by severing delusive thoughts and having no intent to kill or harm, he causes all sentient beings who enter the realms of various ghosts to not dare do them harm. That sutra merely says "entering the realms of various ghosts."
It is not yet known for what reason they entered [the sea]. This clarifies that they were driven by a black wind while seeking jewels;

the significance of this lies in the wind bringing about the three calamities (*trisāhasra-lokadhātu*). Otherwise, the subsequent section’s mention of *rākṣasas* and its statement that the many merchants were carrying various treasures would be redundant in this context.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who is about to be harmed [up to] "the power of his majestic spiritual authority is as lofty and magnificent as this.

Again, below: the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Fifth, by perfuming the faculty of hearing so that it becomes true hearing, the six sense organs are dissolved and restored, becoming identical to the hearing of sound.
It can cause sentient beings... and so forth. "Perfuming the hearing" means that, initially, one uses verbal teachings to perfume and cultivate the faculty of hearing.
This refers to the passage in the Sūtra: "I followed that Buddha's teaching and entered samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
This constitutes "accomplishment through hearing" (*śruta-siddha*), meaning that the ultimate ocean of fruition is truly accomplished by means of the faculty of hearing.

This corresponds to the text in the Sūtra beginning with "First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object," up to "quiescence manifests before one. This is what is called "extracting [the essence] one by one."
"The faculties being detached from their adhesions and lying dormant within" refers to the following:

when the remaining five faculties, such as the eye, are dissolved and returned to their source, and the remaining five objects, such as form, revert to the original truth, it is identical to the case of the sound-object in relation to the ear's hearing.
This is what is meant by "the remaining adhesions of the other five [faculties] should be uprooted for a complete liberation," and so forth. By analogy with that, one should...

When the physical form is destroyed by the blade, one attains liberation; this is because the Bodhisattva’s six sense faculties have been dissolved and restored, resulting in a state where hearing is identical to sound.
According to the verse, regarding those who encounter royal peril and attain liberation—if [the text] says "three thousand [leagues]" and below, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
Sixth: "The brilliance of the permeation of hearing is pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; thus, the nature of all dark obscurations cannot remain intact," and so forth.

In the preceding section on the permeation of the six sense organs, the discussion was limited to a single body. Here, stating that "brilliance is pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm" encompasses the ten Dharma-realms.
According to that [text], it is because the brilliance of the Bodhisattva’s permeation of hearing is pervasive that it causes [the darkness] to expand.
The evil ghosts of the great trichiliocosm, whose nature is to dwell in profound darkness, cannot even look upon one who recites this name with an evil eye, much less dare to harm them.
According to the verse, "evil beasts, snakes, and the like," this is what is being praised.
As Master Zhao said, there are three kinds of yakṣas: first, those on the earth, namely tigers, wolves, cats, and wildcats; second, those in the air.
These are the various birds of prey, such as hawks and falcons. Third is those dwelling in the heavens, namely the various murderous spirits;
*rākṣasa* refers to "frightening ghosts. Furthermore, regarding the descent [into the realms], the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Seventh, when the nature of sound is completely dissolved—meaning the six sense objects are simultaneously liberated—and when hearing is observed to turn back inward, the six faculties flow against the current, one becomes able to leave behind all sensory dusts and delusions. This enables the multitude...
It is said, "When born... and so forth. According to that [scripture], this is because the Bodhisattva has departed from worldly dust (*rajas*).

Thus, those who deserve punishment—such as being bound with shackles and cangues—and those who are innocent—being unjustly fettered and imprisoned—are all liberated from suffering upon the single utterance of his name.
As for the passage beginning, "If a trichiliocosm were filled with enemies and bandits," "enemies" refers to adversaries, and "bandits" refers to thieves. It is filled...
The phrase "in the midst" means there is no place to escape. The merchant leader is one capable of guiding the multitude of merchants;
therefore, he is called a "General. Since wealth is linked to life, it is called "precious. Because the road abounds in enemies and bandits, it is called "perilous.

"Among them, a subordinate" refers to one person among the multitude of merchants who exhorts [them] to invoke the name of the Sage. "The multitude of merchants" refers to the merchants who followed the instruction and were all liberated together.

It is suffering. The wind from above is difficult [to withstand]. When one person utters the name, the multitude are liberated; when this assembly utters it together, they are all liberated. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Eighth, the sounds are extinguished and hearing becomes perfect, universally generating the power of compassion," and so forth. "Extinction of sound" means the cessation of the dust of auditory objects.

It is not annihilation. Yuanwen says: Since even a single sensory object, such as sound, attains quiescence, then the six sensory objects—form, fragrance, and so forth—all become perfectly complete (yuan) just as hearing does; thus, one is able to universally generate the power of compassion.

According to that, it is because the Bodhisattva’s compassion is universal that all the merchants and their enemies and robbers are completely liberated. From "Wujinyi" (Akṣayamati) onwards, it is explained through...

To speak truthfully is called answering. Since kings, punishments, ghosts, harms, prohibitions, shackles, grievances, and bandits are all commonly encountered in the world, yet the Bodhisattva is universally able to deliver and liberate them from these, his majestic power is praised as being vast and sublime.
"Vast and sublime" (*weiwei*) describes a state of towering loftiness; as the saying goes: "How vast! Only Heaven is great."
If there are sentient beings who have much lust... [up to] the benefit of immeasurable and boundless merit.
"If there are sentient beings"—the Jin translation renders this as "if there are those in training" (śaikṣa), which is correct; for they are those who have left the household life.
