For without patience, one cannot renounce the throne to leave the household life; and without leaving the household life to practice the Way, one cannot realize the further shore of patience.
After the king had renounced the world, he constantly practiced with diligent vigor for eighty-four thousand years, cultivating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
This passage describes the king practicing the Way as a monk; it clarifies that his two sons were fully endowed with the path practiced by bodhisattvas.
He caused his father to realize the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
After this, having attained all pure merits, he came to be born into my family for the sake of benefiting me.

"Beyond this, below," refers to the diligent practice of cultivation. After these sutras had passed eighty-four thousand years, through the sutras one attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and through concentration one attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); thus, one was able to ascend into the air.

Although this describes the King’s cultivation of the sutras for the sake of the monks, it actually clarifies that the two sons were fully endowed with the path practiced by Bodhisattvas; therefore, [it says]...
The father has realized the *dhyānapāramitā*, for *samādhi* is a synonym for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Since the previous passage did not describe the height or number of the transformation-pavilions within the void,
this section describes the King ascending into the sky to a height of seven *tāla* trees, and then [the text] below states that although he was described as heading toward the pavilion within...

The Buddha [acted] thus to move his two sons; in reality, it was because he knew that the two sons were fully endowed with the path practiced by Bodhisattvas, and thus caused the Father King to realize the Prajñāpāramitā.
The words spoken to the Buddha were all expressions of wisdom that knows both self and others.
From "Since this time I arose" up to "until I beheld the World-Honored One," this is a narration of himself.
"Only through these two sons did he first believe in the heterodox and ultimately return to Right Enlightenment.

From their emergence until the conclusion of the festival, this describes how his past roots of goodness and the holy fruits of his present life arose because of these two sons. Therefore, these two sons were not merely his children;
they were the King’s spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), manifesting as his sons in order to exhort him to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
These words concerning gratitude and requital of kindness are not for those who have yet realized the Prajñāpāramitā;
who else could possess such roots of goodness from past lives? The Tiantai Commentary states that the king, his consort, and their two sons once practiced the Way in former times.
They had entered into a covenant to dwell in the mountains. Later, due to a lack of food, one man wished to act as a secular messenger.

He entered the marketplace and, upon seeing the king’s wealth and nobility, his mind was moved by worldly desire; he subsequently passed away and took rebirth as that king, named Wondrous Adornment (*Suśobhana*).

He exclusively believed in heterodox paths and did not honor the Buddha-dharma. His three friends lamented his delusion, for there was no Dharma by which they could deliver him. They said, "We must first use the hook of desire."
Their aspirations could not be thwarted. One person vowed to become a beautiful and well-proportioned daughter; this was Lady Jingde.
Two others vowed to become sons endowed with merit, virtue, and wisdom; these were the two princes, Jingzang and Jingyan.

Therefore, it is said that they arose to bring benefit and came to be born into my family. According to this, the mutual relationship between our six kinds of kin—*ṣaḍjñāti*—is as follows: [text continues].
That which is drawn forth as a Buddha-work is none other than the causal conditions of past lives. As the *Śāstra* says: "There are two kinds of differentiated conditions:
either as an enemy or as a kinsman. This is what is meant.
"At that time, the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña... [omitted] ...caused them to abide in right view.
From "At that time" onwards, this describes how that Buddha confirmed the King’s attainment of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); therefore, it says "Thus, etc."

"Regarding the passage 'If a good son' and below: by means of the King's seal of approval, this is extended to mean that all other good sons and daughters alike take the planting of roots of goodness in a single lifetime as the cause, and the meeting with a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in every lifetime as the condition.
Regarding the passage 'That spiritual friend' and below: this clarifies that it is precisely because of this spiritual friend that they are able to act as the condition."
This is because they are able to accomplish the great task of attaining Buddhahood.
First, they demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, setting an example through their own diligent practice, much like a shopkeeper who displays his wares for sale.
Next, they teach the method for attaining that Buddha-knowledge and vision, like a merchant who states the price of the goods to a customer at the shop.
This refers to the distinctions of high and low. Furthermore, it successively causes those who have attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to receive benefit;

finally, it causes those who have attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to give rise to joy. Because these four aspects exist, one is able to lead people into the fruit of Buddhahood, which is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Great King, you should know" and so forth summarizes the preceding points; that is to say, the King should know that [it is through] a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) that...

The superior [action] is able to perform the work of a Buddha; it is the great causal condition for these sons of good family. Therefore, they transform and guide people, causing them to see the Buddha and resolve their minds [on enlightenment].
Since the King has already left the household life to become a monk, the translator should [place the title] "King" beneath the name of the monarch.
Setting aside the words of the bhikṣu for a moment, they are initially consistent. Great King, you see only what is near at hand; let us conclude this by referring to the two bodhisattvas.

You consider these two sons merely to be the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of your own single lifetime, yet you do not yet know that they have served many Buddhas over successive kalpas, that they have upheld their sublime Dharma, and that they are those destined to realize the fruits of enlightenment.

However, out of compassion for those with wrong views and to lead them back to perfect enlightenment, he manifested as dwelling in the stage of a causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), using the way of a son to transform his kinsmen.
To understand this, one should look to the deeds performed by King Subhavyūha;
all these serve as instructions for the two sons regarding the bodhisattva path they were to practice. This is based on the preceding section and these two passages of the sutra. Although this—
The narrative concludes with the Buddha’s seal of approval in response to the King’s words, stating that in truth both bodhisattvas have also fully mastered this samādhi;
thus, it concludes by enjoining the upholding of the Lotus Sūtra.
King Wondrous Adornment immediately descended from mid-air (until) having spoken these words, he paid homage to the Buddha and departed. Regarding King Wondrous Adornment’s descent:

previously, while the Bhikṣu King was contemplating the marks and signs of the emanation body of the Buddha Cloud Thunder Sound in the sky, he first attained renunciation, received a prediction of enlightenment, and gained supernormal powers. Later, relying on the power of those attainments, he ascended into the void; this is related here.

As for the causes and conditions: since he has already received the seal of approval from the Transformation Buddha, he now descends from the realm of emptiness to the earthly plane to offer praise for the marks and signs of the Reward Body of the Buddha Yunlei (Cloud-Thunder), thereby making his vow. This praise encompasses the Three Jewels in their essential unity.

From "The Tathāgata is most rare" onwards, the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is praised. From "The fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head" onwards, the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* is praised, briefly clarifying five of the thirty-two marks:
first, the radiance of the crown-protuberance; second, the long, deep-blue eyes; third, the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows;
fourth, the even and closely set teeth; and fifth, the beautiful color of the lips. From "At that time" onwards, the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are praised in general.
...and all other merits. The above has been the praise of the Buddha Jewel. Below, the Dharma Jewel is praised.

It is clarified that because the two sons were fully endowed with the path practiced by Bodhisattvas, they caused themselves to realize and attain loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
thus, they became completely clear and thoroughly proficient in them. Therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgata’s..."
"Regarding the Dharma and so forth: from this day forward, I shall praise myself for having become the Sangha-treasure through seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma.
I vow to forever sever the afflictions of the great and small latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Therefore, it is said: 'I shall no longer act according to my own whims,' and so forth."
The narrative of the sutra is before our eyes, past and present; how solemn it is!
The Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying: "What do you think? (up to: "...attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena."
The Buddha’s discourse below reconciles the past and the present. The former king is now the Bodhisattva;

although the circumstances of Huade’s inquiry regarding the causes and conditions of Miaoyin differ between the two cases, the sublime Dharma upheld by the wife and husband, as well as the son and father, remains the same.
Below this, [the text] presents the dhāraṇī for those who uphold the Sublime Dharma.
It is taught by as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers, and is therefore not false. Hence it says: "Already, in immeasurable [aeons]," and so forth.
If there are those who even merely hear the names of these two Great Beings, all devas and humans should pay them homage;
how much more so for those who study the dhāraṇī-sūtras of these two Great Beings—how could they not receive the protection of the Buddhas' spells and attain mindfulness?

The Buddha’s teaching concludes here, summarizing the benefits obtained by those who hear this chapter. Among the five eyes of the Buddha, the purity of the Dharma-eye is possessed by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The *Bie xing shu* (Separate Commentary) on the twenty-eighth chapter, the "Exhortation by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva," of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, states:
The Sanskrit term is *Samantabhadra*; this is translated here as "Universal Worthy" (*Puxian*).

According to this sūtra, his sovereign spiritual powers are termed "Universal" (*pu*), and his majestic virtue and renown are termed "Worthy" (*xian*). He is thus [the embodiment of] all [beings] throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
He is the eldest son of all Buddhas. Thus, a sutra says: "All Tathāgatas have an eldest son; his name is the Honored One Samantabhadra.
According to the commentary on that [sutra], there are five interpretations for the person and the dharma. Regarding the dharma, there are two:

first, "Universal" (Samanta) refers to the pervasive nature of the essence, while "Worthy" (Bhadra) refers to the perfection of virtues in accordance with conditions. Second, "Universal" means that one is all, and all is one. All...
The first is called "Worthy" (xian). These two are precisely identical to the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma) of this sutra. There are three types of persons:

first, those Bodhisattvas at the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and dedication who provide universal salvation without exception, which is termed "Universal" (pu); those adjacent to the Ultimate and nearly equal to the Sages are termed "Worthy" (xian).

The first corresponds to the bodhisattvas newly receiving their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) in this sutra. The second corresponds to the bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), who are called "Universal" (*Samantabhadra*) because their virtues pervade the *dharmadhātu*, and "Worthy" (*Bhadra*) because they are perfectly compliant, harmonious, and virtuous.

This precisely corresponds to the eighty trillion *nayuta* bodhisattvas in this sutra who have made vows and uphold the sutra. The third refers to the stage after [the preceding], meaning those who have already attained Buddhahood and completed their practice.

His virtues are fully perfected; all obstructions and karmic burdens are forever dispelled. Having nothing further to seek above, he does not abandon his compassionate vows, but makes the deliverance of sentient beings his sole endeavor.

He conceals his realization while manifesting expedient means; his fruition is so utterly exhaustive that it is called "Universal" (Samantabhadra), and because he does not abandon the gateway of causes, he is called "Worthy" (Bhadra).

This is precisely identical to the great Bodhisattvas who were the primary audience for the eight chapters of the dissemination section of this sutra. Therefore, Samantabhadra is [the embodiment of these].
At the conclusion of the circulation [of this text], that commentary further contains ten points of instruction for universal benefit; fearing prolixity, they are not recorded here.

"Exhortation" (*kuan*) refers to the exhortation of the Buddha to re-proclaim the four dharmas. "Arousing" (*fa*) refers to the arousal of the mind to preach mantras and provide protection, thereby accomplishing these four dharmas.

Because those who obtain this sutra [do so through such means], it is titled the "Chapter on the Universal Worthy’s Exhortation and Arousing. This sutra takes Maitreya and Mañjuśrī as its opening figures.
Chapter: Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra serve as its practitioners; the Wondrous Dharma clarifies that compassion begins with wisdom and concludes with compassionate action.

Yet, true compassion has no end, and true compassion has no beginning. Since one uses compassion to exhort others to resolve their minds and uphold this sutra, how could there ever be an exhaustion or limit?

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... [down to] "How can one obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?"—the section beginning with "At that time" describes the virtues and names of those who are the appropriate recipients (*yogya-pudgala*). "Together with great... describes the abundance of those who share the same name and identical virtues. "From the East...
describes the place from which he comes, clarifying the power of his sovereign supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*). Furthermore, "Together with... [and so on].

The passage beginning with "Narrating his retinue" describes the manifestation of his majestic virtue and renown. The phrase "Arriving below the Sahā world" indicates that, according to the statement that he comes from the east, the Sahā world is situated to the west.
The section beginning with "Bowing his head to the ground" narrates the ritual of the three karmas of reverence performed upon seeing the Buddha.

The section beginning with "Addressing the Buddha" sets forth the names of the Buddhas he served and the worlds from which they came. This concludes the opening of the Dharma assembly. Addressing... [the Buddha].

The light from the ūrṇā-kośa shines from the west to illuminate the east. Now that the Dharma assembly has concluded, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva proceeds from the east to the west, demonstrating the beginning and end of the signs of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*).
"From afar he hears" and so forth: this refers to the "hearing of the mind" (*citta-śravaṇa*) which penetrates the ten directions and is not obstructed by physical forms.
Having finished reciting the two sections of the sūtra—the introduction and the main body—"I only pray" and so forth [is spoken] to receive [the teaching].
Regarding the five chapters within the *parīndanā* (concluding) section, they refer to those who uphold this sutra in the present and the past—

namely, those such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and others, who do so either through ascetic practices, or through the [Buddha] of Wondrous Sound (*Gandhahastin*), or through dhāraṇīs, or through Sublime Adornment (*Sudarśana*).
There is nothing that is not the sovereign activity of the Universal Gate; this is an exceedingly difficult matter.
To teach people of future generations after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa how they may obtain a method that is extremely effortless, saving, and simple—namely, by upholding this sutra.
This is the intention behind my arrival here with the assembly of bodhisattvas to listen and receive [this teaching]. Therefore, it says, "If there are good sons," and so forth.
At the conclusion of the *Avataṃsaka* assembly, Samantabhadra expounded the Ten Great Vows for Sudhana;
at the conclusion of this sutra’s assembly, Samantabhadra requested the Buddha to speak on these four practices. From beginning to end, the two scriptures form a single, continuous whole.
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... [omitted] "...after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you shall certainly obtain this sutra.

From "The Buddha told" onwards, he answers for those who are suited to the teaching—namely, the good sons of the latter age after the Buddha’s extinction—that they must accomplish four dharmas before they can obtain this sutra.
Question: What is meant by "obtaining the sutra"? Does it mean obtaining these seven fascicles?
Is it the written words? Or is it that one attains awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Answer:
It is said that by receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting these seven fascicles of written words, one immediately attains awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. For the sutra states:

"If there are those who hear the Dharma, not one shall fail to become a Buddha. Furthermore, regardless of whether the Buddha is present or has passed into extinction, hearing even a single verse or a single phrase [is sufficient].

...all shall receive a prediction [of enlightenment]. First, the following section lists and explains four dharmas. Question: Since people in the末代 (final age) are far removed from the Buddha, how can they obtain his protective mindfulness?

Answer: That which is called "obtaining the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas" means that when a practitioner gives rise to the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind, they then obtain the protective mindfulness of the Dharmakāya Buddha. This is because of the Dharmakāya...

The Buddha is precisely the innate nature of mind that we all possess. Once one has perceived this nature of mind, to attend to it at every moment is what is meant by "protective mindfulness" (*ārakṣā*).
However, in practicing this path, one must take great compassion as one's dwelling—great kindness in bestowing happiness upon sentient beings and great compassion in uprooting their suffering.
Only those who have realized the Dharma-body Buddha are capable of this. Second, below:
Question: Since we have already attained the Dharma-body and our own selves are thus living Buddhas, why is it necessary to further plant the roots of manifold virtues?
Furthermore, what dharma serves as the root of these manifold virtues? Answer: If one merely attains the Dharma-body but does not plant the manifold virtues, [the realization remains incomplete].
For example, if there is earth but no grain is sown, the earth serves no purpose.
Likewise, although the human mind-nature is inherently complete, if one does not extensively cultivate the six perfections, it will lack adornment;

consequently, the retributive and transformational bodies cannot be perfected, and the saving of sentient beings will remain limited. Therefore, after realizing the Dharma-body, one must further nurture the myriad practices. However...

As one's practice becomes profound, demonic obstacles multiply; therefore, one must take the robe of gentle forbearance as the foundation for cultivating merit, so that demons and afflictions can no longer create hindrances.
Third, below this, the question asks: "Since one has already cultivated the six perfections..."

Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) lies in the middle. Furthermore, why say one enters the "correct assembly" (*samyaktva-niyāma*)? Answer: It does not mean that there is a "correct assembly" existing apart from the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Rather, one cultivates the root of virtue through patience (*kṣānti*). If one does not realize that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty as one's seat, then patience cannot endure for long.
Therefore, seeing that all phenomena are empty is taken as correct concentration; thus, one practices patience without [weariness].

Patience encompasses all the aggregates of the perfections. Fourth, [the section on] "The Lower": Question: Since it has been established that the aggregates of phenomena are empty, then both oneself and sentient beings are empty.

Furthermore, why is it necessary to give rise to the mind that seeks to save all sentient beings? Answer: If one observes from the perspective of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), both others and oneself are indeed empty.
However, if one speaks from the perspective of conventional characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible. If one does not give rise to the mind of salvation, then...
Laziness constitutes its activity; thus, the power of one’s vows is insufficient and the ocean of fruition cannot be perfected.
For this reason, even Bodhisattvas on the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi-bhūmi) still employ the arousal of the mind. As the Sūtra says:

"Thereafter, with a mind free from laziness, [the Buddha] extensively expounded this sūtra for the sake of all Bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly. One should know that only by possessing the three preceding dharmas can one subsequently arouse the single mind. To arouse...

Only after achieving single-mindedness can one finally accomplish the preceding three practices. These four dharmas are fully recorded at the end of the "Dharma Master" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*).

Now, for the sake of Samantabhadra and others, I have revised the title and re-explained them to clarify, both implicitly and explicitly, the ability of a Dharma master who upholds this sutra—this is precisely the practice of Samantabhadra.
For Bodhisattvas of the final age who wish to obtain this sutra, they must practice these four [dharmas].
The Dharma is like the eye and the foot, which assist one another; neither can be lacking. Therefore, it concludes by addressing "good sons" and so forth.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "recite them together until they are thoroughly mastered."

"At that time," and so forth. This refers to those who hear and obtain the sutra according to their capacity. First, because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas, [the Buddhas] likewise give rise to the resolve to protect and remember them.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of protection and remembrance (*anurakṣaṇā*): first, protection and remembrance that eliminates decline and affliction.
"Decline" refers to the withered appearance of one's physical form and the desolation of one's livelihood; "affliction" refers to the suffering and pain of body and mind.
This refers to speech that is harmful and offensive. It is precisely because such speech is absent that one attains peace and security.

Second, through protective mindfulness, one ensures that no malevolent spirits (*māra* or *bhūta*) seek an opportunity to cause harm. "Māra" is translated as "killer," and is also called "extremely evil.

There are distinctions between *māra*, his sons, kings and ministers, and those possessed by *māra*; therefore, it is said, "whether *māra* or the sons of *māra*," and so forth. As for spirits (*bhūta*), there are seven categories.
This is explained in detail in the "Dhāraṇī Chapter. Generally, [demons] find it convenient to afflict and harm the virtuous;
yet, although those who obtain this sūtra have awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as long as they remain in a physical form, they are prone to many outflows and imperfections.

Once they receive the Bodhisattva’s protective mindfulness, even though the various ghosts are evil, none will find it convenient to commit misdeeds; hence it is said that "none can find an opportunity. If such a person should act...

The third [point] regarding the protection and mindfulness of those who obtain this sutra: whether walking or standing, they shall receive the comfort of the Bodhisattva manifesting his body before them.
The six tusks symbolize the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); the white elephant symbolizes the purity of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*; and the True Pure King symbolizes the meaning of sovereignty.

This is also "the lower" [category], meaning that the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s body is not only for the sake of protecting and upholding those who possess the sutra, but also for the purpose of making offerings.

Regarding this method: if this person, while seated, forgets any part of the sutra during the fourfold mindful contemplation, they should be instructed to recite it aloud until it is mastered in their mind.

The phrase "at that time" below serves to connect with the preceding section, clarifying that [the attainment] is due to the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s body, through which they together receive, uphold, read, and recite this sūtra, thereby giving rise to joy and increasing their vigor;
thus they obtain [these attainments]. Third, they enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and obtain...
Second, planting the roots of all virtues; fourth, giving rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings.

Because one immediately attains samādhi, this is the stage of the rightly settled (samyaktva-niyāma). Furthermore, because it possesses the meaning of the fundamental source, there is both the original and the initial.
It can revolve once, twice, and even hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times, circling and returning.
In the worlds of the ten directions, those who uphold this sutra give rise to the resolve to save all sentient beings for the sake of future generations.
By means of skillful dharmic sounds, they preach to sentient beings the *dhāraṇī* of total retention (*saṃgraha*).
Regarding the question asked by Samantabhadra at the outset—“How can one obtain this sutra?”—the Buddha answered with four dharmas; this constitutes having already obtained this sutra. How so?
Samantabhadra further causes [beings] to obtain the four dharmas once more. Does this teaching not mean that one straightens what is crooked? Answer:

When the Buddha answered Samantabhadra, he stated that one obtains the sutra by practicing the four dharmas; this was said with reference to a person who had not yet obtained this sutra at the outset.
That Samantabhadra manifests his body and again causes them to obtain the sutra refers to the renewed practice of the four dharmas; this concerns the subsequent stage.
This refers to attaining the ocean of fruits through the intensification of diligence. Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of "further increasing one's diligence.
Ancient masters attained great enlightenment eighteen times and small enlightenments countless times; was this not also a matter of repetition? Thus, my interpretation is not erroneous.

"Bhagavān, in a future age, during the final five hundred years... [he] then spoke a dhāraṇī before the Buddha, saying: *Atandri* (1), *Dantapāli* (2)... [up to] *Siddhārthakṣemamati* (20). The Jin translation says:
'I pray that you will listen to this dhāraṇī. Its words of invocation are: 'No-self, eliminate self; turn back self through skillful means.'"

The guest is benevolent and harmonious, having removed [all defilements]. He is exceedingly supple and soft. His phrases are weak [in form but strong in meaning]. Having seen all Buddhas through various *dhāraṇīs*, he practices all various teachings.

He covers and transforms [all beings], gathering them all together. He removes the various destinies (*gati*), numbering in the infinite. His phrases are equal in number to those of the three periods of time.
He transcends conditioned learning and all dharmas. He understands the voices of sentient beings. He is the lion’s delight. O World-Honored One, if...

"Later generations" (hòushì) below serves as a general application for all the preceding sections. Thus, whereas previously it spoke of "good sons and good daughters," here it applies this to the fourfold assembly, beginning with the bhikṣus.

"Recite. This refers to the act of writing added after the recitation. The mantra is hereby proclaimed. Regarding such a proclamation: it means that those who have already cultivated the four dharmas and have already obtained this sutra should certainly follow the previous sections.

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly contemplate [this teaching], up to causing it to be widely disseminated so that it shall never be interrupted.
The following section explains, in general terms, the merit of those who are able to attain this sutra through the cultivation of four dharmas.
This merit corresponds to the meaning of the six types of Dharma-preachers mentioned previously: (1) receiving and upholding; (2) reading and reciting;

(3) correct mindfulness—meaning that through proficiency gained from reading and reciting, one maintains silent, mental recollection with a correct mind; and (4) understanding its meaning and purport. That is to say:
By silently recollecting its text, one understands and attains the essential meaning and intent.

Fifth is "acting according to what has been taught," which means practicing in reliance upon the teachings regarding that essential meaning and intent. Through these six kinds of merit, one should know that the following virtues are manifested;
there are four such virtues. First, because of acting according to what has been taught, one knows that such a person has become a Samantabhadra.

Practice. Regarding the phrase "at immeasurable [Buddhas]," there are two causes for such practice: namely, one knows that this person has deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of boundless Buddhas.

Third, because of the great cause of having planted such roots of goodness, they encounter the Buddhas who possess great fruits, who touch their heads with their hands to comfort their hearts. Thus, it is explained by means of these five kinds of dharmas.
This immediately brings about merit in the present life. If one merely practices the lowest [grade], they will not be able to fully possess all five types [of merit];
however, if they can possess at least one type, such as the dharma-master who performs transcription, that person, upon the end of their life, will experience merit in the future.
They shall be born in the second heaven of the desire realm to receive joy. There are three aspects to this joy: first, celestial maidens and musical performances welcome them; second, they wear...
[They wear] crowns of the seven treasures and, thirdly, enjoy themselves together with the palace maidens. How much more so for those below? Furthermore, comparing the inferior with the superior:
if even one who merely possesses the single practice of copying [the scripture] has such merit, then what of one who fully possesses all six?
Their merit is threefold: first, at the end of life, a thousand Buddhas extend their hands to receive them, and they are welcomed by the exquisite celestial maidens of the higher heavens.

Second, because body and mind are free from the fear of falling [into lower realms], this conversely highlights the bliss of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; even when that bliss is exhausted, there is still the fear of falling.

Third, through the guidance of the thousand Buddhas, one attains birth in the Inner Court of Maitreya in the fourth heaven of the desire realm, where one may draw near to the Compassionate Honored One, the Future Successor who will descend to be born here.
Therefore, it is said: "One immediately goes to Tuṣita," and so forth—referring to Maitreya Bodhisattva.
"There are those of lower [capacity]," refers to the bodhisattvas who practice alongside Maitreya Tathāgata.

"There are hundreds of thousands of those of lower [capacity]" refers to the attendants whom Maitreya manifests as receiving celestial blessings; these are not like the sensual pleasures of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

"There are such as these of lower [capacity]" is a summary of the extensive and concise merits, intended to exhort people. "World-Honored One, I now... and so forth, expresses the resolve to protect through supernatural power.

This is the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "within Jambudvīpa" and so forth: Jambudvīpa is the native land where the Buddha generated the aspiration for enlightenment, cultivated the causes, and attained the fruit;
therefore, although it is defiled and evil, because there are many beings with sharp faculties, this section is also presented separately.
Fourth is the generation of the mind to rescue all sentient beings, as the text explains that one generates the resolve to rescue all [beings].
For the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised him, saying: "...is covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha.

From "At that time" downwards, the scribe of the scripture describes how the Buddha honors the one who is the appropriate vessel for the teaching; therefore, he specifically records his name. [The Buddha] praised him, saying:

"Below. This praises the suitability of the recipient for skillfully protecting this sutra. "Causing many below. This praises the suitability of the recipient for skillfully assisting those who uphold this sutra.
"You have already below. This means that whenever a bodhisattva protects the Dharma, it may be for their own sake to achieve the inconceivable merit of the Buddha-fruit;
you, Samantabhadra, have accomplished your karma and are endowed with profound and great compassion.

Furthermore, regarding those who assist in upholding this sutra—some may have only recently first resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whereas you, Samantabhadra, have already resolved your mind since time immemorial. In that case, it might seem unnecessary for you to protect those who uphold the sutra;
yet, by means of your supernatural powers and vows, you are still able to guard both those people and the Dharma. Thus, I...
Śākyamuni, you should especially employ your supernatural powers to protect those who are able to receive and uphold your name, Samantabhadra, as a way of repaying your inconceivable merit.
[The phrase] "If there be one who is inferior... begins the section on the six kinds of Dharma-preachers who are to be protected and assisted by the appropriate recipients.
[The phrase] "One should know that such a person... clarifies the nature of these six kinds of Dharma-preachers.
Although one dwells in the turbid and evil age of the final dharma, being able to obtain the protection and assistance of Samantabhadra is equivalent to the Buddha’s being present in person.

There are six categories: first, personally seeing the Buddha; second, personally hearing the Dharma; third, personally making offerings to the Buddha; fourth, personally receiving the Buddha’s praise;
fifth, personally receiving the Buddha’s touching of the crown of the head; sixth, personally receiving the Buddha’s robe as a covering. This constitutes the seal of authentication.
Regarding the capacity for awakening: those who follow the One are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Such persons no longer crave worldly pleasures (up to) being able to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.
This section follows the preceding one to clarify that in the final age, the six kinds of Dharma-preachers shall receive the protective mindfulness of the Buddha as if he were present.

Consequently, they are able to accomplish two things: first, planting the roots of all virtues; second, because the concluding text describes the cultivation of the practices of Samantabhadra, which constitute the very foundation of these roots of virtue.
There are six categories [of virtues]: first, from "In this way" onwards, it describes planting the virtue of not craving worldly pleasures. Worldly pleasures...
These refer to the five desires of wealth, form, fame, food, and sleep. Second, not to admire the qualities of non-Buddhist practitioners:
"qualities" refers to their scriptures and writings; "persons" refers to the six heretical teachers. Third, not to associate with those of evil character; there are three types of such evil:
first, those who raise pigs and the like; second, hunters; third, those who traffic in female beauty. Fourth, to plant the roots of integrity within oneself.
The virtue of the power of merit (*puṇyabala*). Fifth, the virtue of not being a base person and not being afflicted by the root and secondary latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), great or small.
The "three poisons" refer to greed, hatred, and delusion; these are the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and the dull fetters (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
Envy is a minor secondary affliction. Pride and so forth are the major secondary afflictions and the sharp fetters. Sixth, the virtue of having few desires and cultivating contentment.

This means that because one dwells in the final age, one cannot avoid having few desires amidst the five sensory pleasures; one stops as soon as one has obtained what is needed, and thus it is called "contentment.

This concludes the section on being able to practice. That is to say, if the six kinds of Dharma masters in the final age possess the aforementioned six virtues, they are then said to be able to practice the conduct of Samantabhadra.
"Samantabhadra, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata... you shall sit upon the lion Dharma-seat amidst the great assembly of devas and humans.

This passage from Samantabhadra’s descent through to the seal of verification serves to certify the six kinds of Dharma-preachers in the final age, enabling them to receive appropriate protection and assistance so that people may believe they will attain Buddhahood before long.
"Darkly illuminating the three" refers to entering the true state; this is the gathering for the sake of attaining the Way.
The "place" and so forth constitute the section on the stage of the *samyaktvaniyāma* (the group of those destined for rightness), as it concludes the discourse on the Dharma for one full cycle.

This is because the "Turning of the Wheel of Dharma" and so forth belong to the introductory chapter (*nidāna*) and the chapter on skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), which contain the passage where Mañjuśrī answers Maitreya.

In the preceding section, the cultivation of the practices of Samantabhadra and the six kinds of Dharma-preachers constituted the possession of the great cause; in this section, the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [is established].
These six kinds of Dharma masters possess great fruit.
If Samantabhadra, in a future age, should uphold, receive, read, or recite [this], one should rise to welcome them from afar and treat them with the same reverence as one would the Buddha.

If Samantabhadra appears below, this section universally serves as a seal of authentication for the six kinds of Dharma-preachers in the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age, showing that they receive appropriate protection and assistance.
They should simply offer worship and respect to obtain blessings; it is improper to disparage or revile them, thereby incurring sin. This completes the fourth point:
the arousal of the mind to rescue all sentient beings. Therefore, although such persons do not greedily cling to the four things, beginning with clothing.
Nevertheless, regarding the necessities of life, whatever they may seek or wish for will certainly not be in vain, and they shall receive its meritorious retribution in this present life.
Suppose there were someone who, not understanding their intent, would speak with contempt and disparagement, saying: "These six kinds of Dharma-preachers are madmen;
they perform the practice of upholding the sutras in vain, yet ultimately have no [merit] regarding the four requisites such as clothing."

As for those who have obtained [this merit], such persons, having blinded themselves to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, shall consequently receive the retribution of being sightless in birth after birth.
As for the passage beginning with "If there is one who makes offerings," it means that if another person, seeing one who upholds this sutra,
no longer clings to the four requisites but instead increases their offerings and offers praise, then that person shall likewise [receive the same merit].
Those who uphold this sutra shall obtain the fruition of their wishes in the present life. Thus, it is clear that the demerit of disparaging and the merit of honoring [the Dharma] are manifest.

"Furthermore, if one sees [them receiving offerings]" and so forth means that there are those who, upon seeing a person upholding this sutra, not only disparage them face-to-face but also, behind their backs, expose the actual or alleged faults and evils of that Dharma teacher. Such a person shall receive—

This refers to leprosy (*śvitra*). If one treats it with contempt and, moreover, adds to that transgression by mocking it lightly, then its retribution will manifest as eleven types throughout successive lifetimes: first, sparse and missing teeth; second, deformed lips;
third, a flat nose; fourth, webbed hands; fifth, crooked feet; sixth, eyes with squinting or oblique vision (*tiryag-dṛṣṭi*); and seventh, a foul odor from the body.
1. Foulness; 2. Eight types of malignant sores with pus and blood; 3. Dropsy, namely the disease of abdominal distension; 4. Shortness of breath, the disease of pulmonary consumption (tuberculosis);

5. Various other grave and malignant illnesses. One should know that while the practitioner who upholds this sutra originally intended to save all sentient beings, it is difficult to save those who encounter such conditions as these. Therefore, [the text] below says: "One should simply see them and..."
To go out to meet him from afar and receive him with reverence as if he were a Buddha, hoping thereby that offenses may be extinguished and merit may arise—this is permissible.
This concludes the section of the text consisting of parables, for after the "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta), there is much discussion regarding retribution.
When the Buddha spoke this "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" (up to the point where) the bodhisattvas, as numerous as atoms, were fully endowed with the path of Samantabhadra—

this section was recorded by the scribe to describe the assembly that attained benefit upon hearing this single chapter, thereby concluding the exposition of the causal conditions for one complete cycle of the teaching.
With assemblies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and as many as the atoms of a great trichiliocosm, each possessing the full extent of a Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
they encounter the Buddha’s teaching or the teaching of Samantabhadra as their respective conditions; thus, some realize the revolving *dhāraṇī*, while others perfect the path of Samantabhadra,
each according to their individual capacity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Samantabhadra and the other bodhisattvas (up to) received and upheld the Buddha’s words, prostrated, and departed.

This section concludes the *pratyekānuśaṃsā* (circulation) portion of the entire work. As for the fact that Śāriputra and others are still called "śrāvakas," this is said in reference to their manifested traces (*vyañjana*).
